rows.text: If untreated, it produces severe and permanent intellectual disability; if detected at newborn screening and treated with early dietary Phe restriction, normal cognitive development is the expected outcome [1,2].

judged.citation: Blau N, van Spronsen FJ, Levy HL. Phenylketonuria. Lancet. 2010;376(9750):1417–27.
judged.reason: The abstract states untreated disease causes profound irreversible mental disability and that newborn screening plus early Phe-restricted diet prevents most neuropsychological complications.
judged.quote: if untreated, results in profound and irreversible mental disability. Neonatal screening programmes identify individuals with phenylketonuria. The initiation of a phenylalanine-restricted diet very soon after birth prevents most of the neuropsychological complications.

judged.citation: van Wegberg AMJ et al. The complete European guidelines on phenylketonuria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):162.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that untreated PKU causes severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and behavioural problems, but says nothing about newborn screening detection or normal cognitive development as the expected outcome of early dietary treatment.
judged.quote: If left untreated, PKU results in increased phenylalanine concentrations in blood and brain, which cause severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and behavioural problems.

rows.text: Incidence ranges from ~1:10,000 in European populations to 1:2,600 in Turkey and <1:100,000 in East Asia [1,4].

judged.citation: Blau N, van Spronsen FJ, Levy HL. Phenylketonuria. Lancet. 2010;376(9750):1417–27.
judged.reason: The abstract touches on PKU prevalence only qualitatively and contains none of the population-specific incidence figures (~1:10,000 European, 1:2,600 Turkey, <1:100,000 East Asia) asserted in the sentence.
judged.quote: Phenylketonuria is the most prevalent disorder caused by an inborn error in aminoacid metabolism.

judged.citation: Hillert A et al. The Genetic Landscape and Epidemiology of Phenylketonuria. Am J Hum Genet. 2020;107(2):234–50.
judged.reason: The abstract supports wide geographic variation in PKU prevalence and the very low East Asian figure (Japan 1:125,000), but it does not give ~1:10,000 for European populations or 1:2,600 for Turkey (its highest reported rate is 1:4,500 in Italy).
judged.quote: global prevalence 1:23,930 live births (range 1:4,500 [Italy]-1:125,000 [Japan])

rows.text: Plasma Phe >120 µmol/L defines hyperphenylalaninaemia; >600 µmol/L on an unrestricted diet is classic PKU [5].

judged.citation: Vockley J et al. ACMG — Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency: diagnosis and management guideline. Genet Med. 2014;16(2):188–200.
judged.reason: The abstract is the ACMG guideline on PAH deficiency and mentions 120 µmol/l as the lower bound of the target treatment range, but it never states the diagnostic definition of hyperphenylalaninaemia (>120 µmol/L) nor the >600 µmol/L on unrestricted diet cutoff for classic PKU.
judged.quote: treatment of phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency must be life long, with a goal of maintaining blood phenylalanine in the range of 120-360 µmol/l

rows.text: The Phe/Tyr ratio is a more robust early-life marker than absolute Phe: a ratio >3 raises suspicion, >10 is characteristic of untreated classic PKU and of biopterin disorders [6,7].

judged.citation: Eastman JW et al. Use of the phenylalanine:tyrosine ratio to test newborns for phenylketonuria in a large public health screening programme. J Med Screen. 2000;7(3):131–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that the Phe/Tyr ratio outperforms absolute phenylalanine for newborn screening, but it uses a ratio cut-off of 1.50 and says nothing about the specific thresholds of >3 or >10 or about biopterin disorders.
judged.quote: the clinical sensitivity and specificity of the PKU screening test are higher when the phenylalanine:tyrosine ratio is incorporated into the cut off than when the cut off is based on the phenylalanine concentration alone

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Diagnosis of tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency using filter paper blood spots: further development of the method and 5 years experience. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(3):819–26.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns neopterin/biopterin and dihydropteridine reductase measurement in dried blood spots and never addresses the phenylalanine/tyrosine ratio or its diagnostic thresholds.
judged.quote: Differential diagnosis is most commonly performed by analysis of urinary neopterin and biopterin.

rows.text: Urinary o-hydroxyphenylacetic acid, phenyl-pyruvate and phenyl-lactate may be detected but are insensitive in infancy and should not be used for primary diagnosis [1].

judged.citation: Blau N, van Spronsen FJ, Levy HL. Phenylketonuria. Lancet. 2010;376(9750):1417–27.
judged.reason: The abstract does not mention urinary phenylketone metabolites or their diagnostic sensitivity at all.

rows.text: BH4 loading (20 mg/kg): a ≥30% reduction in Phe at 24 h defines BH4-responsiveness and indicates that sapropterin therapy may be used [8].

judged.citation: Muntau AC et al. Tetrahydrobiopterin as an alternative treatment for mild PKU. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(26):2122–32.
judged.reason: The abstract supports BH4 loading testing and that responsiveness (common in mild phenotypes) permits BH4/sapropterin therapy with diet discontinuation, but it does not state the specific 20 mg/kg dose or the ≥30% reduction at 24 h threshold.
judged.quote: we performed a combined phenylalanine-tetrahydrobiopterin loading test and analyzed the in vivo rates of [13C]phenylalanine oxidation in 38 children with phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency

rows.text: Over 1,000 pathogenic variants have been reported (PAHvdb/BIOPKU); most are missense variants affecting protein stability or BH4 binding [9,10].

judged.citation: Scriver CR et al. PAHdb: a locus-specific knowledgebase. Hum Mutat. 2003;21(4):333–44.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that most pathogenic PAH variants are missense acting largely via protein misfolding/instability, but it records only 439 pathogenic alleles and does not support the "over 1,000 variants" figure or BH4-binding effects.
judged.quote: The majority (63%) of the putative pathogenic PAH alleles are point mutations causing missense in translation of which few have a primary effect on PAH enzyme kinetics. Most apparently have a secondary effect on its function through misfolding, aggregation, and intracellular degradation of the protein.

judged.citation: Himmelreich N et al. Relationship between genotype, phenotype and BH4-responsiveness in PAH deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2018;125(1–2):86–95.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly supports the >1000 PAH variant count but does not state that most are missense variants affecting protein stability or BH4 binding.
judged.quote: The genotypic heterogeneity of PKU, involving >1000 PAH variants and over 2500 different genotypes, makes genotype-based phenotype prediction challenging.

rows.text: Genotype–phenotype correlation is imperfect but useful: p.Arg408Trp (common in Slavic populations) produces classic PKU, while p.Tyr414Cys and p.Ala403Val are typically BH4-responsive [10,11].

judged.citation: Himmelreich N et al. Relationship between genotype, phenotype and BH4-responsiveness in PAH deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2018;125(1–2):86–95.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the general point that genotype–phenotype correlation is established yet imperfect, but it gives no variant-specific assignments (p.Arg408Trp as classic PKU, Slavic frequency, or BH4-responsiveness of p.Tyr414Cys/p.Ala403Val).
judged.quote: While a relationship between PAH variants and the metabolic phenotype is well established, we questioned the importance of PAH expression and residual in vitro activity for the metabolic phenotype.

judged.citation: Blau N. Genetics of phenylketonuria: then and now. Hum Mutat. 2016;37(6):508–15.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the general point that genotype–phenotype correlation is imperfect but useful for predicting BH4 responsiveness and PKU severity, but it names no specific variants, so the claims about p.Arg408Trp, p.Tyr414Cys and p.Ala403Val (and Slavic population frequency) are absent.
judged.quote: While it is possible to predict the level of BH4 responsiveness (∼71%) and PKU severity (∼78%) from the nature of the underlying gene variants, these relationships remain complex and incompletely understood.

rows.text: Untreated classic PKU: severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy, behavioural disturbance, eczema, hypopigmentation and musty body odour developing from ~6 months [1,2].

judged.citation: Blau N, van Spronsen FJ, Levy HL. Phenylketonuria. Lancet. 2010;376(9750):1417–27.
judged.reason: The abstract supports severe irreversible intellectual disability in untreated classic PKU but says nothing about microcephaly, epilepsy, behavioural disturbance, eczema, hypopigmentation, musty odour or onset from ~6 months.
judged.quote: a severe classic phenotype with pronounced hyperphenylalaninaemia, which, if untreated, results in profound and irreversible mental disability

judged.citation: van Wegberg AMJ et al. The complete European guidelines on phenylketonuria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):162.
judged.reason: The abstract supports severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and behavioural disturbance in untreated PKU, but not microcephaly, eczema, hypopigmentation, musty odour or onset from ~6 months.
judged.quote: If left untreated, PKU results in increased phenylalanine concentrations in blood and brain, which cause severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and behavioural problems.

rows.text: Maternal PKU syndrome: babies born to women with poorly-controlled PKU have microcephaly, congenital heart disease and intellectual disability from intrauterine Phe toxicity, regardless of the infant's own PAH genotype — maternal Phe must be maintained <360 µmol/L throughout pregnancy [14,15].

judged.citation: Prick BW et al. Maternal phenylketonuria: pregnancy outcome. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(2):253–61.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the neonatal sequelae in nonphenylketonuric offspring (microcephaly, CHD, intellectual disability) from maternal Phe exposure, but gives no specific target threshold of <360 µmol/L during pregnancy.
judged.quote: Untreated maternal phenylketonuria or hyperphenylalaninemia may result in nonphenylketonuric offspring with neonatal sequelae, especially intellectual disability, microcephaly, and congenital heart disease (CHD).

judged.citation: Rouse B et al. Maternal Phenylketonuria Collaborative Study. Am J Med Genet. 1997;69(1):89–95.
judged.reason: The abstract reports microcephaly, congenital heart disease and mental retardation in offspring of untreated maternal PKU and explicitly recommends maintaining maternal Phe <360 µmol/L throughout pregnancy; only the genotype-independence aside is not directly stated.
judged.quote: These data support the concept that women with PKU should begin a low-phenylalanine diet to achieve Phe levels of < 360 mumol/liter prior to conception and should maintain this throughout pregnancy.

rows.text: Life-long Phe-restricted diet using Phe-free amino acid medical foods, aiming for plasma Phe of 120–360 µmol/L in childhood and <600 µmol/L in adulthood [2,16].

judged.citation: van Wegberg AMJ et al. The complete European guidelines on phenylketonuria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):162.
judged.reason: The abstract is a methodological/structural summary of guideline development and contains no dietary recommendations or target plasma Phe ranges, so the specific 120–360 µmol/L and <600 µmol/L thresholds cannot be checked.
judged.quote: Using these methods 70 statements were formulated based on the highest quality evidence available.

judged.citation: Singh RH et al. Recommendations for the nutrition management of PKU. Genet Med. 2014;16(2):121–31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports lifelong Phe-restricted dietary management with appropriate medical foods and monitoring, but gives no plasma Phe target ranges (120–360 µmol/L childhood, <600 µmol/L adulthood).
judged.quote: The effectiveness of a phenylalanine-restricted diet to improve the outcome of individuals with phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (OMIM no. 261600) has been recognized since the first patients were treated 60 years ago.

rows.text: Sapropterin dihydrochloride (Kuvan®, synthetic BH4; 10–20 mg/kg/day) is an option in BH4-responsive patients and can allow liberalisation of Phe intake [8,17].

judged.citation: Muntau AC et al. Tetrahydrobiopterin as an alternative treatment for mild PKU. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(26):2122–32.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that BH4 is effective in BH4-responsive patients and permits liberalisation/discontinuation of the Phe-restricted diet, but it does not give the 10–20 mg/kg/day dose or address sapropterin dihydrochloride (Kuvan) specifically.
judged.quote: Long-term treatment with tetrahydrobiopterin in five children increased daily phenylalanine tolerance, allowing them to discontinue their restricted diets.

judged.citation: Longo N et al. Sapropterin long-term effectiveness and safety. Mol Genet Metab. 2015;114(4):557–63.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that sapropterin lowers blood Phe and permits liberalisation of dietary Phe intake, but it does not state the 10–20 mg/kg/day dose range (nor explicitly restrict use to BH4-responsive patients).
judged.quote: This drop in blood Phe was associated with an increase in dietary Phe tolerance [from 1000 ± 959 mg/day (pre-sapropterin baseline) to 1539 ± 840 mg/day after 6 years].

rows.text: Pegvaliase (Palynziq®, PEGylated phenylalanine ammonia-lyase) is approved for adults with uncontrolled Phe on conventional therapy [18].

judged.citation: Thomas J et al. Pegvaliase for the treatment of phenylketonuria. Mol Genet Metab. 2018;124(1):27–38.
judged.reason: The abstract supports pegvaliase as PEGylated phenylalanine ammonia lyase therapy shown effective in adults with PKU and uncontrolled blood Phe (>600 µmol/L), but it does not state regulatory approval or the trade name Palynziq®.
judged.quote: Pegvaliase, PEGylated recombinant Anabaena variabilis phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL), converts Phe to trans-cinnamic acid and ammonia, and is a potential enzyme substitution therapy to lower blood Phe in adults with PKU.

rows.text: Large-neutral-amino-acid supplementation provides an adjunct for older patients with poor dietary adherence [19].

judged.citation: Matalon R et al. Large neutral amino acids in PKU. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2007;30(2):153–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports LNAA as a therapeutic adjunct that lowers blood Phe in PKU, but says nothing about it being targeted at older patients or those with poor dietary adherence.
judged.quote: The data from the double-blind placebo control are encouraging, establishing proof of principle of the role of orally administered LNAA in lowering blood Phe concentrations in patients with PKU.

rows.text: Early-treated patients with good lifetime Phe control achieve IQ within the normal range but remain at risk for executive-function deficits, anxiety and depression even with early diagnosis [2,20].

judged.citation: van Wegberg AMJ et al. The complete European guidelines on phenylketonuria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):162.
judged.reason: The abstract does not address outcomes in early-treated patients, IQ, executive function, anxiety or depression.

judged.citation: Bilder DA et al. Psychiatric symptoms in adults with phenylketonuria. Mol Genet Metab. 2013;108(3):155–60.
judged.reason: The abstract supports elevated psychiatric symptom burden in adults with PKU correlated with phe levels, but does not address IQ in the normal range, executive-function deficits, or specifically anxiety/depression subscales in early-treated patients.
judged.quote: The number of BSI scores meeting clinical threshold was significantly elevated for all global indexes and 6 out of 7 symptom subscales in patients with PKU.

rows.text: Discontinuation of diet in adolescence or adulthood causes reversible cognitive slowing and white-matter abnormalities on MRI [21].

judged.citation: Anderson PJ, Leuzzi V. White matter pathology in phenylketonuria. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;99 Suppl 1:S3–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that white-matter MRI abnormalities in PKU relate to metabolic control and are reversible with strict low-Phe diet, but it does not address diet discontinuation in adolescence/adulthood or reversible cognitive slowing specifically.
judged.quote: Research demonstrates that this pathology is associated with metabolic control and may be reversed with adherence to a strict low-phenylalanine (Phe) diet.

rows.text: Women of reproductive age require preconception Phe control to prevent maternal PKU syndrome [14,15].

judged.citation: Prick BW et al. Maternal phenylketonuria: pregnancy outcome. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(2):253–61.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly recommends starting Phe-controlling treatment before conception to prevent maternal PKU sequelae in offspring.
judged.quote: We strongly recommend starting treatment before conception because we showed the deleterious effect of an increased mean first-trimester phenylalanine concentration on FD.

judged.citation: Rouse B et al. Maternal Phenylketonuria Collaborative Study. Am J Med Genet. 1997;69(1):89–95.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly concludes that women with PKU should achieve target Phe levels prior to conception to prevent fetal damage from maternal PKU.
judged.quote: women with PKU should begin a low-phenylalanine diet to achieve Phe levels of < 360 mumol/liter prior to conception

rows.text: BH4 is the cofactor for phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases — PTPS deficiency impairs all three, causing combined hyperphenylalaninaemia plus CNS dopamine and serotonin deficiency [1,2].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract supports combined HPA with dopamine and serotonin deficiency in BH4 disorders but does not state that BH4 is cofactor for the three aromatic amino acid hydroxylases or address PTPS specifically.
judged.quote: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH 4 ) deficiencies comprise a group of six rare neurometabolic disorders characterized by insufficient synthesis of the monoamine neurotransmitters dopamine and serotonin due to a disturbance of BH 4  biosynthesis or recycling. Hyperphenylalaninemia (HPA) is the first diagnostic hallmark for most BH 4  deficiencies

judged.citation: Shintaku H. Disorders of tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism and their treatment. Curr Drug Metab. 2002;3(2):123–31.
judged.reason: The abstract states BH4 is the essential cofactor for hydroxylation of phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan and that its deficiency produces combined hyperphenylalaninaemia plus dopamine/serotonin deficiency, with PTPS among the listed enzyme deficiencies.
judged.quote: BH4 is the essential cofactor in the enzymatic hydroxylation of 3 aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan)... BH4 deficiency without treatment causes combined symptoms of HPA and neurotransmitter (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and serotonin) deficiency

rows.text: Without specific pterin screening, it would be mis-diagnosed as PKU, and the patient would deteriorate neurologically despite strict Phe restriction — which is why every NBS-positive hyperphenylalaninaemia MUST be screened for BH4 disorders [2,3].

judged.citation: Shintaku H. Disorders of tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism and their treatment. Curr Drug Metab. 2002;3(2):123–31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that BH4 deficiency is detected among neonatal-screening hyperphenylalaninaemia cases via pterin/loading/DHPR testing and deteriorates untreated, but does not state that it would otherwise be misdiagnosed as PKU or that patients deteriorate despite strict Phe restriction.
judged.quote: BH4 deficiency has been diagnosed in patients with hyperphenylalaninemia (HPA) by neonatal mass-screening based on BH4 oral loading tests, analysis of urinary or serum pteridines, and measurement of dihydropterindine reductase (DHPR) activity in blood from a Guthrie card.

rows.text: Urine pterin profile is the diagnostic tool: neopterin markedly ELEVATED, biopterin LOW, resulting in a very low biopterin:neopterin ratio [4].

judged.citation: Dhondt JL. Strategy for the screening of tetrahydrobiopterin deficiencies among hyperphenylalaninemic patients. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1991;14(2):117–27.
judged.reason: The abstract supports urine pteridine measurement as a reliable diagnostic test for BH4 (cofactor) deficiency in hyperphenylalaninaemic patients, but it never states the specific pattern of markedly elevated neopterin, low biopterin, or a very low biopterin:neopterin ratio.
judged.quote: DHPR assay in dried blood samples and pteridine measurement in urine collected on filter paper combine convenient sampling and reliable tests for systematic investigation of hyperphenylalaninaemic patients for cofactor deficiency.

rows.text: BH4 loading test: rapid normalisation of plasma Phe after 20 mg/kg oral BH4 — sometimes diagnostic in mild cases [1].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract is a structural summary of a diagnostic/treatment guideline and says nothing about a BH4 loading test or a 20 mg/kg dose.

rows.text: Two clinical forms: severe/typical with both hyperphenylalaninaemia AND CNS neurotransmitter deficiency; peripheral/mild form with transient HPA but preserved CNS neurotransmitter synthesis [1,6].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract does not mention PTPS clinical subtypes (severe/typical versus peripheral/mild) or genotype–phenotype issues.

judged.citation: Werner ER et al. The PTPS enzyme: structure, function and mutations. Biochem J. 2011;438(3):397–414.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses BH4 deficiency as a cause of hyperphenylalaninaemia and its link to monoamine neurotransmitter formation, but never describes the two clinical forms of PTPS deficiency (severe/typical versus peripheral/mild with transient HPA and preserved CNS neurotransmitter synthesis).
judged.quote: BH4 deficiency due to autosomal recessive mutations in all enzymes, except for sepiapterin reductase, has been described as a cause of hyperphenylalaninaemia.

rows.text: Poor without the neurotransmitter precursor arm of therapy [1,2].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract states that early neurotransmitter precursor supplementation significantly improves motor and cognitive outcome, which directly underpins poor prognosis without that arm of therapy.
judged.quote: Early supplementation of neurotransmitter precursors and where appropriate, treatment of HPA results in significant improvement of motor and cognitive function.

judged.citation: Shintaku H. Disorders of tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism and their treatment. Curr Drug Metab. 2002;3(2):123–31.
judged.reason: The abstract notes progressive neurological deterioration without treatment and lists neurotransmitter precursors as part of therapy, but does not specifically state that outcome is poor when the precursor component is omitted.
judged.quote: BH4 deficiency without treatment causes combined symptoms of HPA and neurotransmitter (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and serotonin) deficiency, such as red hair, psychomotor retardation, and progressive neurological deterioration.

rows.text: DHPR activity is measured directly on dried blood spots in most NBS programs with BH4 screening [1].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract makes no mention of dried blood spot DHPR enzyme assays or newborn screening practice.

rows.text: DHPR activity on DBS: <20% of normal — direct diagnostic test [1,4].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract is a high-level guideline summary and gives no biochemical or enzyme-activity diagnostic details such as DHPR activity in dried blood spots.

judged.citation: Ponzone A et al. Dihydropteridine reductase deficiency in man: from biology to treatment. Med Res Rev. 2004;24(2):127–50.
judged.reason: The abstract is a review of DHPR deficiency that mentions screening and diagnosis generally but gives no DBS enzyme activity threshold such as <20% of normal.
judged.quote: major progresses have been made in the understanding of physiopathology, screening, diagnosis, treatment, and molecular genetics of this inherited disease

rows.text: Some mild variants (p.Gly151Ser, p.Phe212Cys) retain partial activity and predominantly affect serotonin synthesis [1,2].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract contains no molecular or variant-level information about QDPR.

judged.citation: Longo N. Disorders of biopterin metabolism. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(3):333–42.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions only generic detection of "causative mutations" and says nothing about specific QDPR variants, residual activity, or preferential serotonin involvement.
judged.quote: causative mutations in the relative genes

rows.text: Regular monitoring CSF neurotransmitter metabolites + CSF 5-methylTHF [2].

judged.citation: Longo N. Disorders of biopterin metabolism. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(3):333–42.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions CSF neurotransmitter and pterin measurement for diagnosis but does not describe regular treatment monitoring or CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate measurement.
judged.quote: neurotransmitters and pterins in the CSF

rows.text: Severe combined hyperphenylalaninaemia + neurotransmitter deficiency [1,2].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract implies recessive GTPCH-I deficiency presents with HPA (only the autosomal dominant form is excepted) plus monoamine deficiency, but does not characterise it as severe.
judged.quote: Hyperphenylalaninemia (HPA) is the first diagnostic hallmark for most BH 4  deficiencies, apart from autosomal dominant guanosine triphosphate cyclohydrolase I deficiency and sepiapterin reductase deficiency.

rows.text: GTPCH-I is regulated by the GTPCH-I regulatory protein (GFRP) which mediates feedback activation by phenylalanine [3].

judged.citation: Harada T et al. Feedback regulation mechanisms for the control of GTP cyclohydrolase I activity. Science. 1993;260(5113):1507–10.
judged.reason: The abstract describes a regulatory protein (p35, i.e., GFRP) mediating BH4 feedback inhibition of GTP cyclohydrolase I that is specifically reversed by phenylalanine, matching the claim of GFRP-mediated feedback activation by phenylalanine.
judged.quote: Inhibition was found to depend specifically on BH4 and the presence of another protein (p35). The inhibition occurred through BH4-dependent complex formation between p35 protein and GTP cyclohydrolase I. Furthermore, the inhibition was specifically reversed by phenylalanine

rows.text: Urine pterin profile: BOTH biopterin AND neopterin LOW (the defining finding — PTPS has high neopterin) [1,4].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract gives no urinary pterin profile data for GTPCH-I or PTPS deficiency.

judged.citation: Niederwieser A et al. GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency, a new enzyme defect causing hyperphenylalaninemia. Eur J Pediatr. 1984;141(4):208–14.
judged.reason: The abstract reports very low urinary excretion of both neopterin and biopterin in the GTP cyclohydrolase I–deficient patient, matching the claimed urine pterin profile; the PTPS contrast is left to the co-cited guideline.
judged.quote: Urinary excretion of neopterin, biopterin, pterin, isoxanthopterin, dopamine, and serotonin was very low, although the relative proportions of pterins were normal.

rows.text: Recessive severe deficiency requires biallelic loss-of-function [6].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. The International Working Group on Neurotransmitter related Disorders (iNTD): a worldwide research project. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;119(3):241–3.
judged.reason: The abstract describes an international network and registry for neurotransmitter disorders and says nothing about GCH1 genetics or biallelic loss-of-function requirements.

rows.text: Similar to PTPS — severe hypotonia, dystonia, oculogyric crises, swallowing difficulties, developmental delay, seizures [1,2].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract does not enumerate clinical signs such as hypotonia, dystonia or oculogyric crises.

rows.text: Often missed for years as 'cerebral palsy' or 'idiopathic dystonia' [1,2].

judged.citation: Wijemanne S, Jankovic J. Dopa-responsive dystonia—clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Nat Rev Neurol. 2015;11(7):414–24.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that DRD is frequently misdiagnosed with delayed levodopa treatment, but does not name 'cerebral palsy' or 'idiopathic dystonia' as the mistaken labels or specify a delay of years.
judged.quote: This heterogeneity of conditions that underlie DRD frequently leads to misdiagnosis, which delays the appropriate treatment with levodopa.

rows.text: Plasma phenylalanine is NORMAL (PAH function adequate in hepatocytes) — DRD is NOT detected by NBS [1].

judged.citation: Wijemanne S, Jankovic J. Dopa-responsive dystonia—clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Nat Rev Neurol. 2015;11(7):414–24.
judged.reason: The abstract lists the phenylalanine loading test among diagnostic tests but says nothing about baseline plasma phenylalanine being normal or about newborn screening detection.
judged.quote: which include a levodopa trial, genetic testing (including whole-exome sequencing), cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter analysis, the phenylalanine loading test, and enzyme activity measurements

rows.text: CSF diagnostic: low HVA, sometimes low 5-HIAA, low biopterin [4].

judged.citation: Tadic V et al. Dopa-responsive dystonia revisited. Mov Disord. 2012;27(6):808–13.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns diagnostic delay, residual motor and nonmotor signs in DRD and says nothing about CSF neurotransmitter metabolite or biopterin levels.

rows.text: Empirical levodopa trial is often used as the practical diagnostic test — dramatic sustained response within days–weeks is essentially diagnostic [1,2].

judged.citation: Wijemanne S, Jankovic J. Dopa-responsive dystonia—clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Nat Rev Neurol. 2015;11(7):414–24.
judged.reason: The abstract endorses a levodopa trial as a diagnostic test and describes a robust, sustained response, but gives no time frame such as days–weeks nor calls the response essentially diagnostic.
judged.quote: exhibit a robust and sustained response to levodopa treatment

rows.text: Heterozygous missense, splicing or deletion variants; ~230 variants reported [5,6].

judged.citation: Ichinose H et al. Hereditary progressive dystonia with marked diurnal fluctuation caused by mutations in the GTP cyclohydrolase I gene. Nat Genet. 1994;8(3):236–42.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms GCH1 mutations cause DRD and maps the gene to 14q22.1-q22.2, but it reports only four mutations and does not give variant classes (missense/splicing/deletion) or the ~230 total variant count.
judged.quote: The identification of four independent mutations of the gene for GTP cyclohydrolase I in patients with HPD, as well as a marked decrease in the enzyme's activity in mononuclear blood cells, confirms that the GTP cyclohydrolase I gene is a causative gene for HPD/DRD.

judged.citation: Clot F et al. GCH1 mutation spectrum and genotype-phenotype correlations. Brain. 2009;132(Pt 7):1753–63.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms heterozygous point mutations (including missense/splicing implied by point mutations) and large deletions in GCH1, but gives no total variant count approaching ~230.
judged.quote: We identified 34 different heterozygous point mutations in 40 patients, and six different large deletions in seven patients in the GCH1 gene.

rows.text: Childhood onset (typical): progressive dystonia, often starting in a lower limb (unilateral foot), with DIURNAL FLUCTUATION (worse in the evening, improved after sleep) — a classic clinical clue [1,3].

judged.citation: Wijemanne S, Jankovic J. Dopa-responsive dystonia—clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Nat Rev Neurol. 2015;11(7):414–24.
judged.reason: Limb-onset, diurnally fluctuating dystonia is stated, but the abstract does not specify lower-limb/unilateral foot onset, progression, or the evening-worse/improved-after-sleep pattern.
judged.quote: typically manifest as limb-onset, diurnally fluctuating dystonia

rows.text: Low-dose levodopa/carbidopa — typical regimens: children <6 years 1–10 mg/kg/day in multiple doses; children ≥6 years 25–50 mg once to three times daily; adults 50 mg once to three times daily; maximum benefit usually at total doses <300–400 mg/day [1,2,7].

judged.citation: Wijemanne S, Jankovic J. Dopa-responsive dystonia—clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Nat Rev Neurol. 2015;11(7):414–24.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms levodopa as the effective treatment but provides none of the specific age-based dosing regimens or the <300–400 mg/day ceiling.
judged.quote: exhibit a robust and sustained response to levodopa treatment

rows.text: Treated patients lead normal lives with essentially normal motor function [1,2].

judged.citation: Wijemanne S, Jankovic J. Dopa-responsive dystonia—clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Nat Rev Neurol. 2015;11(7):414–24.
judged.reason: A robust and sustained levodopa response is stated, but the abstract does not assert that treated patients lead normal lives with essentially normal motor function.
judged.quote: exhibit a robust and sustained response to levodopa treatment

rows.text: A CRITICAL diagnostic trap: the biochemistry is normal peripherally but the patient has progressive neurological disease [1,2].

judged.citation: Friedman J et al. Sepiapterin reductase deficiency: a treatable mimic of cerebral palsy. Ann Neurol. 2012;71(4):520–30.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the diagnostic trap of frequent misdiagnosis/long delay and ongoing brain dysfunction requiring CSF investigation, but never states that peripheral biochemistry (e.g., plasma phenylalanine, newborn screening) is normal.
judged.quote: Average age of onset is 7 months, with delay to diagnosis of 9.1 years. Misdiagnoses of cerebral palsy (CP) are common.

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that sepiapterin reductase deficiency lacks hyperphenylalaninaemia (normal peripheral biochemistry) but does not describe the progressive neurological disease or frame it as a diagnostic trap.
judged.quote: Hyperphenylalaninemia (HPA) is the first diagnostic hallmark for most BH 4  deficiencies, apart from autosomal dominant guanosine triphosphate cyclohydrolase I deficiency and sepiapterin reductase deficiency.

rows.text: SR deficiency (OMIM #612716) was described in 2001 [3].

judged.citation: Bonafé L et al. Mutations in the sepiapterin reductase gene cause a novel tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent monoamine-neurotransmitter deficiency without hyperphenylalaninemia. Am J Hum Genet. 2001;69(2):269–77.
judged.reason: This 2001 paper reports the first description of sepiapterin reductase deficiency as a novel BH4-dependent neurotransmitter deficiency, matching the claim's year of description (OMIM number is bibliographic, not an abstract-checkable fact).
judged.quote: Mutations in the sepiapterin reductase gene cause a novel tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent monoamine-neurotransmitter deficiency without hyperphenylalaninemia.

rows.text: Peripheral biochemistry is normal: plasma Phe normal, urine pterins normal [1,4].

judged.citation: Friedman J et al. Sepiapterin reductase deficiency: a treatable mimic of cerebral palsy. Ann Neurol. 2012;71(4):520–30.
judged.reason: The abstract endorses CSF as the preferred initial biochemical investigation with distinctive findings, implying peripheral testing is uninformative, but it does not state that plasma phenylalanine and urine pterins are specifically normal.
judged.quote: Cerebrospinal fluid findings are distinctive. Diagnosis is confirmed by mutation analysis and/or enzyme activity measurement in cultured fibroblasts.

judged.citation: Blau N, Bonafé L, Thöny B. Tetrahydrobiopterin deficiencies without hyperphenylalaninemia: diagnosis and genetics of dopa-responsive dystonia and sepiapterin reductase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2001;74(1–2):172–85.
judged.reason: The abstract supports normal plasma phenylalanine (absence of hyperphenylalaninemia, undetectable by newborn PKU screening) but says nothing about urine pterins being normal.
judged.quote: In contrast to classical forms of BH4 deficiency DRD and SR deficiency present without hyperphenylalaninemia and thus cannot be detected by the neonatal screening for phenylketonuria (PKU).

rows.text: CSF is the diagnostic specimen: low HVA, low 5-HIAA, ELEVATED DIHYDROBIOPTERIN and SEPIAPTERIN (sepiapterin in CSF is essentially pathognomonic) [5].

judged.citation: Neville BG et al. Sepiapterin reductase deficiency: a congenital dopa-responsive motor and cognitive disorder. Brain. 2005;128(Pt 10):2291–6.
judged.reason: The abstract reports only clinical phenotype, L-dopa response and the SPR gene mutation, and says nothing about CSF neurotransmitter metabolites or pterin levels, so the claim's biochemical content cannot be assessed from it.
judged.quote: All of the subjects had the same novel mutation in the tetrahydrobiopterin pathway involving sepiapterin reductase, and no abnormality in the gene encoding guanosine triphosphate cyclohydrolase 1.

rows.text: SPR at 2p13.2 [6]. >25 pathogenic variants reported.

judged.citation: Bonafé L et al. Mutations in the sepiapterin reductase gene cause a novel tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent monoamine-neurotransmitter deficiency without hyperphenylalaninemia. Am J Hum Genet. 2001;69(2):269–77.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that mutations in the SPR gene cause the disorder (reporting four distinct variants), but it never gives the chromosomal locus 2p13.2 nor supports a total of >25 reported pathogenic variants.
judged.quote: Mutations in the SPR gene were detected in both patients and their family members.

rows.text: Excellent with early treatment; delayed diagnosis leaves residual deficits [2,8].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract supports good outcome with early treatment but says nothing about residual deficits after delayed diagnosis.
judged.quote: Early supplementation of neurotransmitter precursors and where appropriate, treatment of HPA results in significant improvement of motor and cognitive function.

rows.text: However, a subgroup develops HNF-1α-like MODY diabetes in adolescence/adulthood [1,2].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract does not mention PCBD1 deficiency, MODY or HNF-1α-related diabetes.

judged.citation: Thöny B et al. Hyperphenylalaninemia due to defects in tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism: molecular characterization of mutations in 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase. Am J Hum Genet. 1994;54(5):782–92.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns PTPS deficiency mutations and says nothing about pterin-4α-carbinolamine dehydratase deficiency or MODY diabetes.

rows.text: Urine pterins: PRIMAPTERIN (7-biopterin) detectable — this is the pathognomonic marker, a non-enzymatic breakdown product of pterin-4α-carbinolamine when PCD is absent [1,5].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract contains no information on primapterin/7-biopterin or urinary pterin markers.

judged.citation: Curtius HC et al. 7-substituted pterins: a new class of mammalian pterins. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 1990;172(3):1060–6.
judged.reason: The abstract states that 7-substituted pterins arise from a chemical (non-enzymatic) rearrangement of 6-substituted pterins occurring specifically when dehydratase activity is absent, and that this characterises a distinct form of human hyperphenylalaninaemia, which is the substance of the claim (though the urinary matrix and the term 'primapterin' are not named).
judged.quote: We conclude that formation of 7-substituted pterins in humans is a consequence of an absence of dehydratase activity, which might result from a genetic defect. A chemical mechanism for this rearrangement is presented.

rows.text: A few pathogenic variants reported [6,7].

judged.citation: Citron BA et al. Identity of 4a-carbinolamine dehydratase, a component of the phenylalanine hydroxylation system, and DCoH, a transregulator of HNF-1 activity. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 1992;89(24):11891–4.
judged.reason: The abstract reports cloning of the dehydratase and its identity with DCoH but says nothing about pathogenic variants or mutation counts in PCBD1, so the claim's topic is not addressed.
judged.quote: Upon cloning and sequencing the dehydratase, we discovered that this protein is identical to DCoH, the cofactor which regulates the dimerization of hepatic nuclear factor 1 alpha, a homeodomain transcription factor.

judged.citation: Thöny B et al. The human gene locus for the pterin-4α-carbinolamine dehydratase. Genomics. 1995;26(2):295–300.
judged.reason: The abstract characterizes the PCBD gene structure, promoter and encoded bifunctional protein but never addresses patient mutations or the number of pathogenic variants reported.
judged.quote: Using this cDNA as a probe, we isolated and determined the complete nucleotide sequence and flanking regions of the single human PCBD gene.

rows.text: Newborn period: transient HPA at NBS, mostly asymptomatic [1].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract does not describe the newborn presentation of PCBD1 deficiency or its transient, asymptomatic course.

rows.text: No treatment typically required in newborn period; if Phe markedly elevated, transient dietary restriction until spontaneous normalisation [1].

judged.citation: Opladen T et al. Consensus guideline for BH4 deficiencies. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2020;15(1):126.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions treatment of HPA only in general terms and gives no disorder-specific guidance on withholding or transiently restricting diet in PCBD1 deficiency.

rows.text: Long-term: annual screening for diabetes (glucose, HbA1c) and magnesium from adolescence [3,4].

judged.citation: Simaite D et al. Recessive mutations in PCBD1 cause a new type of early-onset diabetes. Diabetes. 2014;63(10):3557–64.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes diabetes risk detectable via newborn screening and treatable with oral drugs, supporting the need for surveillance, but gives no annual screening interval or specific glucose/HbA1c/magnesium monitoring schedule from adolescence.
judged.quote: Finally, patients at risk can be detected through a newborn screening for phenylketonuria.

judged.citation: Ferrè S et al. Mutations in PCBD1 cause hypomagnesemia and renal magnesium wasting. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2014;25(3):574–86.
judged.reason: The abstract recommends monitoring for hypomagnesaemia and MODY diabetes but specifies neither annual frequency, the specific tests (glucose, HbA1c), nor onset from adolescence.
judged.quote: suggest that patients with HPABH4D should be monitored for previously unrecognized late complications, such as hypomagnesemia and MODY diabetes

rows.text: Metabolic-endocrine follow-up warranted for diabetes/hypomagnesaemia risk in adolescence/adulthood [3,4].

judged.citation: Simaite D et al. Recessive mutations in PCBD1 cause a new type of early-onset diabetes. Diabetes. 2014;63(10):3557–64.
judged.reason: The abstract shows adolescence-onset (pubertal) diabetes in PCBD1 deficiency and stresses its clinical importance for these patients, supporting endocrine follow-up; the hypomagnesaemia element is from the co-cited paper.
judged.quote: This condition responds to and can be treated with oral drugs instead of insulin, which is important clinical information for these patients.

judged.citation: Ferrè S et al. Mutations in PCBD1 cause hypomagnesemia and renal magnesium wasting. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2014;25(3):574–86.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly recommends monitoring HPABH4D patients for late-onset diabetes and hypomagnesaemia, matching the call for metabolic-endocrine follow-up.
judged.quote: suggest that patients with HPABH4D should be monitored for previously unrecognized late complications, such as hypomagnesemia and MODY diabetes

rows.text: Overall incidence is ~1:185,000 worldwide but rises to 1:380 in Old Order Mennonite populations due to a founder variant [4].

judged.citation: Puffenberger EG. Genetic heritage of the Old Order Mennonites. Am J Med Genet C. 2003;121C(1):18–31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the elevated Mennonite incidence from a founder BCKDHA variant (given as 1/358, close to but not identical with the claimed 1:380), but says nothing about the worldwide incidence of ~1:185,000.
judged.quote: The incidence of MSUD in the Old Order Mennonites is estimated to be 1/358 births, yielding a corrected carrier frequency of 7.96% and a mutation allele frequency of 4.15%.

rows.text: Alloisoleucine, formed non-enzymatically from elevated α-keto-β-methylvalerate, is pathognomonic: it is essentially absent (<5 µmol/L) from normal plasma and presence of alloisoleucine is considered diagnostic [6,7].

judged.citation: Schadewaldt P et al. Significance of L-alloisoleucine in plasma for diagnosis of MSUD. Clin Chem. 1999;45(10):1734–40.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes normal plasma alloisoleucine well below 5 µmol/L, adopts 5 µmol/L as the cutoff, and concludes it is the most specific and sensitive diagnostic marker for all MSUD forms; only the non-enzymatic derivation mechanism is not spelled out (it states derivation from isoleucine in vivo).
judged.quote: Therefore, a plasma concentration of 5 micromol/L was used as a cutoff value. ... The present findings indicate that plasma L-alloisoleucine above the cutoff value of 5 micromol/L is the most specific and most sensitive diagnostic marker for all forms of MSUD.

judged.citation: Oglesbee D et al. Second-tier test for quantification of alloisoleucine and branched-chain amino acids in dried blood spots to improve newborn screening for maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). Clin Chem. 2008;54(3):542–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms alloisoleucine is the only pathognomonic marker of MSUD, but gives no normal-plasma threshold (<5 µmol/L) and does not describe its non-enzymatic formation from α-keto-β-methylvalerate.
judged.quote: d-Alloisoleucine (allo-Ile) is the only pathognomonic marker of MSUD

rows.text: The (Leu+Ile+Val)/Ala ratio is a useful screening tool — alanine is low-normal as anaplerosis is impaired [8].

judged.citation: Strauss KA et al. Classical maple syrup urine disease and brain development. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;99(4):333–45.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that MSUD patients have episodic alanine (and glutamine/glutamate) depletion from reverse transamination, but it never mentions a (Leu+Ile+Val)/Ala ratio as a screening tool nor attributes low alanine to impaired anaplerosis.
judged.quote: compensate for episodic depletions of glutamine, glutamate, and alanine caused by reverse transamination

rows.text: Intermittent forms can have NORMAL plasma BCAA between episodes — alloisoleucine may persist and is the only reliable marker during remission [7].

judged.citation: Oglesbee D et al. Second-tier test for quantification of alloisoleucine and branched-chain amino acids in dried blood spots to improve newborn screening for maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). Clin Chem. 2008;54(3):542–9.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns a newborn-screening second-tier LC-MS/MS assay and says nothing about intermittent MSUD variants, normal interictal BCAA levels, or marker reliability during remission.

rows.text: BCKDC is a 4-MDa mitochondrial complex comprising E1α (BCKDHA, 19q13.2), E1β (BCKDHB, 6q14.1), E2/DBT (1p21.2), E3/DLD (7q31.1) and regulatory kinase/phosphatase subunits [1,9].

judged.citation: Aevarsson A et al. Crystal structure of human BCKDC E1. Structure. 2000;8(3):277–91.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that E1b is an α2β2 heterotetrameric component of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase multienzyme complex, but it does not state the 4-MDa complex size, the chromosomal loci of BCKDHA/BCKDHB/DBT/DLD, the E2/E3 components, or the regulatory kinase/phosphatase subunits.
judged.quote: we determined the crystal structure of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase (E1), the 170 kDa alpha(2)beta(2) heterotetrameric E1b component of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase multienzyme complex

rows.text: The Mennonite founder variant is BCKDHA p.Tyr438Asn [4].

judged.citation: Puffenberger EG. Genetic heritage of the Old Order Mennonites. Am J Med Genet C. 2003;121C(1):18–31.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies the BCKDHA 1312T→A mutation (which encodes p.Tyr438Asn) as the founder mutation causing classical MSUD in the Old Order Mennonites.
judged.quote: The population genetics of the 1312T --> A BCKDHA gene mutation, which causes classical MSUD, are presented in detail.

rows.text: MRI shows characteristic cytotoxic oedema in dorsal brainstem, cerebellar white matter, globus pallidus and thalami — the 'MSUD oedema' pattern [11].

judged.citation: Ha JS et al. MRI of the brain in maple syrup urine disease. AJNR. 2004;25(7):1219–27.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the anatomical distribution of MRI abnormalities (brainstem, thalamus, globus pallidus) in MSUD but describes chronic dysmyelination/disturbed white-matter water content in adolescents and adults rather than the acute 'MSUD oedema' cytotoxic pattern, and does not mention cerebellar white matter.
judged.quote: Areas affected most commonly were mesencephalon, brain stem, thalamus and globus pallidus; supratentorial lesions seem to be restricted to severe cases.

rows.text: Valine and isoleucine supplementation (20–40 mg/kg/day each) is essential to prevent selective BCAA deficiency once leucine is restricted [13].

judged.citation: Strauss KA et al. Classical maple syrup urine disease and brain development: principles of management and formula design. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;99(4):333–45.
judged.reason: The abstract details MSUD formula design and enrichment (LAT1 substrates, glutamine, alanine, zinc, selenium, alpha-linolenic acid) but nowhere addresses valine/isoleucine supplementation or the 20–40 mg/kg/day dose to prevent selective BCAA deficiency.
judged.quote: The formula was enriched with LAT1 amino acid substrates, glutamine, alanine, zinc, selenium, and alpha-linolenic acid (18:3n-3).

rows.text: Orthotopic liver transplantation is curative for classic MSUD and an increasingly standard option to liberalise diet and prevent further crises [15,16].

judged.citation: Mazariegos GV et al. Liver transplantation for classical MSUD. J Pediatr. 2012;160(1):116–21.
judged.reason: The abstract reports 100% patient/graft survival, immediate and sustained correction of branched-chain amino acid levels and >10-fold increase in leucine tolerance, concluding transplantation is an effective long-term treatment for classical MSUD, which carries the claim's substance about metabolic cure and dietary liberalisation.
judged.quote: Branched-chain amino acid levels were corrected within hours after surgery and remained stable, with leucine tolerance increasing more than 10-fold.

judged.citation: Shellmer DA et al. Cognitive and adaptive functioning after liver transplantation for MSUD. J Pediatr. 2011;159(4):614–20.
judged.reason: The abstract states liver transplantation is a metabolic cure and limits further CNS damage, but says nothing about dietary liberalisation or its increasing adoption as a standard option.
judged.quote: Although liver transplantation provides a metabolic cure for MSUD, changes in cognitive and adaptive functioning following transplantation have not been investigated.

rows.text: With NBS detection and prompt dietary management, neurological outcomes have improved substantially but remain vulnerable: residual cognitive deficits, attention problems and anxiety are common even with excellent control [17].

judged.citation: Muelly ER et al. Biochemical correlates of neuropsychiatric illness in MSUD. J Clin Invest. 2013;123(4):1809–20.
judged.reason: The abstract supports elevated risk of cognitive, attention and mood problems in treated MSUD patients, but does not support the specific qualifier that these persist even with excellent metabolic control (it instead reports that stringent biochemical control optimized mental health), nor does it address NBS detection or anxiety specifically.
judged.quote: Compared with 26 age-matched controls, MSUD patients were at higher risk for disorders of cognition, attention, and mood.

rows.text: Liver transplantation normalises metabolism and prevents future crises; neurocognitive outcomes are stabilised at the pre-transplant level [15,16].

judged.citation: Mazariegos GV et al. Liver transplantation for classical MSUD. J Pediatr. 2012;160(1):116–21.
judged.reason: The abstract documents corrected and stable BCAA homeostasis with no statistically significant change in IQ one year post-transplant and states transplantation may arrest but not reverse brain damage, matching the claim of metabolic normalisation with neurocognitive stabilisation at the pre-transplant level.
judged.quote: One-third of our patients were mentally impaired (IQ ≤ 70) before transplantation, with no statistically significant change 1 year later. Liver transplantation is an effective long-term treatment for classical MSUD and may arrest brain damage, but will not reverse it.

judged.citation: Shellmer DA et al. Cognitive and adaptive functioning after liver transplantation for MSUD. J Pediatr. 2011;159(4):614–20.
judged.reason: The abstract reports no significant change or improvement in IQ and adaptive scores post-transplant with prevention of further CNS injury, matching the claim of stabilisation at pre-transplant level.
judged.quote: Findings show either no significant change (n=8) or improvement (n=5) in IQ scores pre- to post-liver transplantation. ... findings indicate that liver transplantation minimizes the likelihood of additional central nervous system damage, providing an opportunity for possible stabilization or improvement in neurocognitive functioning.

rows.text: Pyridoxine-responsive forms have a markedly milder natural history than non-responsive forms [1,2].

judged.citation: Morris AA et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):49–74.
judged.reason: The abstract contrasts severely affected childhood-onset patients requiring diet/betaine with mildly affected pyridoxine-responsive patients presenting only in adulthood, i.e. a milder natural history.
judged.quote: Severely affected patients usually present in childhood with ectopia lentis, learning difficulties and skeletal abnormalities. These patients generally require treatment with a low-methionine diet and/or betaine. In contrast, mildly affected patients are likely to present as adults with thromboembolism and to respond to treatment with pyridoxine.

rows.text: Worldwide incidence is ~1:200,000–1:335,000, but founder effects change the picture entirely: in Qatar the incidence is at least 1:3,000 — the highest reported anywhere — driven by a single CBS variant (p.R336C) in one tribe, and every patient in whom it was assessed was pyridoxine-NON-responsive [4].

judged.citation: El-Said MF et al. A common mutation in the CBS gene explains a high incidence of homocystinuria in the Qatari population. Hum Mutat. 2006;27(7):719.
judged.reason: The abstract fully supports the Qatar incidence of ≥1:3,000 as the world's highest, the p.R336C founder variant in tribe M, and universal B6-nonresponsiveness, but it does not mention the worldwide incidence figure of ~1:200,000–1:335,000.
judged.quote: The incidence of homocystinuria in Qatar was calculated to be > or =1:3000, the highest in the world known so far. All patients in whom data were available were vitamin B6-nonresponsive.

rows.text: The disorder is often under-diagnosed in adulthood — prevalence of undetected CBS deficiency in ectopia-lentis cohorts is as high as 5% [5].

judged.citation: Cruysberg JR et al. Delay in diagnosis of homocystinuria. BMJ. 1996;313(7058):1037–40.
judged.reason: The abstract documents substantial diagnostic delay/under-recognition of CBS deficiency including in patients with ectopia lentis, but gives no prevalence figure (e.g., 5%) for undetected CBS deficiency within ectopia-lentis cohorts — it reports the converse (76% of homocystinuria patients had ectopia lentis).
judged.quote: Even when ectopia lentis was diagnosed (in 26 (76%) patients, mean age 18 (1-50) years), this did not lead to adequate biochemical analysis for homocystinuria at the time of detection, causing a mean diagnostic delay of 8 (0-24) years in these patients.

rows.text: Plasma total homocysteine (tHcy) is markedly elevated (typically >100 µmol/L untreated, often >200) [1,6].

judged.citation: Refsum H et al. Facts and recommendations about total homocysteine determinations. Clin Chem. 2004;50(1):3–32.
judged.reason: The abstract covers total homocysteine measurement and its use in diagnosing homocystinuria, but gives no concentration values, so the specific thresholds (>100 µmol/L, often >200) are not verifiable from it.
judged.quote: risk assessment and disease diagnosis (homocystinuria, folate and cobalamin deficiencies, cardiovascular disease, renal failure, psychiatric disorders and cognitive impairment, pregnancy complications and birth defects, and screening of elderly and newborns)

rows.text: Plasma methionine is elevated (usually 40–200 µmol/L, occasionally >1000) because trans-sulfuration is blocked — this is the biochemical hallmark that distinguishes CBS deficiency from remethylation defects (cblC/D/E/F/G/J and MTHFR), in which methionine is low [2,7].

judged.citation: Morris AA et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):49–74.
judged.reason: This guideline summary mentions only the methionine catabolic pathway and homocysteine measurement; it gives no plasma methionine concentrations and does not discuss remethylation defects, so the claim cannot be assessed from the abstract.
judged.quote: We strongly recommend measuring the plasma total homocysteine concentrations in any patient whose clinical features suggest the diagnosis.

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that remethylation defects impair conversion of homocysteine to methionine (implying low methionine) but gives no plasma methionine values for CBS deficiency and never states the 40–200 µmol/L range or the >1000 µmol/L extreme.
judged.quote: Remethylation defects are rare inherited disorders in which impaired remethylation of homocysteine to methionine leads to accumulation of homocysteine and perturbation of numerous methylation reactions.

rows.text: Free homocystine appears in urine only above plasma tHcy ≈50 µmol/L, which is why NBS using free-Hcy DBS misses milder forms; second-tier plasma tHcy is essential [8].

judged.citation: Peterschmitt MJ et al. Reduction of false-negative results in screening for homocystinuria. N Engl J Med. 1999;341(21):1572–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the general point that newborn screening misses milder/less markedly elevated cases (false negatives from slightly raised analyte levels), but it concerns methionine-based screening and says nothing about urinary free homocystine appearing only above plasma tHcy ≈50 µmol/L, free-Hcy DBS assays, or second-tier plasma tHcy testing.
judged.quote: Many infants with this disorder, however, are not identified by screening and have irreversible brain damage.

rows.text: Pyridoxine responsiveness: pharmacological doses (200–500 mg/day) reduce tHcy by ≥30% in ~50% of patients [1,9].

judged.citation: Wilcken DE, Turnbull DM. Homocystinuria—the effects of betaine in the treatment of patients not responsive to pyridoxine. N Engl J Med. 1983;309(8):448–53.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns betaine therapy in pyridoxine-nonresponsive homocystinuria and, while it invokes the responsive/nonresponsive distinction, it provides no pyridoxine dose range, no ≥30% tHcy reduction threshold, and no ~50% responsiveness proportion.
judged.quote: Ten patients with cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency that was not responsive to pyridoxine and one patient with homocystinuria due to a defect in cobalamin metabolism were treated with 6 g daily of betaine added to conventional therapy

rows.text: CBS is located at 21q22.3, a 23-kb gene encoding a 551-amino-acid PLP-dependent haem enzyme [10].

judged.citation: Kraus JP et al. Cystathionine beta-synthase mutations in homocystinuria. Hum Mutat. 1999;13(5):362–75.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns CBS gene mutations and enzyme deficiency but gives none of the claimed structural facts (21q22.3 locus, 23-kb gene, 551 amino acids, PLP/haem cofactors).
judged.quote: The major cause of homocystinuria is mutation of the gene encoding the enzyme cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS).

rows.text: The two commonest are p.Ile278Thr (typically B6-responsive) and p.Gly307Ser (almost always B6-non-responsive, Celtic founder) [1,10,11].

judged.citation: Kraus JP et al. Cystathionine beta-synthase mutations in homocystinuria. Hum Mutat. 1999;13(5):362–75.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the two most frequent mutations and their pyridoxine-responsiveness, but does not mention a Celtic founder origin for G307S.
judged.quote: The two most frequently encountered of these mutations are the pyridoxine-responsive I278T and the pyridoxine-nonresponsive G307S.

judged.citation: Matthews A, Moat SJ et al. An indirect response model of homocysteine suppression by betaine: optimising the dosage regimen of betaine in homocystinuria. Br J Clin Pharmacol. 2002;54(2):140–6.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns betaine pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics dosing in CBS deficiency and says nothing about specific CBS variants or their B6-responsiveness.

rows.text: Genotype reliably predicts B6-responsiveness and is the basis of stratifying newly-diagnosed patients [11].

judged.citation: Matthews A, Moat SJ et al. An indirect response model of homocysteine suppression by betaine: optimising the dosage regimen of betaine in homocystinuria. Br J Clin Pharmacol. 2002;54(2):140–6.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses betaine dosage optimisation, not genotype prediction of pyridoxine responsiveness or genotype-based stratification.

rows.text: Classic untreated CBS deficiency has four cardinal features: (1) ectopia lentis (downward, bilateral, typically by age 8 but may present in infancy) [1,12]; (2) marfanoid body habitus with osteoporosis, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity and genu valgum [1]; (3) thromboembolism — venous or arterial, responsible for ~20% of deaths, highest perioperative risk [1,13]; (4) intellectual disability, commoner in B6-non-responsive forms [1,14].

judged.citation: Mulvihill A et al. Ocular findings in homocystinuria. J AAPOS. 2001;5(5):311–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports ectopia lentis as a cardinal feature of untreated/poorly controlled homocystinuria, but does not state the downward direction or the "typically by age 8/may present in infancy" timing, and says nothing about marfanoid habitus, thromboembolism (~20% of deaths) or intellectual disability.
judged.quote: Lens subluxation is a principal feature of untreated HCU, yet we found a median lag period of 5.5 years in 4 cases before diagnosis.

judged.citation: Yap S et al. Vascular complications of severe hyperhomocysteinaemia. Semin Thromb Hemost. 2000;26(3):335–40.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that thromboembolic/vascular events (venous and arterial) are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in untreated CBS deficiency, but it gives no figure for ~20% of deaths and does not mention perioperative risk or the other cardinal features (ectopia lentis, marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability).
judged.quote: Vascular events (VE) remain the major cause of morbidity and mortality in the untreated patients with HCU.

judged.citation: Yap S et al. Vascular outcome in patients with homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency treated chronically: a multicenter observational study. Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol. 2001;21(12):2080–5.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms thromboembolic/vascular events (venous and arterial) as the main life-threatening complication of untreated CBS deficiency, but gives no figure for ~20% of deaths, no mention of perioperative risk, and nothing on ectopia lentis, marfanoid habitus or intellectual disability.
judged.quote: Premature vascular events are the main life-threatening complication.

rows.text: Pyridoxine-responsive patients may escape diagnosis until their second or third decade, often with thromboembolism as the presenting event [14].

judged.citation: Yap S et al. Vascular outcome in patients with homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency treated chronically: a multicenter observational study. Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol. 2001;21(12):2080–5.
judged.reason: The abstract reports vascular outcomes in chronically treated CBS patients and never addresses pyridoxine responsiveness, delayed diagnosis, or thromboembolism as a presenting event leading to diagnosis.

rows.text: If B6-responsive, titrate to normal tHcy [2,15].

judged.citation: Morris AA et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):49–74.
judged.reason: The abstract supports pyridoxine responsiveness and tHcy-based treatment targets but specifies a target below 100 µmol/L rather than titration to a normal tHcy.
judged.quote: Nevertheless, we recommend keeping the concentration below 100 μmol/L because levels fluctuate and the complications associated with high levels are so serious.

judged.citation: Wilcken DE, Wilcken B. The natural history of vascular disease in homocystinuria and the effects of treatment. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1997;20(2):295–300.
judged.reason: The abstract reports that all pyridoxine-responsive patients on vitamin therapy were maintained at essentially normal plasma total free homocyst(e)ine (<20 µmol/L) with markedly reduced vascular risk, which underpins the recommendation to treat B6-responsive patients to normal tHcy.
judged.quote: There were 17 pyridoxine-responsive patients and all maintained plasma total free homocyst(e)ine levels < 20 mumol/L over an average treatment period of 16.6 years.

rows.text: If B6-non-responsive: methionine-restricted diet with cystine-supplemented medical food, keeping tHcy <50 µmol/L [1,2].

judged.citation: Morris AA et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):49–74.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a low-methionine diet for severely (non-pyridoxine-responsive) affected patients but does not mention cystine-supplemented medical food or a tHcy target of <50 µmol/L (it recommends <100 µmol/L).
judged.quote: These patients generally require treatment with a low-methionine diet and/or betaine.

rows.text: Betaine (3–20 g/day in divided doses) provides an alternative remethylation route via BHMT and is added when diet alone cannot reach target — note the paradoxical rise in methionine [16].

judged.citation: Singh RH et al. Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency: effects of betaine supplementation after methionine restriction in B6-nonresponsive homocystinuria. Genet Med. 2004;6(2):90–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports adding betaine after optimal dietary methionine restriction in B6-nonresponsive homocystinuria to lower tHcy, but it gives no 3–20 g/day dosing, no BHMT remethylation mechanism, and reports methionine as unchanged rather than paradoxically rising.
judged.quote: Betaine improves metabolic control in B6-nonresponsive patients with homocystinuria after optimum dietary control.

rows.text: Aspirin thromboprophylaxis and avoidance of dehydration, immobility, and oestrogen-containing contraceptives are routine [2].

judged.citation: Morris AA et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):49–74.
judged.reason: The abstract summarises diagnostic and homocysteine-lowering recommendations only and says nothing about aspirin, dehydration, immobility or oestrogen-containing contraceptives.

rows.text: The evidence cited here is preclinical — in the I278T mouse, ERT held plasma homocysteine near 100 µmol/L, normalised cysteine for up to 9 months, and partially rescued the ocular, bone and hair phenotypes when given from birth [17].

judged.citation: Majtan T et al. Enzyme replacement therapy ameliorates multiple symptoms of murine homocystinuria. Mol Ther. 2018;26(3):834–44.
judged.reason: The abstract states ERT in the I278T mouse sustained plasma homocysteine near 100 µM, normalized plasma cysteine for up to 9 months, and prevented/reversed alopecia, low bone mass, and partially rescued the ocular phenotype when given from birth.
judged.quote: ERT substantially reduced and sustained plasma homocysteine concentration at around 100 μM and normalized plasma cysteine for up to 9 months of treatment.

rows.text: Untreated: 50% of patients have had a thromboembolic event by age 30, and mean IQ is 57 [1,14].

judged.citation: Yap S et al. Vascular outcome in patients with homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency treated chronically: a multicenter observational study. Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol. 2001;21(12):2080–5.
judged.reason: The abstract directly supports the untreated 50%-by-age-30 thromboembolic figure but says nothing about mean IQ of 57.
judged.quote: Half of all untreated patients have a vascular event by 30 years of age.

rows.text: Early NBS detection with lifelong compliance normalises IQ trajectory and cuts thromboembolic risk sharply: across 2,822 patient-years in 158 treated patients there were 17 vascular events against 112 predicted from untreated historical controls — relative risk 0.09 — and that held despite plasma homocysteine usually remaining moderately elevated, so imperfect biochemical control is still worth having [14].

judged.citation: Yap S et al. Vascular outcome in patients with homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency treated chronically: a multicenter observational study. Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol. 2001;21(12):2080–5.
judged.reason: All the vascular figures (158 patients, 2822 patient-years, 17 vs 112 events, RR 0.09, imperfect biochemical control) are directly supported, but the abstract says nothing about newborn screening detection or normalisation of IQ trajectory.
judged.quote: There were 2822 patient-years of treatment, with an average of 17.9 years per patient. Plasma homocysteine levels were markedly reduced from pretreatment levels but usually remained moderately elevated. There were 17 vascular events in 12 patients... Without treatment, 112 vascular events would have been expected, for a relative risk of 0.09 (95% CI 0.036 to 0.228; P<0.0001).

rows.text: Read the untreated figures with care, however: molecular screening in Denmark finds far more p.I278T homozygotes than are ever diagnosed clinically, implying the classic natural-history curves were built on an ascertainment-biased sample and that a substantial share of homozygotes may remain unaffected or present only in the third decade [18].

judged.citation: Skovby F, Gaustadnes M, Mudd SH. A revisit to the natural history of homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;99(1):1–3.
judged.reason: The abstract directly states that Danish molecular screening predicts far more p.I278T homozygotes than are clinically identified, that most may be unaffected or present with thromboembolism in the third decade, and that the previously published natural-history curves were ascertainment-biased and should be used with care.
judged.quote: the number of individuals identified with homocystinuria due to homozygosity for the widespread c.833T>C (p.I278T) mutation in the gene that encodes cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) falls far short of the number of such individuals expected on the basis of the heterozygote frequency for this mutation found by molecular screening. We conclude that the predominant portion of such homozygotes may be clinically unaffected, or may be ascertained for thromboembolic events occurring no sooner than the third decade of life. If so, there was significant ascertainment bias in the time-to-event curves previously published

rows.text: Pregnancy requires intensified tHcy monitoring because thrombotic risk is amplified [19].

judged.citation: Levy HL et al. Pregnancy in women with homocystinuria. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2002;25(4):299–314.
judged.reason: The abstract supports careful monitoring (with metabolic therapy and possible anticoagulation) during pregnancy, but it does not establish that thrombotic risk is amplified — it reports thromboembolic events as infrequent and outcomes usually normal.
judged.quote: The infrequent occurrences of pregnancy complications, offspring abnormalities and maternal thromboembolic events in this series suggest that pregnancy and outcome in maternal homocystinuria are usually normal. Nevertheless, a cautious approach would include careful monitoring of these pregnancies with attention to metabolic therapy and possibly anticoagulation.

rows.text: Since the introduction of nitisinone (NTBC) the natural history has been transformed from uniformly fatal to long-term survival with near-normal liver function [1,2].

judged.citation: Chinsky JM et al. Diagnosis and treatment of tyrosinemia type I: US and Canadian consensus group recommendations. Genet Med. 2017;19(12).
judged.reason: The abstract confirms NTBC is an effective treatment allowing most early-identified infants to remain asymptomatic, but does not state the pre-NTBC course was uniformly fatal or document long-term near-normal liver function.
judged.quote: An effective medical treatment with 2-[2-nitro-4-trifluoromethylbenzoyl]-1,3-cyclohexanedione (NTBC) exists but requires early identification of affected children for optimal long-term results... If identified early and treated appropriately, the majority of affected infants can remain asymptomatic.

judged.citation: de Laet C et al. Recommendations for the management of tyrosinaemia type 1. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms nitisinone revolutionised HT1 management but gives no data on survival transformation from uniformly fatal to long-term survival with near-normal liver function.
judged.quote: The management of tyrosinaemia type 1 (HT1, fumarylacetoacetase deficiency) has been revolutionised by the introduction of nitisinone

rows.text: Global incidence is ~1:100,000 but rises to ~1:1,846 in Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean (Quebec) due to a founder variant [4].

judged.citation: De Braekeleer M, Larochelle J. Genetic epidemiology of hereditary tyrosinemia in Quebec. Am J Hum Genet. 1990;47(2):302–7.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the 1/1,846 birth prevalence in Saguenay–Lac-St-Jean and a founder effect, but gives no global incidence figure of ~1:100,000.
judged.quote: The prevalence at birth was estimated at 1/1,846 live borns, and the carrier rate was estimated at 1/20 inhabitants in the SLSJ region.

rows.text: It is the only tyrosinaemia causing severe multi-system disease and the only one on the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (via succinylacetone measurement) [5].

judged.citation: Stinton C et al. Newborn screening for tyrosinemia type 1 using succinylacetone: a systematic review of test accuracy. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):48.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms newborn screening for tyrosinemia type 1 via succinylacetone in dried blood spots, but says nothing about the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel or that HT1 is the only tyrosinaemia with severe multi-system disease or on the panel.
judged.quote: Newborn screening allows for earlier identification, but there is uncertainty regarding the test accuracy of the current method: succinylacetone measurement in dried blood spots using tandem mass spectrometry.

rows.text: Succinylacetone in urine or dried blood spot is pathognomonic — detectable at trace levels (>0.5 µmol/L DBS) even before the plasma tyrosine rises [5,6].

judged.citation: Stinton C et al. Newborn screening for tyrosinemia type 1 using succinylacetone: a systematic review of test accuracy. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):48.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the high diagnostic accuracy of succinylacetone in dried blood spots (100% sensitivity/specificity in case-control studies) but gives no cut-off such as >0.5 µmol/L and does not address detection before plasma tyrosine rises.
judged.quote: Sensitivity (29 cases in total) and specificity (34,403 controls in total) were 100% in the case-control studies

judged.citation: Allard P et al. Newborn screening for hepatorenal tyrosinemia by MS/MS succinylacetone. Clin Biochem. 2004;37(11):1010–5.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms succinylacetone is markedly elevated in DBS of HT1 patients versus unaffected newborns (<2 µmol/L), but its limit of quantitation is 1 µmol/L and it never establishes a >0.5 µmol/L trace-level threshold nor that SA rises before plasma tyrosine.
judged.quote: The reference range in the control group of unaffected newborn was determined to be <2 micromol/L, while SA in retrieved DBS from HT patients was significantly elevated, measuring 46.7, 36.5, and 23.2 micromol/L.

rows.text: Plasma alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is markedly elevated at presentation (often >100,000 µg/L) and serves as a tumour surveillance marker during NTBC therapy [1,7].

judged.citation: Chinsky JM et al. Diagnosis and treatment of tyrosinemia type I: US and Canadian consensus group recommendations. Genet Med. 2017;19(12).
