judged.reason: The abstract discusses succinylacetone and tyrosine as screening markers and mentions HCC risk but says nothing about alpha-fetoprotein levels or tumour surveillance, and is too summary-level to judge.

judged.citation: Holme E, Lindstedt S. Tyrosinaemia type I and NTBC. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1998;21(5):507–17.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns NTBC treatment outcomes and hepatocellular carcinoma risk in tyrosinaemia type I but never addresses alpha-fetoprotein levels or its use as a surveillance marker, so the claim's topic is not engaged.

rows.text: NBS using tyrosine alone has unacceptably high false-negative rate; succinylacetone MS/MS-based second-tier testing is the standard of care [5,6].

judged.citation: Stinton C et al. Newborn screening for tyrosinemia type 1 using succinylacetone: a systematic review of test accuracy. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):48.
judged.reason: The abstract endorses succinylacetone MS/MS as the current screening method with high accuracy but does not report false-negative rates for tyrosine-only screening, and describes the approach as "promising" rather than established standard of care with second-tier testing.
judged.quote: Screening for Tyrosinemia type 1 using tandem mass spectrometry measurement of succinylacetone from dried blood spots appears to be promising.

judged.citation: Allard P et al. Newborn screening for hepatorenal tyrosinemia by MS/MS succinylacetone. Clin Biochem. 2004;37(11):1010–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports MS/MS succinylacetone as a feasible, highly sensitive/specific newborn screening test for HT1, but says nothing about tyrosine-alone screening or its false-negative rate, nor about second-tier standard of care.
judged.quote: We report a simple method that can be used for screening HT in newborns. Based on our limited experience, a 2 micromol/L cutoff could result in up to 100% sensitivity and specificity.

rows.text: Over 100 pathogenic variants are known (FAH mutation database) [8].

judged.citation: St-Louis M, Tanguay RM. Mutations in the FAH gene in hereditary tyrosinemia type I. Hum Mutat. 1997;9(4):291–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms mutations in FAH cause HT1 but reports only 26 mutations known at the time, not over 100, so the specific count is not supported.
judged.quote: At present 26 mutations have been reported, all consisting of single base substitutions resulting in 16 amino acid replacements, one silent mutation causing a splicing defect, five nonsense codons, and four putative splicing defects.

rows.text: No genotype–phenotype correlation — the same variant can produce acute neonatal liver failure in one sibling and chronic presentation in another [1,8].

judged.citation: Chinsky JM et al. Diagnosis and treatment of tyrosinemia type I: US and Canadian consensus group recommendations. Genet Med. 2017;19(12).
judged.reason: The abstract addresses screening and management only and does not discuss FAH variants or genotype–phenotype relationships.

judged.citation: St-Louis M, Tanguay RM. Mutations in the FAH gene in hereditary tyrosinemia type I. Hum Mutat. 1997;9(4):291–9.
judged.reason: The abstract discusses mutation types, locations and diagnostic/counseling implications but says nothing about genotype–phenotype correlation or intrafamilial phenotypic variability.
judged.quote: The identification of these mutations in subpopulations and groups at high risk should help in the diagnosis of, and genetic counseling for, HT1.

rows.text: FAH protein is cytosolic and tissue distribution is highest in hepatocytes and proximal renal tubules, explaining the hepatorenal phenotype [1].

judged.citation: Chinsky JM et al. Diagnosis and treatment of tyrosinemia type I: US and Canadian consensus group recommendations. Genet Med. 2017;19(12).
judged.reason: The abstract does not describe FAH protein localisation or tissue distribution, only that the condition has hepatic, renal and neurologic involvement.

rows.text: Three clinical forms based on age of onset [1]: (1) Acute infantile (<6 mo): severe hepatic crisis with coagulopathy, oedema, ascites, cabbage-like odour, and Fanconi syndrome.

judged.citation: Chinsky JM et al. Diagnosis and treatment of tyrosinemia type I: US and Canadian consensus group recommendations. Genet Med. 2017;19(12).
judged.reason: The abstract lists organ systems affected but does not describe age-of-onset clinical forms or the specific acute infantile features listed.

rows.text: Mortality without NTBC: ~60% in first year; (2) Subacute (6 mo–2 yr): hepatomegaly, growth failure, rickets from tubulopathy, coagulopathy; (3) Chronic (>2 yr): rickets, hypophosphataemic bone disease, porphyria-like neurological crises (from succinylacetone inhibition of δ-aminolevulinate dehydratase), and 20–40% risk of hepatocellular carcinoma by age 5 without treatment [9,10].

judged.citation: van Spronsen FJ et al. Tyrosinemia type I: risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatology. 1994;20(5):1187–91.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the ~60% first-year mortality for very early-onset disease (38% 1-yr survival) and the existence of porphyria-like crises and HCC as causes of death, but it does not support the specific "20–40% risk of hepatocellular carcinoma by age 5" figure (it reports HCC as 17% of deaths) nor the rickets/hypophosphataemic bone findings.
judged.quote: Liver failure and recurrent bleeding (67%), hepatocellular carcinoma (17%) and the porphyria-like syndrome with respiratory failure (10%) were the most common causes of death. The 1- and 2-yr survival probability after the onset of symptoms in patients in whom symptoms developed before 2 mo, between 2 and 6 mo and after 6 mo were 38%/29%, 74%/74% and 96%/96%, respectively.

judged.citation: Mitchell GA et al. Neurologic crises in hereditary tyrosinemia. N Engl J Med. 1990;322(7):432–7.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the porphyria-like neurological crises with elevated δ-aminolevulinic acid, but does not provide the ~60% first-year mortality, the rickets/hypophosphataemic bone disease, or the 20–40% HCC risk by age 5 (the latter covered by the co-cited paper).
judged.quote: Urinary excretion of delta-aminolevulinic acid, a neurotoxic intermediate of porphyrin biosynthesis, was elevated during crises but also during the asymptomatic periods... We conclude that episodes of acute, severe peripheral neuropathy are common in hereditary tyrosinemia and resemble the crises of the neuropathic porphyrias.

rows.text: Nitisinone (NTBC, 1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses) inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, preventing formation of toxic downstream metabolites including succinylacetone [11,12].

judged.citation: Lindstedt S et al. Treatment of hereditary tyrosinaemia type I by inhibition of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase. Lancet. 1992;340(8823):813–7.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms NTBC inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase and abolishes succinylacetone/succinylacetoacetate formation, but the stated dose of 1 mg/kg/day in two divided doses is not supported — the reported oral daily dose was 0.1–0.6 mg/kg.
judged.quote: We have treated one acute and four subacute-chronic cases with 2-(2-nitro-4-trifluoromethylbenzoyl)-1,3-cyclohexanedione (NTBC), a potent inhibitor of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (EC 1.13.11.27), to prevent the formation of maleylacetoacetate and fumarylacetoacetate and their saturated derivatives. The oral daily dose was 0.1-0.6 mg/kg.

judged.citation: Larochelle J et al. Effect of nitisinone treatment on HCC in tyrosinaemia type 1. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;107(1–2):49–54.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms nitisinone blocks tyrosine degradation upstream of toxic metabolites such as succinylacetone, but it does not name 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase as the target nor give the 1 mg/kg/day divided-dose regimen.
judged.quote: Nitisinone (NTBC, Orfadin ®) inhibits tyrosine degradation prior to the formation of toxic metabolites like succinylacetone

rows.text: Combined with tyrosine + phenylalanine-restricted diet (target plasma Tyr 200–600 µmol/L to prevent oculocutaneous toxicity from NTBC-induced hypertyrosinaemia) [1,13].

judged.citation: Chinsky JM et al. Diagnosis and treatment of tyrosinemia type I: US and Canadian consensus group recommendations. Genet Med. 2017;19(12).
judged.reason: The abstract endorses combined NTBC and dietary treatment but gives no target plasma tyrosine range or mention of oculocutaneous toxicity from hypertyrosinaemia.
judged.quote: followed by diagnostic confirmation and early treatment with NTBC and diet

judged.citation: van Ginkel WG et al. Neurocognitive outcome in tyrosinemia type 1 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;118(3):138–42.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns neurocognitive outcomes in NTBC- and diet-treated HT1 patients and says nothing about tyrosine/phenylalanine restriction targets or oculocutaneous toxicity thresholds.

rows.text: NTBC reverses porphyria-like crises within hours, stabilises liver function and dramatically reduces HCC risk when started <1 month of age (HCC risk ~1% vs. ~35% if started >2 years) [12,14].

judged.citation: Larochelle J et al. Effect of nitisinone treatment on HCC in tyrosinaemia type 1. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;107(1–2):49–54.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that nitisinone abolishes acute complications and that treatment before 1 month prevents detectable liver disease, but it gives no HCC risk figures (~1% vs ~35%) and does not describe reversal of porphyria-like crises within hours.
judged.quote: Nitisinone treatment abolishes the acute complications of HT1. Some patients with established liver disease before nitisinone treatment eventually require hepatic transplantation. Patients who receive nitisinone treatment before 1 month had no detectable liver disease after more than 5 years.

judged.citation: Mayorandan S et al. Cross-sectional study of 168 patients with hepatorenal tyrosinaemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:107.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that early NTBC treatment prevents liver failure and hepatocellular carcinoma, but gives no data on reversal of porphyria-like crises within hours or the quantified HCC risks (~1% if started <1 month vs ~35% if started >2 years).
judged.quote: Early treatment by NTBC accompanied by diet is essential to prevent serious complications such as liver failure, hepatocellular carcinoma and renal disease.

rows.text: Liver transplantation is reserved for NTBC-unresponsive acute liver failure or established HCC [15].

judged.citation: Arnon R et al. Liver transplantation for hereditary tyrosinemia type I. Pediatr Transplant. 2011;15(4):400–5.
judged.reason: The abstract states LT is indicated for fulminant liver failure, HCC, or chronic liver disease refractory to NTBC, matching the claim.
judged.quote: LT is indicated in patients with fulminant liver failure, HCC or decompensated chronic liver disease refractory to NTBC.

rows.text: Pre-NTBC era: 5-year survival ~30%; HCC was almost inevitable after age 5 [16].

judged.citation: Weinberg AG et al. The occurrence of hepatoma in chronic form of hereditary tyrosinemia. J Pediatr. 1976;88(3):434–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a substantial HCC risk in patients surviving infancy (16/43, 37%) but gives no 5-year survival figure (~30%) and does not show HCC was "almost inevitable after age 5".
judged.quote: have disclosed 16 cases of hepatocarcinoma occurring in 43 patients surviving beyond 2 years of age (37%)

rows.text: With NTBC started at NBS (prior to 1 month of age): 10-year survival >95%, HCC risk near 1%, normal growth, minimal hepatic fibrosis [12,14].

judged.citation: Larochelle J et al. Effect of nitisinone treatment on HCC in tyrosinaemia type 1. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;107(1–2):49–54.
judged.reason: The abstract supports reduced mortality and absence of detectable liver disease in patients treated before 1 month, but does not report a 10-year survival figure >95%, an HCC risk near 1%, growth outcomes, or fibrosis assessment.
judged.quote: Ten deaths occurred in non-nitisinone treated patients versus two in treated patients (p<0.01). Both of the latter deaths were from complications of transplantation unrelated to HT1.

judged.citation: Mayorandan S et al. Cross-sectional study of 168 patients with hepatorenal tyrosinaemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:107.
judged.reason: The abstract endorses early NTBC treatment (with newborn screening) to prevent complications but provides none of the specific outcome figures claimed (10-year survival >95%, HCC risk ~1%, normal growth, minimal hepatic fibrosis).
judged.quote: Early treatment by NTBC accompanied by diet is essential to prevent serious complications such as liver failure, hepatocellular carcinoma and renal disease. As patients may remain initially asymptomatic or develop uncharacteristic clinical symptoms in the first months of life newborn mass screening using succinylacetone (SA) as a screening parameter in dried blood is mandatory for early diagnosis.

rows.text: Long-term cognitive outcomes on NTBC are subtly impaired (IQ 5–10 points below siblings), attributed partly to chronic tyrosine elevation [17].

judged.citation: Bendadi F et al. Impaired cognitive functioning in patients with tyrosinemia type I receiving NTBC. J Pediatr. 2014;164(2):398–401.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that cognition is impaired on nitisinone but contradicts both the magnitude (20-point deficit, 71±13 vs 91±13, not 5–10 points) and the attribution to tyrosine elevation (no significant association found).
judged.quote: Average total IQ score in 10 patients with tyrosinemia type I receiving nitisinone was significantly lower compared with their unaffected siblings (71 ± 13 vs 91 ± 13; P = .008)... No significant association was found between IQ score and either plasma tyrosine or phenylalanine concentration.

rows.text: Lifelong AFP, α-fetoprotein imaging (liver US every 6 months), and renal function surveillance are required [2].

judged.citation: de Laet C et al. Recommendations for the management of tyrosinaemia type 1. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:8.
judged.reason: The abstract only announces that detailed management recommendations are made, without stating any monitoring modality or interval, so the specific surveillance schedule cannot be checked.
judged.quote: The added value of this paper is that it summarises in detail current clinical knowledge about HT1 and makes recommendations for the management.

rows.text: Oculocutaneous features (painful dendritic keratitis and hyperkeratosis of palms/soles) dominate the phenotype and respond fully to a tyrosine-restricted diet [1,2].

judged.citation: Chitayat D et al. Hereditary tyrosinaemia type II in a consanguineous Ashkenazi Jewish family: intrafamilial variation in phenotype; absence of parental phenotype effects on the fetus. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1992;15(2):198–203.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the oculocutaneous (Richner-Hanhart) phenotype in TAT deficiency but says nothing about response to a tyrosine-restricted diet, and in fact reports one affected sib without oculocutaneous disease.
judged.quote: because it is associated with the oculocutaneous manifestations of Richner-Hanhart syndrome

rows.text: Eyes: painful pseudo-dendritic keratitis (photophobia, tearing, redness) from early infancy — tyrosine crystals deposit in cornea; can cause corneal scarring if untreated [1,2].

judged.citation: Chitayat D et al. Hereditary tyrosinaemia type II in a consanguineous Ashkenazi Jewish family: intrafamilial variation in phenotype; absence of parental phenotype effects on the fetus. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1992;15(2):198–203.
judged.reason: The abstract records only generic "oculocutaneous signs" and gives no detail on pseudo-dendritic keratitis, infantile onset, corneal tyrosine crystals, or scarring.
judged.quote: The affected female sib (age 41 years) has hypertyrosinaemia and oculocutaneous signs

rows.text: Skin: painful hyperkeratosis of palms and soles (unique to TYR2 among tyrosinaemias) [6].

judged.citation: Macsai MS et al. Tyrosinemia type II: nine cases of ocular signs and symptoms. Am J Ophthalmol. 2001;132(4):522–7.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms cutaneous involvement in tyrosinemia type II but never specifies palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, its painful nature, or that it is unique among the tyrosinaemias.
judged.quote: Three patients presented with cutaneous manifestations, and one patient had mild mental impairment at the time of diagnosis.

rows.text: Tyrosine + phenylalanine-restricted diet — target plasma Tyr <500 µmol/L; eye and skin findings rapidly resolve [2].

judged.citation: Chitayat D et al. Hereditary tyrosinaemia type II in a consanguineous Ashkenazi Jewish family: intrafamilial variation in phenotype; absence of parental phenotype effects on the fetus. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1992;15(2):198–203.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns phenotypic variation and fetal risk and does not address dietary therapy or any plasma tyrosine treatment target.

rows.text: Excellent with early dietary management — eye and skin manifestations fully reversible, cognitive outcomes good if treated from infancy [1,2].

judged.citation: Chitayat D et al. Hereditary tyrosinaemia type II in a consanguineous Ashkenazi Jewish family: intrafamilial variation in phenotype; absence of parental phenotype effects on the fetus. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1992;15(2):198–203.
judged.reason: The abstract reports untreated adults with persistent hypertyrosinaemia and offers no data on reversibility of eye/skin findings or cognitive outcome with early dietary treatment.
judged.quote: two adults, offspring of consanguineous parents, have persistent hypertyrosinaemia (770-1110 mumol/L; normal less than 110 mumol/L)

rows.text: Variable phenotype, from asymptomatic to intellectual disability [1,2].

judged.citation: Ellaway CJ et al. Outcome of tyrosinaemia type III. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2001;24(8):824–32.
judged.reason: Abstract describes both asymptomatic screening-detected patients and patients with neurological symptoms, supporting a variable phenotype.
judged.quote: The majority of the nine previously reported patients have presented with neurological symptoms after the neonatal period, while others detected by neonatal screening have been asymptomatic.

rows.text: The pharmacological block produced by NTBC in TYR1 treatment is biochemically equivalent to TYR3 — which is why on-NTBC tyrosine levels must be controlled to prevent oculocutaneous toxicity [3].

judged.citation: Lindstedt S et al. Treatment of hereditary tyrosinaemia type I by inhibition of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase. Lancet. 1992;340(8823):813–7.
judged.reason: The abstract describes the NTBC-induced enzymatic block but never draws the biochemical equivalence to tyrosinaemia type III, nor mentions plasma tyrosine control or oculocutaneous toxicity — it explicitly reports no side-effects.
judged.quote: No side-effects were encountered.

rows.text: Urine: markedly elevated 4-OH-phenylpyruvate (4OHpp) + 4-OH-phenyllactate — out of proportion to the plasma tyrosine elevation, which is the biochemical clue [4].

judged.citation: Rüetschi U et al. Mutations in the 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase gene cause tyrosinemia type III. Hum Genet. 2000;106(6):654–62.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms increased excretion of tyrosine and phenolic metabolites in tyrosinemia III but does not name 4-OH-phenylpyruvate or 4-OH-phenyllactate specifically, nor state that their elevation is out of proportion to plasma tyrosine as a diagnostic clue.
judged.quote: The enzyme deficiency results in an accumulation and increased excretion of tyrosine and phenolic metabolites.

rows.text: HPD dominant mutations cause hawkinsinuria (different phenotype) [5].

judged.citation: Tomoeda K et al. Mutations in the 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid dioxygenase gene are responsible for tyrosinemia type III and hawkinsinuria. Mol Genet Metab. 2000;71(3):506–10.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies a heterozygous HPD missense mutation (A33T) in two hawkinsinuria patients and describes hawkinsinuria as an autosomal dominant disorder distinct from tyrosinemia type III.
judged.quote: A heterozygous missense mutation predicting an Ala to Thr change at codon 33 (A33T) was found in the same HPD gene in the two patients with hawkinsinuria.

rows.text: Variable phenotype [1,2]: some patients identified on NBS are entirely asymptomatic; others present with intellectual disability, seizures, ataxia.

judged.citation: Ellaway CJ et al. Outcome of tyrosinaemia type III. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2001;24(8):824–32.
judged.reason: Abstract supports the variable phenotype (asymptomatic on screening vs neurological symptoms) and absence of skin/eye and liver/renal abnormalities, but does not specify intellectual disability, seizures or ataxia.
judged.quote: All have had normal liver and renal function and none has skin or eye abnormalities.

rows.text: Tyrosine + phenylalanine-restricted diet in symptomatic cases [2].

judged.citation: Ellaway CJ et al. Outcome of tyrosinaemia type III. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2001;24(8):824–32.
judged.reason: Abstract mentions a low tyrosine diet with uncertain benefit but does not state phenylalanine restriction or restriction specifically for symptomatic cases.
judged.quote: It is not clear whether a strict low tyrosine diet alters the natural history of tyrosinaemia type III, although there remains a suspicion that treatment may be important, at least in infancy.

rows.text: Generally favourable; severity of neurological phenotype likely correlates with duration/magnitude of tyrosine elevation [1,2].

judged.citation: Ellaway CJ et al. Outcome of tyrosinaemia type III. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2001;24(8):824–32.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses outcome and hints treatment may matter in infancy, but does not state a generally favourable prognosis or a correlation between neurological severity and duration/magnitude of tyrosine elevation.
judged.quote: although there remains a suspicion that treatment may be important, at least in infancy

rows.text: Long-term, HGA polymerises into ochronotic pigment depositing in cartilage, heart valves and kidneys, causing a progressive arthropathy and cardiac valve disease in mid-adulthood [1,2].

judged.citation: Phornphutkul C et al. Natural history of alkaptonuria. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(26):2111–21.
judged.reason: Abstract states HGA accumulation, ochronosis and connective tissue destruction with joint replacement at mean age 55, renal stones at 64 and cardiac-valve involvement at 54 years, matching progressive arthropathy and valve disease in mid-adulthood.
judged.quote: Alkaptonuria, caused by mutations in the HGO gene and a deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, results in an accumulation of homogentisic acid (HGA), ochronosis, and destruction of connective tissue... Life-table analyses showed that joint replacement was performed at a mean age of 55 years and that renal stones developed at 64 years, cardiac-valve involvement at 54 years

judged.citation: Ranganath LR et al. Recent advances in management of alkaptonuria. J Clin Pathol. 2013;66(5):367–73.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms HGA oxidation to a melanin-like polymer (ochronosis) binding connective tissue with resulting spondyloarthropathy, renal damage and aortic valve disease, but gives no age of onset, so the "mid-adulthood" timing is not carried here (it rests on the natural-history paper).
judged.quote: Oxidative conversion of HGA leads to production of a melanin-like polymer in a process termed ochronosis. The binding of ochronotic pigment to the connective tissues of the body leads to multisystem disorder dominated by premature severe spondylo-arthropathy. Other systemic features include stones (renal, prostatic, salivary, gall bladder), renal damage/failure, osteopenia/fractures, ruptures of tendons/muscle/ligaments, respiratory compromise, hearing loss and aortic valve disease.

rows.text: Worldwide prevalence ~1:250,000, with clusters in Slovakia (~1:19,000) and the Dominican Republic due to founder variants [4].

judged.citation: Zatková A et al. High frequency of alkaptonuria in Slovakia: evidence for the appearance of multiple mutations in HGO involving different mutational hot spots. Am J Hum Genet. 2000;67(5):1333–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the ~1:250,000 worldwide prevalence and the Slovak cluster at 1:19,000, but it does not mention the Dominican Republic and explicitly argues against a classical founder effect in Slovakia, favoring an increased mutation rate at multiple hot spots.
judged.quote: AKU shows a very low prevalence (1:100,000-250,000) in most ethnic groups. One notable exception is in Slovakia, where the incidence of AKU rises to 1:19,000. This high incidence is difficult to explain by a classical founder effect

rows.text: The NTBC treatment paradigm developed for TYR1 has been extended to alkaptonuria with striking success [5].

judged.citation: Ranganath LR et al. Suitability of nitisinone in alkaptonuria 1 (SONIA 1). Ann Rheum Dis. 2016;75(2):362–7.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that nitisinone markedly lowers homogentisic acid in alkaptonuria (98.8% reduction, well tolerated), but it does not mention tyrosinaemia type 1 or that the paradigm was developed for TYR1, and shows only a 4-week biochemical rather than clinical outcome.
judged.quote: For the most efficacious dose, 8 mg daily, this corresponds to a mean reduction of u-HGA24 of 98.8% compared with baseline.

rows.text: Urine darkens to brown-black on alkalinisation or prolonged standing as HGA oxidises and polymerises [1,6].

judged.citation: Phornphutkul C et al. Natural history of alkaptonuria. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(26):2111–21.
judged.reason: The abstract quantifies urinary HGA excretion but never mentions urine darkening to brown-black on alkalinisation or standing, nor HGA oxidation/polymerisation in urine.
judged.quote: urinary HGA excretion fell from 2.9 to 0.13 g per day after a 10-day course of nitisinone

judged.citation: Fernandez-Cañón JM et al. The molecular basis of alkaptonuria. Nat Genet. 1996;14(1):19–24.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that accumulated homogentisic acid darkens the urine but says nothing about the brown-black colour developing on alkalinisation or prolonged standing via oxidation and polymerisation.
judged.quote: Affected individuals accumulate large quantities of homogentisic acid, an intermediary product of the catabolism of tyrosine and phenylalanine, which darkens the urine and deposits in connective tissues causing a debilitating arthritis.

rows.text: Urine darkening on standing (detectable from birth if observed) — often goes unnoticed [1].

judged.citation: Phornphutkul C et al. Natural history of alkaptonuria. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(26):2111–21.
judged.reason: Although the paper delineates the natural history, the abstract makes no mention of urine darkening on standing, detectability from birth, or its going unnoticed.
judged.quote: We performed a study to delineate the natural history of alkaptonuria.

rows.text: OCHRONOTIC ARTHROPATHY: progressive spondyloarthritis and hip/knee arthritis in the 4th–5th decade — the dominant clinical burden in adulthood, often leading to joint replacement [1,8].

judged.citation: Phornphutkul C et al. Natural history of alkaptonuria. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(26):2111–21.
judged.reason: Abstract documents radiographic spinal and joint damage worsening after age 30 with joint replacement at a mean age of 55, consistent with progressive arthropathy in the 4th–5th decade leading to joint replacement.
judged.quote: A radiographic scoring system was devised to assess the severity of spinal and joint damage... joint replacement was performed at a mean age of 55 years... the radiographic score for the severity of disease began increasing after the age of 30 years

judged.citation: Helliwell TR et al. Alkaptonuria — a review of surgical and autopsy pathology. Histopathology. 2008;53(5):503–12.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms advanced degenerative changes in synovial and intervertebral joints as the clinical burden (and reviews surgical pathology, implying joint failure surgery), but gives no age of onset such as the 4th–5th decade.
judged.quote: In symptomatic patients, degenerative changes in synovial and intervertebral joints are usually well advanced, while early changes include diffuse cartilage pigmentation and chondrocyte necrosis.

rows.text: Nitisinone (NTBC) 2 mg/day ADULT — inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (same enzyme as TYR1) and reduces HGA production by >90% [5,9].

judged.citation: Ranganath LR et al. Suitability of nitisinone in alkaptonuria 1 (SONIA 1). Ann Rheum Dis. 2016;75(2):362–7.
judged.reason: The abstract reports a dose-response study in which the 2 mg daily dose lowered adjusted geometric mean u-HGA24 to 1.44 mmol versus 31.53 mmol untreated (~95% reduction, >90% as claimed), though the enzymatic mechanism itself is not spelled out.
judged.quote: At 4"u2005weeks, the adjusted geometric mean u-HGA24 was 31.53 mmol, 3.26 mmol, 1.44 mmol, 0.57 mmol and 0.15"u2005mmol for the no treatment or 1 mg, 2 mg, 4 mg and 8"u2005mg doses, respectively.

judged.citation: Ranganath LR et al. Efficacy of nitisinone in alkaptonuria (SONIA 2). Mol Genet Metab. 2020;131(4):357–63.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a >90% reduction in HGA (99.7% decrease in urinary HGA) but uses a 10 mg daily dose rather than the claimed 2 mg/day and never states the 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase mechanism.
judged.quote: Patients aged 25 years or older with confirmed alkaptonuria and any clinical disease manifestations were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either oral nitisinone 10 mg daily or no treatment.

rows.text: SONIA 2 trial showed nitisinone significantly slows ochronosis and arthropathy progression [9].

judged.citation: Ranganath LR et al. Efficacy of nitisinone in alkaptonuria (SONIA 2). Mol Genet Metab. 2020;131(4):357–63.
judged.reason: The abstract reports SONIA 2 findings that nitisinone decreased ochronosis and significantly reduced the increase in clinical severity (cAKUSSI) score, indicating slower disease progression, though "arthropathy" is not named explicitly.
judged.quote: At 48 months, the increase in cAKUSSI score from baseline was significantly lower in the nitisinone group compared with the control group (adjusted mean difference -8·6 points [-16·0 to -1·2], p=0·023)... Nitisinone decreased ochronosis and improved clinical signs, indicating a slower disease progression.

rows.text: Without treatment: progressive disabling arthropathy from 4th–5th decade; aortic valve replacement may be needed [1,8].

judged.citation: Phornphutkul C et al. Natural history of alkaptonuria. N Engl J Med. 2002;347(26):2111–21.
judged.reason: Progressive arthropathy from the 4th–5th decade is supported, but the abstract reports only cardiac-valve involvement at a mean age of 54 years, not that aortic valve replacement may be needed.
judged.quote: joint replacement was performed at a mean age of 55 years and that renal stones developed at 64 years, cardiac-valve involvement at 54 years

judged.citation: Helliwell TR et al. Alkaptonuria — a review of surgical and autopsy pathology. Histopathology. 2008;53(5):503–12.
judged.reason: The abstract supports progressive joint degeneration and clinically significant aortic stenosis/valve failure (the indication for valve replacement) but does not state the 4th–5th decade timing or explicitly mention valve replacement.
judged.quote: Pigmentation of the aortic and mitral valve cusps and valve rings is a result of intracellular and extracellular pigment deposition and is associated with calcification and clinically significant aortic stenosis.

rows.text: Nitisinone: large reductions in HGA and measurable slowing of ochronosis/arthropathy in SONIA 2 [9].

judged.citation: Ranganath LR et al. Efficacy of nitisinone in alkaptonuria (SONIA 2). Mol Genet Metab. 2020;131(4):357–63.
judged.reason: The abstract documents a 99.7% reduction in urinary HGA excretion and significantly less progression in the clinical severity score with decreased ochronosis in SONIA 2.
judged.quote: u-HGA 24  at 12 months was significantly decreased by 99·7% in the nitisinone group compared with the control group

rows.text: GCS is a mitochondrial tetrameric complex (P-, T-, H- and L-proteins); defects in any subunit cause NKH [3].

judged.citation: Kure S et al. Molecular analysis of the glycine cleavage system in NKH. Hum Mutat. 2006;27(4):343–52.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms GCS is a multi-enzyme system whose deficiency causes NKH, but names only three components (GLDC, AMT, GCSH) rather than a mitochondrial tetramer including the L-protein, and it explicitly found no GCSH mutations, so "defects in any subunit" is not established here.
judged.quote: NKH is caused by deficiency of the glycine cleavage multi-enzyme system with three specific components encoded by GLDC, AMT, and GCSH.

rows.text: The CSF:plasma glycine ratio is THE diagnostic test — >0.08 confirms NKH (normal <0.04); values >0.25 correlate with severe phenotype [2,4].

judged.citation: Hoover-Fong JE et al. Natural history of nonketotic hyperglycinemia in 65 patients. Neurology. 2004;63(10):1847–53.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns natural history, mortality and development in NKH and never addresses CSF or plasma glycine measurement or any diagnostic ratio thresholds.

rows.text: The glycine/serine relationship is a CSF measure, not a plasma screen: in 61 genetically proven patients CSF serine was DECREASED and CSF threonine increased, so the CSF serine/threonine ratio separates patients from controls and the CSF glycine/serine ratio helps distinguish severe from attenuated disease in neonates — but after age-adjustment CSF glycine alone discriminated outcome classes best, and no validated plasma glycine/serine cutoff exists [5].

judged.citation: Swanson MA et al. Cerebrospinal fluid amino acids glycine, serine, and threonine in nonketotic hyperglycinemia. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(4):734–47.
judged.reason: The abstract states all the specific elements: 61 genetically proven patients, decreased CSF serine and increased threonine, serine/threonine ratio discriminating patients from controls, glycine/serine aiding severe vs attenuated neonatal discrimination, and CSF glycine alone best after age-adjustment; only the negative statement about plasma cutoffs is not addressed but is consistent with the CSF-only framing.
judged.quote: In addition to elevated CSF glycine, NKH patients had significantly decreased levels of CSF serine and increased levels of CSF threonine, even after age-adjustment. The CSF serine/threonine ratio discriminated between NKH patients and controls. The CSF glycine/serine aided in discrimination between severe and attenuated neonates with NKH. ... After age-adjustment, only the CSF glycine level provided good discrimination between outcome classes.

rows.text: GLDC (P-protein, 9p24.1) accounts for ~70% of cases; AMT (T-protein, 3p21.31) ~20%; GCSH (H-protein, 16q23.2) very rare [3,6].

judged.citation: Kure S et al. Molecular analysis of the glycine cleavage system in NKH. Hum Mutat. 2006;27(4):343–52.
judged.reason: The abstract's mutation counts (36 GLDC vs 11 AMT families, no GCSH mutations found) support the approximate ~70%/~20%/very rare distribution, but it gives no chromosomal loci (9p24.1, 3p21.31, 16q23.2) for the three genes.
judged.quote: GLDC mutations were identified in 36 families, and AMT mutations were detected in 11 families.

judged.citation: Coughlin CR et al. The genetic basis of classic non-ketotic hyperglycinemia. Genet Med. 2017;19(1):104–11.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms GLDC as the predominant gene with AMT second, but reports 80% (not ~70%) for GLDC, gives no AMT percentage, no GCSH data, and no chromosomal loci.
judged.quote: 80% of subjects had mutations in GLDC.

rows.text: Over 400 pathogenic variants reported; many are deep-intronic or copy-number, requiring MLPA or WGS [6].

judged.citation: Coughlin CR et al. The genetic basis of classic non-ketotic hyperglycinemia. Genet Med. 2017;19(1):104–11.
judged.reason: The abstract supports over 400 unique mutations and a large contribution from copy-number variants, but it does not mention deep-intronic variants or the specific requirement for MLPA or WGS (it refers only generically to sequencing and CNV analysis).
judged.quote: In 578 families, genetic analyses identified 410 unique mutations, including 246 novel mutations... Intragenic copy-number variations (CNVs) in GLDC were noted in 140 subjects, with biallelic CNVs present in 39 subjects.

rows.text: Atypical/attenuated NKH (10–20% of cases): later presentation with mild–moderate developmental delay, behavioural problems and variable seizures — these are the patients carrying hypomorphic GLDC variants that retain residual enzyme activity, which is why genotype has prognostic value here [9].

judged.citation: Bravo-Alonso I et al. Nonketotic hyperglycinemia: functional assessment of missense variants in GLDC to understand phenotypes of the disease. Hum Mutat. 2017;38(6):678–91.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that hypomorphic GLDC variants with residual activity underlie attenuated phenotypes and that genotype carries prognostic value, but it gives no 10–20% frequency figure and no clinical description of later presentation, developmental delay or behavioural problems.
judged.quote: We identify hypomorphic variants that produce attenuated phenotypes with improved prognosis of the disease. Structural analysis allows us to interpret the effects of mutations on protein stability and catalytic activity, providing molecular evidence for clinical outcome and disease severity.

rows.text: Sodium benzoate (250–750 mg/kg/day) conjugates glycine with benzoyl-CoA → hippurate (excreted) and reduces plasma glycine; CSF levels partially follow [7].

judged.citation: Bjoraker KJ et al. Neurodevelopmental outcome and treatment efficacy of benzoate and dextromethorphan in siblings with attenuated nonketotic hyperglycinemia. J Pediatr. 2016;170:234–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms benzoate dosing was titrated to normalize plasma glycine, but gives no mg/kg/day range, no benzoyl-CoA/hippurate mechanism, and says nothing about CSF glycine.
judged.quote: using dextromethorphan and benzoate at dosing sufficient to normalize plasma glycine levels

rows.text: In the original long-term series benzoate normalised plasma glycine but only partly lowered CSF glycine, and dextromethorphan was a potent anticonvulsant in some patients and not others, with marked interpatient variability in its metabolism — so dose response has to be judged individually rather than assumed [8].

judged.citation: Hamosh A et al. Long-term use of high-dose benzoate and dextromethorphan for the treatment of nonketotic hyperglycinemia. J Pediatr. 1998;132(4):709–13.
judged.reason: The abstract directly states benzoate normalized plasma glycine but only substantially (not fully) reduced CSF glycine, and that dextromethorphan was a potent anticonvulsant in some but not all patients with remarkable interpatient metabolic variability, supporting individualized dosing.
judged.quote: Benzoate reduced to normal the glycine concentration in plasma and substantially reduced but did not normalize the glycine concentration in cerebrospinal fluid. Dextromethorphan was a potent anticonvulsant in some but not all patients. There was remarkable interpatient variability in dextromethorphan metabolism.

rows.text: In four sibling pairs, the second child — diagnosed at birth and treated from the neonatal period at doses sufficient to normalise plasma glycine — reached more developmental milestones and had a higher developmental quotient than the older sibling treated late, and in three of the four pairs had no seizures at all where the first child had epilepsy [7].

judged.citation: Bjoraker KJ et al. Neurodevelopmental outcome and treatment efficacy of benzoate and dextromethorphan in siblings with attenuated nonketotic hyperglycinemia. J Pediatr. 2016;170:234–9.
judged.reason: The abstract reports exactly the four sibling-pair comparison, earlier/more milestones and higher developmental quotient in the neonatally treated sibling, and absence of seizures in 3 of 4 younger siblings.
judged.quote: In each sibling set, the second sibling treated from the neonatal period achieved earlier and more developmental milestones, and had a higher developmental quotient. In 3 of the 4 sibling pairs, the younger sibling had no seizures whereas the first child had a seizure disorder.

rows.text: Classic NKH: ~30% neonatal mortality; virtually all survivors have profound intellectual disability and intractable epilepsy [1,10].

judged.citation: Dinopoulos A et al. Atypical variants of nonketotic hyperglycinemia. Mol Genet Metab. 2005;86(1–2):61–9.
judged.reason: The abstract corroborates that classical NKH is characterized by uniform severe neurological symptoms (in contrast to atypical forms), but gives no neonatal mortality figure (~30%) and does not specify profound intellectual disability or intractable epilepsy in survivors.
judged.quote: Clinical symptoms in atypical nonketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH) are heterogeneous, in sharp contrast to uniform severe neurological symptoms in the classical NKH.

rows.text: The single best predictor of outcome is the CSF:plasma glycine ratio at diagnosis [4].

judged.citation: Hoover-Fong JE et al. Natural history of nonketotic hyperglycinemia in 65 patients. Neurology. 2004;63(10):1847–53.
judged.reason: The abstract does engage outcome prediction in NKH but attributes prognostic value to gender and corpus callosum/hydrocephalus abnormalities, with no mention of the CSF:plasma glycine ratio as the best predictor.
judged.quote: An abnormal corpus callosum and/or hydrocephalus were associated with especially poor gross motor and speech development.

rows.text: Once considered benign, there is now robust evidence of association with schizophrenia and with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome — the PRODH gene lies within the 22q11.2 deletion region, so del22q11 patients are haploinsufficient for PRODH [1,2].

judged.citation: Jacquet H et al. Hyperprolinemia is a risk factor for schizoaffective disorder. Mol Psychiatry. 2005;10(5):479–85.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms PRODH lies in the 22q11 DiGeorge region and links moderate hyperprolinemia to psychosis, but its positive finding is for schizoaffective disorder specifically (with no association found between PRODH polymorphisms and schizophrenia), so the claim's 'robust evidence of association with schizophrenia' and the haploinsufficiency statement are not directly carried.
judged.quote: we identified several heterozygous alterations, including a complete deletion, of the proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) gene, which were associated with moderate hyperprolinemia in a subset of DSM III schizophrenic patients

rows.text: Genetic studies have since linked PRODH haploinsufficiency (via 22q11.2 deletion) and hypomorphic variants to increased risk of schizophrenia, autism and intellectual disability [3,4].

judged.citation: Liu H et al. Genetic variation at the 22q11.2 PRODH locus deregulates translation in schizophrenia. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2002;99(6):3717–22.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a link between 22q11 microdeletions/PRODH (PRODH2) variants and schizophrenia susceptibility, but says nothing about autism or intellectual disability.
judged.quote: In three independent samples, we provide evidence for a contribution of the PRODH2/DGCR6 locus in 22q11-associated schizophrenia.

judged.citation: Afenjar A et al. Early neurological phenotype in 4 children with biallelic PRODH mutations. Brain Dev. 2007;29(9):547–52.
judged.reason: The abstract states that heterozygous and homozygous PRODH mutations occur in patients with schizophrenia, 22q11 microdeletions and neurological defects, and describes cognitive defects and autistic features in the biallelic cohort.
judged.quote: Heterozygous and homozygous mutations have been identified in patients with variable hyperprolinemia and various features (patients with schizophrenia, chromosome 22q11 microdeletions and/or neurological defects).

rows.text: Over 20 variants described; some hypomorphic variants (p.Leu441Pro, p.Arg453Cys) are common in schizophrenia cohorts [3,5]. 22q11.2 deletion patients have haploinsufficiency.

judged.citation: Liu H et al. Genetic variation at the 22q11.2 PRODH locus deregulates translation in schizophrenia. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2002;99(6):3717–22.
judged.reason: The abstract reports pseudogene-like missense variants at conserved residues that may impair enzyme function in schizophrenia samples, but gives neither a variant count (>20) nor the specific p.Leu441Pro/p.Arg453Cys changes.
judged.quote: Several of the pseudogene-like variants we identified result in missense changes at conserved residues and may prevent synthesis of a fully functional enzyme.

judged.citation: Bender HU et al. Functional consequences of PRODH missense mutations. Am J Hum Genet. 2005;76(3):409–20.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that L441P and R453C are hypomorphic (severe POX reduction) alleles associated with schizophrenia and that PRODH lies in the 22q11 deleted region with large deletions causing severe hyperprolinemia, but it reports "at least 16" missense mutations rather than the claim's "over 20 variants," and does not establish these alleles as common in schizophrenia cohorts.
judged.quote: At least 16 PRODH missense mutations have been identified in studies of type I hyperprolinemia (HPI) and schizophrenia

rows.text: Heterogeneous: from incidental biochemical finding to intellectual disability, seizures, psychiatric illness (schizophrenia) [3,4]. 22q11.2 deletion syndrome patients with PRODH variant on the remaining allele have more severe neuropsychiatric phenotype than those without.

judged.citation: Liu H et al. Genetic variation at the 22q11.2 PRODH locus deregulates translation in schizophrenia. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2002;99(6):3717–22.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the schizophrenia/psychiatric association with the 22q11 PRODH locus but does not address intellectual disability, seizures, incidental biochemical findings, or the claim that a PRODH variant on the remaining allele worsens the neuropsychiatric phenotype in deletion carriers.
judged.quote: Our results have implications for understanding the genetic basis of the 22q11-associated psychiatric phenotypes

judged.citation: Afenjar A et al. Early neurological phenotype in 4 children with biallelic PRODH mutations. Brain Dev. 2007;29(9):547–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the heterogeneous spectrum from asymptomatic to neurological/psychiatric involvement, but provides no comparison showing that 22q11.2 deletion patients with a PRODH variant on the remaining allele are more severely affected than those without.
judged.quote: whereas various patients were asymptomatic, others had neurological and extraneurological defects

rows.text: Isolated biochemical finding in many; in others, contributes to neuropsychiatric morbidity — particularly when combined with 22q11.2 deletion [3,4].

judged.citation: Liu H et al. Genetic variation at the 22q11.2 PRODH locus deregulates translation in schizophrenia. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2002;99(6):3717–22.
judged.reason: The abstract supports PRODH locus variation contributing to neuropsychiatric (schizophrenia) morbidity in the context of 22q11 deletion, but does not address the claim that it is an isolated benign biochemical finding in many patients.
judged.quote: approximately 20-30% of individuals with 22q11 microdeletions develop schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder in adolescence and adulthood

judged.citation: Afenjar A et al. Early neurological phenotype in 4 children with biallelic PRODH mutations. Brain Dev. 2007;29(9):547–52.
judged.reason: The abstract describes both asymptomatic patients and those with severe early neuropsychiatric features, including a case combining PRODH alteration with a 22q11 microdeletion.
judged.quote: Patients with biallelic PRODH alterations resulting in severely impaired POX activity had an early onset and severe neurological features.

rows.text: Early recognition and urea-scavenging therapy are life-saving [1,2].

rows.text: Acute: as for OTC — stop protein, high-calorie glucose, Ammonul® (sodium benzoate + phenylacetate) 250 mg/kg + continuous infusion, IV arginine 600 mg/kg (especially effective because it rescues urea-cycle flux around the block), haemodiafiltration if ammonia >250–500 µmol/L [10].

judged.reason: The abstract supports combined sodium phenylacetate/benzoate plus IV arginine hydrochloride, adequate calories and hemodialysis in urea-cycle disorders, but gives none of the specific doses (250 mg/kg, 600 mg/kg) or the ammonia threshold of 250–500 µmol/L for haemodiafiltration.
judged.quote: treatment with both sodium phenylacetate and sodium benzoate, in conjunction with other therapies, such as intravenous arginine hydrochloride and the provision of adequate calories to prevent catabolism, effectively lower plasma ammonium levels

rows.text: Chronic: moderate protein restriction 0.8–1.4 g/kg/day, L-arginine supplementation 200–400 mg/kg/day, sodium phenylbutyrate or glycerol phenylbutyrate for chronic scavenging [1,2].

judged.citation: Häberle J et al. Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2019;42(6):1192–230.

rows.text: Liver transplantation normalises biochemistry and prevents further crises [11,12].

judged.reason: The abstract concerns conservative long-term dietary/pharmacological management and survival, and never addresses liver transplantation or its biochemical effects.

rows.text: Common in East Asian populations [1,2].

rows.text: Citrin deficiency (OMIM #605814 NICCD; #603471 CTLN2) has an estimated carrier frequency of ~1:65 in Japanese, Chinese and Korean populations; clinical incidence ~1:17,000–1:34,000 in East Asia and much lower in Western populations [3,4].

judged.reason: The abstract establishes that citrin (SLC25A13) deficiency causes both NICCD in neonates and CTLN2 in adults, matching the sentence's framing of the two entities, but it gives no carrier frequency (~1:65) or clinical incidence figures (~1:17,000–1:34,000) and no comparison with Western populations.
judged.quote: We conclude that citrin deficiency causes NICCD in neonates and CTLN2 in adults through the additional effects of genetic or environmental modifiers.

judged.quote: 16 novel pathogenic mutations ... were identified in CTLN2 or NICCD patients from China, Japan and Malaysia, respectively

rows.text: Galactose elevated on NBS; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; elevated AFP [1,5].

judged.quote: Laboratory data showed elevated serum bile acid levels, hypoproteinemia, low levels of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors, and hypergalactosemia.

rows.text: CTLN2: strikingly elevated citrulline (often 100–300) with elevated Arg and Thr, recurrent hyperammonaemia during carbohydrate loading or alcohol [1,2].

rows.text: NICCD (neonatal): conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, hypoproteinaemia, coagulopathy — usually resolves spontaneously by 12 months with appropriate formula, though failure to thrive (FTTDCD) may persist [1,5].

rows.text: CTLN2 (second decade to adulthood): episodic hyperammonaemic encephalopathy typically precipitated by high-carbohydrate meals, alcohol, or glycerol infusions; characteristic aversion to sweets/carbohydrates and preference for protein/fats from childhood ('self-selected diet'); fatty liver, hypertriglyceridaemia; can progress to hepatocellular carcinoma if unrecognised [2,8].

judged.reason: The abstract supports adult-onset CTLN2 with hyperammonaemic encephalopathy and progression to hepatocellular carcinoma, but says nothing about carbohydrate/alcohol/glycerol precipitants, the self-selected diet, fatty liver, or hypertriglyceridaemia.
judged.quote: She was also found to have hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and underwent palliative surgery consisting of partial liver section of the HCC.

rows.text: NICCD: switch to lactose-free, MCT-supplemented formula; most resolve spontaneously [5].

rows.text: CTLN2: AVOID high-carbohydrate diet and infusions (including IV dextrose during acute episodes — paradoxically worsens encephalopathy); low-carbohydrate high-protein-fat diet (opposite of UCD dietary advice); sodium pyruvate or arginine supplementation; liver transplantation curative for severe/recurrent disease [1,9].

rows.text: The 'self-selected' protein-preference diet is protective and should NOT be corrected aggressively [2,8].

judged.quote: Twelve patients with argininosuccinate lyase deficiency were ascertained between 4 and 6 weeks of age by urine amino acid screening... Diagnosis was confirmed by enzyme assay in red blood cells and/or skin fibroblasts.

rows.text: ASL is uniquely non-redundant for both urea cycle AND arginine-citrulline NO-synthesis cycles in endothelium [4].

judged.reason: The abstract demonstrates that ASL is required for systemic NO production via both endogenous arginine synthesis and use of extracellular arginine, in addition to its urea-cycle catalytic role, supporting non-redundancy in both pathways.
judged.quote: Loss of Asl in both humans and mice leads to reduced NO synthesis, owing to both decreased endogenous arginine synthesis and an impaired ability to use extracellular arginine for NO production.

rows.text: OAT has dual metabolic roles depending on age: (1) neonatal — net flux synthesises ornithine from glutamate (P5CS→OAT), so deficiency causes low Orn/Cit/Arg and paradoxical hyperammonaemia; (2) after 3–6 months — flux reverses to ornithine catabolism, so deficiency causes hyperornithinaemia [6].

judged.quote: an autosomal recessive chorioretinal degeneration with a 10-20-fold elevation of plasma ornithine due to deficient activity of ornithine aminotransferase

rows.text: Creatine deficiency: high ornithine inhibits glycine transamidinase (GATM, first enzyme of creatine biosynthesis) — reduced brain and serum creatine; low serum creatinine is a useful clinical marker [7].

judged.quote: Hyperornithinemia-associated Cr deficiency in GA also affects the CNS, further supporting the possibility that Cr deficiency also has a pathogenetic role in the retina.

rows.text: Gyrate atrophy: nyctalopia from early childhood → progressive constriction of visual fields → tunnel vision → blindness typically by age 45–65 [1,9].

rows.text: Arginine-restricted diet to lower plasma ornithine (target <200 µmol/L) — slows chorioretinal progression [10].

judged.quote: Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI) is an inherited defect of cationic amino acid (lysine, arginine and ornithine) transport at the basolateral membrane of intestinal and renal tubular cells caused by mutations in SLC7A7 encoding the y(+)LAT1 protein.

rows.text: Prevalence ~1:60,000 in Finland (founder variant p.Leu334Arg) but much rarer elsewhere [4].

judged.citation: Torrents D et al. Identification of SLC7A7, encoding y+LAT-1, as the lysinuric protein intolerance gene. Nat Genet. 1999;21(3):293–6.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms high prevalence in Finland and a Finnish founder mutation, but gives no prevalence figure (~1:60,000) and does not name the variant p.Leu334Arg.
judged.quote: a rare, recessive disorder with a worldwide distribution, but with a high prevalence in the Finnish population

rows.text: Plasma lysine, arginine and ornithine LOW (often <50% of reference), whereas urinary excretion of these dibasic amino acids is HIGH (fractional excretion inappropriate for plasma level) — the classic pattern [1,2].

judged.citation: Ogier de Baulny H et al. Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI): a multi organ disease. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;106(1):12–7.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies the defective basolateral transport of lysine, arginine and ornithine in intestinal and renal tubular cells, which underlies the described pattern, but it never states low plasma levels, the "<50% of reference" threshold, or high urinary dibasic amino acid excretion/fractional excretion.
judged.quote: Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI) is an inherited defect of cationic amino acid (lysine, arginine and ornithine) transport at the basolateral membrane of intestinal and renal tubular cells caused by mutations in SLC7A7 encoding the y(+)LAT1 protein.

rows.text: SLC7A7 at 14q11.2 encodes y+LAT1, the light chain of a heterodimeric transporter with the heavy chain 4F2hc [5]. ~60 pathogenic variants reported.

judged.citation: Mykkänen J et al. Functional analysis of novel mutations in y+LAT-1. Hum Mol Genet. 2000;9(3):431–8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms SLC7A7 encodes y+LAT-1 which functions together with the 4F2 heavy chain, but it does not state the 14q11.2 locus and reports only 10 novel mutations in 20 patients, not a total of ~60 pathogenic variants.
judged.quote: LPI is caused by mutations in the SLC7A7 (solute carrier family 7, member 7) gene encoding y(+)LAT-1 (y(+)L amino acid transporter-1), which co-induces together with 4F2 heavy chain (4F2hc) system y(+)L in Xenopus oocytes.

rows.text: Finnish founder p.Leu334Arg (c.1001T>G) accounts for ~90% of Finnish alleles [4].

judged.citation: Torrents D et al. Identification of SLC7A7, encoding y+LAT-1, as the lysinuric protein intolerance gene. Nat Genet. 1999;21(3):293–6.
judged.reason: The abstract shows all 31 Finnish patients homozygous for a single founder mutation, consistent with a predominant Finnish allele, but neither the ~90% figure nor the specific designation p.Leu334Arg (c.1001T>G) appears.
judged.quote: The Finnish patients are homozygous for a founder missense mutation leading to a premature stop codon.

rows.text: Infantile: recurrent vomiting and feeding refusal after weaning (which increases protein load), failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, muscle hypotonia [1,6].

judged.citation: Tanner LM et al. Nutrient intake in 42 patients with lysinuric protein intolerance. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2007;30(5):716–21.
judged.reason: The abstract supports early-life protein aversion/feeding refusal and hyperammonaemia after normal protein loads, but says nothing about recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly or muscle hypotonia as infantile features.
judged.quote: As a protective mechanism, most patients develop strong aversion to protein-rich foods early in life.

rows.text: Childhood/adult multi-system complications: (1) Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis — progressive dyspnoea, can be fatal in early adulthood [7]; (2) Renal: proteinuria, chronic kidney disease; (3) Haematologic: pancytopenia, haemophagocytic syndrome; (4) Immune: abnormal lymphocyte function, increased infection susceptibility; (5) Osteoporosis from lysine deficiency; (6) Erythroblastophagocytic syndrome (MAS-like).

judged.citation: Parto K et al. Pulmonary manifestations in lysinuric protein intolerance. Chest. 1993;104(4):1176–82.
judged.reason: The abstract supports pulmonary alveolar proteinosis as a fatal pulmonary complication of LPI, but the deaths described occurred in children rather than early adulthood, and the renal, haematologic, immune, bone and erythroblastophagocytic components of the sentence are not addressed.
judged.quote: During the follow-up period, four children with LPI died in respiratory insufficiency... At autopsy, three patients showed pulmonary alveolar proteinosis and one had pulmonary hemorrhage and cholesterol granulomas.

rows.text: Moderate protein restriction + oral L-citrulline supplementation (3–8 g/day) — citrulline is neutral (absorbed via separate transporter) and generates arginine + ornithine intracellularly [1,2].

judged.citation: Ogier de Baulny H et al. Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI): a multi organ disease. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;106(1):12–7.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms treatment with a low-protein diet plus L-citrulline supplementation but gives no 3–8 g/day dose (indeed it advises lowering citrulline dosage) and does not mention citrulline's neutral amino acid transport or intracellular conversion to arginine and ornithine.
judged.quote: when appropriately treated with low-protein diet and l-citrulline supplementation

rows.text: Adequate citrulline + protein restriction largely prevents hyperammonaemic crises, but the multi-system phenotype (lungs, kidneys, bone, immune) progresses regardless of ammonia control [8].

judged.citation: Mauhin W et al. Update on lysinuric protein intolerance, a multi-faceted disease: retrospective cohort analysis from birth to adulthood. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):3.
judged.reason: The abstract supports progressive multi-system involvement (lung, kidney, immune/HLH, pancreas, cardiovascular) during long-term follow-up, but it does not state that citrulline plus protein restriction largely prevents hyperammonaemic crises (indeed 5 patients had acute hyperammonaemia on follow-up), nor does it address bone disease or independence from ammonia control.
judged.quote: Kidney disease was observed in all patients: tubulopathy (11/11), proteinuria (4/16) and kidney failure (7/16), which was more common in older patients

rows.text: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is the leading cause of death in young adults with LPI [7].

judged.citation: Parto K et al. Pulmonary manifestations in lysinuric protein intolerance. Chest. 1993;104(4):1176–82.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms fatal respiratory insufficiency with alveolar proteinosis in LPI, but the fatalities were in children while adults mostly had only radiologic signs, and no comparison establishing it as the leading cause of death in young adults is given.
judged.quote: During the follow-up period, four children with LPI died in respiratory insufficiency, 1 adult had an episode of respiratory insufficiency... Most adult LPI patients show radiologic signs of interstitial lung disease but only a few show clinical impairment.

rows.text: Triple therapy (creatine + ornithine + arginine restriction) is highly effective and GAMT was added to the RUSP in the US in 2023 [1,2].

judged.citation: Stockler-Ipsiroglu S et al. Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency: outcomes in 48 individuals. Mol Genet Metab. 2014;111(1):16–25.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the efficacy of combined creatine, l-ornithine and arginine restriction, but says nothing about GAMT being added to the US RUSP in 2023.
judged.quote: Increase of cerebral creatine and decrease of plasma/CSF guanidinoacetate levels were achieved by supplementation with creatine-monohydrate combined with high dosages of l-ornithine and/or an arginine-restricted diet (250 mg/kg/d l-arginine). Therapy was associated with improvement or stabilization of symptoms in all of the symptomatic cases.

rows.text: GAMT deficiency (OMIM #612736) was the first cerebral creatine deficiency to be described (Stöckler 1994) [3].

judged.citation: Stöckler S et al. Creatine deficiency in the brain: a new, treatable inborn error of metabolism. Pediatr Res. 1994;36(3):409–13.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly reports the first patient with complete cerebral creatine deficiency, attributed to guanidinoacetate methyltransferase defect, published 1994.
judged.quote: This is the first report of a patient with complete creatine deficiency in the brain. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy during arginine and creatine treatment point to an inborn error of creatine biosynthesis at the level of guanidinoacetete-methyltransferase.

rows.text: Plasma and urine GAA markedly elevated (often 5–30× ULN) — the pathognomonic marker [1,5].

judged.citation: Hanna-El-Daher L, Braissant O. Creatine synthesis and exchanges between brain cells. Amino Acids. 2016;48(8):1877–95.
judged.reason: The abstract implies guanidinoacetate accumulation in GAMT deficiency and reviews biochemical characteristics of creatine-deficient patients, but it gives no plasma/urine GAA values, no 5–30× ULN magnitude, and does not call GAA pathognomonic.
judged.quote: This review also addresses the question of guanidinoacetate toxicity for brain cells, as probably found under GAMT deficiency.

rows.text: Brain MR spectroscopy shows ABSENT creatine peak — visually striking and diagnostic [6].

judged.citation: Stöckler S et al. Creatine deficiency in the brain: a new, treatable inborn error of metabolism. Pediatr Res. 1994;36(3):409–13.
judged.reason: The abstract reports in vivo proton MRS showing generalized brain creatine depletion (complete creatine deficiency) with no detectable creatine-phosphate, which pointed to a defect at guanidinoacetate methyltransferase.
judged.quote: in vivo proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy disclosed a generalized depletion of creatinine in the brain ... This is the first report of a patient with complete creatine deficiency in the brain. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy during arginine and creatine treatment point to an inborn error of creatine biosynthesis at the level of guanidinoacetete-methyltransferase.

rows.text: Over 60 pathogenic variants; c.327G>A (splice variant) common in Portuguese population, p.Trp20Ser in Arab populations [8].

judged.citation: Almeida LS et al. Creatine deficiency syndromes: molecular characterization. Mol Genet Metab. 2004;82(3):214–9.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns biochemical diagnostic markers (GAA and creatine measurement) in GAMT and SLC6A8 deficiency and contains no mutation counts or specific variants such as c.327G>A or p.Trp20Ser despite involving GAMT-deficient patients.
judged.quote: Eight guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficient patients and eight creatine transporter SLC6A8 deficient patients were investigated.

rows.text: Infantile onset (most): global developmental delay recognised 6–12 months, progressive to severe intellectual disability with little-to-no speech, autistic features, hypotonia progressing to spasticity, drug-resistant epilepsy (often myoclonic), movement disorder [1,2].

judged.citation: Stockler-Ipsiroglu S et al. Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency: outcomes in 48 individuals. Mol Genet Metab. 2014;111(1):16–25.
judged.reason: The abstract supports global developmental delay/intellectual disability with speech delay, behavioral problems, epilepsy and movement disorder, but does not state onset at 6–12 months, autistic features, hypotonia progressing to spasticity, or that epilepsy is drug-resistant/myoclonic.
judged.quote: Global developmental delay/intellectual disability (DD/ID) with speech/language delay and behavioral problems as the most affected domains was present in 44 participants, with additional epilepsy present in 35 and movement disorder in 13.

rows.text: Triple therapy: (1) Creatine monohydrate 400–800 mg/kg/day (3–6 divided doses) — replaces missing brain creatine; (2) L-ornithine 400–800 mg/kg/day (3–6 divided doses) — feedback-inhibits GATM, reducing GAA production; (3) Arginine-restricted diet, typically targeting 15–25 mg/kg/day arginine intake — reduces GATM substrate, further lowers GAA [1,2,9].

judged.citation: Stockler-Ipsiroglu S et al. Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency: outcomes in 48 individuals. Mol Genet Metab. 2014;111(1):16–25.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the triple-therapy combination of creatine monohydrate, high-dose L-ornithine and arginine restriction, but gives none of the claimed mg/kg/day ranges for creatine or ornithine and cites an arginine figure (250 mg/kg/d) rather than the claimed 15–25 mg/kg/day target.
judged.quote: Increase of cerebral creatine and decrease of plasma/CSF guanidinoacetate levels were achieved by supplementation with creatine-monohydrate combined with high dosages of l-ornithine and/or an arginine-restricted diet (250 mg/kg/d l-arginine).

judged.citation: Schulze A. Creatine deficiency syndromes. Mol Cell Biochem. 2003;244(1–2):143–50.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the three treatment components (oral creatine, ornithine substitution, arginine restriction) and their rationale of lowering GAA, but gives no dosing figures such as 400–800 mg/kg/day or the 15–25 mg/kg/day arginine target.
judged.quote: Treatment with oral creatine supplementation is in part successful in GAMT and AGAT deficiency... Treatment of combined arginine restriction and ornithine substitution in GAMT deficiency is capable to decrease guanidinoacetic acid permanently and improves the clinical outcome.

rows.text: Early-treated (presymptomatic) patients have near-normal developmental outcomes — this is one of the great justifications for GAMT NBS [4,10].

judged.citation: El-Gharbawy AH et al. Elevation of guanidinoacetate before measurable symptoms in GAMT. Mol Genet Metab. 2013;109(2):215–7.
judged.reason: The abstract reports a patient treated from birth with normal developmental outcome and states early treatment appears to improve outcomes, making GAMT a good newborn screening candidate.
judged.quote: GAMT) deficiency is a good candidate disorder for newborn screening because early treatment appears to improve outcomes. ... We also report a new case of a patient treated from birth with normal developmental outcome at the age of 42 months.

rows.text: Established brain injury: partial response — seizures and movement disorders often improve, but cognitive gains are limited once injury has occurred [10].

judged.citation: El-Gharbawy AH et al. Elevation of guanidinoacetate before measurable symptoms in GAMT. Mol Genet Metab. 2013;109(2):215–7.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses treatment outcomes in GAMT but says nothing about partial response in patients with established brain injury, seizure/movement improvement, or limited cognitive gains.
judged.quote: early treatment appears to improve outcomes

rows.text: The phenotype is milder than GAMT deficiency and responds excellently to oral creatine supplementation alone [1,2].

judged.citation: Sykut-Cegielska J, Stockler-Ipsiroglu S et al. Biochemical and clinical characteristics of creatine deficiency syndromes. Acta Biochim Pol. 2004;51(4):875–82.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms AGAT deficiency is treatable by oral creatine supplementation but never states that the phenotype is milder than GAMT deficiency.
judged.quote: GAMT and AGAT deficiency are treatable by oral creatine supplementation, while patients with CRTR deficiency do not respond to this type of treatment.

rows.text: GATM deficiency (OMIM #612718) was described in 2001 by Item et al. [3].

judged.citation: Item CB et al. Arginine:glycine amidinotransferase deficiency. Am J Hum Genet. 2001;69(5):1127–33.
judged.reason: This 2001 paper by Item et al. reports AGAT (GATM) deficiency as a newly identified genetic defect of creatine metabolism, matching the claim of first description in 2001.
judged.quote: AGAT deficiency was identified as a new genetic defect in creatine metabolism

rows.text: Absent brain creatine on MR spectroscopy (same as GAMT and SLC6A8) [4].

judged.citation: Battini R et al. Arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) deficiency in a newborn. Mol Genet Metab. 2006;77(4):326–31.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns early diagnosis and creatine treatment outcome in an AGAT-deficient newborn and never addresses MR spectroscopy or brain creatine levels, so the imaging claim cannot be assessed from it.
judged.quote: We describe a patient in whom arginine:glycine amidinotransferase was diagnosed at birth and treated at 4 months with creatine supplementation.

rows.text: Plasma and urinary GAA LOW — the key distinguisher from GAMT [1,2].

judged.citation: Sykut-Cegielska J, Stockler-Ipsiroglu S et al. Biochemical and clinical characteristics of creatine deficiency syndromes. Acta Biochim Pol. 2004;51(4):875–82.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly contrasts low guanidinoacetate in AGAT deficiency with high concentration in GAMT deficiency as the discriminating measurement.
judged.quote: Measurement of guanidinoacetate in body fluids may discriminate between the GAMT (high concentration), AGAT (low concentration) and CRTR (normal concentration) deficiencies.

rows.text: The pathogenic dominant-negative GATM variants that cause a different (adult-onset renal Fanconi) syndrome are not implicated in the creatine-deficient phenotype [6].

judged.citation: Reichold M et al. Glycine amidinotransferase variants causing dominant renal Fanconi syndrome. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2018;29(7):1849–58.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that monoallelic/dominant GATM missense mutations cause a distinct renal Fanconi syndrome via a gain-of-function aggregation mechanism, separate from the recessive creatine deficiency disorder, but it does not state the age of onset ("adult-onset") nor explicitly document that these patients lack the creatine-deficient phenotype.
judged.quote: The renal disease in these patients resulted from monoallelic mutations in the gene encoding glycine amidinotransferase (GATM), a renal proximal tubular enzyme in the creatine biosynthetic pathway that is otherwise associated with a recessive disorder of creatine deficiency.

rows.text: Mild-moderate intellectual disability (less severe than GAMT), delayed speech, mild hypotonia, sometimes autistic features, occasional myopathy [1,2].

judged.citation: Sykut-Cegielska J, Stockler-Ipsiroglu S et al. Biochemical and clinical characteristics of creatine deficiency syndromes. Acta Biochim Pol. 2004;51(4):875–82.
judged.reason: The abstract supports intellectual disability/mental retardation and speech delay as features of creatine deficiency syndromes generally, but does not state that AGAT is less severe than GAMT nor mention hypotonia, autistic features, or myopathy.
judged.quote: The common clinical feature of creatine deficiency syndromes is mental retardation and epilepsy suggesting main involvement of cerebral gray matter.

rows.text: Oral creatine monohydrate 400–800 mg/kg/day (3–6 divided doses) — alone is highly effective because there is no neurotoxic GAA to suppress (unlike GAMT which needs the triple regimen) [1,2,7].

judged.citation: Sykut-Cegielska J, Stockler-Ipsiroglu S et al. Biochemical and clinical characteristics of creatine deficiency syndromes. Acta Biochim Pol. 2004;51(4):875–82.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms oral creatine supplementation treats AGAT deficiency but gives no dose (400–800 mg/kg/day), dosing frequency, or rationale about absent neurotoxic GAA.
judged.quote: GAMT and AGAT deficiency are treatable by oral creatine supplementation

rows.text: Brain cells cannot import creatine despite normal plasma synthesis; unlike GAMT and GATM, oral creatine supplementation is largely ineffective because the transporter needed to import it is the defective protein [1,2].

judged.citation: van de Kamp JM et al. X-linked creatine transporter deficiency: clinical aspects and pathophysiology. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(5):715–33.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms cerebral creatine deficiency in transporter deficiency and that no treatment has proven effective, but it does not state the contrast with GAMT/GATM where oral creatine works, nor normal plasma/peripheral creatine synthesis.
judged.quote: Over the past years several treatment options have been explored but no treatment has been proven effective.

rows.text: Creatine transporter deficiency (OMIM #300352) was described by Salomons in 2001 [3].

judged.citation: Salomons GS et al. X-linked creatine-transporter gene (SLC6A8) defect: a new creatine-deficiency syndrome. Am J Hum Genet. 2001;68(6):1497–500.
judged.reason: The 2001 Salomons paper reports the first X-linked creatine transporter deficiency, matching the claim of first description by Salomons in 2001 (OMIM number not stated but is a database identifier).
judged.quote: We report the first X-linked creatine-deficiency syndrome caused by a defective creatine transporter.

rows.text: Prevalence in unexplained X-linked intellectual disability ~2%, making it among the most common X-linked ID syndromes after fragile X [4].

judged.citation: Clark AJ et al. X-linked creatine transporter (SLC6A8) mutations in individuals with nonsyndromic X-linked intellectual disability. Hum Genet. 2006;119(6):604–10.
judged.reason: The abstract engages the prevalence question in males with ID of unknown cause but reports about 1%, not ~2%, and says nothing about ranking among X-linked ID syndromes relative to fragile X.
judged.quote: Our findings of a minimum of four pathogenic mutations and two potentially pathogenic mutations indicate that about 1% of males with MR of unknown etiology might have a SLC6A8 mutation.

rows.text: Elevated URINE creatine:creatinine ratio is the diagnostic biochemical finding (creatine not reabsorbed by renal tubular transporter of same family) — can be used as a screening test [1,5].

judged.citation: Arias A et al. Guanidinoacetate and creatine/creatinine levels in controls and patients with urea cycle defects. Mol Genet Metab. 2004;82(3):220–3.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns GC-MS methodology, age-related reference values for urinary guanidinoacetate and creatine/creatinine, and low guanidinoacetate in urea cycle defects; it does not address creatine transporter deficiency, an elevated urine creatine:creatinine ratio as a diagnostic/screening finding, or renal tubular creatine reabsorption.
judged.quote: We determined the reference values in urine and plasma. In urine both guanidinoacetate concentration and creatine/creatinine ratio decrease as age increases, but no significant differences were found in plasma.

rows.text: Brain MR spectroscopy: ABSENT creatine peak despite normal plasma creatine — a striking finding and essentially diagnostic in a male with intellectual disability [6].

judged.citation: Bianchi MC et al. Reversible brain creatine deficiency in two sisters with normal blood creatine level. Ann Neurol. 2000;47(4):511–3.
judged.reason: The abstract supports brain creatine depletion detected by in vivo proton MRS with normal blood examination, but it describes two female siblings with a reversible, creatine-responsive depletion (not an absent peak that is 'essentially diagnostic in a male with intellectual disability'), so the specifying part of the claim is not carried.
judged.quote: Diagnosis was established only by means of in vivo proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which disclosed generalized depletion of creatine in the brain.

rows.text: Over 100 pathogenic variants. 0.5–3% of males with intellectual disability of unknown cause [4,8].

judged.citation: Clark AJ et al. X-linked creatine transporter (SLC6A8) mutations in individuals with nonsyndromic X-linked intellectual disability. Hum Genet. 2006;119(6):604–10.
judged.reason: The abstract's ~1% estimate falls within the stated 0.5–3% range, but it reports only six novel variants and provides no support for the claim of over 100 pathogenic variants.
judged.quote: indicate that about 1% of males with MR of unknown etiology might have a SLC6A8 mutation

judged.citation: Rosenberg EH et al. High prevalence of SLC6A8 deficiency in X-linked mental retardation. Am J Hum Genet. 2004;75(1):97–105.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the prevalence figure in males with nonsyndromic intellectual disability (at least 2.1%, within the 0.5–3% range) but says nothing about over 100 pathogenic variants, reporting only six mutations.
