judged.quote: Six pathogenic mutations, of which five were novel, were identified in a total of 288 patients with XLMR, showing a prevalence of at least 2.1% (6/288).

rows.text: Affected males: moderate-severe intellectual disability, absent/minimal expressive speech, autistic features, seizures (commonly febrile + subsequent complex partial), hyperactivity, hypotonia evolving to spasticity [1,2,4].

judged.citation: van de Kamp JM et al. X-linked creatine transporter deficiency: clinical aspects and pathophysiology. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(5):715–33.
judged.reason: The abstract supports intellectual disability as the core phenotype and notes relative sparing of muscle, but none of the specific features (absent speech, autistic features, febrile then complex partial seizures, hyperactivity, hypotonia to spasticity) appear in this review abstract.
judged.quote: Creatine transporter deficiency was discovered in 2001 as an X-linked cause of intellectual disability characterized by cerebral creatine deficiency.

judged.citation: Clark AJ et al. X-linked creatine transporter (SLC6A8) mutations in individuals with nonsyndromic X-linked intellectual disability. Hum Genet. 2006;119(6):604–10.
judged.reason: The abstract is a mutation-frequency screening study reporting SLC6A8 mutation prevalence in males with intellectual disability and does not describe the clinical phenotype features (speech, autistic features, seizures, hypotonia/spasticity) asserted in the claim.
judged.quote: Our findings of a minimum of four pathogenic mutations and two potentially pathogenic mutations indicate that about 1% of males with MR of unknown etiology might have a SLC6A8 mutation.

rows.text: Limited efficacy — the transporter required to import creatine into brain is the defective protein [1,2].

judged.citation: van de Kamp JM et al. X-linked creatine transporter deficiency: clinical aspects and pathophysiology. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(5):715–33.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly reports that despite exploration of several treatment options none has proven effective in this transporter-defect disorder.
judged.quote: Over the past years several treatment options have been explored but no treatment has been proven effective.

rows.text: Cyclocreatine and gene therapy in development [9,10].

judged.citation: Kurosawa Y et al. Cyclocreatine treatment improves cognition in mice with creatine transporter deficiency. J Clin Invest. 2012;122(8):2837–46.
judged.reason: The abstract reports preclinical cyclocreatine treatment improving cognition in a CRT-deficient mouse model and calls it a promising potential therapy, supporting the cyclocreatine-in-development portion of the sentence (gene therapy is carried by the other citation).
judged.quote: Thus, cyclocreatine appears promising as a potential therapy for CRT deficiency.

rows.text: Despite NBS detection and optimal management, long-term outcomes remain significantly compromised [1,2].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract supports persistently poor long-term outcome despite apparently effective therapy, but says nothing about newborn-screening detection (it instead cites delayed diagnosis and under-recognition as contributors).
judged.quote: Except for vitamin B12 responsive forms of MMA the outcome remains poor despite the existence of apparently effective therapy with a low protein diet and carnitine.

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic acidaemia and propionic acidaemia: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: The abstract is a purely structural guideline summary describing methodology and recommendation counts; it says nothing about newborn screening detection or long-term outcomes.
judged.quote: As a result, 21 updated recommendations were compiled in a more concise paper with a focus on the existing evidence to enable well-informed decisions in the context of MMA and PA patient care.

rows.text: Incidence is ~1:100,000 worldwide but much higher where founder variants exist: a founder allele makes PA strikingly common among the Inuit of Greenland [4], and in the Saudi national newborn-screening programme PA is the commonest inborn error detected, at 1:14,000 [5].

judged.citation: Ravn K et al. High incidence of propionic acidemia in Greenland Inuit. Hum Genet. 2000;107(5):455–8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms PA is highly prevalent among Greenland Inuit due to a likely founder mutation, which is the portion of the sentence cited to this paper (the ~1:100,000 and Saudi 1:14,000 figures come from the other citation).
judged.quote: Surprisingly, PA is highly prevalent among Inuits in Greenland.

judged.citation: Alfadhel M et al. Expanded Newborn Screening Program in Saudi Arabia: incidence of screened disorders. J Paediatr Child Health. 2017;53(6):585–91.
judged.reason: The abstract directly states that propionic acidaemia had the highest incidence among inborn errors in the Saudi national newborn screening programme at 1:14,000, which is the portion of the sentence this paper is cited for.
judged.quote: The highest incidence among the IEM was propionic acidaemia with an incidence rate of 1:14/! oud...

rows.text: PCC converts propionyl-CoA (derived from ~50% of propionate from intestinal flora, and from catabolism of Ile, Val, Met, Thr, cholesterol side chain and odd-chain fatty acids) to D-methylmalonyl-CoA [1].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms PA arises from propionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency with propionic acid accumulation, but says nothing about the conversion product D-methylmalonyl-CoA or the precursor sources (~50% gut flora, Ile/Val/Met/Thr, cholesterol side chain, odd-chain fatty acids).
judged.quote: characterized by accumulation of propionic acid and/or methylmalonic acid due to deficiency of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MUT) or propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC)

rows.text: Block produces: elevated plasma C3 (propionylcarnitine), C3/C2 and C3/(C16+C18) ratios [6]; elevated urinary methylcitric acid (MCA), 3-hydroxypropionate, propionylglycine and tiglylglycine; and secondary hyperglycinaemia due to C3-CoA inhibition of the glycine cleavage system [1,7].

judged.citation: Rinaldo P et al. Sudden and unexpected neonatal death: a protocol for the postmortem diagnosis of fatty acid oxidation disorders. Semin Perinatol. 1999;23(2):204–10.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns postmortem diagnosis of fatty acid oxidation disorders and says nothing about propionic acidemia markers such as C3, C3/C2 ratios, methylcitrate or hyperglycinaemia.
judged.quote: Bile carnitine analysis and acylcarnitine profiling have expanded significantly the effectiveness of the initial protocol

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The guideline abstract only notes accumulation of propionic/methylmalonic acid and does not address acylcarnitine markers, urinary organic acid profiles or secondary hyperglycinaemia.

judged.citation: Hayasaka K et al. Glycine cleavage system in PA. Pediatr Res. 1982;16(3):220–4.
judged.reason: The abstract directly demonstrates that propionyl-CoA (and related CoA esters) inhibit the glycine cleavage system, which is the clause this paper is cited for; the urinary/plasma marker details are carried by the co-cited references.
judged.quote: It was found that CoA derivatives including tiglyl CoA, isobutyryl CoA, succinyl CoA, methylmalonyl CoA, isovaleryl CoA, propionyl CoA and CoA itself and cysteamine significantly inhibited the glycine cleavage system of the liver extracts.

rows.text: On newborn screening, multivariate post-analytical scoring of the whole marker pattern (CLIR) followed by a second-tier test measuring homocysteine, methylmalonic acid and methylcitric acid reduces the false-positive rate for the propionate disorders to below 0.01% — far better than manipulating single-analyte cutoffs [8].

judged.citation: Gavrilov DK et al. The combined impact of CLIR post-analytical tools and second tier testing on the performance of newborn screening for disorders of propionate, methionine, and cobalamin metabolism. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2020;6(2):33.
judged.reason: The abstract describes exactly this three-step algorithm for propionate/methionine/cobalamin disorders and states it reduces false positives to <0.01%, presented as an alternative to cutoff manipulation.
judged.quote: As an alternative to subjective manipulation of cutoff values and overutilization of molecular testing, here we describe the performance outcome of an algorithm for disorders of methionine, cobalamin, and propionate metabolism ... further evaluation of abnormal scores by a second tier test measuring homocysteine, methylmalonic acid, and methylcitric acid. This approach can consistently reduce false positive rates to a <0.01% level

rows.text: MCA is markedly more elevated in PA than in MMA, providing biochemical separation [1].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract makes no mention of methylcitric acid or its comparative levels in PA versus MMA.

rows.text: It can now be quantified rather than merely reported as present — in dried urine spots the control range is 0.4–3.4 mmol/mol creatinine against 8.3–591 in affected patients [9].

judged.citation: Al Dhahouri N et al. Quantification of methylcitrate in dried urine spots by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry for the diagnosis of propionic and methylmalonic acidemias. Clin Chim Acta. 2018;487:41–5.
judged.reason: The abstract gives exactly the control reference interval and patient range for methylcitrate in dried urine spots and frames the method as providing quantification where previously it was measured without quantification.
judged.quote: In controls (n = 135), methylcitrate reference interval of 0.4-3.4 mmol/mol creatinine. In patients, methylcitrate ranged between 8.3 and 591 mmol/mol creatinine.

rows.text: PCCA (13q32.3) encodes the biotin-binding α-subunit; PCCB (3q22.3) encodes the β-subunit [10].

judged.citation: Ugarte M et al. Overview of mutations in the PCCA and PCCB genes causing propionic acidemia. Hum Mutat. 1999;14(4):275–82.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms PCCA encodes the alpha subunit and PCCB the beta subunit, but gives neither the chromosomal loci (13q32.3, 3q22.3) nor the biotin-binding property of the α-subunit.
judged.quote: The enzyme is composed of alpha and beta subunits which are encoded by the PCCA and PCCB genes, respectively.

rows.text: The Inuit founder variant is PCCA c.1540+1G>A [4].

judged.citation: Ravn K et al. High incidence of propionic acidemia in Greenland Inuit. Hum Genet. 2000;107(5):455–8.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies the Inuit founder variant as a 3-bp insertion, 1540insCCC, in PCCB (beta-subunit), not a splice-site variant c.1540+1G>A in PCCA, so the claim's gene and variant are contradicted.
judged.quote: A 3-bp insertion, 1540insCCC, was found in homozygous form in three patients and in compound heterozygous form in one patient.

rows.text: A founder effect also underlies the high Saudi incidence [5].

judged.citation: Alfadhel M et al. Expanded Newborn Screening Program in Saudi Arabia: incidence of screened disorders. J Paediatr Child Health. 2017;53(6):585–91.
judged.reason: The abstract documents a high Saudi incidence of propionic acidaemia (1:14 000) but says nothing about a founder effect or founder variant underlying it.
judged.quote: The highest incidence among the IEM was propionic acidaemia with an incidence rate of 1:14\u2009000.

rows.text: Genotype does NOT reliably predict phenotype — the same genotype produces classic neonatal and late-onset cases in different individuals [11].

judged.citation: Pérez-Cerdá C et al. Potential relationship between genotype and clinical outcome in PA patients. Hum Genet. 2000;107(4):378–84.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the idea that genotype alone does not determine phenotype (other genetic/environmental factors contribute to variability), but it reports a 'good correlation' between null mutations and severe phenotype and never states that the same genotype produces both classic neonatal and late-onset presentations in different individuals.
judged.quote: we have found a good correlation between certain mutations which can be considered as null with a severe phenotype, while certain missense mutations tend to be related to the late and mild forms of the disease. Expression studies, particularly of the missense mutations identified are necessary but other genetic and environmental factors probably contribute to the phenotypic variability observed in PA.

rows.text: Acute neonatal (most common): days 1–7 of life, lethargy progressing to coma, vomiting, severe acidosis, hyperammonaemia, seizures, pancytopenia — mortality ~25% at first crisis [1,12].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract supports an acute neonatal presentation with acidosis and hyperammonaemia leading to early death, but gives no day 1–7 window, no seizures/pancytopenia, and no ~25% mortality figure for the first crisis.
judged.quote: Patients present either shortly after birth with acute deterioration, metabolic acidosis and hyperammonemia or later at any age with a more heterogeneous clinical picture, leading to early death or to severe neurological handicap in many survivors.

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. Propionic acidemia: clinical course and outcome in 55 pediatric and adolescent patients. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:6.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms neonatal metabolic decompensation as the dominant presentation and hematologic complications, but gives no mortality figure (~25%) at first crisis or the specific day 1–7 symptom details.
judged.quote: The vast majority of patients (>85%) presented with metabolic decompensation in the neonatal period.

rows.text: Cardinal long-term complications in all survivors: (1) Basal ganglia injury producing dystonic cerebral palsy (~35%); (2) Dilated cardiomyopathy (25–30% over time, sometimes without preceding decompensation); (3) Optic atrophy; (4) Chronic kidney disease (late); (5) Acute pancreatitis; (6) Osteoporosis [1,2,13].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract supports cardiomyopathy as a mainly PA late complication and poor neurological outcome, but the stated frequencies (~35% dystonic CP, 25–30% cardiomyopathy) and optic atrophy, pancreatitis and osteoporosis are absent.
judged.quote: Mental outcome tends to be worse in PA and late complications include chronic kidney disease almost exclusively in MMA and cardiomyopathy mainly in PA.

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic acidaemia and propionic acidaemia: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: The abstract is purely structural, describing the guideline revision process and GRADE methodology without reporting any long-term complications or their frequencies in propionic acidaemia.
judged.quote: As a result, 21 updated recommendations were compiled in a more concise paper with a focus on the existing evidence to enable well-informed decisions in the context of MMA and PA patient care.

judged.citation: Pena L et al. Natural history of propionic acidemia. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):5–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that long-term survivors develop neurological, cardiac and gastrointestinal complications plus intellectual difficulties, but gives no frequencies (~35% dystonic CP, 25–30% cardiomyopathy) and does not mention optic atrophy, chronic kidney disease, pancreatitis or osteoporosis.
judged.quote: As patients age, the natural progression of propionic acidemia illuminates intellectual difficulties, increased risk for neurological complications, including stroke-like episodes, cardiac complications, and gastrointestinal difficulties, as well as a number of other complications.

rows.text: Acute decompensation: stop protein for ≤24 h, high-calorie glucose + intralipid, IV L-carnitine 100 mg/kg, IV N-carbamylglutamate and/or sodium benzoate for hyperammonaemia, haemofiltration if ammonia >500 µmol/L [2,14].

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic acidaemia and propionic acidaemia: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: The abstract only states that updated recommendations were compiled and gives no acute-management content, drugs, doses or ammonia thresholds.
judged.quote: the full body of evidence up until autumn 2019 was re-evaluated, analysed and graded

judged.citation: Filippi L et al. N-carbamylglutamate in emergency management of hyperammonemia in neonatal acute onset propionic and methylmalonic aciduria. Neonatology. 2010;97(3):286–90.
judged.reason: The abstract supports N-carbamylglutamate use for hyperammonaemia in acute neonatal propionic/methylmalonic aciduria (though given orally, not IV), but says nothing about protein cessation for ≤24 h, glucose/intralipid, the 100 mg/kg L-carnitine dose, sodium benzoate, or the >500 µmol/L haemofiltration threshold — those specifics rest on the guideline citation.
judged.quote: N-carbamylglutamate, added to the classic treatment, quickly normalized plasma ammonia levels in both patients and avoided the need of hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.

rows.text: Chronic management: moderate protein restriction with Ile/Val/Met/Thr-restricted medical food, target natural protein 0.8–1.2 g/kg/day; L-carnitine 50–100 mg/kg/day; biotin 10 mg/day trial (rarely responsive); metronidazole cycles to reduce propionate from gut flora; N-carbamylglutamate for chronic hyperammonaemia [2].

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic acidaemia and propionic acidaemia: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the guideline updates evidence on precursor-free amino acid mixtures (medical foods) but contains none of the specific chronic-management figures (protein 0.8–1.2 g/kg/day, carnitine 50–100 mg/kg/day, biotin 10 mg/day, metronidazole, N-carbamylglutamate).
judged.quote: a growing body of evidence on transplant outcomes in MMA and PA patients and use of precursor free amino acid mixtures allows for updates of the guidelines

rows.text: Use the Ile/Val-restricted medical foods judiciously: they are high in leucine and devoid of valine and isoleucine, and liberal use drives plasma valine and isoleucine down, predicts impaired brain uptake of other essential amino acids, and has been associated with adverse growth outcomes [15].

judged.citation: Myles JG, Manoli I, Venditti CP. Effects of medical food leucine content in the management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemias. Curr Opin Clin Nutr Metab Care. 2018;21(1):42–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the leucine-high/Val-Ile-devoid composition, lowered plasma Val and Ile, predicted impaired brain amino acid uptake, and judicious use, but says nothing about adverse growth outcomes.
judged.quote: The combination of protein restriction and medical food use in MMA and propionic acidemia results in an imbalanced branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) dietary content with a high Leu-to-Val and/or Ile ratio. This leads to decreased plasma levels of Val and Ile and predicts impaired brain uptake of multiple essential amino acids.

rows.text: Neurological assessment methods differed widely between the pooled studies and longer-term outcomes are still uncertain [16].

judged.citation: Zhou GP et al. Liver transplantation for propionic acidemia: evidence from a systematic review and meta-analysis. Transplantation. 2021;105(10):2272–82.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly notes diversity in neurological assessment methods across studies and that longer-term outcomes require further investigation.
judged.quote: Given the diversity in neurological assessment methods and the inconsistency in the achievement of dietary protein liberalization across different studies, consensus on neurological evaluation methods and posttransplant protein intake is necessary. Longer-term clinical outcomes of LT for PA warrants further investigation.

rows.text: Pre-NBS mortality at first crisis ~25%; 50% of survivors had major disability at 5-year follow-up [1,12].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract supports poor outcome with early death or severe handicap in many survivors, but neither the ~25% mortality at first crisis nor the 50% major disability at 5-year follow-up appears.
judged.quote: leading to early death or to severe neurological handicap in many survivors

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. Propionic acidemia: clinical course and outcome in 55 pediatric and adolescent patients. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:6.
judged.reason: The abstract documents an unfavourable outcome with major neurocognitive disability in about three quarters of patients, but reports neither the ~25% mortality at first crisis nor the 50%-disability-at-5-year figure.
judged.quote: About three quarters of the study population was mentally retarded, median IQ was 55.

rows.text: Post-NBS: mortality reduced to ~10% but long-term disease burden remains heavy — 30–50% of patients have developmental delay, 25–30% develop cardiomyopathy, and recurrent hospitalisation is the norm [2,13].

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic acidaemia and propionic acidaemia: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: The abstract describes only the scope and methodology of the guideline revision and contains no mortality, developmental-delay, cardiomyopathy or hospitalisation figures against which the claim's numbers could be checked.
judged.quote: Since that time, a growing body of evidence on transplant outcomes in MMA and PA patients and use of precursor free amino acid mixtures allows for updates of the guidelines.

judged.citation: Pena L et al. Natural history of propionic acidemia. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):5–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports improved survival beyond the neonatal period with a heavy burden of intellectual and cardiac complications, but provides none of the specific figures (~10% mortality, 30–50% developmental delay, 25–30% cardiomyopathy) or the newborn-screening comparison.
judged.quote: Recent advancements in treatment have allowed patients with propionic acidemia to live beyond the neonatal period and acute presentation.

rows.text: IQ drops 3–4 points per decompensation [13].

judged.citation: Pena L et al. Natural history of propionic acidemia. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):5–9.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses natural history including intellectual difficulties but gives no quantitative IQ decline per decompensation.
judged.quote: As patients age, the natural progression of propionic acidemia illuminates intellectual difficulties, increased risk for neurological complications, including stroke-like episodes, cardiac complications, and gastrointestinal difficulties

rows.text: PA remains one of the metabolic disorders with the greatest ongoing need for new therapies — dual-mRNA enzyme replacement encoding both PCC subunits has restored metabolic function in long-term studies in PA mice, but the published evidence is still preclinical [17].

judged.citation: Jiang L et al. Dual mRNA therapy restores metabolic function in long-term studies in mice with propionic acidemia. Nat Commun. 2020;11(1):5339.
judged.reason: The abstract reports dual mRNA encoding both PCCA and PCCB restoring functional PCC enzyme and reducing disease toxins in long-term 3- and 6-month studies in PA mice, i.e., preclinical evidence, consistent with the claim.
judged.quote: Dual mRNAs additionally restore functional PCC enzyme in liver and thus reduce primary disease-associated toxins in a dose-dependent manner in long-term 3- and 6-month repeat-dose studies in PA mice.

rows.text: Distinct from combined MMA+homocystinuria (cblC/D/F/J) by normal plasma homocysteine [1,2].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns isolated MMA/PA and does not discuss homocysteine or the combined MMA-with-homocystinuria (cblC/D/F/J) differential.

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of MMA/PA: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: The abstract refers to "isolated" MMA but does not discuss combined MMA with homocystinuria or plasma homocysteine as a discriminator.
judged.quote: Isolated methylmalonic acidaemia (MMA) and propionic acidaemia (PA) are rare inherited metabolic diseases.

rows.text: The classic distinction is between mut0 (no enzyme activity, B12-unresponsive, severe), mut- (residual activity, partially B12-responsive) and cblA/cblB (B12-responsive adenosylcobalamin synthesis defects) [1,4].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract acknowledges MUT deficiency and the existence of vitamin B12-responsive forms of MMA, but does not present the mut0/mut-/cblA/cblB classification or their respective responsiveness and severity.
judged.quote: Except for vitamin B12 responsive forms of MMA the outcome remains poor

judged.citation: Fowler B, Leonard JV, Baumgartner MR. Causes of and diagnostic approach to methylmalonic acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2008;31(3):350–60.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the mut0/mut-/cblA/cblB complementation classes and that cblA/cblB relate to adenosylcobalamin synthesis, but does not state the B12-responsiveness or severity/residual-activity attributes assigned to each class.
judged.quote: The mut(0) and mut(-) defects result from deficiency of MMCoA mutase apoenzyme which requires adenosyl-cobalamin (Ado-Cbl) as coenzyme. The cblA, cblB and the variant 2 form of cblD complementation groups are linked to processes unique to Ado-Cbl synthesis.

rows.text: Renal failure is the defining long-term complication — occurs in almost all mut0 cases by adolescence [5].

judged.citation: Hörster F et al. Long-term outcome in methylmalonic acidurias is influenced by the underlying defect. Pediatr Res. 2007;62(2):225–30.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that chronic renal failure is a leading long-term complication most frequent in mut0, but reports 61% of mut0 patients rather than "almost all" and gives no adolescent time-point (median follow-up 18 y in patients aged 7–33 y).
judged.quote: Chronic renal failure (CRF) was found most frequently in mut0 (61%) and cblB patients (66%), and was predicted by the urinary excretion of methylmalonic acid (MMA) before CRF.

rows.text: Block produces: urine MMA 100–10,000× ULN (often >1,000 mmol/mol Cr in mut0) — far higher than in PA [1,6]; plasma C3 elevated; MMA/MCA ratio >5 (distinguishes from PA where MCA predominates) [7]; secondary hyperglycinaemia and methionine may be low-normal (NOT low as in cblC — this distinguishes isolated MMA from cblC) [1,4].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms methylmalonic acid accumulation from MUT deficiency but contains none of the specific biochemical discriminators (MMA 100–10,000× ULN, >1,000 mmol/mol Cr, MMA/MCA ratio >5, methionine status).
judged.quote: accumulation of propionic acid and/or methylmalonic acid due to deficiency of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MUT)

judged.citation: Dionisi-Vici C et al. 'Classical' organic acidurias, PA, MMA, IVA. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(2–3):383–9.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns long-term outcome and newborn screening detection rates for classical organic acidurias, and says nothing about urine MMA levels, C3, MMA/MCA ratios, glycine or methionine biochemistry.

judged.citation: Al Dhahouri N et al. Quantification of methylcitrate in dried urine spots by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry for the diagnosis of propionic and methylmalonic acidemias. Clin Chim Acta. 2018;487:41–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that quantified methylcitrate is a diagnostic marker in propionic acidemia, methylmalonic aciduria and cobalamin defects, but it gives no MMA/MCA ratio threshold of >5 and does not state that methylcitrate predominates in PA relative to MMA.
judged.quote: Quantification of methylcitrate provides important diagnostic clues for propionic acidemia, methylmalonic aciduria and cobalamin disorders.

judged.citation: Fowler B, Leonard JV, Baumgartner MR. Causes of and diagnostic approach to methylmalonic acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2008;31(3):350–60.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the markedly elevated urinary MMA in severe mutase deficiency (up to >20000 mmol/mol creatinine, vs 10–20 in mild disturbances), but says nothing about plasma C3, the MMA/methylcitrate ratio >5, secondary hyperglycinaemia, or methionine being low-normal versus low in cblC.
judged.quote: MMA levels in urine range from 10-20 mmol/mol creatinine in mild disturbances of MMA metabolism to over 20000 mmol/mol creatinine in severe MMCoA mutase deficiency, but show considerable overlap and are of limited value for differential diagnosis.

rows.text: Plasma total homocysteine is NORMAL in isolated MMA — elevated tHcy immediately redirects the diagnosis to cblC/D/F/J [8].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that cobalamin remethylation disorders (cblC/D/F/J) accumulate homocysteine, but says nothing about homocysteine being normal in isolated methylmalonic acidemia.
judged.quote: Remethylation defects are rare inherited disorders in which impaired remethylation of homocysteine to methionine leads to accumulation of homocysteine and perturbation of numerous methylation reactions.

rows.text: Cobalamin responsiveness testing (1 mg hydroxocobalamin IM daily for 5–7 days, with ≥50% reduction in MMA) distinguishes cblA/B from mut [1,9].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract acknowledges vitamin B12-responsive forms of MMA but gives no testing protocol (1 mg hydroxocobalamin IM for 5–7 days, ≥50% MMA reduction) or cblA/B versus mut distinction.
judged.quote: Except for vitamin B12 responsive forms of MMA the outcome remains poor

judged.citation: Matsui SM et al. The natural history of the inherited methylmalonic acidemias. N Engl J Med. 1983;308(15):857–61.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that cobalamin responsiveness differentiates cblA/cblB from mut forms, but gives no dosing protocol (1 mg hydroxocobalamin IM for 5–7 days) or ≥50% MMA reduction threshold.
judged.quote: in response to cobalamin supplements, marked decreases in the concentration of methylmalonic acid in blood or urine were reported in most cbl A patients and in nearly half the cbl B patients, but not in mut degrees or mut- patients

rows.text: MMUT at 6p12.3 encodes the mitochondrial apoenzyme [10].

judged.citation: Ledley FD et al. Molecular cloning of L-methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 1988;85(10):3518–21.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms cloning of the cDNA for the mitochondrial methylmalonyl-CoA mutase apoenzyme deficient in methylmalonic acidemia, but says nothing about the gene's 6p12.3 chromosomal localization.
judged.quote: L-Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM, EC 5.4.99.2) is a mitochondrial adenosylcobalamin-requiring enzyme that catalyzes the isomerization of L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. This enzyme is deficient in methylmalonic acidemia

rows.text: Over 300 MMUT variants reported; mut0 variants produce no activity, mut- variants retain partial activity [4,11]. cblA has better prognosis than mut0.

judged.citation: Fowler B, Leonard JV, Baumgartner MR. Causes of and diagnostic approach to methylmalonic acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2008;31(3):350–60.
judged.reason: The abstract names mut0 and mut- defects but gives no variant count (>300) and does not state residual activity in mut- or a better prognosis for cblA than mut0.
judged.quote: The mut(0) and mut(-) defects result from deficiency of MMCoA mutase apoenzyme

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Novel mutations in the MUT gene identified from a database of 216 patients with MMA. Hum Mutat. 2016;37(8):745–62.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the mut0 vs mut- distinction (mut- retaining partial/residual activity with higher propionate incorporation) and a large mutation landscape, but it reports 110 different MUT mutations rather than the claimed >300 variants, and says nothing about cblA prognosis.
judged.quote: As per the definition, mut(-) patients showed a higher propionate incorporation ratio in vitro, which was correlated to a considerably later age of onset compared with mut(0) patients. In all patients, we found a total of 110 different mutations, of which 41 were novel.

rows.text: Unique MMA complementation classes are resolved by cultured fibroblast studies [4].

judged.citation: Fowler B, Leonard JV, Baumgartner MR. Causes of and diagnostic approach to methylmalonic acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2008;31(3):350–60.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly states that the underlying defect in isolated MMAuria is characterized in cultured skin fibroblasts including complementation analysis.
judged.quote: The underlying defect in isolated MMAuria can be characterized in cultured skin fibroblasts using several assays, e.g. conversion of propionate to succinate, specific activity of MMCoA, cobalamin adenosyltransferase assay, cellular uptake of CN-[(57)Co] cobalamin and its conversion to cobalamin coenzymes and complementation analysis.

rows.text: Neonatal (mut0 most common): first week of life with lethargy, vomiting, severe ketoacidosis, hyperammonaemia >500 µmol/L, pancytopenia — mortality ~30% at first crisis [1,12].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract supports neonatal acute deterioration with metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia and early death, but omits the first-week timing, ammonia >500 µmol/L, pancytopenia and the ~30% first-crisis mortality.
judged.quote: Patients present either shortly after birth with acute deterioration, metabolic acidosis and hyperammonemia

rows.text: Cardinal long-term complications: (1) CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE — interstitial nephritis progressing to ESRF in nearly all mut0 patients by 3rd decade [5,13]; (2) METABOLIC STROKE — bilateral globus pallidus infarction during acidotic crisis producing fixed dystonia [14]; (3) Pancreatitis; (4) Optic atrophy; (5) Cardiomyopathy (less common than in PA).

judged.citation: Hörster F et al. Long-term outcome in methylmalonic acidurias is influenced by the underlying defect. Pediatr Res. 2007;62(2):225–30.
judged.reason: This paper carries the chronic kidney disease element as a cardinal long-term complication predominating in mut0, but does not state interstitial nephritis, ESRF in nearly all mut0 patients by the third decade, or the other listed complications (stroke, pancreatitis, optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy), which are attributed to the co-cited papers.
judged.quote: Chronic renal failure (CRF) was found most frequently in mut0 (61%) and cblB patients (66%)

judged.citation: Cosson MA et al. Long-term outcome in methylmalonic aciduria. Mol Genet Metab. 2009;97(3):172–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports chronic kidney disease as a major long-term complication that is earlier and more severe in mut(o) patients, but it does not support the specific claim that nearly all mut0 patients progress to ESRF by the third decade (CRD occurred in only 47% of the whole cohort, median onset 6.5 y, with no ESRF rate given), and it says nothing about metabolic stroke, pancreatitis, optic atrophy or cardiomyopathy.
judged.quote: Chronic renal disease (CRD) occurred in 14 patients (47%) with a median age of onset of 6.5 y (range 1.5-18.6). ... Patients with mut(o) phenotype have a more severe phenotype and probably an earlier and more severe CRD than patients with mut-/cblA phenotype.

judged.citation: Heidenreich R et al. Acute extrapyramidal syndrome in methylmalonic acidemia. Neurology. 1988;38(12):1916–9.
judged.reason: The abstract directly describes bilateral globus pallidus destruction with acute extrapyramidal disease after metabolic decompensation in methylmalonic acidemia, termed a "metabolic stroke" — the specific component this paper is cited for.
judged.quote: We report four patients with methylmalonic acidemia who developed acute extrapyramidal disease after metabolic decompensation. The neurologic findings resulted from bilateral destruction of the globus pallidus

rows.text: Acute: as for PA (stop protein, glucose/lipid, carnitine, ammonia removal with Carbaglu®/benzoate/phenylacetate, haemofiltration if ammonia >500) [2,15].

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of MMA/PA: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: No acute treatment details, ammonia-removal agents or haemofiltration threshold appear in this structural guideline abstract.

judged.citation: Chapman KA et al. Acute management of propionic and methylmalonic acidemia. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):16–25.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that consensus recommendations exist for acute management of metabolic decompensation in propionic acidemia (the framework the claim invokes), but none of the specific interventions (protein cessation, glucose/lipid, carnitine, Carbaglu®/benzoate/phenylacetate, or haemofiltration at ammonia >500) are stated in the abstract.
judged.quote: The following manuscript provides recommendations for initial treatment and evaluation, a discussion of issues concerning transport to a metabolic center (if patient presents to a non-metabolic center), acceleration of management and preparation for discharge.

rows.text: TRIAL HYDROXOCOBALAMIN 1–2 mg/day IM at diagnosis — cblA/cblB patients show dramatic MMA reduction; mut- shows partial response; mut0 shows none [2,9].

judged.citation: Forny P et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of MMA/PA: first revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(3):566–92.
judged.reason: The abstract makes no mention of hydroxocobalamin dosing or differential responsiveness by cblA/cblB/mut- /mut0 subtype.

judged.citation: Matsui SM et al. The natural history of the inherited methylmalonic acidemias. N Engl J Med. 1983;308(15):857–61.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the cobalamin-responsiveness pattern (marked MMA decreases in most cblA and nearly half of cblB, none in mut0), but it gives no hydroxocobalamin dose/route (1–2 mg/day IM) and it groups mut- with mut0 as non-responders rather than showing a partial response.
judged.quote: in response to cobalamin supplements, marked decreases in the concentration of methylmalonic acid in blood or urine were reported in most cbl A patients and in nearly half the cbl B patients, but not in mut degrees or mut- patients

rows.text: Liver transplantation + combined liver-kidney transplantation is increasingly used — reverses acute decompensation risk, partially normalises MMA, and addresses renal failure but does not reverse basal ganglia injury [16]. mRNA therapy in trial for MMUT deficiency [17].

judged.citation: Niemi AK et al. Treatment of methylmalonic acidemia by liver or combined liver-kidney transplantation. J Pediatr. 2015;166(6):1455–61.
judged.reason: The abstract supports elimination of decompensation/hyperammonemia episodes, substantial but incomplete MMA normalisation, and use of combined liver-kidney grafts, but says nothing about basal ganglia injury (indeed it reports neurodevelopmental stabilisation/improvement); the mRNA trial element belongs to the co-cited paper.
judged.quote: LT or LKT for MMA eradicates episodes of hyperammonemia, results in excellent long-term survival, and suggests stabilization of neurocognitive development.

judged.citation: An D et al. Systemic messenger RNA therapy as a treatment for methylmalonic acidemia. Cell Rep. 2017;21(12):3548–58.
judged.reason: The abstract supports mRNA therapy targeting methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMUT) deficiency, but it reports preclinical mouse-model work rather than a clinical trial; the liver/combined liver-kidney transplantation content is carried by the other cited paper.
judged.quote: we generated a pseudoU-modified codon-optimized mRNA encoding human methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (hMUT), the enzyme most frequently mutated in MMA, and encapsulated it into biodegradable lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Intravenous (i.v.) administration of hMUT mRNA in two different mouse models of MMA resulted in a 75%-85% reduction in plasma methylmalonic acid

rows.text: Pre-NBS, mut0 mortality ~30% at first presentation; long-term disability rate 60% [1,12].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130.
judged.reason: The abstract conveys poor outcome with early death or severe neurological handicap but provides neither the ~30% mut0 mortality at first presentation nor a 60% long-term disability rate.
judged.quote: leading to early death or to severe neurological handicap in many survivors

rows.text: NBS detection reduces mortality but long-term natural history remains severe: mut0 patients have ~50% probability of ESRF by age 30 [5]. cblA has best prognosis — near-normal development possible with B12 therapy. cblB intermediate. mut- variable.

judged.citation: Hörster F et al. Long-term outcome in methylmalonic acidurias is influenced by the underlying defect. Pediatr Res. 2007;62(2):225–30.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that long-term outcome depends on the enzymatic subgroup and that renal failure is common in mut0, but it does not give the specific ~50% probability of ESRF by age 30, says nothing about newborn screening reducing mortality, and its data place cblB alongside mut0 as the worst rather than 'intermediate'.
judged.quote: Chronic renal failure (CRF) was found most frequently in mut0 (61%) and cblB patients (66%), and was predicted by the urinary excretion of methylmalonic acid (MMA) before CRF.

rows.text: The number-one therapeutic advance of the decade has been combined liver-kidney transplantation, which largely eliminates decompensation and prevents renal deterioration [16].

judged.citation: Niemi AK et al. Treatment of methylmalonic acidemia by liver or combined liver-kidney transplantation. J Pediatr. 2015;166(6):1455–61.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that transplantation largely eliminates metabolic decompensation and reports 100% kidney allograft survival, but it explicitly leaves unresolved whether renal deterioration is prevented long-term.
judged.quote: Long-term follow-up is underway to evaluate whether patients who undergo early LT need kidney transplantation later in life.

rows.text: The triad of elevated plasma total homocysteine, elevated urinary methylmalonic acid and LOW plasma methionine distinguishes this from isolated MMA (normal Hcy) and from CBS deficiency (high Met). cblC is the commonest inherited disorder of intracellular cobalamin metabolism and a preventable cause of thromboembolism, dementia and pigmentary retinopathy [1,2].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders cblC, cblD, cblE, cblF, cblG, cblJ and MTHFR deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: The abstract supports homocysteine elevation and the value of detecting these treatable disorders in thrombosis/visual/haematological presentations, but does not state the MMA + low-methionine triad, the contrast with CBS deficiency, or that cblC is the commonest intracellular cobalamin disorder.
judged.quote: We strongly recommend measuring plasma total homocysteine in any patient presenting with the combination of neurological and/or visual and/or haematological symptoms, subacute spinal cord degeneration, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or unexplained vascular thrombosis.

rows.text: Two clinical phenotypes: early-onset (<1 yr of age, severe, multi-system) and late-onset (adolescent/adult, with isolated neurological features — dementia, psychiatric disturbance, myelopathy, thromboembolism) — often decades-delayed diagnosis [4,5]. cblD is much rarer and can present with isolated MMA, isolated Hcy elevation, or combined.

judged.citation: Rosenblatt DS et al. Clinical heterogeneity and prognosis in combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria (cblC). J Inherit Metab Dis. 1997;20(4):528–38.
judged.reason: The abstract supports two distinct phenotypes with early presentation in the first year of life (severe, multi-system) and a later-onset form with neurological/psychiatric features (extrapyramidal signs, dementia, delirium, psychosis), but it describes the later form as childhood-onset rather than adolescent/adult, does not mention myelopathy, thromboembolism or decades-delayed diagnosis, and says nothing about cblD.
judged.quote: We identified two distinct phenotypes; they differed in age of onset, presence of systemic symptoms, type of neurological symptoms, and outcome after diagnosis and treatment. Forty-four patients presented in the first year of life.

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Three new cases of late-onset cblC defect. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:161.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the late-onset phenotype (onset >12 months) with neurological/psychiatric features and diagnostic delays of up to more than 20 years, but says nothing about cblD or its isolated MMA/Hcy presentations.
judged.quote: patients with the late-onset form of the disease (onset >12 fnths)... Time between first symptoms and diagnosis ranged from three months to more than 20 years. ... In older children/adolescents, psychiatric symptoms, cognitive impairment, ataxia and myelopathy were frequently observed while thromboembolic events and glomerulopathies were almost exclusively seen in adults.

rows.text: Block produces the triad: elevated MMA, elevated tHcy AND LOW-LOW-NORMAL methionine (unlike CBS deficiency where Met is HIGH) [1].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders cblC, cblD, cblE, cblF, cblG, cblJ and MTHFR deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: Only the homocysteine-accumulation/impaired-remethylation element is present; the abstract does not report methylmalonic acid elevation, low-normal methionine values, or the contrast with high methionine in CBS deficiency.
judged.quote: Remethylation defects are rare inherited disorders in which impaired remethylation of homocysteine to methionine leads to accumulation of homocysteine and perturbation of numerous methylation reactions.

rows.text: The Met/Hcy ratio is LOW — a useful discriminator [1].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders cblC, cblD, cblE, cblF, cblG, cblJ and MTHFR deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses biochemical diagnosis of remethylation disorders (recommending plasma total homocysteine) but never mentions a methionine/homocysteine ratio as a discriminator.

rows.text: On newborn screening the first-tier acylcarnitine markers alone discriminate poorly; multivariate post-analytical scoring (CLIR) followed by a second-tier test measuring homocysteine, methylmalonic acid and methylcitric acid is what brings the false-positive rate for this group below 0.01% [8].

judged.citation: Gavrilov DK et al. The combined impact of CLIR post-analytical tools and second tier testing on the performance of newborn screening for disorders of propionate, methionine, and cobalamin metabolism. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2020;6(2):33.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly includes cobalamin metabolism disorders in the algorithm (CLIR scoring plus second-tier homocysteine/MMA/methylcitric acid) achieving a <0.01% false-positive rate, with poor first-tier specificity as the stated motivation; only the phrase about acylcarnitine markers discriminating poorly is implicit.
judged.quote: an algorithm for disorders of methionine, cobalamin, and propionate metabolism that includes ... a score of likelihood of disease for each target condition calculated by post-analytical interpretive tools created byCollaborative Laboratory Integrated Reports (CLIR) ... This approach can consistently reduce false positive rates to a <0.01% level

rows.text: MMACHC at 1p34.1 encodes a multifunctional protein (cobalamin dealkylase + glutathione-dependent reductase) that processes incoming cobalamin into either methyl- or adenosyl-cobalamin [9].

judged.citation: Lerner-Ellis JP et al. Identification of the gene responsible for methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria, cblC type. Nat Genet. 2006;38(1):93–100.
judged.reason: The abstract supports identification of MMACHC on chromosome 1p as the cblC gene, but it does not state the precise 1p34.1 locus nor the claimed dealkylase/glutathione-dependent reductase activities or processing into methyl-/adenosylcobalamin (only a predicted TonB-like C-terminal fold related to cobalamin uptake).
judged.quote: The cblC locus was mapped to chromosome region 1p by linkage analysis. We refined the chromosomal interval using homozygosity mapping and haplotype analyses and identified the MMACHC gene.

rows.text: The c.271dupA variant accounts for ~40% of alleles in Caucasian cases (early-onset phenotype); c.482G>A is associated with milder late-onset phenotype [5,10].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Three new cases of late-onset cblC defect. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:161.
judged.reason: The abstract describes the clinical spectrum, biochemistry and treatment response of late-onset cblC defect but never addresses MMACHC genotypes, allele frequencies, or genotype–phenotype correlations such as c.271dupA or c.482G>A.
judged.quote: Reports on 58 cases (30 females, 22 males, 6	hree new cases undernderlined the clinical heterogeneity of the disease.

judged.citation: Morel CF et al. cblC MMACHC mutations and outcome. Mol Genet Metab. 2006;88(4):315–21.
judged.reason: The abstract supports c.271dupA as the predominant mutation in early-onset cblC, but gives no ~40% allele frequency in Caucasians and never mentions c.482G>A (it cites c.394C>T as the late-onset-associated variant).
judged.quote: 25/37 had early-onset disease, presenting in the first 6 months of life: 17/25 were found to be either homozygous for the c.271dupA mutation (n=9) or for the c.331C>T mutation (n=3), or compound heterozygotes for these 2 mutations (n=5).

rows.text: Early-onset cblC (<1 year of age): failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, pigmentary retinopathy (pathognomonic and progressive — requires URGENT ophthalmology), microcephaly, developmental delay, haemolytic uraemic syndrome, progressive neurodegeneration [4]. cblC can also present in adults as thrombotic microangiopathy: the first reported adult-onset case was treated as eculizumab-resistant atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome until homocysteine was measured, which is why plasma homocysteine belongs in the work-up of unexplained HUS [11].

judged.citation: Rosenblatt DS et al. Clinical heterogeneity and prognosis in combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria (cblC). J Inherit Metab Dis. 1997;20(4):528–38.
judged.reason: The abstract supports feeding difficulties, hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay and unspecified ophthalmological and haematological abnormalities in infantile presentation, but does not specifically mention pigmentary retinopathy, microcephaly or haemolytic uraemic syndrome (the adult thrombotic microangiopathy portion belongs to the other cited paper).
judged.quote: Feeding difficulties, neurological dysfunction (hypotonia, seizures, developmental delay), and ophthalmological and haematological abnormalities characterized their clinical picture.

judged.citation: Cornec-Le Gall E et al. Adult-onset eculizumab-resistant hemolytic uremic syndrome associated with cobalamin C deficiency. Am J Kidney Dis. 2014;63(1):119–23.
judged.reason: The abstract describes exactly the adult-onset cblC case treated as eculizumab-resistant atypical HUS until homocysteine was measured, and recommends homocysteine testing in HUS work-up; the early-onset symptom list is attributed to a different reference.
judged.quote: To our knowledge, this is the first report of adult-onset cobalamin C-related HUS. Considering the wide availability and low cost of the homocysteine assay, we suggest that it be included in the diagnostic algorithm for adult patients who present with HUS.

rows.text: Late-onset (adolescent/adult): subacute combined spinal cord degeneration (MYELOPATHY mimicking B12 deficiency), dementia, psychiatric disorder, venous thromboembolism, pulmonary hypertension — often misdiagnosed for years before the combined MMA+Hcy pattern is recognised [5,6,12]. cblD: variable phenotype.

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Three new cases of late-onset cblC defect. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:161.
judged.reason: Myelopathy, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, thromboembolism and long diagnostic delay are all supported, but the abstract attributes pulmonary hypertension to preschool children rather than adolescents/adults and does not address cblD phenotype.
judged.quote: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome and pulmonary hypertension were main presenting symptoms in preschool children. In older children/adolescents, psychiatric symptoms, cognitive impairment, ataxia and myelopathy were frequently observed while thromboembolic events and glomerulopathies were almost exclusively seen in adults.

judged.citation: Ben-Omran TI et al. Late-onset cobalamin-C disorder: a challenging diagnosis. Am J Med Genet A. 2007;143A(9):979–84.
judged.reason: The abstract supports late-onset cblC presenting with neuropsychiatric symptoms and being easily missed/difficult to diagnose, but does not mention subacute combined spinal cord degeneration, dementia, venous thromboembolism or pulmonary hypertension specifically (only nonspecific "vasculopathy").
judged.quote: we describe clinical and biochemical findings of two unrelated patients with late-onset cblC disease who presented with neuropsychiatric symptoms

judged.citation: Wang SJ et al. Late-onset cblC deficiency: a review of 17 cases. Front Neurol. 2018;9:919.
judged.reason: The abstract is about somatic SMARCB1 mutation in sporadic multiple meningiomas and does not address cblC deficiency or its late-onset presentation at all.

rows.text: Treatment initiated pre-symptomatically (NBS detection) lowers overall morbidity, but in the 238-patient E-HOD registry early treatment was distinctly LESS effective against eye disease and cognitive impairment than against other outcomes — so early diagnosis should not be presented to families as protecting vision or cognition [2,7,13,16].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Phenotype, treatment practice and outcome in the cobalamin-dependent remethylation disorders and MTHFR deficiency: data from the E-HOD registry. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2019;42(2):333–52.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly reports the 238-patient E-HOD cohort and that early treatment lowers overall morbidity but is less effective against eye disease and cognitive impairment.
judged.quote: This review comprises 238 patients ... Early treatment correlates with lower overall morbidity but is less effective in preventing eye disease and cognitive impairment.

judged.citation: Weisfeld-Adams JD et al. Newborn screening and early management of cblC deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2013;110(3):241–7.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that early (NBS-detected) treatment fails to protect cognition and that metabolite levels poorly predict neurodevelopmental outcome, but contains nothing about the 238-patient E-HOD registry or its comparison of outcome domains.
judged.quote: All patients showed evidence of developmental delay with the exception of one patient with a genotype predictive of attenuated disease and near-normal biochemical parameters.

judged.citation: Ahrens-Nicklas RC et al. Efficacy of early treatment in patients with cobalamin C disease identified by newborn screening: a 16-year experience. Genet Med. 2017;19(8):926–35.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that early NBS-initiated treatment prevents metabolic decompensation yet fails to protect cognition and vision, but the specific 238-patient E-HOD registry figure and comparison come from another cited paper.
judged.quote: Of the patients, 87.5% had intellectual disability and 75% had retinopathy; 16.7% had one episode of mild acidosis. However, no patients manifested major metabolic decompensation.

rows.text: Early treatment does NOT prevent the retinal disease: maculopathy appears in the first year and progresses over months, 75% of a newborn-screened cohort developed retinopathy despite treatment from birth, and ophthalmic progression correlates poorly with metabolic status — cblC has a developmental as well as a degenerative ocular phenotype, so damage laid down before birth is not recoverable by postnatal control [14,15,16].

judged.citation: Gerth C et al. Ocular phenotype in patients with methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria, cobalamin C type. J AAPOS. 2008;12(6):591–6.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms retinopathy occurred despite systemic treatment and that early-onset patients had progressive retinal disease while late-onset did not, but it provides no support for the 75% newborn-screened cohort figure, the first-year onset/months-long progression timeline, or the poor correlation with metabolic status.
judged.quote: Retinopathy occurred despite systemic treatment for cblC.

judged.citation: Brooks BP et al. Ophthalmic manifestations and long-term visual outcomes in patients with cobalamin C deficiency. Ophthalmology. 2016;123(3):571–82.
judged.reason: The abstract directly states that ophthalmic manifestations lacked strict correlation to metabolic status, that early/prenatal treatment did not prevent progression to severe macular degeneration, and that cblC has a developmental as well as degenerative ocular phenotype; only the 75% newborn-screened figure comes from the co-cited Ahrens-Nicklas paper.
judged.quote: The pace and chronicity of ophthalmic manifestations lacked strict correlation to metabolic status as measured during visits. Prenatal or early treatment, or both, may have mitigated ocular disease, leading to better functional acuity, but patients still progressed to severe macular degeneration.

judged.citation: Ahrens-Nicklas RC et al. Efficacy of early treatment in patients with cobalamin C disease identified by newborn screening: a 16-year experience. Genet Med. 2017;19(8):926–35.
judged.reason: The abstract directly reports 75% retinopathy in a newborn-screened cblC cohort with poor outcomes despite early therapy initiation, and notes outcomes tracked initial rather than long-term metabolic control; the maculopathy-timing and ophthalmic-progression details are carried by the co-cited ocular papers.
judged.quote: Of the patients, 87.5% had intellectual disability and 75% had retinopathy

rows.text: What early or prenatal treatment does appear to buy is better functional visual acuity, even in patients who still progress to severe macular degeneration [15].

judged.citation: Brooks BP et al. Ophthalmic manifestations and long-term visual outcomes in patients with cobalamin C deficiency. Ophthalmology. 2016;123(3):571–82.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly states prenatal or early treatment may have mitigated ocular disease leading to better functional acuity while patients still progressed to severe macular degeneration.
judged.quote: Prenatal or early treatment, or both, may have mitigated ocular disease, leading to better functional acuity, but patients still progressed to severe macular degeneration.

rows.text: Late-onset patients show no definite retinal degeneration [14].

judged.citation: Gerth C et al. Ocular phenotype in patients with methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria, cobalamin C type. J AAPOS. 2008;12(6):591–6.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly states late-onset patients showed no definite evidence of retinal degeneration.
judged.quote: Patients with late-onset disease showed no definite evidence of retinal degeneration.

rows.text: Pre-NBS early-onset cblC: 50% mortality in infancy, severe disability in survivors, retinopathy with legal blindness by age 5 [4,14].

judged.citation: Rosenblatt DS et al. Clinical heterogeneity and prognosis in combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria (cblC). J Inherit Metab Dis. 1997;20(4):528–38.
judged.reason: The abstract supports early-onset presentation with severe neurological impairment in survivors, but gives mortality as about one-quarter rather than 50%, and says nothing about retinopathy or legal blindness by age 5 (covered by the co-cited ocular paper).
judged.quote: About one-quarter of those patients died. Survival was associated with neurological impairment; only one infant was neurologically intact at follow-up.

judged.citation: Gerth C et al. Ocular phenotype in patients with methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria, cobalamin C type. J AAPOS. 2008;12(6):591–6.
judged.reason: The abstract documents severe visual loss (down to counting fingers) with macular and optic atrophy in early-onset cblC, but reports no mortality rate and does not establish legal blindness by age 5.
judged.quote: Visual acuity was reduced from 0.2 logMAR to counting fingers and from 0.0 to 0.3 logMAR in the early- (3 of 7) and in the late-onset group (4 of 7), respectively.

rows.text: NBS + prompt hydroxocobalamin + betaine: near-normal cognitive outcomes possible if treatment starts within the first month of life [13].

judged.citation: Weisfeld-Adams JD et al. Newborn screening and early management of cblC deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2013;110(3):241–7.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses cognitive outcomes in newborn-screened, early-treated cblC but reports developmental delay in essentially all such children (the sole exception being an attenuated genotype), rather than near-normal cognition with treatment begun in the first month.
judged.quote: All patients showed evidence of developmental delay with the exception of one patient with a genotype predictive of attenuated disease and near-normal biochemical parameters. Neurodevelopmental deficits were noted most prominently in motor skills

rows.text: Late-onset cases diagnosed as adults: partial improvement of myelopathy and thromboembolic risk on treatment, but residual deficits often persist [5,12].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Three new cases of late-onset cblC defect. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:161.
judged.reason: The abstract supports treatment response with worse outcomes in late-treated patients, but does not specifically document partial improvement of myelopathy and thromboembolic risk with persisting residual deficits in adult-diagnosed cases.
judged.quote: The majority of patients showed marked biochemical and clinical response to treatment with parenteral hydroxocobalamin combined with oral betaine, folate, carnitine and rarely methionine. The course was less favourable in late treated or untreated patients.

judged.citation: Wang SJ et al. Late-onset cblC deficiency: a review of 17 cases. Front Neurol. 2018;9:919.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns meningioma genetics and says nothing about late-onset cblC treatment outcomes.

rows.text: Metabolic control does not track visual or cognitive outcome closely enough to be used as a proxy for either [7].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Phenotype, treatment practice and outcome in the cobalamin-dependent remethylation disorders and MTHFR deficiency: data from the E-HOD registry. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2019;42(2):333–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that eye and neurocognitive outcomes respond poorly to treatment, but it does not report any analysis showing metabolic control (tHcy/MMA) fails to track visual or cognitive outcome, so the proxy claim itself is not carried.
judged.quote: Treatment improves the clinical course of remethylation disorders and reduces morbidity, especially if started early, but neurocognitive and eye symptoms are less responsive.

rows.text: NBS detection and protein-restricted diet with glycine/carnitine supplementation give excellent outcomes [1,2].

judged.citation: Vockley J, Ensenauer R. Isovaleric acidemia: new aspects of genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity. Am J Med Genet C. 2006;142C(2):95–103.
judged.reason: The abstract states that early diagnosis and treatment with protein restriction plus carnitine and glycine supplementation promote normal development, and describes newborn screening detection of mild cases.
judged.quote: Early diagnosis and treatment with a protein restricted diet and supplementation with carnitine and glycine are effective in promoting normal development in severely affected individuals.

judged.citation: Thimm E et al. Practical considerations for the diagnosis and management of isovaleryl-CoA-dehydrogenase deficiency (isovaleric acidemia): systematic search and review and expert opinions. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2025;11(4).
judged.reason: The abstract confirms NBS is established and that treatment is a protein-restricted diet with carnitine and/or glycine, but it does not state that outcomes are excellent (indeed it notes evidence-based recommendations are lacking).
judged.quote: Newborn screening for IVA has been established in many countries. Treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet combined with supplementation of carnitine and/or glycine and emergency treatment in catabolic episodes.

rows.text: Global incidence is ~1:200,000 on NBS; clinically-ascertained incidence is lower because many NBS-detected cases carry the mild c.932C>T (p.Ala282Val) variant and remain asymptomatic [4,5].

judged.citation: Ensenauer R et al. A common mutation is associated with a mild, potentially asymptomatic phenotype in patients with isovaleric acidemia diagnosed by newborn screening. Am J Hum Genet. 2004;75(6):1136–42.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that NBS-detected cases frequently carry the mild c.932C>T (A282V) variant and can be asymptomatic, but it gives no incidence figure such as ~1:200,000.
judged.quote: Molecular genetic analysis of the IVD gene for 19 subjects whose condition was detected through NBS led to the identification of one recurring mutation, 932C-->T (A282V), in 47% of mutant alleles. Surprisingly, family studies identified six healthy older siblings with identical genotype and biochemical evidence of IVA.

judged.citation: Schlune A et al. Aspects of newborn screening in isovaleric acidemia. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2018;4(1):7.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the mild/asymptomatic c.932C>T (p.A282V) phenotype detected via NBS, but gives no incidence figure such as ~1:200,000.
judged.quote: An additional biochemically mild and potentially asymptomatic form of IVA and its association with a common missense mutation, c.932C>T (p.A282V), was discovered in subjects identified through NBS.

rows.text: Elevated plasma C5 (isovalerylcarnitine) is the NBS marker — but C5 is ISOBARIC with 2-methylbutyrylcarnitine (SBCAD) and pivaloylcarnitine (pivalic-acid drugs) [6,7].

judged.citation: Rinaldo P et al. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Diagnosis by stable-isotope dilution measurement of urinary n-hexanoylglycine and 3-phenylpropionylglycine. N Engl J Med. 1988;319(20):1308–13.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns MCAD deficiency diagnosis via urinary hexanoylglycine and 3-phenylpropionylglycine and says nothing about C5 acylcarnitine, isovaleric acidemia, or isobaric interference in newborn screening.

judged.citation: Miller MJ et al. Laboratory analysis of acylcarnitines, 2020 update: a technical standard of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). Genet Med. 2021;23(2):249–58.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that isomeric and isobaric acylcarnitine species exist and may require chromatographic separation, but it never names C5, isovalerylcarnitine, 2-methylbutyrylcarnitine, or pivaloylcarnitine, nor identifies C5 as the IVA newborn screening marker.
judged.quote: Alternative methods utilize liquid chromatographic separation of isomeric and isobaric species and/or detection by selected reaction monitoring.

rows.text: Definitive diagnosis requires urine acylglycines — isovalerylglycine (IVG) is specific and markedly elevated (100–1000× ULN) [8].

judged.citation: Ombrone D, Salvatore F, Ruoppolo M. Quantitative liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry analysis of urinary acylglycines: application to the diagnosis of inborn errors of metabolism. Anal Biochem. 2011;417(1):122–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports urinary acylglycine analysis by LC-MS/MS as a diagnostic tool with reference intervals, demonstrated in an isovaleric acidemia patient, but it does not state that isovalerylglycine is specific or quantify the elevation as 100–1000× ULN.
judged.quote: The diagnostic usefulness of the method was demonstrated in three patients with propionic acidemia (PA), one patient with isovaleric acidemia (IVA)

rows.text: IVD is at 15q15.1, encoding a mitochondrial flavoprotein (FAD-dependent) [9].

judged.citation: Vockley J et al. Molecular characterization of four different classes of mutations in the isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase gene responsible for isovaleric acidemia. Am J Hum Genet. 1991;49(1):147–57.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms IVD is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial matrix enzyme deficient in isovaleric acidemia, but never states the 15q15.1 chromosomal locus nor that the protein is an FAD-dependent flavoprotein.
judged.quote: caused by a genetically determined deficiency of isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (IVD), a mitochondrial matrix enzyme

rows.text: Genotype is a useful adjunct to decide on intensity of treatment for NBS-detected cases [5,10].

judged.citation: Schlune A et al. Aspects of newborn screening in isovaleric acidemia. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2018;4(1):7.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the genotype–phenotype link (c.932C>T with a mild/potentially asymptomatic form found via NBS) but does not state that genotype guides intensity of treatment; it instead says management recommendations for the mild phenotype are still needed.
judged.quote: An additional biochemically mild and potentially asymptomatic form of IVA and its association with a common missense mutation, c.932C>T (p.A282V), was discovered in subjects identified through NBS.

judged.citation: Hertecant JL et al. Clinical and molecular analysis of isovaleric acidemia patients in the United Arab Emirates reveals remarkable phenotypes and four novel mutations in the IVD gene. Eur J Med Genet. 2012;55(12):671–6.
judged.reason: The abstract shows genotype–phenotype heterogeneity including an asymptomatic homozygote for p.R392H, which is consistent with genotype informing prognosis, but it does not address newborn screening detection or using genotype to set treatment intensity.
judged.quote: Furthermore, we found an unusual case of a 17 years old female homozygous for the p.R392H mutation with no clinical symptoms. Our results illustrate a heterogeneous mutation spectrum and clinical presentation in the relatively small UAE population.

rows.text: Two phenotypes [1]: (1) Acute neonatal: days 3–14 of life, acidotic crisis, poor feeding, vomiting, encephalopathy, pancytopenia, 'sweaty feet' odour — mortality ~30% if untreated; (2) Chronic intermittent: later presentation with recurrent episodes of ketoacidosis precipitated by illness or high-protein meal, milder developmental phenotype.

judged.citation: Vockley J, Ensenauer R. Isovaleric acidemia: new aspects of genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity. Am J Med Genet C. 2006;142C(2):95–103.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the two classic phenotypes (acute neonatal and chronic intermittent) but gives none of the specific clinical details (days 3–14, pancytopenia, sweaty feet odour) or the ~30% untreated mortality figure.
judged.quote: Initially, two phenotypes with either an acute neonatal or a chronic intermittent presentation were described.

rows.text: NBS-detected asymptomatic form (mild c.932C>T genotype): often no clinical disease but lifelong biochemical abnormality [4,5].

judged.citation: Ensenauer R et al. A common mutation is associated with a mild, potentially asymptomatic phenotype in patients with isovaleric acidemia diagnosed by newborn screening. Am J Hum Genet. 2004;75(6):1136–42.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies the recurring 932C>T (A282V) mutation in NBS-detected patients and describes a mild, potentially asymptomatic phenotype with healthy siblings showing biochemical evidence of IVA.
judged.quote: Molecular genetic analysis of the IVD gene for 19 subjects whose condition was detected through NBS led to the identification of one recurring mutation, 932C-->T (A282V), in 47% of mutant alleles. Surprisingly, family studies identified six healthy older siblings with identical genotype and biochemical evidence of IVA. Our findings indicate the frequent occurrence of a novel mild and potentially asymptomatic phenotype of IVA.

judged.citation: Schlune A et al. Aspects of newborn screening in isovaleric acidemia. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2018;4(1):7.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly describes a biochemically mild, potentially asymptomatic NBS-detected form associated with the c.932C>T variant.
judged.quote: An additional biochemically mild and potentially asymptomatic form of IVA and its association with a common missense mutation, c.932C>T (p.A282V), was discovered in subjects identified through NBS.

rows.text: Acute management: stop protein, high-calorie glucose/lipid (≥10 mg/kg/min glucose), IV L-glycine 150–250 mg/kg/day (conjugates free isovaleryl-CoA to excretable isovalerylglycine), L-carnitine 100 mg/kg/day, correct acidosis with bicarbonate, haemofiltration if ammonia >500 µmol/L [2,11].

judged.citation: Thimm E et al. Practical considerations for the diagnosis and management of isovaleryl-CoA-dehydrogenase deficiency (isovaleric acidemia): systematic search and review and expert opinions. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2025;11(4).
judged.reason: The abstract supports the general acute-management framework (emergency treatment in catabolic episodes, carnitine/glycine) but contains none of the specific doses, glucose infusion rate, or the ammonia >500 µmol/L haemofiltration threshold.
judged.quote: Treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet combined with supplementation of carnitine and/or glycine and emergency treatment in catabolic episodes.

judged.citation: Hine DG, Tanaka K. The identification and the excretion pattern of isovaleryl glucuronide in the urine of patients with isovaleric acidemia. Pediatr Res. 1984;18(6):508–12.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the biochemical rationale that glycine conjugation of isovaleryl-CoA (via glycine-N-acylase) is the main detoxification route in IVA, but contains none of the treatment specifics — glycine or carnitine dosing, glucose infusion rate, bicarbonate, or the ammonia >500 µmol/L haemofiltration threshold.
judged.quote: Conjugation of isovaleryl-CoA with glycine, by the action of glycine-N-acylase, is the main detoxification mechanism in isovaleric acidemia.

rows.text: Chronic management: moderate protein restriction (1.5–2.0 g/kg/day infants; ~1 g/kg/day older children) using leucine-restricted medical food if needed; oral glycine 150–250 mg/kg/day; L-carnitine 50–100 mg/kg/day [2,12].

judged.citation: Thimm E et al. Practical considerations for the diagnosis and management of isovaleryl-CoA-dehydrogenase deficiency (isovaleric acidemia): systematic search and review and expert opinions. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2025;11(4).
judged.reason: The abstract endorses chronic protein restriction with glycine and/or carnitine supplementation but gives no protein intake targets or mg/kg/day dose ranges.
judged.quote: Treatment consists of a protein-restricted diet combined with supplementation of carnitine and/or glycine

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. Proposed guidelines for the diagnosis and management of methylmalonic and propionic acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2014;9:130 [also applicable principles].
judged.reason: The abstract is about methylmalonic and propionic acidemia and gives no isovaleric acidemia chronic management regimen or glycine/carnitine/protein dosing.

rows.text: Pre-NBS classic cases: ~30% neonatal mortality; survivors have mild cognitive impairment if early crises occur [1].

judged.citation: Vockley J, Ensenauer R. Isovaleric acidemia: new aspects of genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity. Am J Med Genet C. 2006;142C(2):95–103.
judged.reason: The abstract notes significant morbidity and mortality and that early treatment promotes normal development, but does not state a ~30% neonatal mortality rate or mild cognitive impairment in survivors.
judged.quote: It was the first organic acidemia recognized in humans and can cause significant morbidity and mortality.

rows.text: Post-NBS: most cases identified pre-symptomatically — with glycine + carnitine + dietary management, crises are infrequent and developmental outcomes are normal [2,13].

judged.citation: Thimm E et al. Practical considerations for the diagnosis and management of isovaleryl-CoA-dehydrogenase deficiency (isovaleric acidemia): systematic search and review and expert opinions. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2025;11(4).
judged.reason: The abstract confirms NBS is widespread, that an asymptomatic biochemical phenotype exists, and that statements on outcome were formulated, but it does not state that crises are infrequent or that developmental outcomes are normal post-NBS.
judged.quote: Newborn screening for IVA has been established in many countries.
