judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. Clinical and neurocognitive outcome in symptomatic isovaleric acidemia. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:9.
judged.reason: The abstract studies clinically (pre-NBS) diagnosed symptomatic patients and supports only that earlier diagnosis/treatment relates to better cognitive outcome and that IVA qualifies for newborn screening; it provides no post-NBS cohort data showing pre-symptomatic detection, infrequent crises, or normal development on glycine/carnitine/dietary therapy.
judged.quote: The potential to avoid neonatal mortality and to improve neurologic and cognitive outcome under early treatment reinforces IVA to be qualified for newborn screening.

rows.text: NBS detects many 3-MCC-deficient infants who remain clinically asymptomatic — the natural history of isolated 3-MCC deficiency is remarkably benign in most cases, and it is among the most common NBS-positive organic acidemias with the most uncertain clinical significance [1,2].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. The molecular basis of human 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency. J Clin Invest. 2001;107(4):495–504.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that isolated MCC deficiency is the most frequent organic aciduria on MS/MS newborn screening and that phenotypes range to asymptomatic adults, but it does not state that the natural history is benign in most cases or quantify how many NBS-detected infants stay asymptomatic.
judged.quote: appears to be the most frequent organic aciduria detected in tandem mass spectrometry-based neonatal screening programs. The phenotype is variable, ranging from neonatal onset with severe neurological involvement to asymptomatic adults.

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency: clinical, biochemical, enzymatic and molecular studies in 88 patients. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that many NBS-identified individuals are asymptomatic and that penetrance is low, but it does not state that 3-MCC deficiency is among the most common NBS-positive organic acidemias.
judged.quote: Fifty-seven percent of patients were asymptomatic while 43% showed clinical symptoms, many of which were probably not related to MCC deficiency but due to ascertainment bias.

rows.text: BIOTIN-RESPONSIVE 3-MCC deficiency usually indicates biotinidase deficiency or holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency (MCD) rather than isolated 3-MCC deficiency [4].

judged.citation: Wolf B. Biotinidase deficiency: 'if you have to have an inherited metabolic disease, this is the one to have'. Genet Med. 2012;14(6):565–75.
judged.reason: The abstract is a general overview of biotinidase deficiency and never addresses 3-MCC deficiency or the interpretation of biotin-responsiveness in isolated 3-MCC deficiency.

rows.text: Elevated plasma C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine) and urinary 3-methylcrotonylglycine (MCG) + 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid (3-OHIV) [1,5].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. The molecular basis of human 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency. J Clin Invest. 2001;107(4):495–504.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns cloning of MCCA/MCCB, complementation groups and mutant alleles, and says nothing about C5-OH, 3-methylcrotonylglycine or 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid.

judged.citation: Stadler SC, Ranieri E et al. Newborn screening for 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency: population heterogeneity of MCCA and MCCB mutations and impact on risk assessment. Hum Mutat. 2006;27(8):748–59.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms elevated 3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine (C5-OH) as the biochemical marker used to detect MCCD, but says nothing about urinary 3-methylcrotonylglycine or 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid.
judged.quote: we screened 677,852 neonates for 25 conditions, including MCCD, based on elevated concentrations of 3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine (3-HIVA-C)

rows.text: MATERNAL 3-MCC deficiency is a common cause of an NBS-positive infant with elevated C5-OH — the mother is usually asymptomatic and the infant is a carrier [6].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR. Molecular mechanism of dominant expression in 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2005;28(3):301–9.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns a dominant-negative MCCA allele and biotin responsiveness in heterozygotes, and never addresses newborn screening, maternal 3-MCC deficiency, or carrier status of screened infants.
judged.quote: Evidence is presented that MCCA-R385S is a dominant negative allele leading to biochemical abnormalities and clinical symptoms in heterozygous individuals

rows.text: Serum biotinidase activity should be checked to exclude biotinidase deficiency [4].

judged.citation: Wolf B. Biotinidase deficiency: 'if you have to have an inherited metabolic disease, this is the one to have'. Genet Med. 2012;14(6):565–75.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions newborn screening and the enzyme's function but says nothing about measuring serum biotinidase activity as a confirmatory or exclusionary test in a C5-OH workup.

rows.text: Genotype does not reliably predict phenotype [7].

judged.citation: Uematsu M et al. Molecular basis of four cases of 3-MCC deficiency. J Hum Genet. 2007;52(12):1040–3.
judged.reason: The abstract shows severely truncating MCCA/MCCB mutations in asymptomatic patients while missense mutations were found in a patient with severe neurological impairment and another with Reye-like syndrome, directly illustrating lack of genotype–phenotype correlation and explicit clinical/genetic heterogeneity.
judged.quote: No obvious clinical symptoms were observed in patients 1, 2, and 3. Patient 4 had severe neurological impairment and patient 5 developed Reye-like syndrome. The increasing use of MS/MS newborn screening in Japan will further clarify the clinical and genetic heterogeneity among patients with MCC deficiency

rows.text: Overwhelmingly asymptomatic in NBS cohorts — ~90% of NBS-identified cases have no clinical disease [2,8].

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency: clinical, biochemical, enzymatic and molecular studies in 88 patients. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports low penetrance and reports that only 5 of 53 newborn-screening-identified individuals had acute metabolic decompensations (~90% without), but it does not state an asymptomatic proportion specifically for the NBS subgroup (overall asymptomatic rate given is 57%), so the exact ~90% "no clinical disease" figure is only inferable, not stated.
judged.quote: Fifty-seven percent of patients were asymptomatic while 43% showed clinical symptoms, many of which were probably not related to MCC deficiency but due to ascertainment bias. However, 12 patients (5 of 53 identified by newborn screening) presented with acute metabolic decompensations.

judged.citation: Jung CW et al. Uneventful clinical courses of Korean patients with methylcrotonylglycinuria and their common mutations. J Hum Genet. 2012;57(1):62–4.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that NBS-identified MCC deficiency patients are typically asymptomatic with uneventful courses, but it does not provide the ~90% proportion (its own small cohort was 11/11 asymptomatic).
judged.quote: 11 Korean MCG patients from nine unrelated families, who were identified by newborn screening or family member testing and normally developed without experiencing an metabolic crisis during the follow-up period of 2.6±1.96 years

rows.text: The clinical picture of isolated 3-MCC deficiency in clinically-ascertained cohorts may be more severe than NBS cohorts — selection bias [2,8].

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency: clinical, biochemical, enzymatic and molecular studies in 88 patients. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:31.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly invokes ascertainment bias and reports that only 5 of 53 NBS-identified individuals had metabolic decompensations versus 12 overall, implying greater severity in clinically ascertained cases.
judged.quote: However, 12 patients (5 of 53 identified by newborn screening) presented with acute metabolic decompensations.

judged.citation: Jung CW et al. Uneventful clinical courses of Korean patients with methylcrotonylglycinuria and their common mutations. J Hum Genet. 2012;57(1):62–4.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the benign course of NBS-identified patients and a highly variable phenotype, but does not itself compare clinically-ascertained cohorts with NBS cohorts or invoke selection bias.
judged.quote: With the introduction of newborn screening using tandem mass spectrometry, most patients with MCG are identified in their asymptomatic neonatal periods.

rows.text: Excellent for NBS-detected cases — most remain asymptomatic through childhood and adulthood [1,2].

judged.citation: Baumgartner MR et al. The molecular basis of human 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency. J Clin Invest. 2001;107(4):495–504.
judged.reason: The abstract notes that the phenotypic spectrum includes asymptomatic adults, but does not address outcomes of newborn-screening-detected cases or state that most remain asymptomatic through childhood and adulthood.
judged.quote: The phenotype is variable, ranging from neonatal onset with severe neurological involvement to asymptomatic adults.

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency: clinical, biochemical, enzymatic and molecular studies in 88 patients. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that most individuals (including NBS-identified) are asymptomatic and penetrance is low, but it provides no longitudinal follow-up showing they remain asymptomatic through childhood and adulthood, and notes 5 of 53 NBS-detected cases had decompensations.
judged.quote: Our data confirm that MCC deficiency, despite low penetrance, may lead to a severe clinical phenotype resembling classical organic acidurias.

rows.text: Accumulation of HMG-CoA and its derivatives impairs ketogenesis, so patients present with HYPOKETOTIC hypoglycaemia (resembling FAO disorders) plus metabolic acidosis (resembling organic acidaemias) — a diagnostically distinctive combination [1,2].

judged.citation: Menao S et al. Clinical, biochemical and molecular study of 24 patients with HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2009;30(8):E520–40.
judged.reason: The abstract states the disorder affects ketogenesis and leucine catabolism and that acute symptoms include both hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic acidosis, which is the combination claimed.
judged.quote: 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaric aciduria is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder that affects ketogenesis and L-leucine catabolism. The clinical acute symptoms include vomiting, convulsions, metabolic acidosis, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and lethargy.

judged.citation: Pié J et al. Molecular genetics of HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2007;92(3):198–209.
judged.reason: The abstract supports impaired ketogenesis, reduced ketone body synthesis and hypoglycaemia, but does not mention metabolic acidosis or the diagnostic overlap with FAO disorders/organic acidaemias.
judged.quote: 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase (HL) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder that affects ketogenesis and l-leucine catabolism... Patients with HL deficiency have a reduced capacity to synthesize ketone bodies.

rows.text: Worldwide rare (~1:250,000) but relatively common in Saudi Arabia and Portugal due to founder variants [4].

judged.citation: Mitchell GA et al. HMG CoA lyase deficiency: identification of five causal point mutations in codons 41 and 42, including a frequent Saudi Arabian mutation, R41Q. Am J Hum Genet. 1998;62(2):295–300.
judged.reason: The abstract supports high frequency in Saudi Arabia with a recurrent (founder-type) R41Q mutation, but gives no worldwide incidence figure (~1:250,000) and does not mention Portugal.
judged.quote: is reported to be frequent and clinically severe in Saudi Arabia. We found genetic diversity among nine Saudi HL-deficient probands: six were homozygous for the missense mutation R41Q

rows.text: Urine organic acids during crisis: markedly elevated 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaric acid (HMG) — the pathognomonic metabolite — plus 3-methylglutaric acid, 3-methylglutaconic acid and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid [1,5].

judged.citation: Menao S et al. Clinical, biochemical and molecular study of 24 patients with HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2009;30(8):E520–40.
judged.reason: The abstract is a mutation/enzyme-expression study and does not report urine organic acid profiles or the individual metabolites listed in the claim.

judged.citation: Wysocki SJ et al. 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A lyase deficiency. Clin Chim Acta. 1976;73(3):553–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaric aciduria in a patient with HMG-CoA lyase deficiency, but says nothing about the accompanying metabolites (3-methylglutaric, 3-methylglutaconic, 3-hydroxyisovaleric acids), the crisis context, or the pathognomonic status of HMG.
judged.quote: A marked deficiency of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A lyase activity is present in cultured skin fibroblasts from a baby with 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaric aciduria.

rows.text: Plasma C6DC (3-methylglutarylcarnitine) and C5-OH elevated on acylcarnitines [2,6].

judged.citation: Pié J et al. Molecular genetics of HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2007;92(3):198–209.
judged.reason: The abstract is confined to mutational spectrum and enzyme structure and says nothing about acylcarnitine profiles such as C6DC or C5-OH.

judged.citation: Ozand PT et al. HMG-CoA lyase deficiency in Saudi Arabia. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1991;14(2):174–88.
judged.reason: The abstract reports diagnosis by enzyme assay and urine organic acid GC/MS but never addresses plasma acylcarnitine species such as C6DC or C5-OH.
judged.quote: The diagnosis was established by the measurement of enzyme activity in lymphocytes, in fibroblasts and, in seven patients, by the gas chromatography/mass spectrometer pattern of excreted organic acids in the urine.

rows.text: Over 50 variants reported; p.Glu37* founder in Saudi Arabia [4,7].

judged.citation: Mitchell GA et al. HMG CoA lyase deficiency: identification of five causal point mutations in codons 41 and 42, including a frequent Saudi Arabian mutation, R41Q. Am J Hum Genet. 1998;62(2):295–300.
judged.reason: The abstract directly addresses Saudi Arabian founder mutations in HMGCL but identifies R41Q (and F305fs(-2)), not p.Glu37*, and says nothing about a total of over 50 reported variants.
judged.quote: We found genetic diversity among nine Saudi HL-deficient probands: six were homozygous for the missense mutation R41Q, and two were homozygous for the frameshift mutation F305fs(-2).

judged.citation: Casals N et al. Structural (beta-alpha)8 TIM barrel model of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A lyase. J Biol Chem. 2003;278(31):29016–23.
judged.reason: The abstract contributes to and reviews the HMGCL mutation spectrum (three novel missense mutations plus localization of all missense mutations reported to date), but it does not state a total of over 50 variants and says nothing about a p.Glu37* founder variant in Saudi Arabia.
judged.quote: We also report the localization of all missense mutations reported to date and show that these mutations are located in the beta-sheets around the substrate cavity.

rows.text: Acute: IV 10% dextrose, correct acidosis with bicarbonate, IV carnitine, low-protein diet [1,2].

judged.citation: Menao S et al. Clinical, biochemical and molecular study of 24 patients with HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2009;30(8):E520–40.
judged.reason: The abstract is a mutation/enzyme-expression study and does not discuss acute management such as dextrose, bicarbonate, carnitine or protein restriction.

judged.citation: Pié J et al. Molecular genetics of HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2007;92(3):198–209.
judged.reason: The abstract is confined to mutational spectrum, enzyme structure and genotype–phenotype correlation and says nothing about acute or chronic management.

rows.text: Chronic: avoid fasting (age-specific limits), moderate leucine restriction + low-fat diet (fat cannot be ketogenic so minimising fat reduces acetoacetate precursor burden); L-carnitine 50–100 mg/kg/day; emergency protocol with IV glucose for illness [2].

judged.citation: Pié J et al. Molecular genetics of HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2007;92(3):198–209.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses molecular genetics and genotype-phenotype correlation, not dietary management, carnitine dosing or emergency protocols.

rows.text: Pre-NBS mortality 20% at first crisis; ~50% developmental delay in survivors [1,8].

judged.citation: Menao S et al. Clinical, biochemical and molecular study of 24 patients with HMG-CoA lyase deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2009;30(8):E520–40.
judged.reason: The abstract reports genotypes and enzyme activity only, with no mortality or developmental outcome data.

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency: clinical presentation and outcome. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):162.
judged.reason: The abstract supports ~50% developmental delay in survivors, but reports only that 6/37 patients (~16%) died prior to data collection, without establishing a 20% mortality at first crisis.
judged.quote: Six patients died prior to data collection. Long-term neurological complications were common. Half of the patients had a normal cognitive development while the remainder showed psychomotor deficits.

rows.text: NBS + prompt emergency protocol markedly improves outcomes — neurological outcome is largely determined by the severity of presenting crisis [8].

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency: clinical presentation and outcome. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):162.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the general principle that early diagnosis and avoidance of metabolic crises matter for outcome, but it does not present newborn-screening/emergency-protocol data showing markedly improved outcomes, nor does it establish that neurological outcome is determined by severity of the presenting crisis (it only reports absence of genotype-phenotype correlation and that half the patients had psychomotor deficits).
judged.quote: The overall outcome in HMGCLD appears limited, thus rendering early diagnosis and strict avoidance of metabolic crises important.

rows.text: Beta-ketothiolase deficiency (mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase deficiency, T2 deficiency; OMIM #203750) was first described by Daum in 1971 [3].

judged.citation: Daum RS et al. A 'new' disorder of isoleucine catabolism. Lancet. 1971;2(7737):1289–90.
judged.reason: The 1971 Daum paper describes a 'new' disorder of isoleucine catabolism with accumulation of alpha-methylacetoacetate, i.e., the first description of beta-ketothiolase deficiency, consistent with the historical first-description claim.
judged.quote: A disorder of isoleucine catabolism was found in a child with intermittent metabolic acidosis. The block occurs at the stage of propionate synthesis, and two intermediates--alpha-methylacetoacetate and alpha-methyl-beta-hydroxybutyrate--accumulate.

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. Molecular basis of beta-ketothiolase deficiency: mutations and polymorphisms in the human mitochondrial acetoacetyl-coenzyme A thiolase gene. Hum Mutat. 1995;5(2):113–20.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns mutation and polymorphism spectra in the T2 gene and says nothing about disease incidence or epidemiological frequency.

rows.text: ACAT1 acts in two metabolic pathways: (1) the terminal step of isoleucine catabolism (2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA → propionyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA) and (2) the activation of cytosolic ketone bodies (acetoacetyl-CoA ↔ 2 acetyl-CoA) in extrahepatic tissues [5].

judged.citation: Abdelkreem E et al. Mutation update on ACAT1 variants associated with mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase (T2) deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2019;40(10):1641–63.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms T2/ACAT1 functions in both ketone body and isoleucine metabolism, but does not state the specific reactions (2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA → propionyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA; acetoacetyl-CoA ↔ 2 acetyl-CoA), the subcellular compartment, or the extrahepatic tissue localization.
judged.quote: Mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase (T2, encoded by the ACAT1 gene) deficiency is an inherited disorder of ketone body and isoleucine metabolism.

rows.text: During a ketoacidotic crisis: elevated urinary tiglylglycine (TG) + 2-methylacetoacetic acid (2MAA) + 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyric acid — this triad is pathognomonic [1,6].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. The clinical phenotype and outcome of mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase deficiency (beta-ketothiolase or T2 deficiency) in 26 enzymatically proved and mutation-defined patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2001;72(2):109–14.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions urinary tiglylglycine excretion during ketoacidosis but does not report 2-methylacetoacetic acid or 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyric acid, nor describe the triad as pathognomonic.
judged.quote: only the absence of or a low urinary excretion of tiglyglycine during ketoacidosis correlated with a mild genotype

rows.text: Over 70 pathogenic variants reported; ~75% are missense, some with residual activity [5,10].

judged.citation: Abdelkreem E et al. Mutation update on ACAT1 variants associated with mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase (T2) deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2019;40(10):1641–63.
judged.reason: The abstract supports >70 reported variants (105) and residual in vivo activity, but the ~75% missense proportion conflicts with the 56 of 105 missense variants (~53%) reported here.
judged.quote: To date, 105 ACAT1 variants have been reported in 149 T2-deficient patients. The 56 disease-associated missense ACAT1 variants have been mapped onto the crystal structure of T2.

judged.citation: Vakili R, Hashemian S. A novel mutation of beta-ketothiolase deficiency: the first report from Iran and review of literature. Iran J Child Neurol. 2018;12(3):113–21.
judged.reason: The abstract reports a single novel missense ACAT1 variant (a case report plus literature review) but gives no count of >70 variants, no ~75% missense proportion, and no residual-activity data.
judged.quote: In genetic assessment, we detected a novel homozygous mutation c.664A> C (p. Ser 222 Arg) in ACAT gene.

rows.text: Enzyme assay on cultured fibroblasts (acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase activity) is the gold-standard diagnostic test when biochemistry is equivocal [1].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. The clinical phenotype and outcome of mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase deficiency (beta-ketothiolase or T2 deficiency) in 26 enzymatically proved and mutation-defined patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2001;72(2):109–14.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that fibroblast acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase enzyme activity was used to prove the diagnosis in all 26 patients, but does not assert it is the gold standard when biochemistry is equivocal.
judged.quote: We determined the molecular basis of T2 enzyme deficiency in 26 patients at the levels of skin fibroblast enzyme activity, protein integrity, and DNA nucleotide sequence.

rows.text: Classic: previously-well child aged 6 months–3 years presents with severe ketoacidosis during an intercurrent viral illness or fasting — vomiting, tachypnoea, dehydration, impaired consciousness, profound ketonuria [1,2].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. The clinical phenotype and outcome of mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase deficiency (beta-ketothiolase or T2 deficiency) in 26 enzymatically proved and mutation-defined patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2001;72(2):109–14.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the age window of first ketoacidotic presentation but does not describe the triggers (viral illness, fasting) or the specific clinical features listed (vomiting, tachypnoea, dehydration, impaired consciousness, ketonuria).
judged.quote: The median age at onset for the first ketoacidotic episode is 15 months (range 3 days to 48 months).

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports episodic ketoacidotic decompensation in ketolysis defects but gives no age range (6 months–3 years) or the specific clinical features listed.
judged.quote: inborn errors of ketolysis are characterized by metabolic decompensations with ketoacidosis

rows.text: Chronic sequelae are uncommon with good crisis management; movement disorders (dystonia, extrapyramidal features) have been reported in a minority after severe episodes [11].

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. Clinical and molecular outcomes in BKT deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2017;122(1–2):67–75.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that chronic sequelae are uncommon with early diagnosis and preventive measures, but says nothing about movement disorders such as dystonia or extrapyramidal features after severe episodes.
judged.quote: Only 7% developed a major mental disability while the vast majority was cognitively normal.

rows.text: Crisis frequency decreases with age; most patients become clinically stable by adolescence [1,11].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. The clinical phenotype and outcome of mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase deficiency (beta-ketothiolase or T2 deficiency) in 26 enzymatically proved and mutation-defined patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2001;72(2):109–14.
judged.reason: The abstract directly reports declining attack frequency with age with the last episode at 10 years and generally favourable outcome.
judged.quote: The frequency of attacks falls with age, the last in our series occurring at 10 years of age; 11 patients had only one episode and 3 patients had none.

judged.citation: Grünert SC et al. Clinical and molecular outcomes in BKT deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2017;122(1–2):67–75.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a good overall prognosis and that manifestation occurred only in early childhood (5 months–6.8 years) in a cohort followed to age 27, but it does not state that crisis frequency decreases with age or that most patients become clinically stable by adolescence.
judged.quote: Our study underlines that the prognosis in MAT deficiency is good and MAT deficient individuals may remain asymptomatic, if diagnosed early and preventive measures are applied.

rows.text: Prognosis is favourable with fasting avoidance [1,2].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. Ketone body metabolism and its defects. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(4):541–51.
judged.reason: The abstract describes ketone body metabolism and diagnostic features of SCOT deficiency but says nothing about prognosis or fasting-avoidance management.

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a generally good clinical outcome for ketone body metabolism defects but does not specify fasting avoidance as the determinant.
judged.quote: patients with inborn errors of ketone body metabolism often have a good clinical outcome

rows.text: SCOT deficiency (OMIM #245050) was described in 1972 by Tildon and Cornblath [3].

judged.citation: Tildon JT, Cornblath M. Succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase deficiency: a cause of ketoacidosis in infancy. J Clin Invest. 1972;51(3):493–8.
judged.reason: The 1972 paper by Tildon and Cornblath reports the first description of absent succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA-transferase activity as a cause of infantile ketoacidosis, matching the claimed first description.
judged.quote: No measurable succinyl-CoA: 3-ketoacid CoA-transferase (CoA-transferase) activity could be detected in homogenates of the post mortem brain, muscle and kidney tissue, or in the cultured skin fibroblasts.

rows.text: Persistent non-diabetic ketonaemia: elevated β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) and acetoacetate (AcAc) even in the fed state, with further marked elevation during fasting or illness [1,2].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. Ketone body metabolism and its defects. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(4):541–51.
judged.reason: The abstract states permanent ketosis is pathognomonic for SCOT deficiency (i.e. ketonaemia including the fed state) and frames ketone body levels in relation to fasting time and ketogenic stresses, with AcAc and 3HB as the two main ketone bodies.
judged.quote: Permanent ketosis is pathognomonic for SCOT deficiency.

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies SCOT as the rate-limiting ketolytic enzyme whose deficiency causes ketoacidotic decompensation, but does not describe persistent fed-state ketonaemia or any threshold values.
judged.quote: The rate-limiting enzyme of ketone body utilization (ketolysis) is succinyl-coenzyme A:3-oxoacid coenzyme A transferase.

rows.text: OXCT1 gene sequencing confirms [4].

judged.citation: Shafqat N et al. A structural mapping of mutations causing succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (SCOT) deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(6):983–7.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that OXCT1 encodes SCOT and that ~20 disease-associated alleles are known, which underpins molecular testing, but it does not state that OXCT1 sequencing is used to confirm the diagnosis.
judged.quote: To date there are ~20 disease-associated alleles on the OXCT1 gene that encodes the mitochondrial enzyme SCOT.

rows.text: Genotype does track phenotype to a degree: patients whose variants retain no residual activity have PERMANENT ketosis, whereas those with a 'mild' variant retaining significant residual activity may have normal ketone levels between crises while still suffering severe ketoacidotic episodes [4,5].

judged.citation: Shafqat N et al. A structural mapping of mutations causing succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (SCOT) deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(6):983–7.
judged.reason: The abstract notes the phenotype of ketoacidotic episodes with often permanent ketosis and maps mutations to structural effects, but it does not report the genotype–phenotype relationship in which residual-activity ('mild') variants give normal interictal ketone levels versus permanent ketosis with null variants.
judged.quote: characterized by ketoacidotic episodes and often permanent ketosis

judged.citation: Hori T et al. Inborn errors of ketone body utilization. Pediatr Int. 2015;57(1):41–8.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly states permanent ketosis is pathognomonic of severe-genotype SCOT deficiency (no residual activity) while mild-genotype patients may lack permanent ketosis yet develop severe ketoacidotic episodes.
judged.quote: Permanent ketosis is a pathognomonic characteristic of SCOT-deficient patients with severe genotype. Patients with mild genotype, however, may not have permanent ketosis, although they may develop severe ketoacidotic episodes similar to patients with severe genotype.

rows.text: Classic: first crisis in the first year of life, precipitated by intercurrent illness or fasting — severe metabolic acidosis with profound ketosis (BHB often >15 mmol/L), Kussmaul breathing, dehydration, lethargy [1,2].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. Ketone body metabolism and its defects. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(4):541–51.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms SCOT deficiency is a ketolysis defect with permanent ketosis and that ketone levels must be read against fasting/ketogenic stress, but gives no age of first crisis, no BHB >15 mmol/L threshold, and no clinical signs such as Kussmaul breathing, dehydration or lethargy.
judged.quote: Succinyl-CoA-3-oxoacid CoA transferase (SCOT) deficiency and beta-ketothiolase (T2) deficiency are two defects in ketolysis. Permanent ketosis is pathognomonic for SCOT deficiency.

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: Ketoacidotic decompensation is supported, but the abstract gives no age of first crisis, precipitants, or BHB >15 mmol/L figure.
judged.quote: inborn errors of ketolysis are characterized by metabolic decompensations with ketoacidosis

rows.text: Acute crisis: IV 10% dextrose (≥10 mg/kg/min) + fluid + bicarbonate — episodes resolve rapidly with glucose administration [2].

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies SCOT as the rate-limiting ketolytic enzyme and notes ketoacidotic decompensation, but gives no acute management details such as 10% dextrose at ≥10 mg/kg/min, bicarbonate, or rapid response to glucose.
judged.quote: The rate-limiting enzyme of ketone body utilization (ketolysis) is succinyl-coenzyme A:3-oxoacid coenzyme A transferase.

rows.text: Generally favourable — most patients have normal long-term cognitive and physical development once fasting is avoided [1,2].

judged.citation: Fukao T et al. Ketone body metabolism and its defects. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(4):541–51.
judged.reason: The abstract announces a review of disease course in adults but reports no outcome data on cognitive or physical development or on fasting avoidance.

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports frequently good outcome with early recognition and treatment but says nothing about normal cognitive/physical development or fasting avoidance specifically.
judged.quote: If those diseases are considered early and appropriate treatment is initiated without delay, patients with inborn errors of ketone body metabolism often have a good clinical outcome.

rows.text: Prognosis is favourable with fasting avoidance [1,2].

judged.citation: Aledo R et al. Genetic basis of mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase deficiency. Hum Genet. 2001;109(1):19–23.
judged.reason: The abstract is confined to molecular/genetic findings and clinical-biochemical recognition; it says nothing about prognosis or fasting-avoidance management.

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: Good outcome with timely treatment of ketogenesis defects is stated, but fasting avoidance as the specific measure is not.
judged.quote: While disorders of ketogenesis can present with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, inborn errors of ketolysis are characterized by metabolic decompensations with ketoacidosis. If those diseases are considered early and appropriate treatment is initiated without delay, patients with inborn errors of ketone body metabolism often have a good clinical outcome.

rows.text: DURING A CRISIS: inappropriately low ketones (BHB <1 mmol/L) with hypoglycaemia, elevated free fatty acids (FFA) — FFA:BHB ratio markedly elevated (>3), which distinguishes from normal fasting physiology [1,2].

judged.citation: Aledo R et al. Genetic basis of mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase deficiency. Hum Genet. 2001;109(1):19–23.
judged.reason: The abstract supports hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting but gives no BHB threshold, free fatty acid levels, or FFA:BHB ratio >3.
judged.quote: a recessive disorder of ketogenesis that has been previously diagnosed in two children with hypoglycaemic hypoketotic coma during fasting periods

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in ketogenesis defects but provides no BHB threshold or FFA:BHB ratio value.
judged.quote: disorders of ketogenesis can present with hypoketotic hypoglycemia

rows.text: UOA: mild dicarboxylic aciduria during crises (non-specific) — 4-hydroxy-6-methyl-2-pyrone has been described as relatively specific [4].

judged.citation: Lee T et al. A Japanese case of mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase deficiency who presented with severe metabolic acidosis and fatty liver without hypoglycemia. JIMD Rep. 2019;48(1):19–25.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms dicarboxylic aciduria and the presence of 4-hydroxy-6-methyl-2-pyrone on urinary organic acid analysis in mHS deficiency, but does not characterise the pyrone as relatively specific (indeed it emphasises poor biochemical markers).
judged.quote: Urinary organic acid analysis revealed hypoketotic dicarboxylic aciduria, and increased excretions of glutarate, and, retrospectively, 4-hydroxy-6-methyl-2-pyrone.

rows.text: ENZYME assay requires liver tissue (HMGCS2 is liver-expressed) — molecular genetics is the preferred confirmatory test [5].

judged.citation: Pitt JJ et al. Mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase deficiency. Pediatr Res. 2015;77(6):697–703.
judged.reason: The abstract supports molecular testing as the confirmatory approach but says nothing about enzyme assay requiring liver tissue or hepatic expression of HMGCS2.
judged.quote: The diagnosis was confirmed by sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of the HMGCS2 gene.

rows.text: HMGCS2 at 1p12 encodes the mitochondrial isoform of HMG-CoA synthase (the cytosolic HMGCS1 is unaffected and handles cholesterol synthesis) [6]. ~20 pathogenic variants reported [5].

judged.citation: Boukaftane Y, Mitchell GA. Cloning and characterization of the human mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA synthase gene. Gene. 1997;195(2):121–6.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms HMGCS2 encodes the mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase and maps to chromosome 1p12-13, but says nothing about the cytosolic HMGCS1 isoform/cholesterol synthesis or the ~20 reported pathogenic variants.
judged.quote: The human mHS locus (HMGCS2) on chromosome 1p12-13 spans 25 kb and contains 10 exons.

judged.citation: Pitt JJ et al. Mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase deficiency. Pediatr Res. 2015;77(6):697–703.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses the mutation tally but reports 26 known HMGCS2 mutations rather than ~20, and does not address the 1p12 locus or the cytosolic HMGCS1 isoform (covered by the co-cited paper).
judged.quote: There are now 26 known HMGCS2 mutations, which are reviewed in the text.

rows.text: Infantile/toddler: Reye-like hepatopathy with hypoglycaemia during first prolonged fast (weaning, illness, gastroenteritis) — encephalopathy, hepatomegaly, elevated transaminases, coagulopathy [1,2].

judged.citation: Aledo R et al. Genetic basis of mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase deficiency. Hum Genet. 2001;109(1):19–23.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms fasting-triggered hypoglycaemic coma in children but does not mention hepatomegaly, transaminase elevation, coagulopathy, or a Reye-like hepatopathy.
judged.quote: two children with hypoglycaemic hypoketotic coma during fasting periods

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia is supported, but the Reye-like hepatopathy features (hepatomegaly, transaminitis, coagulopathy, encephalopathy) and fasting triggers are not described.
judged.quote: disorders of ketogenesis can present with hypoketotic hypoglycemia

rows.text: Acute: IV 10% dextrose (≥10 mg/kg/min), correct coagulopathy [2].

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract covers mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase deficiency as a ketogenesis defect with hypoketotic hypoglycemia but provides no acute treatment specifics such as IV 10% dextrose at ≥10 mg/kg/min or correction of coagulopathy.
judged.quote: While disorders of ketogenesis can present with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, inborn errors of ketolysis are characterized by metabolic decompensations with ketoacidosis.

rows.text: Chronic: avoid prolonged fasting (as for MCAD), uncooked cornstarch at bedtime in young children or continuous nasogastric feeds if tolerated poorly, high-carbohydrate low-fat diet, emergency protocol for illness [2,7].

judged.citation: Sass JO. Inborn errors of ketogenesis and ketone body utilization. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(1):23–8.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions treatment only in the generic sense of early initiation and contains no dietary or cornstarch/nasogastric feeding recommendations.
judged.quote: If those diseases are considered early and appropriate treatment is initiated without delay, patients with inborn errors of ketone body metabolism often have a good clinical outcome.

judged.citation: Conboy E et al. Mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA synthase deficiency: unique presenting laboratory values. JIMD Rep. 2018;40:63–9.
judged.reason: The abstract describes a case presentation, biomarkers and differential diagnosis of HMGCS2D but says nothing about chronic management measures such as fasting avoidance, cornstarch, nasogastric feeds, diet composition or emergency protocols.

rows.text: Adult life is typically unremarkable on maintenance regimen [7].

judged.citation: Conboy E et al. Mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA synthase deficiency: unique presenting laboratory values. JIMD Rep. 2018;40:63–9.
judged.reason: The abstract reports an acute infant presentation and biochemical findings and makes no statement about long-term or adult outcomes on a maintenance regimen.

rows.text: With newborn-screening detection and strict adherence to lysine-restricted diet and an emergency regimen during illnesses, neurological injury is preventable in the majority of affected children [1,2].

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Diagnosis and management of glutaric aciduria type I — revised recommendations. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(3):677–94.
judged.reason: The abstract states that striatal injury can be prevented in the majority of neonatally (screening) diagnosed patients with combined treatment comprising low lysine diet, carnitine and intensified emergency treatment during illness.
judged.quote: It has been shown that in the majority of neonatally diagnosed patients striatal injury can be prevented by combined metabolic treatment. Metabolic treatment that includes a low lysine diet, carnitine supplementation and intensified emergency treatment during acute episodes of intercurrent illness should be introduced and monitored by an experienced interdisciplinary team.

judged.citation: Boy N et al. Proposed recommendations for diagnosing and managing individuals with glutaric aciduria type I: third revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):75–101.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that newborn screening plus low-lysine diet, carnitine and emergency treatment improves neurological outcome when diagnosed early, but does not quantify that injury is preventable in the majority of children.
judged.quote: Metabolic treatment, consisting of low lysine diet, carnitine supplementation, and intensified emergency treatment during catabolism, is effective treatment and improves neurologic outcome in those individuals diagnosed early; treatment after symptom onset, however, is less effective.

rows.text: Worldwide incidence is ~1:100,000; it rises to ~1:300 in Amish and Lumbee communities from founder variants [4,5].

judged.citation: Morton DH et al. Glutaric aciduria type I: a common cause of episodic encephalopathy among the Amish. Am J Med Genet. 1991;41(1):89–95.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms GA-I is unusually common in the Lancaster County Amish (14 children from 7 families), but gives no incidence figures — neither the ~1:100,000 worldwide rate nor the ~1:300 Amish/Lumbee rate — and does not mention founder variants or the Lumbee.
judged.quote: An otherwise rare disorder, GA-I appears to be a common cause of acute encephalopathy and cerebral palsy among the Amish.

judged.citation: Basinger AA et al. Glutaric acidemia type I in patients of Lumbee heritage. Mol Genet Metab. 2006;88(1):90–2.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms a founder mutation causing GA-I in the Lumbee community but gives no incidence figures (neither ~1:100,000 worldwide nor ~1:300 in Lumbee/Amish).
judged.quote: Five Lumbee individuals with GA-I had homozygous 1240G>A mutations in GCD. This is a rare, known mutation that was likely introduced by a Lumbee founder.

rows.text: Loss of activity causes accumulation of glutaryl-CoA, glutaric acid (GA), 3-hydroxyglutaric acid (3-OHGA), glutaconic acid and glutarylcarnitine (C5DC) [1].

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Diagnosis and management of glutaric aciduria type I — revised recommendations. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(3):677–94.
judged.reason: The abstract attributes the disorder to glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency and lists the accumulating metabolites named in the claim.
judged.quote: This defect gives rise to elevated glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, glutaconic acid, and glutarylcarnitine

rows.text: C5DC on DBS acylcarnitines is the most sensitive NBS marker; C5DC/C8 ratio further improves specificity (distinguishing from medium-chain FAO disorders) [6,7].

judged.citation: Schulze A et al. Expanded newborn screening for inborn errors of metabolism. Pediatrics. 2003;111(6 Pt 1):1399–406.
judged.reason: The abstract reports overall yield, false-positive rate and outcomes of MS/MS newborn screening for 23 disorders but never discusses C5DC, the C5DC/C8 ratio, or differentiation from medium-chain FAO disorders.
judged.quote: During the period of study, 250,000 neonates in a German population were investigated for 23 inborn errors of metabolism by electrospray ionization-MS/MS.

rows.text: Urinary 3-OHGA/GA ratio helps distinguish GA1 from GA3 (SUGCT): >0.3 favours GA1 [8].

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Natural history, outcome and treatment efficacy in children with GA1. Pediatr Res. 2006;59(6):840–7.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns natural history, outcome and treatment efficacy in GCDH deficiency and mentions biochemical phenotype only to say it does not predict clinical phenotype; it says nothing about a urinary 3-OHGA/GA ratio, a >0.3 threshold, or differentiation from glutaric aciduria type III.
judged.quote: Notably, the biochemical phenotype did not predict the clinical phenotype.

rows.text: LOW EXCRETER phenotype — approximately 25% of genetically-confirmed GA1 patients have near-normal urinary GA and 3-OHGA; C5DC may also be borderline [9,10].

judged.citation: Christensen E et al. Correlation of genotype and phenotype in glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2004;27(6):861–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the existence of a low-excreter phenotype (mild mutations with residual activity showing low/normal urinary glutaric acid and mild 3-hydroxyglutaric acid elevation) but gives no ~25% prevalence figure and does not mention borderline C5DC.
judged.quote: Patients with a mild mutation on at least one chromosome frequently show unusual biochemical findings such as low or normal urinary excretion of glutaric acid and mild or only slightly increased excretion of 3-hydroxyglutaric acid.

judged.citation: Baric I et al. Diagnosis of glutaric acidemia type I: R402W allele in low excretors. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1999;22(7):867–81.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms a low-excretor group exists but gives 12/25 (~48%), not ~25%, and directly contradicts the claim that 3-OHGA is also near-normal, since quantitative 3-OHGA achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity in all patients regardless of GA excretion; C5DC is not addressed.
judged.quote: Low excretors (12 patients) were defined by a urinary glutaric acid below 100 mmol/mol creatinine down into the normal range, while high excretors (13 patients) had glutaric acid excretions well above this value... Diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of 100% could only be achieved by the quantitative determination of 3-hydroxyglutaric acid with the newly developed stable-isotope dilution assay, allowing an accurate diagnosis of all patients, regardless of the amount of glutaric acid excreted in urine.

rows.text: Low excreters carry IDENTICAL neurological risk to high excreters; molecular confirmation is required whenever clinical suspicion exists [9]. 3-OHGA is the more neurotoxic intermediate and its concentration in CSF correlates with basal-ganglia injury [11].

judged.citation: Christensen E et al. Correlation of genotype and phenotype in glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2004;27(6):861–8.
judged.reason: The abstract reports no correlation between biochemical phenotype (excretion pattern) and clinical outcome, and notes enzyme studies cannot always distinguish mild cases from carriers, supporting the part of the sentence attributed to this paper; the 3-OHGA/CSF claim is carried by the co-cited paper.
judged.quote: Clinical data were available for a subgroup of 79 patients. No correlation with the biochemical phenotype or the genotype could be established.

judged.citation: Funk CB et al. Neuropathological, biochemical and molecular findings in a GA-I cohort. Brain. 2005;128(Pt 4):711–22.
judged.reason: The abstract engages the topic of 3-OH-GA concentrations and striatal injury but measured brain (not CSF) levels and found no regional correlation with the selective basal-ganglia damage, and it does not establish 3-OHGA as the more neurotoxic intermediate; it also does not address low-excreter risk equivalence.
judged.quote: All brain regions demonstrated markedly elevated concentrations of GA (3770-21 200 nmol/g protein) and 3-OH-GA (280-740 nmol/g protein), with no evidence of striatal specificity or age dependency.

rows.text: The Amish founder variant is p.Ala421Val; the Lumbee variant is p.Arg402Trp (which uniquely predicts low-excreter phenotype) [5,10].

judged.citation: Basinger AA et al. Glutaric acidemia type I in patients of Lumbee heritage. Mol Genet Metab. 2006;88(1):90–2.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a rare Lumbee founder mutation in GCDH but reports it as "1240G>A" without naming p.Arg402Trp, and says nothing about the low-excreter phenotype or the Amish p.Ala421Val variant.
judged.quote: Five Lumbee individuals with GA-I had homozygous 1240G>A mutations in GCD. This is a rare, known mutation that was likely introduced by a Lumbee founder.

judged.citation: Baric I et al. Diagnosis of glutaric acidemia type I: R402W allele in low excretors. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1999;22(7):867–81.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns the diagnostic sensitivity/specificity of stable-isotope dilution assays for glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and defines low versus high excretors biochemically, but it reports no genotype data and never mentions p.Ala421Val, p.Arg402Trp, or Amish/Lumbee founder populations, so the variant-specific claim cannot be assessed from it.
judged.quote: Low excretors (12 patients) were defined by a urinary glutaric acid below 100 mmol/mol creatinine down into the normal range, while high excretors (13 patients) had glutaric acid excretions well above this value.

rows.text: Genotype–phenotype correlation for residual excretion exists but not for neurological outcome — low and high excreters have the same cerebral disease risk [9,12].

judged.citation: Christensen E et al. Correlation of genotype and phenotype in glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2004;27(6):861–8.
judged.reason: The abstract shows mild versus severe genotypes track with residual activity and urinary metabolite excretion while explicitly finding no correlation with clinical phenotype.
judged.quote: Patients with a mild mutation on at least one chromosome frequently show unusual biochemical findings such as low or normal urinary excretion of glutaric acid ... No correlation with the biochemical phenotype or the genotype could be established.

rows.text: Macrocephaly is present in ~50% at birth or develops progressively; it should prompt metabolic investigation in any infant [1].

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Diagnosis and management of glutaric aciduria type I — revised recommendations. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(3):677–94.
judged.reason: This guideline abstract summarises GA-I pathophysiology, diagnosis and treatment but never addresses macrocephaly or its frequency, so the claim's specific content cannot be judged from the abstract alone.
judged.quote: Untreated patients characteristically develop dystonia during infancy resulting in a high morbidity and mortality.

rows.text: Acute encephalopathic crisis: typically between 6 and 18 months, precipitated by fever, infection or prolonged fasting — sudden onset hypotonia, seizures, loss of developmental milestones and a fixed dystonic movement disorder from bilateral striatal injury [1,13].

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Diagnosis and management of glutaric aciduria type I — revised recommendations. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(3):677–94.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms infection-precipitated encephalopathic crises causing striatal injury and dystonia in infancy, but gives no 6–18 month age window and does not mention fasting, hypotonia, seizures or loss of milestones.
judged.quote: The neuropathological correlate is striatal injury which results from encephalopathic crises precipitated by infectious diseases, immunizations and surgery during a finite period of brain development

judged.citation: Hoffmann GF et al. Clinical course, early diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of disease in glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Neuropediatrics. 1996;27(3):115–23.
judged.reason: The abstract supports an acute encephalopathic crisis triggered by intercurrent illness with hypotonia, extrapyramidal symptoms and basal ganglia atrophy, but gives a mean onset of 12 months rather than the stated 6–18 month window, and does not mention seizures or prolonged fasting as a precipitant.
judged.quote: The patients often showed symptoms such as hypotonia, irritability, and jitteriness followed by an acute encephalopathic crisis occurring on average at 12 months of age.

rows.text: MRI findings: widened Sylvian fissures, fronto-temporal atrophy, subdural haematomas (may be mistaken for non-accidental injury), and in symptomatic patients, bilateral putaminal and caudate injury [1,15].

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Diagnosis and management of glutaric aciduria type I — revised recommendations. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(3):677–94.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions striatal injury as the neuropathological correlate but does not address neuroimaging findings such as widened Sylvian fissures, frontotemporal atrophy or subdural haematomas.

judged.citation: Twomey EL et al. Neuroimaging findings in glutaric aciduria type I. Pediatr Radiol. 2003;33(12):823–30.
judged.reason: The abstract documents widened Sylvian fissures, expanded CSF spaces anterior to the temporal lobes, subdural collections and basal ganglia signal abnormality, but does not mention confusion with non-accidental injury nor specify putaminal and caudate (rather than general basal ganglia) involvement.
judged.quote: Widening of the sylvian fissures and of the fluid spaces anterior to the temporal lobes was seen in 93% of cases... Abnormal high-signal intensity on T2-weighted (T2-W) images was seen in the basal ganglia and periventricular white matter in 64% of children. Subdural collections were found in 3 patients

rows.text: After age 6 years the risk of crisis falls markedly [1].

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Diagnosis and management of glutaric aciduria type I — revised recommendations. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(3):677–94.
judged.reason: The abstract refers to vulnerability during a 'finite period of brain development' but specifies no age threshold, so the age-6 cut-off is not carried.
judged.quote: during a finite period of brain development

rows.text: Three pillars of management [2]: (1) Lysine-restricted diet using a lysine-free, tryptophan-reduced amino acid formula, from diagnosis until at least age 6; (2) L-carnitine supplementation 100–200 mg/kg/day to maintain free carnitine and facilitate C5DC excretion; (3) Emergency protocol during any febrile illness, gastroenteritis or fasting: hospital admission if fever >38.5 °C, IV glucose (≥10 mg/kg/min), protein restriction for 24–48 h and doubled carnitine.

judged.citation: Boy N et al. Proposed recommendations for diagnosing and managing individuals with glutaric aciduria type I: third revision. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):75–101.
judged.reason: The abstract names the three treatment components (low-lysine diet, carnitine, intensified emergency treatment) but gives none of the specific doses, thresholds or durations (100–200 mg/kg/day, fever >38.5 °C, ≥10 mg/kg/min glucose, 24–48 h protein restriction).
