judged.reason: Doses of 10, 20 and 40 mg/day biotin are reported, but the abstract does not mention requirements up to 80 mg/day or variant-dependent biotin responsiveness.
judged.quote: Biotin therapy (20 or 40 mg/day) prevented further episodes and normalized biochemical parameters

rows.text: Block causes accumulation of γ-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB) and succinic semialdehyde, producing a clinical tetrad of non-progressive intellectual disability, disproportionate expressive language delay, hypotonia/ataxia and seizures — with a striking neuropsychiatric phenotype (OCD, aggression, sleep disturbance) that often dominates adolescent and adult care [1,2].

judged.citation: Pearl PL et al. Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency: lessons from mice and men. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(3):343–52.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms GABA/GHB elevation and the intellectual disability, hypotonia, ataxia, epilepsy, sleep and psychiatric features, but does not mention succinic semialdehyde accumulation, the non-progressive course, disproportionate expressive language delay, or OCD/aggression dominating adolescent/adult care.
judged.quote: a disorder of GABA degradation with subsequent elevations in brain GABA and GHB, is a neurometabolic disorder with intellectual disability, epilepsy, hypotonia, ataxia, sleep disorders, and psychiatric disturbances

rows.text: Standard urine organic-acid analysis detects GHB only if the laboratory integrates early-eluting hydroxy acids — many screens miss it and the test must be specifically requested [1,4].

judged.citation: Pearl PL et al. Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency: lessons from mice and men. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(3):343–52.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns pathophysiology, neuroimaging, EEG, mouse models and therapeutics, and says nothing about urine organic-acid analysis or detection of early-eluting hydroxy acids.

judged.citation: Gibson KM et al. Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency: an inborn error of γ-aminobutyric acid metabolism. Clin Chim Acta. 1984;141(1):73–83.
judged.reason: The abstract reports GHB accumulation and a lymphocyte enzyme assay but says nothing about organic-acid screening methodology, elution of hydroxy acids, or missed detection on routine screens.

rows.text: Over 70 pathogenic variants reported without a strong genotype–phenotype correlation [5].

judged.citation: Akaboshi S et al. Mutational spectrum of the succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase gene and functional analysis of 27 novel disease-causing mutations in patients with SSADH deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2003;22(6):442–50.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the absence of a strong genotype–phenotype correlation but documents a far smaller mutational spectrum (27 novel plus 8 previously reported, ~34 total), so the "over 70 pathogenic variants" figure is not carried.
judged.quote: This indicates that residual expression is not likely to be an important factor contributing to the large phenotypic differences observed among different families and even among siblings, suggesting that other modifying factors are of great importance in disease pathology.

rows.text: MRI shows bilateral symmetric globus pallidus and dentate nucleus T2 hyperintensity, reflecting GHB toxicity — a useful imaging clue [6,7].

judged.citation: Pearl PL et al. MRI findings in 4-hydroxybutyric aciduria (SSADH deficiency). J Inherit Metab Dis. 2003;26(6):635–8.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns behavioral/psychiatric features and CSF neurotransmitter metabolites in SSADH deficiency and never addresses MRI or globus pallidus/dentate nucleus signal changes.
judged.quote: To explore the potential biochemical basis of these behavioral abnormalities, we studied cerebrospinal fluid derived from 13 patients, which revealed significantly elevated GHB (65- to 230-fold), high free and total GABA (up to threefold), and low glutamine.

judged.citation: Ziyeh S et al. Selective involvement of the globus pallidus and dentate nucleus in succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency. Neuroradiology. 2002;44(7):567–71.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms T2 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus and dentate nucleus as a pattern suggestive of SSADH deficiency, but it does not state bilateral symmetry (single case) nor attribute the finding to GHB toxicity.
judged.quote: MRI showed an unusual pattern with hyperintense signal in the globus pallidus and cerebellar dentate nucleus in T2-weighted images.

rows.text: Adolescent and adult phase is often dominated by a challenging neuropsychiatric phenotype — OCD, aggression, hallucinations, sleep disturbance, anxiety — which frequently determines the level of care required [2,8].

judged.citation: Knerr I et al. Neuropsychiatric morbidity in adolescent and adult succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency patients. CNS Spectr. 2008;13(7):598–605.
judged.reason: The abstract supports prominent, persisting neuropsychiatric morbidity in adolescents/adults including aggression and anxiety, but does not mention OCD, hallucinations, sleep disturbance, or that these symptoms determine the level of care required.
judged.quote: Eighty-two percent demonstrated behavioral problems, such as attention deficit, hyperactivity, anxiety, or aggression, and 33% had >or=3 behavior problems.

rows.text: Vigabatrin (GABA-transaminase inhibitor) is NOT generally recommended — despite being a rational therapeutic target because it reduces GHB generation upstream, in practice it further elevates GABA and may exacerbate manifestations; it is reserved at most for selected cases under specialist supervision [9].

judged.citation: Casarano M et al. Efficacy of vigabatrin intervention in a mild phenotypic expression of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency. JIMD Rep. 2011;2:119–23.
judged.reason: The abstract supports only the notion that vigabatrin can be used beneficially in a selected case with close clinical/neurochemical monitoring, and says nothing about vigabatrin not being generally recommended, further elevating GABA, or exacerbating manifestations.
judged.quote: To reduce the GHB levels in body fluids, a treatment with vigabatrin at low dose (25 mg/kg per day) was started, monitoring its efficacy by clinical and neurochemical follow-up.

rows.text: Experimental: SGS-742 (GABA-B antagonist) failed in phase II trials; AAV9-ALDH5A1 gene therapy is in preclinical development [10].

judged.citation: Keller M, Opladen T et al. Assessment of intellectual impairment, health-related quality of life, and behavioral phenotype in patients with neurotransmitter related disorders: data from the iNTD registry. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(6):1489–502.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns IQ, quality of life, and behavioral phenotypes in neurotransmitter disorders and says nothing about SGS-742 trials or AAV9-ALDH5A1 gene therapy.

rows.text: No disease-modifying therapy is currently available [2,10].

judged.citation: Keller M, Opladen T et al. Assessment of intellectual impairment, health-related quality of life, and behavioral phenotype in patients with neurotransmitter related disorders: data from the iNTD registry. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(6):1489–502.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses cognitive, behavioral, and quality-of-life outcomes but does not discuss the availability or absence of disease-modifying therapy.

rows.text: The clinical phenotype is a slowly progressive infantile–childhood leukodystrophy with macrocephaly, cerebellar ataxia, seizures and intellectual disability, plus a substantial brain-tumour risk [1,2].

judged.citation: Steenweg ME et al. L-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria: pattern of MR imaging abnormalities in 56 patients. Radiology. 2009;251(3):856–65.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the slowly progressive leukodystrophy component (subcortical cerebral white matter abnormalities worsening with disease duration) but says nothing about macrocephaly, cerebellar ataxia, seizures, intellectual disability, or brain-tumour risk.
judged.quote: L2HGA has a distinct highly characteristic pattern of MR imaging abnormalities: a combination of predominantly subcortical cerebral WM abnormalities and abnormalities of the dentate nucleus, globus pallidus, putamen, and caudate nucleus. With increasing disease duration, WM abnormalities and basal ganglia signal intensity abnormalities become more diffuse and cerebral WM atrophy ensues.

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. Progress in understanding 2-hydroxyglutaric acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):571–87.
judged.reason: The review abstract only states that these disorders cause neurological impairment at a young age and announces that clinical characterization is presented, without any phenotypic detail (leukodystrophy, macrocephaly, ataxia, tumour risk) to assess.
judged.quote: The organic acidurias D: -2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D-2-HGA), L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (L-2-HGA), and combined D,L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D,L-2-HGA) cause neurological impairment at young age.

rows.text: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (OMIM #236792) was first described by Duran et al. in 1980 [3].

judged.citation: Duran M et al. L-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria: an inborn error of metabolism? J Inherit Metab Dis. 1980;3(4):109–12.
judged.reason: The 1980 Duran paper describes the first case of L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, with chiral confirmation of the L-configuration, matching the first-description claim.
judged.quote: A 5-year-old boy, excreting large amounts of 2-hydroxyglutaric acid in the urine (3.3-7.6 mmol/l), is described. ... The 2-hydroxyglutaric acid was found to have the L-configuration

rows.text: It must be distinguished from D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D2HGDH/IDH2 deficiency) — a biochemically and clinically different disorder — by STEREOSPECIFIC chiral chromatographic analysis of urine 2-hydroxyglutarate [4,5].

judged.citation: Struys EA et al. Measurement of urinary D- and L-2-hydroxyglutarate enantiomers by stable-isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS. Clin Chem. 2004;50(8):1391–5.
judged.reason: The abstract states that differential diagnosis of D-2-HGA versus L-2-HGA requires measurement of the corresponding enantiomer and presents a chiral derivatization chromatographic method for that purpose.
judged.quote: The differential diagnosis of D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D-2-HGA), L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (L-2-HGA), and the combined D/L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D/L-2-HGA) can be accomplished only by the measurement of the corresponding 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG).

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. IDH2 mutations in patients with D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Science. 2010;330(6002):336.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria is a distinct neurometabolic disorder caused by IDH2 mutations, but says nothing about stereospecific chiral chromatographic differentiation of urinary 2-hydroxyglutarate enantiomers (carried by the co-cited Struys method paper).
judged.quote: heterozygous germline mutations in IDH2 that alter enzyme residue Arg(140) in 15 unrelated patients with d-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D-2-HGA), a rare neurometabolic disorder characterized by supraphysiological levels of D-2-HG

rows.text: Elevation is specifically of the L-stereoisomer; D-form elevation points instead to D2HGDH or IDH2 deficiency (or, in adults, somatic IDH1/IDH2 mutation in gliomas or AML) [4,6].

judged.citation: Struys EA et al. Measurement of urinary D- and L-2-hydroxyglutarate enantiomers by stable-isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS. Clin Chem. 2004;50(8):1391–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that the distinct disorders are defined by which enantiomer is elevated, but says nothing about D2HGDH/IDH2 deficiency or somatic IDH1/IDH2 mutations in gliomas or AML.
judged.quote: The differential diagnosis of D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D-2-HGA), L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (L-2-HGA), and the combined D/L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D/L-2-HGA) can be accomplished only by the measurement of the corresponding 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG).

judged.citation: Topçu M et al. L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria: a report of 29 patients from Turkey. Turk J Pediatr. 2005;47(1):1–7.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that L2HGA is diagnosed by increased urinary excretion of the L-stereoisomer, but says nothing about D-form elevation indicating D2HGDH/IDH2 deficiency or somatic IDH1/IDH2 mutations in gliomas or AML.
judged.quote: Diagnosis was confirmed by increased urinary excretion of L-2-hydroxyglutaric acid in all patients

rows.text: Over 50 pathogenic variants (missense, splice, nonsense) reported without strong genotype–phenotype correlation [7,8].

judged.citation: Rzem R et al. A gene encoding a putative FAD-dependent L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase is mutated in L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2004;101(48):16849–54.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies L2HGDH mutations (three, in a few families) and the 14q22.1 locus but does not report over 50 variants nor address genotype–phenotype correlation.
judged.quote: Three mutations that replaced a highly conserved residue (Lys-71-Glu and Glu-176-Asp) or removed exon 9 were identified in homozygous state in patients from three distinct families and were found to cosegregate with the disease.

judged.citation: Vilarinho L et al. Novel L2HGDH mutations in 21 patients with L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria of Portuguese origin. Hum Mutat. 2005;26(4):395–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the variant classes (missense, nonsense, splice) and explicitly the absence of genotype–phenotype correlation, but it reports only seven novel mutations and does not support the tally of over 50 pathogenic variants.
judged.quote: All the mutations presumably lead to loss-of-function with no relationship between clinical signs, progression of the disease, levels of L-2-HGA and site of the mutation.

rows.text: MRI is highly characteristic and often triggers the diagnosis: bilateral SUBCORTICAL white-matter T2 hyperintensity (centripetal pattern — central white matter relatively spared, unlike most leukodystrophies) with additional signal change in the dentate nuclei, globus pallidus and putamen [9,10].

judged.citation: Barth PG et al. L-2-hydroxyglutaric acidaemia: clinical and biochemical findings in 12 patients and preliminary report on L-2-hydroxyacid dehydrogenase. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1993;16(4):753–61.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms subcortical leukoencephalopathy with cerebellar atrophy on MRI as a consistent feature, but does not mention the centripetal pattern with central white-matter sparing or signal change in the dentate nuclei, globus pallidus and putamen.
judged.quote: expressed as progressive ataxia, mental deficiency with subcortical leukoencephalopathy and cerebellar atrophy on magnetic resonance imaging

judged.citation: van der Knaap MS et al. D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria: further clinical delineation. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1999;22(4):404–13.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria and describes an entirely different MRI profile (ventriculomegaly, subependymal cysts, delayed maturation), without addressing the L-2-HGA subcortical/centripetal white-matter pattern or basal ganglia and dentate involvement that the sentence claims.
judged.quote: The most consistent MRI finding is enlargement of the lateral ventricles, occipital more than frontal. Regardless of the clinical phenotype, early MRI shows in addition subependymal cysts and signs of delayed cerebral maturation.

rows.text: A well-described complication is BRAIN TUMOUR — gliomas and medulloblastomas — attributed to oncometabolite activity of L-2-HG (competitive inhibition of TET-family DNA demethylases and histone demethylases); incidence ~5–10% of reported cases, warranting imaging surveillance [11,12].

judged.citation: Patay Z et al. Diffuse leukoencephalopathy associated with L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. AJNR Am J Neuroradiol. 2012;33(5):940–3.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the tumour predisposition and a ~5% prevalence with a 2-HG oncometabolite role, but does not state the 5–10% range, the specific tumour types (gliomas, medulloblastomas), the TET/histone demethylase inhibition mechanism, or a recommendation for imaging surveillance.
judged.quote: In 14 patients, the metabolic disorder was associated with cerebral neoplasms, suggesting an approximately 5% prevalence rate of CNS neoplasms in patients with L2-HGA

judged.citation: Moroni I et al. L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria and brain malignant tumours: a predisposing condition? Neurology. 2004;62(10):1882–4.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the association between L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria and malignant brain tumours as a predisposing condition, but gives no incidence figure (~5–10%), no tumour histology breakdown (gliomas/medulloblastomas), no oncometabolite/TET-demethylase mechanism, and no surveillance recommendation.
judged.quote: The authors report on four patients who developed a malignant brain tumor during the course of the disease. This association points to a possible role of L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria in predisposing to brain tumorigenesis.

rows.text: Riboflavin (50–400 mg/day) and FAD have been trialled (enzyme is FAD-dependent) with occasional biochemical improvement but no proven clinical benefit [2,7].

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. Progress in understanding 2-hydroxyglutaric acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):571–87.
judged.reason: The abstract makes no mention of therapy, riboflavin, FAD supplementation or treatment outcomes.

judged.citation: Rzem R et al. A gene encoding a putative FAD-dependent L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase is mutated in L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2004;101(48):16849–54.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the FAD-dependent nature of the deficient enzyme (the stated rationale) but says nothing about riboflavin or FAD trials, the 50–400 mg/day dosing, or biochemical versus clinical response.
judged.quote: Evidence is provided for the existence in rat tissues of a FAD-dependent enzyme catalyzing specifically the oxidation of L-2-hydroxyglutarate to alpha-ketoglutarate.

rows.text: Serial MRI every 1–3 years is recommended from childhood because of brain-tumour risk [11].

judged.citation: Patay Z et al. Diffuse leukoencephalopathy associated with L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. AJNR Am J Neuroradiol. 2012;33(5):940–3.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the brain-tumour predisposition and an approximate 5% CNS neoplasm prevalence that motivates surveillance, but it gives no imaging schedule such as every 1–3 years or a starting age in childhood.
judged.quote: In 14 patients, the metabolic disorder was associated with cerebral neoplasms, suggesting an approximately 5% prevalence rate of CNS neoplasms in patients with L2-HGA

rows.text: Earlier diagnosis enables imaging surveillance but does not modify the primary neurodegenerative course [2,11].

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. Progress in understanding 2-hydroxyglutaric acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):571–87.
judged.reason: The abstract says nothing about diagnosis timing, imaging surveillance or the natural history/neurodegenerative course.

judged.citation: Patay Z et al. Diffuse leukoencephalopathy associated with L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. AJNR Am J Neuroradiol. 2012;33(5):940–3.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the tumour risk that underpins imaging surveillance but says nothing about earlier diagnosis or about failure to modify the underlying neurodegenerative course.
judged.quote: Increasing evidence suggests that patients with L2-HGA have a predisposition to cerebral neoplasms.

rows.text: Monoallelic germline FH variants in adults cause hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) — a cancer-predisposition syndrome entirely distinct from the biallelic metabolic disorder but caused by the same gene [1,2].

judged.citation: Bourgeron T et al. Mutation of the fumarase gene in two siblings with progressive encephalopathy and fumarase deficiency. J Clin Invest. 1994;93(6):2514–8.
judged.reason: The abstract describes biallelic fumarase deficiency in two siblings and heterozygous carrier parents with half-normal enzyme activity, but says nothing about cancer predisposition or HLRCC, which is the claim's subject.
judged.quote: Both parents exhibited half the expected fumarase activity in their lymphocytes and were found to be heterozygous for this substitution.

judged.citation: Tomlinson IPM et al. Germline mutations in FH predispose to dominantly inherited uterine fibroids, skin leiomyomata and papillary renal-cell cancer. Nat Genet. 2002;30(4):406–10.
judged.reason: The abstract states that heterozygous germline FH mutations cause dominantly inherited leiomyomata/renal cell carcinoma while biallelic mutations cause the recessive fumarate hydratase deficiency, with very different clinical phenotypes from the same gene.
judged.quote: Mutations in FH also occur in the recessive condition fumarate hydratase deficiency, and some parents of people with this condition are susceptible to leiomyomata. Thus, heterozygous and homozygous or compound heterozygous mutants have very different clinical phenotypes.

rows.text: Fumarase deficiency (OMIM #606812) was first described biochemically by Zinn et al. in 1986 [3].

judged.citation: Zinn AB et al. Fumarase deficiency: a new cause of mitochondrial encephalomyopathy. N Engl J Med. 1986;315(8):469–75.
judged.reason: This is the 1986 Zinn et al. report presenting fumarase deficiency as a newly recognized biochemical defect, matching the claim of first biochemical description.
judged.quote: We observed a deficiency of both the mitochondrial and cytosolic forms of fumarase in a male infant with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy

rows.text: It is very rare (fewer than ~100 published cases) but is notable for its consistent and severe phenotype, highly distinctive brain-imaging findings, and the dual-phenotype biology of the FH gene: biallelic loss of function causes infantile metabolic encephalopathy, while heterozygous germline variants cause HLRCC — an autosomal-dominant tumour syndrome [4,5].

judged.citation: Menko FH, Schmidt LS, Linehan WM et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): renal cancer risk, surveillance and treatment. Fam Cancer. 2014;13(4):637–44.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that germline (heterozygous) FH mutations cause the autosomal-dominant tumour syndrome HLRCC, but says nothing about biallelic infantile metabolic encephalopathy, brain-imaging findings, or the "fewer than ~100 published cases" figure.
judged.quote: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC) is an autosomal dominant condition in which susceptible individuals are at risk for the development of cutaneous leiomyomas, early onset multiple uterine leiomyomas and an aggressive form of type 2 papillary renal cell cancer. HLRCC is caused by germline mutations in the fumarate hydratase (FH) gene

judged.citation: Ottolenghi C et al. Clinical and biochemical heterogeneity associated with fumarate hydratase deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2011;32(9):1046–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the rarity (<30 unrelated cases, consistent with fewer than ~100) and the dual-phenotype FH biology (biallelic FD with severe neurological impairment vs heterozygous mutations causing HLRCC), but it explicitly documents clinical and biochemical heterogeneity, which conflicts with the claim of a "consistent" phenotype, and it does not address autosomal-dominant inheritance of HLRCC.
judged.quote: Fumarase deficiency (FD), caused by biallelic alteration of the Fumarase Hydratase gene (FH), and a rare metabolic disorder that affects the Krebs cycle, causes severe neurological impairment and fumaric aciduria. Less than 30 unrelated cases are known to date. In addition, heterozygous mutations of the FH gene are responsible for hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC).

rows.text: Enzyme assay: FH activity in cultured fibroblasts, lymphocytes or muscle <20% of normal [1,6].

judged.citation: Bourgeron T et al. Mutation of the fumarase gene in two siblings with progressive encephalopathy and fumarase deficiency. J Clin Invest. 1994;93(6):2514–8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms enzyme assay diagnosis of profound fumarase deficiency in multiple tissues including lymphocytes, but gives no quantitative residual activity figure supporting the specific <20% of normal threshold.
judged.quote: The deficiency was profound and present in all tissues investigated, affecting the cytosolic and the mitochondrial fumarase isoenzymes to the same degree.

judged.citation: Kerrigan JF et al. Fumaric aciduria: clinical and imaging features. Ann Neurol. 2000;47(5):583–8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the disorder results from deficient fumarate hydratase activity but gives no enzyme assay data, no tissue sources (fibroblasts, lymphocytes, muscle), and no <20%-of-normal residual activity threshold.
judged.quote: Fumaric aciduria (fumaric acidemia, fumarase deficiency) is a rare inborn error of metabolism caused by deficient activity of fumarate hydratase

rows.text: Monoallelic germline variants cause HLRCC (hereditary leiomyomatosis + renal cell cancer, type 2 papillary subtype, often aggressive) [2,4].

judged.citation: Tomlinson IPM et al. Germline mutations in FH predispose to dominantly inherited uterine fibroids, skin leiomyomata and papillary renal-cell cancer. Nat Genet. 2002;30(4):406–10.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that monoallelic germline FH mutations predispose to dominantly inherited leiomyomatosis and papillary renal cell cancer, but does not specify the type 2 papillary subtype or its aggressive behaviour.
judged.quote: Germline mutations in FH predispose to dominantly inherited uterine fibroids, skin leiomyomata and papillary renal cell cancer.

judged.citation: Menko FH, Schmidt LS, Linehan WM et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): renal cancer risk, surveillance and treatment. Fam Cancer. 2014;13(4):637–44.
judged.reason: The abstract directly states that germline FH mutations cause HLRCC with aggressive type 2 papillary renal cell cancer.
judged.quote: an aggressive form of type 2 papillary renal cell cancer. HLRCC is caused by germline mutations in the fumarate hydratase (FH) gene

rows.text: Parents of infants with fumarase deficiency are obligate heterozygotes and are at HLRCC risk — cascade screening and surveillance should be offered [4].

judged.citation: Menko FH, Schmidt LS, Linehan WM et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): renal cancer risk, surveillance and treatment. Fam Cancer. 2014;13(4):637–44.
judged.reason: The abstract supports predictive FH testing and surveillance within HLRCC families, but does not address parents of infants with fumarase deficiency as obligate heterozygotes.
judged.quote: periodic renal imaging and, when available, predictive testing for a FH mutation is recommended from 8 to 10 years of age

rows.text: Fumarate itself is oncometabolic (competitive inhibitor of α-KG-dependent dioxygenases), linking the two phenotypes mechanistically [7].

judged.citation: Isaacs JS et al. HIF overexpression correlates with biallelic loss of fumarate hydratase in renal cancer. Cancer Cell. 2005;8(2):143–53.
judged.reason: The abstract shows elevated intracellular fumarate acts as a competitive inhibitor of HIF prolyl hydroxylase (an α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase) with resulting HIF stabilization in FH-mutant renal cancer, supporting fumarate's oncometabolite role linking FH loss to tumorigenesis.
judged.quote: We demonstrate that FH inhibition, together with elevated intracellular fumarate, coincides with HIF upregulation. Further, we show that fumarate acts as a competitive inhibitor of HPH.

rows.text: Brain imaging — highly characteristic — shows combinations of polymicrogyria, agenesis of the corpus callosum, open opercula, enlarged lateral ventricles, delayed myelination and sometimes brainstem hypoplasia [6,8].

judged.citation: Kerrigan JF et al. Fumaric aciduria: clinical and imaging features. Ann Neurol. 2000;47(5):583–8.
judged.reason: Polymicrogyria, open opercula and enlarged ventricles are explicitly reported, but corpus callosum agenesis, delayed myelination and brainstem hypoplasia are not addressed in the abstract.
judged.quote: Magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple abnormalities, including diffuse polymicrogyria, decreased cerebral white matter, large ventricles, and open opercula.

rows.text: Adult heterozygous HLRCC / FH Tumour Predisposition Syndrome: cutaneous piloleiomyomas (present in ~50–80%), uterine fibroids (~40–90% of females, mean diagnosis age ~30 y) and renal cell carcinoma (~10–15% lifetime risk; histologic subtypes include type 2 papillary, tubulocystic, unclassified and collecting-duct carcinoma) [2,4].

judged.citation: Tomlinson IPM et al. Germline mutations in FH predispose to dominantly inherited uterine fibroids, skin leiomyomata and papillary renal-cell cancer. Nat Genet. 2002;30(4):406–10.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that heterozygous germline FH mutations predispose to cutaneous leiomyomata, uterine fibroids and papillary renal cell cancer with a phenotype distinct from the recessive deficiency, but gives none of the specific quantitative details (~50–80% piloleiomyomas, ~40–90% fibroids, mean age ~30 y, ~10–15% RCC risk) or the RCC histologic subtypes.
judged.quote: Germline mutations in FH predispose to dominantly inherited uterine fibroids, skin leiomyomata and papillary renal cell cancer.

judged.citation: Menko FH, Schmidt LS, Linehan WM et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): renal cancer risk, surveillance and treatment. Fam Cancer. 2014;13(4):637–44.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the HLRCC triad of cutaneous leiomyomas, early-onset multiple uterine leiomyomas and type 2 papillary RCC with a 15% lifetime renal cancer risk, but gives no penetrance percentages for skin/uterine lesions, no mean age of fibroid diagnosis, and does not mention tubulocystic, unclassified or collecting-duct histologies.
judged.quote: susceptible individuals are at risk for the development of cutaneous leiomyomas, early onset multiple uterine leiomyomas and an aggressive form of type 2 papillary renal cell cancer... The lifetime renal cancer risk for FH mutation carriers is estimated to be 15 %.

rows.text: Experimental ketogenic-diet and high-dose multivitamin regimens have no proven benefit [1].

judged.citation: Bourgeron T et al. Mutation of the fumarase gene in two siblings with progressive encephalopathy and fumarase deficiency. J Clin Invest. 1994;93(6):2514–8.
judged.reason: The abstract is purely a biochemical and molecular characterisation and does not mention any therapy, including ketogenic diet or high-dose vitamins.

rows.text: For metastatic disease: erlotinib + bevacizumab, or cabozantinib + nivolumab [4,9].

judged.citation: Menko FH, Schmidt LS, Linehan WM et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): renal cancer risk, surveillance and treatment. Fam Cancer. 2014;13(4):637–44.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses systemic treatment of metastatic HLRCC disease but names no specific regimens, recommending clinical trial enrolment instead of erlotinib/bevacizumab or cabozantinib/nivolumab.
judged.quote: The choice for systemic treatment in metastatic disease should, if possible, be part of a clinical trial.

judged.citation: Grubb RL et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer: a syndrome associated with an aggressive form of inherited renal cancer. J Urol. 2007;177(6):2074–9.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses surgical management and surveillance of HLRCC renal tumours only and says nothing about systemic therapy or the named drug regimens for metastatic disease.
judged.quote: We report the clinical characteristics and urological treatment of patients with hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer associated renal tumors.

rows.text: Early surveillance-detected surgical resection is therefore the key to reducing mortality [4,9].

judged.citation: Menko FH, Schmidt LS, Linehan WM et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): renal cancer risk, surveillance and treatment. Fam Cancer. 2014;13(4):637–44.
judged.reason: The abstract recommends surveillance imaging with prompt wide-margin surgical excision because of early-onset aggressive RCC, which is the substance of the claim.
judged.quote: In view of the potential for early onset of RCC in HLRCC, periodic renal imaging and, when available, predictive testing for a FH mutation is recommended from 8 to 10 years of age.... Treatment of renal tumours should be prompt and generally consist of wide-margin surgical excision

judged.citation: Grubb RL et al. Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer: a syndrome associated with an aggressive form of inherited renal cancer. J Urol. 2007;177(6):2074–9.
judged.reason: The abstract shows HLRCC tumours metastasise while small and concludes that prompt surgery rather than observation plus careful follow-up of at-risk individuals is required, which is the substance of the claim, though it does not quantify mortality reduction.
judged.quote: In contrast to other familial renal cancer syndromes, the observation of 3 cm or less renal tumors associated with hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer is not recommended. Careful followup of affected and at risk individuals in families is necessary.

rows.text: Uniquely among FAO disorders, treatment (lifelong oral L-carnitine) is fully replete and prevents virtually all disease sequelae [1,2].

judged.citation: Magoulas PL, El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency: an overview. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:68.
judged.reason: The abstract supports lifelong oral L-carnitine as primary treatment with favorable long-term prognosis, but does not address the comparative claim that this is unique among FAO disorders or that virtually all sequelae are prevented.
judged.quote: Primary treatment involves supplementation of oral levocarnitine (L-carnitine) at a dose of 50-400 mg/kg/day divided into three doses... the long-term prognosis is favorable as long as individuals remain on carnitine supplementation.

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency. GeneReviews®. 2012 [updated 2022].
judged.reason: The abstract supports that oral levocarnitine improves decompensation and muscle function, but it conditions this on starting before irreversible organ damage and never claims prevention of virtually all sequelae or uniqueness among FAO disorders.
judged.quote: Metabolic decompensation and skeletal and cardiac muscle function improve with 100-200 mg/kg/day oral levocarnitine if it is started before irreversible organ damage occurs.

rows.text: Incidence varies dramatically with population: ~1:40,000 in NBS cohorts overall but 1:300 in the Faroe Islands (c.95A>G founder variant) [4,5].

judged.citation: Lund AM et al. Primary carnitine deficiency: Faroese population. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2007;30(3):341–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms CTD is unusually frequent in the Faroe Islands and gives a carrier frequency of ~1:20, but it does not state the 1:300 incidence, the ~1:40,000 NBS figure, or the c.95A>G founder variant.
judged.quote: Estimates of carrier frequency of about 1:20 for both disorders indicate that some enzyme-deficient individuals remain undiagnosed.

judged.citation: Rasmussen J et al. Carnitine levels in 26,462 individuals from the nationwide screening program for primary carnitine deficiency in the Faroe Islands. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2014;37(2):215–22.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the Faroe Islands prevalence of ~1:300 and the c.95A>G variant, but says nothing about the ~1:40,000 incidence in general newborn screening cohorts.
judged.quote: The prevalence of PCD in the Faroe Islands is the highest reported in the world (1:297).

rows.text: NBS has dramatically increased ascertainment, including detection of asymptomatic carrier mothers via their infant's low C0 [6].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW et al. Maternal systemic primary carnitine deficiency uncovered by newborn screening. Genet Med. 2010;12(1):19–24.
judged.reason: The abstract reports five families in which infants' low free carnitine on newborn screening led to diagnosis of maternal PCD in mostly asymptomatic mothers, supporting NBS-driven ascertainment (though the mothers are affected rather than merely carriers).
judged.quote: We report five families in which low free carnitine levels in the infants' newborn screening have led to the diagnosis of maternal systemic primary carnitine deficiency.

rows.text: Plasma free carnitine (C0) is profoundly low, often <5 µmol/L (normal >20), and total carnitine <10 µmol/L [1].

judged.citation: Magoulas PL, El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency: an overview. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:68.
judged.reason: The abstract gives low plasma free carnitine <5 µM with normal 25-50 µM, but says nothing about total carnitine <10 µmol/L.
judged.quote: established by demonstration of low plasma free carnitine concentration (<5 μM, normal 25-50 μM)

rows.text: Acylcarnitine profile shows LOW absolute values across all species (not elevated, which differentiates from secondary depletion caused by organic acidaemia or FAO disorders) [2,7].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency. GeneReviews®. 2012 [updated 2022].
judged.reason: The abstract refers only generically to "consistent biochemical analyte findings" and low carnitine levels and does not discuss the acylcarnitine profile or its differentiation from secondary carnitine depletion.
judged.quote: The diagnosis of PCD is established in a proband with consistent biochemical analyte findings and/or suggestive clinical and laboratory features

judged.citation: Wang Y et al. Phenotype and genotype variation in primary carnitine deficiency. Genet Med. 2001;3(6):387–92.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns SLC22A5 mutational analysis, transporter function in CHO cells, and clinical variability, and never addresses acylcarnitine profile values or the distinction from secondary carnitine depletion.

rows.text: Urinary fractional excretion of carnitine is INAPPROPRIATELY HIGH despite low plasma levels — the hallmark of renal transporter dysfunction [1,8].

judged.citation: Magoulas PL, El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency: an overview. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:68.
judged.reason: The abstract lists plasma carnitine, fibroblast transport and molecular testing but never addresses urinary carnitine excretion or renal fractional excretion, so the claim's topic is not engaged.

judged.citation: Koizumi A et al. Genetic epidemiology of the carnitine transporter OCTN2 gene. Hum Mol Genet. 1999;8(12):2247–54.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses OCTN2 mutation epidemiology, serum carnitine screening and cardiac hypertrophy, but says nothing about urinary carnitine excretion or renal wasting.

rows.text: Oglesbee 2017 reported ~75.7% clinical sensitivity of NBS for PCD, reflecting the subtle biochemistry at birth [9].

judged.citation: Hall PL, Wittenauer A, Hagar A. Post-analytical tools for the triage of newborn screening results in follow-up can reduce confirmatory testing and guide performance improvement. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2020;6(1):20.
judged.reason: The abstract does not address primary carnitine deficiency or any clinical sensitivity estimate for newborn screening of it.

rows.text: Over 100 pathogenic variants reported; most are loss-of-function [11].

judged.citation: Rose EC, di San Filippo CA, Longo N et al. Genotype-phenotype correlation in primary carnitine deficiency. Hum Mutat. 2012;33(1):118–23.
judged.reason: The abstract engages the SLC22A5 mutation spectrum and documents nonsense (loss-of-function) and missense variants, but never gives a total count of over 100 pathogenic variants, and it notes many missense mutations retain residual transport activity rather than establishing that most variants are loss-of-function.
judged.quote: DNA sequencing indicated an increased frequency of nonsense mutations in symptomatic patients (P < 0.001). Expression of the missense mutations in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells indicated that many mutations retained residual carnitine transport activity

rows.text: Heterozygotes have half-normal carnitine levels but are asymptomatic except for mild biochemical findings [12].

judged.citation: Amat di San Filippo C et al. Cardiomyopathy and carnitine deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2008;94(2):162–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that heterozygotes have only mildly reduced carnitine and are not meaningfully at risk of cardiomyopathy, but it does not state the specific "half-normal" carnitine level and it notes possible benign cardiac hypertrophy rather than purely biochemical findings.
judged.quote: Heterozygotes for primary carnitine deficiency can have mildly reduced plasma carnitine levels and can develop benign cardiac hypertrophy.

rows.text: Three phenotypes [1,2]: (1) Infantile metabolic: 3 months–2 years, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy during fasting/illness, hepatomegaly; (2) Childhood cardiomyopathic: progressive dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure in infancy or toddlerhood — can be fatal if untreated; (3) Adult myopathic: exercise intolerance, muscle pain, sometimes arrhythmia; sometimes asymptomatic 'MATERNAL PCD' identified only when their NBS-positive infant triggers testing.

judged.citation: Magoulas PL, El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency: an overview. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:68.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the infantile hypoketotic hypoglycaemic, childhood myopathic/cardiomyopathic and adult presentations, but does not give the 3 months–2 years age window nor describe asymptomatic maternal PCD detected via an infant's newborn screen.
judged.quote: typically characterized by episodes of hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, elevated transaminases, and hyperammonemia in infants; skeletal myopathy, elevated creatine kinase (CK), and cardiomyopathy in childhood; or cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, or fatigability in adulthood

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency. GeneReviews®. 2012 [updated 2022].
judged.reason: The abstract describes the infantile metabolic presentation (3 months–2 years with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly), childhood cardiac/skeletal myopathy, adult fatigability/arrhythmia, and asymptomatic mothers detected via their infant's newborn screening.
judged.quote: (1) metabolic decompensation in infancy typically presenting between age three months and two years with episodes of hypoketotic hypoglycemia, poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, hepatomegaly, elevated liver transaminases, and hyperammonemia triggered by fasting or common illnesses ... (2) childhood myopathy involving heart and skeletal muscle with onset between age two and four years; ... The latter two categories often include mothers diagnosed with PCD after newborn screening has identified low carnitine levels in their infants.

rows.text: MATERNAL PCD is an important pitfall — mother may be asymptomatic but has low plasma carnitine detectable via the infant's NBS [6].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW et al. Maternal systemic primary carnitine deficiency uncovered by newborn screening. Genet Med. 2010;12(1):19–24.
judged.reason: The abstract directly describes asymptomatic mothers with PCD detected through their infants' low free carnitine on newborn screening and urges maternal evaluation.
judged.quote: Three mothers are asymptomatic, one had decreased stamina during pregnancy, and one has mild fatigability and developed preeclampsia.

rows.text: Lifelong oral L-carnitine 100–200 mg/kg/day in 3–4 divided doses (100 mg/kg in adults) [1,2].

judged.citation: Magoulas PL, El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency: an overview. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:68.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms oral L-carnitine as primary treatment in divided doses but states 50-400 mg/kg/day in three doses, not the claim's 100–200 mg/kg/day in 3–4 doses or the adult-specific 100 mg/kg figure.
judged.quote: supplementation of oral levocarnitine (L-carnitine) at a dose of 50-400 mg/kg/day divided into three doses

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency. GeneReviews®. 2012 [updated 2022].
judged.reason: The 100–200 mg/kg/day oral levocarnitine dose is stated, but the abstract does not specify 3–4 divided doses or a 100 mg/kg adult dose.
judged.quote: 100-200 mg/kg/day oral levocarnitine

rows.text: Compliance is critical — discontinuation can precipitate fatal cardiomyopathy [13].

judged.citation: Lee NC et al. Diagnoses of newborns and mothers with carnitine uptake defects through newborn screening. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;100(1):46–50.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses carnitine supplementation and cardiomyopathy in CUD but says nothing about treatment compliance or fatal cardiomyopathy following discontinuation; it only reports improvement of cardiac function with treatment.
judged.quote: One mother had dilated cardiomyopathy at diagnosis and her cardiac function improved after treatment.

rows.text: Maternal cases: low-dose carnitine continuation is prudent to protect maternal cardiac function, particularly through pregnancy [6].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW et al. Maternal systemic primary carnitine deficiency uncovered by newborn screening. Genet Med. 2010;12(1):19–24.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns diagnosis and molecular findings in maternal PCD and says nothing about carnitine supplementation dosing, continuation, or cardiac protection during pregnancy.

rows.text: Untreated: cardiomyopathy can be fatal by age 5 [1,14].

judged.citation: Magoulas PL, El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency: an overview. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2012;7:68.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses prognosis and its dependence on continued carnitine supplementation but gives no untreated mortality timeline such as death from cardiomyopathy by age 5.
judged.quote: The prognosis for individuals with CDSP depends on the age, presentation, and severity of symptoms at the time of diagnosis

judged.citation: Crefcoeur LL et al. Clinical characteristics of primary carnitine deficiency: a structured review using a case-by-case approach. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(3):386–405.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms cardiomyopathy is the most prevalent manifestation, that symptoms cluster in early childhood, and that severe cardiac events occur, but it gives no data on fatality by age 5.
judged.quote: cardiac symptoms (predominantly cardiomyopathy) were the most prevalent (23.8%)

rows.text: On adequate carnitine supplementation: normal life expectancy, normal cardiac function, normal cognitive development [2,14].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Systemic primary carnitine deficiency. GeneReviews®. 2012 [updated 2022].
judged.reason: The abstract supports clinical improvement with treatment started before irreversible organ damage but makes no statement about normal life expectancy, normal cardiac function, or normal cognitive development.
judged.quote: Metabolic decompensation and skeletal and cardiac muscle function improve with 100-200 mg/kg/day oral levocarnitine if it is started before irreversible organ damage occurs.

judged.citation: Crefcoeur LL et al. Clinical characteristics of primary carnitine deficiency: a structured review using a case-by-case approach. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(3):386–405.
judged.reason: The abstract characterizes the phenotypic spectrum and mode of identification but does not address outcomes on carnitine supplementation, life expectancy, cardiac recovery, or cognitive development.

rows.text: In a structured review of 757 published patients, 6 of 194 adults (3.1%) suffered a severe event with no preceding symptom at all: five cardiac events and one coma [14].

judged.citation: Crefcoeur LL et al. Clinical characteristics of primary carnitine deficiency: a structured review using a case-by-case approach. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(3):386–405.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly reports 757 individual patients and 6 of 194 adults (3.1%) with a severe event without preceding symptoms, comprising five cardiac events and one coma.
judged.quote: Adult onset of symptoms occurred in 16 of 194 adult patients, of whom 6 (3.1%) patients suffered a severe event without any preceding symptom (five cardiac events and one coma).

rows.text: MCAD deficiency (OMIM #201450) was described in the 1980s by Stanley and colleagues [3].

judged.citation: Stanley CA et al. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency in children with non-ketotic hypoglycemia and low carnitine levels. Pediatr Res. 1983;17(11):877–84.
judged.reason: This 1983 Stanley et al. paper defines MCAD deficiency as a newly recognized disorder, matching the claim of description in the 1980s by Stanley and colleagues (the OMIM number is a database identifier, not an abstract-level fact).
judged.quote: These results define a previously unrecognized inherited metabolic disorder of fatty acid oxidation due to deficiency of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.

rows.text: Worldwide incidence is ~1:10,000–1:20,000, rising to 1:4,900 in parts of Northern Europe [11].

judged.citation: Maier EM et al. Population spectrum of ACADM genotypes correlated to biochemical phenotypes in newborn screening for MCAD. Hum Mutat. 2005;25(5):443–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that MCADD is a frequent disorder with an elevated birth incidence in a Northern European population, but it reports 1 in 8,456 in Bavaria and gives neither the stated worldwide range of ~1:10,000–1:20,000 nor the figure of 1:4,900.
judged.quote: Among 524,287 newborns, we identified 62 cases of MCADD, indicating a birth incidence of 1 in 8,456.

rows.text: It accounts for a substantial fraction of previously-unexplained 'sudden infant death syndrome' cases in retrospective cohorts [5].

judged.citation: Chace DH et al. Rapid diagnosis of MCAD deficiency by tandem mass spectrometry. Clin Chem. 1997;43(11):2106–13.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns tandem-MS newborn screening methodology and disease frequency, and never mentions sudden infant death syndrome or retrospective SIDS cohorts.

rows.text: Inclusion of MCAD on NBS panels from the early 2000s is considered one of the highest-yield interventions in expanded metabolic screening [1].

judged.citation: Wilcken B et al. Outcome of neonatal screening for medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Lancet. 2007;369(9555):37–42.
judged.reason: The abstract supports MCAD as the disorder most justifying tandem-MS newborn screening and shows screening reduces deaths/severe events, but it does not document the "early 2000s" timing of MCAD's inclusion on NBS panels.
judged.quote: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is the disorder thought most to justify neonatal screening by tandem-mass spectrometry because, without screening, there seems to be substantial morbidity and mortality.

rows.text: Loss of activity causes accumulation of C8-acyl-CoA, which is transesterified to octanoylcarnitine (C8) and shunted into glycine conjugation (hexanoylglycine, suberylglycine, phenylpropionylglycine) [2,8].

judged.citation: Rinaldo P et al. Fatty acid oxidation disorders. Annu Rev Physiol. 2002;64:477–502.
judged.reason: The abstract is a general overview of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation disorders and contains no MCAD-specific metabolite data such as octanoylcarnitine or glycine conjugates.
judged.quote: This review addresses the normal process of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation and discusses the clinical, metabolic, and molecular aspects of more than 20 known inherited diseases of this pathway that have been described to date.

rows.text: Plasma C8 >0.3 µmol/L and C8/C10 ratio >2 (often >5) are diagnostic on acylcarnitine analysis [5].

judged.citation: Chace DH et al. Rapid diagnosis of MCAD deficiency by tandem mass spectrometry. Clin Chem. 1997;43(11):2106–13.
judged.reason: The abstract supports an octanoylcarnitine (C8) cutoff near 0.3 µmol/L (healthy newborn maximum 0.22 µmol/L versus affected ranges of 3.1–28.3 and 0.33–4.4 µmol/L), but says nothing about the C8/C10 ratio thresholds of >2 or >5.
judged.quote: The maximum concentration of octanoylcarnitine was 0.22 mumol/L, with the majority being at or below the detection limit. In all 16 blood spots from newborns with confirmed MCAD deficiency, octanoylcarnitine was highly increased [median 8.4 mumol/L (range 3.1-28.3 mumol/L)]

rows.text: On newborn screening, multivariate post-analytical scoring of the whole marker pattern rather than single-analyte cutoffs correctly triages true positives while sharply reducing confirmatory testing [6].

judged.citation: Hall PL, Wittenauer A, Hagar A. Post-analytical tools for the triage of newborn screening results in follow-up can reduce confirmatory testing and guide performance improvement. Int J Neonatal Screen. 2020;6(1):20.
judged.reason: The abstract describes CLIR multivariate post-analytical tools (superior to multiple cutoffs) that correctly assigned all true positives, including MCAD deficiency, while reducing confirmatory testing.
judged.quote: The post-analytical tools appropriately assigned all true positive cases to the higher levels of follow-up testing and reduced the level of intervention for a significant number of cases as well.

rows.text: Urinary acylglycines — hexanoylglycine (HG) and suberylglycine (SG) — are more specific than organic acids and are the confirmatory biochemical test [8].

judged.citation: Rinaldo P et al. Fatty acid oxidation disorders. Annu Rev Physiol. 2002;64:477–502.
judged.reason: The abstract makes no mention of urinary acylglycines, hexanoylglycine, suberylglycine, or comparative diagnostic specificity, being only a structural description of the review's scope.
judged.quote: This review addresses the normal process of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation and discusses the clinical, metabolic, and molecular aspects of more than 20 known inherited diseases of this pathway that have been described to date.

rows.text: Between crises, urine organic acids are often normal and do not exclude the diagnosis — acylcarnitines and acylglycines remain abnormal [2,8].

judged.citation: Rinaldo P et al. Fatty acid oxidation disorders. Annu Rev Physiol. 2002;64:477–502.
judged.reason: Nothing in the abstract addresses interictal urine organic acid results or the persistence of acylcarnitine/acylglycine abnormalities between crises.

rows.text: The c.985A>G (p.Lys329Glu) variant accounts for ~80% of pathogenic alleles in Northern European populations; homozygotes have classic phenotype [4,9].

judged.reason: The abstract confirms the A985-G (p.Lys329Glu) variant is the predominant mutation, with 31 of 34 patients homozygous and complete loss of detectable MCAD protein, but it does not state the ~80% pathogenic allele frequency or specify Northern European populations.

judged.reason: The abstract supports that c.985A>G is the predominant pathogenic allele with a northwestern European founder effect, but gives ~90% (not ~80%) of disease-causing alleles in diagnosed patients and says nothing about homozygotes having the classic phenotype.
judged.quote: Approximately 90% of the disease-causing alleles in diagnosed patients are due to a single base mutation, an A (adenine) to G (guanine) transition at position 985 of MCAD cDNA (G985).

rows.text: Over 90 additional variants are described; compound heterozygotes with milder alleles (e.g., c.199T>C, p.Tyr67His) may have attenuated biochemistry and NBS false negatives [10,11].

judged.citation: Andresen BS et al. MCAD deficiency: identification by MS/MS-based prospective screening of all pathogenic variants. Am J Hum Genet. 2001;68(6):1408–18.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that c.199T>C is a prevalent mild folding mutation with attenuated enzyme activity found in newborn-screening-positive samples, but it does not give the count of over 90 additional variants and does not state that such compound heterozygotes cause NBS false negatives (indeed these cases were acylcarnitine-positive).
judged.quote: Our identification of a new mutation, 199T-->C, which has never been observed in patients with clinically manifested disease but was present in a large proportion of the acylcarnitine-positive samples, may explain this skewed ratio. judged.citation: Maier EM et al. Population spectrum of ACADM genotypes correlated to biochemical phenotypes in newborn screening for MCAD. Hum Mutat. 2005;25(5):443–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that c.199T>C (Tyr67His) is a mild variant often compound heterozygous with c.985A>G and shows statistically lower acylcarnitine markers (attenuated biochemistry), but it does not state that over 90 additional variants are described (it reports 18 variations, 13 novel) nor that these alleles cause newborn-screening false negatives.
judged.quote: The mild folding variant c.199T>C (Tyr67His) was identified in nine individuals, six of them being compound heterozygous with c.985A>G (Lys329Glu).

rows.text: Genotype alone does not reliably predict disease severity — the same genotype can produce fatal neonatal presentation or lifelong asymptomatic status, with unpredictable individual susceptibility [1,12].

judged.reason: The abstract reports screening outcomes and does not discuss ACADM genotypes or genotype–phenotype correlation at all.

judged.citation: Derks TG et al. The natural history of medium-chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase deficiency in the Netherlands: clinical presentation and outcome. J Pediatr. 2006;148(5):665–70.

rows.text: Classic MCAD: a previously-well infant (median age 12 months) develops a Reye-like episode with vomiting, lethargy, seizures and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia after a prolonged fast or intercurrent illness [1,2].
