judged.reason: The abstract gives the 22% mortality, 21% disability, ~35/31/39% follow-up complaints (a third of patients reporting fatigue, muscle pain or reduced exercise tolerance) and prominent overweight after treatment.
judged.quote: On follow-up, a total of 44 patients reported fatigue (35%; 28/80), muscle pain (31%; 25/80), and/or reduced exercise tolerance (39%; 31/80).

rows.text: Adult life expectancy is normal on adequate fasting avoidance [14].

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U et al. Treatment recommendations in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(4):498–505.
judged.reason: No statement about MCAD adult life expectancy; the paper addresses long-chain FAOD treatment only.

rows.text: Pregnancy is well-tolerated with careful intrapartum glucose management [14].

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U et al. Treatment recommendations in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(4):498–505.
judged.reason: Pregnancy management in MCAD is not addressed anywhere in the abstract.

rows.text: Early NBS detection and MCT-based fat-modified diet markedly improve outcome [1,2].

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U. Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation disorders: clinical presentation of long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects before and after newborn screening. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(5):527–32.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that newborn screening improves outcome but says nothing about MCT-based fat-modified diet, only generic "sufficient energy supply".
judged.quote: Implementation of newborn screening has significantly reduced morbidity and mortality of long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects.

rows.text: VLCAD deficiency (OMIM #201475) was separated from the LCAD-deficient phenotype in 1992 when it was shown that the originally-reported 'LCAD' cases actually had VLCAD mutations; true LCAD deficiency does not appear to cause human disease [3,4].

judged.citation: Strauss AW et al. Molecular basis of human mitochondrial very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 1995;92(23):10496–500.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that patients with this phenotype carry VLCAD gene mutations, but it says nothing about the 1992 reclassification of previously reported 'LCAD' cases, nor that true LCAD deficiency does not cause human disease.
judged.quote: Polymerase chain reaction amplification of VLCAD mRNA and genomic exons defined the molecular defects in two patients with VLCAD deficiency who presented with unexplained cardiac arrest and cardiomyopathy.

judged.citation: Aoyama T et al. Molecular features of the CPT-I deficiency; purified LCAD does not catalyse oxidation of palmitoyl-CoA. J Clin Invest. 1995;95(6):2465–73.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes VLCAD as the enzyme accounting for nearly all mitochondrial palmitoyl-CoA dehydrogenation and documents VLCAD deficiency in patients previously suspected of a beta-oxidation disorder, which supports the biochemical basis for LCAD's negligible role, but it never mentions LCAD, the reclassification of the originally-reported 'LCAD' cases, or the 1992 date.
judged.quote: The enzyme was found to catalyze the major part of mitochondrial palmitoylcoenzyme A dehydrogenation in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, and skin fibroblasts (89-97, 86-99, 96-99, and 78-87%, respectively).

rows.text: VLCAD is on the RUSP; C14:1 is the primary NBS marker [5].

judged.citation: Miller MJ et al. Laboratory analysis of acylcarnitines, 2020 update: a technical standard of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). Genet Med. 2021;23(2):249–58.
judged.reason: The abstract is a general technical-standard summary of acylcarnitine methodology and does not mention VLCAD, the RUSP, or C14:1, so it is too structural at abstract level to judge this marker claim.

rows.text: Elevated tetradecenoylcarnitine (C14:1) is the defining acylcarnitine marker; C14:1/C16 ratio and C14:1/C14 ratios are more specific than absolute C14:1, particularly for second-tier confirmation after a borderline NBS result [6,7].

judged.citation: Lindner M, Hoffmann GF, Matern D. Newborn screening for disorders of fatty-acid oxidation: experience and recommendations from an expert meeting. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(5):521–6.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses incidence, program-level policy and general recommendations for newborn screening of fatty-acid oxidation disorders, but says nothing about specific acylcarnitine markers such as C14:1 or the discriminatory ratios or second-tier confirmation cut-offs asserted in the claim.
judged.quote: Confirmatory diagnostic procedures should be agreed upon to ensure international comparability of results and evidence-based modifications.

judged.citation: Merritt JL 2nd et al. Infants suspected to have very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency from newborn screening. Mol Genet Metab. 2014;111(4):484–92.
judged.reason: The abstract supports C14:1 as the NBS marker and shows C14:1/C16 (and C14:1/C2) discriminating true from false positives, but it does not report a C14:1/C14 ratio nor establish that ratios are more specific than absolute C14:1 for second-tier confirmation.
judged.quote: Comparison of analytes and analyte ratios from the NBS demonstrated statistically significant differences between true positive and false positive groups for C14:1, C14, C14:1/C2, and C14:1/C16.

rows.text: Miller (2021) endorses (C16+C18:1)/C2, C14:1/C12 and C14:1/C12:1 as additional discriminatory ratios [5].

judged.citation: Miller MJ et al. Laboratory analysis of acylcarnitines, 2020 update: a technical standard of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). Genet Med. 2021;23(2):249–58.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses acylcarnitine analysis standards generally but never mentions VLCAD-specific discriminatory ratios such as (C16+C18:1)/C2, C14:1/C12 or C14:1/C12:1.
judged.quote: These technical standards were developed as a resource for diagnostic laboratory practices in acylcarnitine analysis, interpretation, and reporting.

rows.text: In-vitro fatty-acid oxidation probe flux assay on cultured fibroblasts is the gold-standard second-tier test, and VLCAD enzyme activity on lymphocytes is a non-invasive alternative [8].

judged.citation: Diekman EF et al. Fatty acid oxidation flux predicts the clinical severity of VLCAD deficiency. Genet Med. 2015;17(12):989–94.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the fibroblast LC-FAO flux assay as the superior/most predictive confirmatory measure (versus VLCAD activity and acylcarnitine ratios), but says nothing about VLCAD enzyme activity in lymphocytes as a non-invasive alternative.
judged.quote: Our results demonstrate a very strong correlation between LC-FAO flux in fibroblasts and the clinical severity of VLCADD. LC-FAO flux measurements may thus predict whether patients are likely to develop symptoms.

rows.text: Over 200 pathogenic variants are reported [9].

judged.citation: Andresen BS et al. Clear correlation of genotype with disease phenotype in VLCAD deficiency. Am J Hum Genet. 1999;64(2):479–94.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that many pathogenic ACADVL mutations have been reported but documents only 58 different mutations, so the specific figure of over 200 is not carried.
judged.quote: we investigated 58 different mutations in 55 unrelated patients representing all known clinical phenotypes

rows.text: Three phenotypes [1,2]: (1) Severe early-onset (cardiomyopathic): neonatal hypertrophic/dilated cardiomyopathy, pericardial effusion, arrhythmia, hepatomegaly, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia — high mortality; (2) Intermediate (hepatic): infantile/toddler presentation with Reye-like episodes during illness — hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, transaminitis; (3) Late-onset (myopathic): exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis, muscle pain and CK rises in adolescence/adulthood, without cardiomyopathy.

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U. Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation disorders: clinical presentation of long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects before and after newborn screening. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(5):527–32.
judged.reason: The abstract supports heterogeneous phenotypes of differing severity affecting heart, liver and skeletal muscle and late-onset exercise-induced myopathy, but does not enumerate the three named phenotypes or their specific features (pericardial effusion, arrhythmia, Reye-like episodes, transaminitis, CK rises).
judged.quote: The different long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects present with similar heterogeneous clinical phenotypes of different severity. Organs mainly affected comprise the heart, liver, and skeletal muscles.

rows.text: Avoid prolonged fasting (infant limits as for MCAD) [13].

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U et al. Treatment recommendations in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects: consensus from a workshop. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(4):498–505.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that recommendations on maximal fasting duration were produced for long-chain FAOD, but gives no specific infant fasting limits or comparison with MCAD.
judged.quote: recommendations are given with regard to the fat and carbohydrate content of the diet, the maximal length of fasting periods and the use of l-carnitine in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects

rows.text: TRIHEPTANOIN (Dojolvi®, UX007) is now first-line medium-chain substrate in many US metabolic centres — FDA-approved 2020 for LC-FAOD including VLCAD; delivers ~25–35% of caloric intake as C7-triglyceride (anaplerotic via propionyl-CoA), and phase 2 extension data showed ~48% reduction in major clinical events vs pre-triheptanoin baseline [15,16].

judged.citation: Vockley J et al. Effects of triheptanoin (UX007) in patients with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders: results from an open-label, long-term extension study. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(1):253–63.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms US approval of triheptanoin for molecularly confirmed LC-FAOD and an open-label extension showing reduced major clinical event rates (1.76→0.96/year, ~45% in the rollover group), but it does not give the 2020 approval date, the ~25–35% caloric dosing, VLCAD-specific data, or the precise ~48% figure.
judged.quote: In the rollover group, mean annualized MCE rate decreased from 1.76 events/year pre-triheptanoin to 0.96 events/year with triheptanoin (P =".0319)

judged.citation: Shirley M. Triheptanoin: first approval. Drugs. 2020;80(15):1595–1600.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the June 2020 US approval of triheptanoin for molecularly confirmed LC-FAOD but does not give the ~25–35% caloric dosing, the anaplerotic propionyl-CoA mechanism detail, the ~48% event reduction, or first-line status in US centres.
judged.quote: In June 2020, triheptanoin received its first regulatory approval, in the USA, for use as a source of calories and fatty acids for the treatment of pediatric and adult patients with molecularly confirmed long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders (LC-FAOD).

rows.text: MCT oil (C8-rich, 10–30% of calories) remains an alternative, particularly where triheptanoin is unavailable or cost-prohibitive; no formal society has declared triheptanoin preferred [15].

judged.citation: Vockley J et al. Effects of triheptanoin (UX007) in patients with long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders: results from an open-label, long-term extension study. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2021;44(1):253–63.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns triheptanoin efficacy and safety only and says nothing about MCT oil as an alternative, its dosing range, or society preference statements.

rows.text: L-CARNITINE supplementation is NOT routine in VLCAD — concern that supplementation increases toxic long-chain acylcarnitine production (animal VLCAD models show arrhythmogenic risk); selective use only if plasma free carnitine <10 µmol/L [13,17].

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U et al. Treatment recommendations in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects: consensus from a workshop. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(4):498–505.
judged.reason: The abstract states that recommendations address l-carnitine use in long-chain FAOD but does not state that carnitine is non-routine, the acylcarnitine-toxicity rationale, or the <10 µmol/L threshold.
judged.quote: the use of l-carnitine in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects

judged.citation: Primassin S et al. Carnitine supplementation induces acylcarnitine production in tissues of VLCAD-deficient mice. Pediatr Res. 2008;63(6):632–7.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that carnitine supplementation in a VLCAD animal model induces accumulation of potentially toxic long-chain acylcarnitines, but it says nothing about arrhythmogenic risk or the selective <10 µmol/L free-carnitine threshold.
judged.quote: The present study demonstrates that carnitine supplementation results in significant accumulation of potentially toxic acylcarnitines in tissues.

rows.text: Pre-NBS severe phenotype: mortality 50% in infancy [1].

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U. Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation disorders: clinical presentation of long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects before and after newborn screening. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(5):527–32.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that pre-screening long-chain FAO defects carried high morbidity/mortality reduced by newborn screening, but gives no 50% infant mortality figure for the severe VLCAD phenotype.
judged.quote: Implementation of newborn screening has significantly reduced morbidity and mortality of long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects.

rows.text: Post-NBS with early fat-modified diet: neonatal cardiomyopathy is often reversible; long-term survival is substantially improved [17].

judged.citation: Primassin S et al. Carnitine supplementation induces acylcarnitine production in tissues of VLCAD-deficient mice. Pediatr Res. 2008;63(6):632–7.
judged.reason: This murine carnitine-supplementation study does not address newborn screening, fat-modified diet outcomes, cardiomyopathy reversibility or survival.

rows.text: Incidence is ~1:100,000–1:250,000, with higher frequency in Finland and Poland due to the common p.Glu474Gln founder variant [3,4].

judged.citation: IJlst L et al. Common missense mutation G1528C in long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase. J Clin Invest. 1996;98(4):1028–33.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that the disorder is frequent and that G1528C (p.Glu474Gln) is a common allele, but gives no incidence figures (1:100,000–1:250,000) and no data on Finnish or Polish founder frequency.
judged.quote: Furthermore, it is clear that this inborn error of fatty acid oxidation is very frequent, second to medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.

judged.citation: Sykut-Cegielska J, Piekutowska-Abramczuk D et al. Urgent metabolic service improves survival in long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency detected by symptomatic identification and pilot newborn screening. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2011;34(1):185–95.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a Polish incidence within the cited range and a prevalent HADHA mutation in essentially all Polish patients, but it does not name the p.Glu474Gln (G1528C) founder variant, does not address Finland, and its figures (~1:110,000–115,000) do not themselves demonstrate a frequency higher than the general range.
judged.quote: The disease frequency estimated on the patients number was 1: 115 450, whereas in the pilot NBS - 1: 109 750 (658 492 neonates tested).

rows.text: Plasma 3-hydroxy-long-chain fatty acids can be measured for confirmation [2].

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U et al. Treatment recommendations in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects: consensus from a workshop. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(4):498–505.
judged.reason: The abstract is about treatment recommendations and does not discuss plasma 3-hydroxy-long-chain fatty acid measurement or any confirmatory biochemistry.

rows.text: Isolated LCHAD deficiency is usually due to HADHA p.Glu474Gln (c.1528G>C), accounting for ~87% of alleles in European cases [3,9].

judged.citation: IJlst L et al. Common missense mutation G1528C in long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase. J Clin Invest. 1996;98(4):1028–33.
judged.reason: The abstract reports the G1528C mutation causes loss of LCHAD activity and gives the 87% allele frequency in LCHAD-deficient patients.
judged.quote: The finding of an 87% allele frequency of the G1528C mutation in 34 LCHAD deficient patients makes this a valuable test for prenatal diagnosis.

judged.citation: Tyni T, Pihko H. Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Acta Paediatr. 1999;88(3):237–45.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms G1528C is the cause in the vast majority of LCHAD deficiency patients but gives no allele frequency figure such as ~87% in European cases.
judged.quote: In the vast majority of patients, LCHAD deficiency is caused by a common autosomal recessive mutation G1528C.

rows.text: Three main phenotypes [1,2]: (1) Severe neonatal/infantile: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, hepatic failure, lactic acidosis — onset days to months; (2) Hepatic/myopathic childhood: Reye-like hepatic episodes triggered by illness, hypoglycaemia; (3) Late-onset myopathic: exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis.

judged.citation: Spiekerkoetter U et al. Treatment recommendations in long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects: consensus from a workshop. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(4):498–505.
judged.reason: The abstract notes that severity varies with the underlying enzyme deficiency but offers no phenotype classification of neonatal, hepatic/myopathic and late-onset myopathic forms.

rows.text: UNIQUE to LCHAD/MTP: peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy (demyelinating) and pigmentary retinopathy — these progressive sequelae occur even in well-managed patients and distinguish LCHAD from other long-chain FAO disorders [12,13].

judged.citation: Tyni T et al. Mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation in the human eye and brain: implications for the retinopathy of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Pediatr Res. 2004;56(5):744–50.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that a retinopathy (affecting RPE/choriocapillaris) is associated with LCHAD deficiency and probes its pathogenesis, but it says nothing about demyelinating peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, progression despite optimal management, or the contrast with other long-chain FAO disorders.
judged.quote: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the choriocapillaris are affected early in the retinopathy associated with long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) deficiency.

judged.citation: Gillingham MB, Harding CO et al. Effect of optimal dietary therapy upon visual function in children with long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase and trifunctional protein deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2005;86(1–2):124–33.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms severe progressive chorioretinopathy in LCHAD/TFP deficiency despite optimal dietary therapy, but says nothing about peripheral demyelinating sensorimotor neuropathy or that these features distinguish LCHAD from other long-chain FAO disorders.
judged.quote: Eleven subjects who were homozygote and heterozygote for the common mutation, c.1528G>C, had no change to severe progression of atrophy of the choroid and retina with time.

rows.text: MATERNAL CLUE: mothers of affected fetuses may have had AFLP or HELLP in the index pregnancy — this should prompt testing of both the surviving infant and siblings [10,11].

judged.citation: Yang Z, Ibdah JA et al. Prospective screening for pediatric mitochondrial trifunctional protein defects in pregnancies complicated by liver disease. JAMA. 2002;288(17):2163–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the maternal AFLP clue and prompting newborn screening plus family counselling/prenatal diagnosis, but it does not support HELLP as a clue (only 1 HELLP mother was heterozygous with no mutations in the newborn) and does not address testing of existing siblings.
judged.quote: We detected mutations causing pediatric long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency in 5 families (19%) with maternal history of AFLP ... Only 1 woman with HELLP syndrome was heterozygous for the E474Q mutation; no mutations were detected in the newborn.

judged.citation: Browning MF et al. Fetal fatty acid oxidation defects and maternal liver disease in pregnancy. Obstet Gynecol. 2006;107(1):115–20.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the strong association between fetal fatty acid oxidation defects and maternal AFLP/HELLP in the index pregnancy, but says nothing about the recommended action of testing the surviving infant and siblings.
judged.quote: Maternal liver disease was noted in 16.00% of all fatty acid oxidation defect pregnancies compared with 0.88% in the general population (odds ratio 20.4, 95% confidence interval 7.82-53.2).

rows.text: Fat-modified diet: long-chain fat restricted to ~10% of energy, medium-chain substrate (either MCT oil 10–30% of energy, or triheptanoin 25–35% of energy) as the main caloric substrate, essential fatty acid supplementation [14].

judged.citation: Solis JO, Singh RH. Management of FAO disorders: a survey. J Am Diet Assoc. 2002;102(12):1800–3.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that dietary/nutritional treatment strategies are surveyed for LCHAD/TFP deficiency but reports no specific figures for long-chain fat restriction (~10% energy), MCT oil (10–30%), triheptanoin (25–35%), or essential fatty acid supplementation, and indeed emphasizes a lack of standardization.
judged.quote: Questionnaire responses provided by dietitians specializing in metabolic disorders evaluated practices used for treatment of fatty acid oxidation disorders, medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCAD), very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (VLCAD), long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (LCHAD), long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (LCAD), and Trifunctional Protein deficiency (TFP).

rows.text: TRIHEPTANOIN (Dojolvi®, UX007) received FDA approval in 2020 for LC-FAOD (including LCHAD/TFP) and is increasingly used as first-line medium-chain therapy in symptomatic patients — open-label extension data showed ~48% reduction in major clinical events and reduced cardiomyopathy and hypoglycaemia versus pre-triheptanoin baseline; many US metabolic centres now favour triheptanoin over MCT as standard initial therapy although no society has issued a formal preference [15,16].

judged.citation: Vockley J et al. Triheptanoin for long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders: phase 2 open-label extension. Mol Genet Metab. 2021;132(3):185–94.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the open-label extension finding of reduced major clinical event rate and duration with triheptanoin in LC-FAOD, but does not report the 2020 approval date, LCHAD/TFP-specific outcomes, separate reductions in cardiomyopathy and hypoglycaemia, or first-line/US-centre practice preference; the composite reduction figures (45% and 70%) do not match the stated ~48%.
judged.quote: Triheptanoin reduced rate and duration of MCEs.

judged.citation: Shirley M. Triheptanoin: first approval. Drugs. 2020;80(15):1595–1600.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the 2020 FDA approval for LC-FAOD but contains no open-label extension outcome data (~48% event reduction, cardiomyopathy/hypoglycaemia effects) and nothing about first-line preference over MCT or absence of society guidance.
judged.quote: In June 2020, triheptanoin received its first regulatory approval, in the USA, for use as a source of calories and fatty acids for the treatment of pediatric and adult patients with molecularly confirmed long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders (LC-FAOD).

rows.text: Severe deficiency is probably a complex condition involving additional modifier factors [1,2].

judged.citation: Gregersen N, Andresen BS, Corydon MJ et al. Mutation analysis in mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation defects: exemplified by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiencies, with special focus on genotype-phenotype relationship. Hum Mutat. 2001;18(3):169–89.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly proposes that the effect of disease-causing mutations in the SCAD gene may be modified by variations in other genes and by protein quality control systems, i.e., a complex condition with modifier factors.
judged.quote: The realization that the effect of the monogene, such as disease-causing mutations in the VLCAD, MCAD, and SCAD genes, may be modified by variations in other genes presages the need for profile analyses of additional genetic variations.

judged.citation: van Maldegem BT et al. Clinical, biochemical, and genetic heterogeneity in short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. JAMA. 2006;296(8):943–52.
judged.reason: The abstract shows no genotype–phenotype correlation and asymptomatic relatives with identical genotypes, which is consistent with additional modifying factors, but it does not state that severe deficiency involves modifier factors.
judged.quote: The ACADS genotype showed a statistically significant association with EMA and C4-C levels, but not with clinical characteristics.

rows.text: Early reports of developmental delay and hypoglycaemia have not been reproducibly confirmed in NBS-detected cohorts; most such children are asymptomatic [2,3].

judged.citation: van Maldegem BT et al. Clinical, biochemical, and genetic heterogeneity in short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. JAMA. 2006;296(8):943–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that symptoms (including developmental delay and hypoglycaemia) are nonspecific, transient and of doubtful clinical significance, but this is a clinically diagnosed Dutch cohort rather than an NBS-detected cohort and the abstract in fact lists developmental delay and hypoglycaemia as frequent findings.
judged.quote: clinical symptoms in SCADD are nonspecific, generally uncomplicated, often transient, and not correlated with specific ACADS genotypes

judged.citation: Gallant NM et al. Biochemical, molecular, and clinical characteristics of children with short chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency detected by newborn screening in California. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;106(1):55–61.
judged.reason: The abstract reports that NBS-detected SCADD cases were largely asymptomatic, with no epilepsy/behavioural disorders and only isolated speech delay in three, and hypoglycaemia in two with confounders, supporting non-reproduction of earlier symptom reports.
judged.quote: None developed epilepsy or behavioral disorders, and three patients had isolated speech delay. Hypoglycemia occurred in two patients, both in the neonatal period.

rows.text: The common c.625G>A variant is present in ~14% of the general population and does not reliably cause disease — many consider SCAD a biochemical finding rather than a clinical disorder unless additional rare variants are present [2,4].

judged.citation: van Maldegem BT et al. Clinical, biochemical, and genetic heterogeneity in short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. JAMA. 2006;296(8):943–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that c.625G>A is a susceptibility variant lacking reliable clinical significance and that SCADD often lacks clinical relevance, but it gives no general-population frequency such as ~14%.
judged.quote: a mutation and/or the c.511C>T or c.625G>A susceptibility variants on each SCAD-encoding (ACADS) allele

judged.citation: Pedersen CB et al. The ACADS gene variation spectrum in 114 patients with short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD) deficiency is dominated by missense variations leading to protein misfolding at the cellular level. Hum Genet. 2008;124(1):43–56.
judged.reason: The abstract reports the common c.625G>A variant among variants present in up to 14% of normal populations with questionable clinical relevance and near-normal enzyme activity, and concludes disease arises only in combination with other genetic and environmental factors, matching the claim (the 14% figure is stated for the two common variants collectively).
judged.quote: two common variations, c.511C > T (p.Arg171Trp) and c.625G > A (p.Gly209Ser), have been identified in patients, but these are also present in up to 14% of normal populations leading to questions of their clinical relevance

rows.text: Rare loss-of-function variants may cause a true clinical phenotype when homozygous or compound with the common variants — but penetrance is incomplete and modifier genes likely contribute [2,4,5].

judged.citation: van Maldegem BT et al. Clinical, biochemical, and genetic heterogeneity in short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. JAMA. 2006;296(8):943–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports incomplete penetrance (asymptomatic relatives with the same genotype) and absence of genotype–phenotype correlation, but does not address rare loss-of-function variants causing a true clinical phenotype or modifier genes specifically.
judged.quote: Seven out of 8 SCADD relatives were free of symptoms.

judged.citation: Pedersen CB et al. The ACADS gene variation spectrum in 114 patients with short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD) deficiency is dominated by missense variations leading to protein misfolding at the cellular level. Hum Genet. 2008;124(1):43–56.
judged.reason: The abstract clearly supports incomplete penetrance and modifier/environmental contributions, but does not state the specific genotype claim that rare loss-of-function variants cause true clinical disease when homozygous or compound heterozygous with the common variants.
judged.quote: However, no correlation was found between the clinical phenotype and the degree of SCAD dysfunction. We propose that SCAD deficiency should be considered as a disorder of protein folding that can lead to clinical disease in combination with other genetic and environmental factors.

judged.citation: Nagan N et al. SCAD deficiency: identification of a novel missense mutation. Mol Genet Metab. 2003;78(3):239–46.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that the common variants are susceptibility rather than true disease-causing alleles and that phenotype is heterogeneous with some asymptomatic individuals (consistent with incomplete penetrance), but it does not address rare loss-of-function variants in homozygous/compound state or modifier gene contributions.
judged.quote: Although they alter the structural and catalytic properties of the SCAD protein, these variants are not true disease-causing mutations but confer disease susceptibility.

rows.text: Occasional reports of developmental delay, seizures, hypotonia, hypoglycaemia, failure to thrive — but these are not convincingly causal in NBS-detected cohorts [2,3].

judged.citation: van Maldegem BT et al. Clinical, biochemical, and genetic heterogeneity in short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. JAMA. 2006;296(8):943–52.
judged.reason: The abstract carries the symptom list and the doubt about clinical significance/causality, but its cohort is clinically ascertained rather than NBS-detected and it reports most patients as symptomatic rather than mostly asymptomatic.
judged.quote: Developmental delay, epilepsy, behavioral disturbances, and hypoglycemia were the most frequently reported symptoms.

judged.citation: Gallant NM et al. Biochemical, molecular, and clinical characteristics of children with short chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency detected by newborn screening in California. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;106(1):55–61.
judged.reason: The abstract lists the clinically diagnosed phenotype (developmental delay, hypoglycaemia, epilepsy) and shows these were not convincingly seen or causal in the NBS cohort.
judged.quote: This study also provides evidence to suggest that, even when associated with deleterious mutations, SCADD diagnosed by newborn screening presents largely as a benign condition.

rows.text: The main clinical implication is avoiding over-treatment and over-counselling: families should be informed the abnormality may be benign [2,3,6].

judged.citation: van Maldegem BT et al. Clinical, biochemical, and genetic heterogeneity in short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. JAMA. 2006;296(8):943–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that the biochemical abnormality may be clinically insignificant/benign in many individuals, but it does not discuss avoiding over-treatment or how families should be counselled.
judged.quote: including a lack of clinical significance in many patients and that it is not possible to differentiate diseased and nondiseased individuals

judged.citation: Gallant NM et al. Biochemical, molecular, and clinical characteristics of children with short chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency detected by newborn screening in California. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;106(1):55–61.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the benign nature of NBS-detected SCADD but does not explicitly discuss counselling or avoiding over-treatment of families.

judged.citation: Froese DS et al. Structural basis for the regulation of human 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase by phosphorylation and S-adenosylmethionine inhibition. Nat Commun. 2018;9(1):2261.
judged.reason: The abstract is a structural/enzymology study of MTHFR regulation and says nothing about numbers of reported kindreds or clinical phenotypic spectrum.

rows.text: CSF 5-methyl-THF is low [1,5].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Update and new concepts in vitamin-responsive disorders of folate transport and metabolism. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):665–70.
judged.reason: No CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate data are reported; cerebral folate deficiency is discussed only in relation to FOLR1 and DHFR defects, not MTHFR biochemical findings.

rows.text: The common thermolabile c.677C>T polymorphism (present in 10–15% homozygous in Caucasian populations) causes only modest enzyme thermolability; tHcy rarely exceeds 30 µmol/L in polymorphism homozygotes and this variant does NOT cause homocystinuria [6,7].

judged.citation: Frosst P et al. A candidate genetic risk factor for vascular disease: a common mutation in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase. Nat Genet. 1995;10(1):111–3.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the common thermolabile 677 variant, its ~38% allele frequency (consistent with ~10–15% homozygotes) and elevated homocysteine in homozygotes, but gives no tHcy threshold (~30 µmol/L) and does not state that the variant fails to cause homocystinuria or that thermolability is only modest.
judged.quote: We have identified a common mutation in MTHFR which alters a highly-conserved amino acid; the substitution occurs at a frequency of approximately 38% of unselected chromosomes. The mutation in the heterozygous or homozygous state correlates with reduced enzyme activity and increased thermolability in lymphocyte extracts

judged.citation: Hickey SE et al. ACMG Practice Guideline: lack of evidence for MTHFR polymorphism testing. Genet Med. 2013;15(2):153–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that the MTHFR polymorphism is associated only with mild hyperhomocysteinemia (implying it does not cause homocystinuria), but it gives neither the 10–15% homozygote prevalence, the modest thermolability, nor the <30 µmol/L tHcy figure.
judged.quote: It was previously hypothesized that reduced enzyme activity of MTHFR led to mild hyperhomocysteinemia

rows.text: Severe disease: compound heterozygous or homozygous loss-of-function variants with residual enzyme activity <20% [8].

judged.citation: Goyette P et al. Human methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase: isolation of cDNA, mapping and mutation identification. Nat Genet. 1994;7(2):195–200.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms MTHFR deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function (missense and nonsense) mutations, but it gives no residual enzyme activity data and does not support the specific <20% activity threshold for severe disease.
judged.quote: MTHFR deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder, results in homocysteinemia. ... Two mutations were identified in MTHFR-deficient patients: a missense mutation (Arg to Gln), in a residue conserved in bacterial enzymes, and a nonsense mutation (Arg to Ter).

rows.text: The thermolabile c.677C>T (Ala222Val; reported as c.665C>T on the newer NM_005957.5 transcript — same p.Ala222Val) and c.1298A>C (Glu429Ala) polymorphisms are common in the general population and are NOT causes of overt disease; they are modifiers of tHcy and have been debated historically as thrombotic risk factors without consistent modern evidence [6,7].

judged.citation: Frosst P et al. A candidate genetic risk factor for vascular disease: a common mutation in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase. Nat Genet. 1995;10(1):111–3.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the thermolabile c.677C>T (Ala222Val) as a common variant that raises plasma homocysteine and was proposed as a vascular risk factor, but it says nothing about c.1298A>C (Glu429Ala), nor that these variants are not causes of overt disease, nor about the lack of consistent modern evidence for thrombotic risk.
judged.quote: We have identified a common mutation in MTHFR which alters a highly-conserved amino acid; the substitution occurs at a frequency of approximately 38% of unselected chromosomes.

judged.citation: Hickey SE et al. ACMG Practice Guideline: lack of evidence for MTHFR polymorphism testing. Genet Med. 2013;15(2):153–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that MTHFR polymorphism status has been hypothesised and debated as a thrombotic/vascular risk factor via mild hyperhomocysteinemia but has been disproven by modern meta-analyses, yet it never names c.677C>T or c.1298A>C, gives no population frequency, and does not state they are not causes of overt disease.
judged.quote: Recent meta-analyses have disproven an association between hyperhomocysteinemia and risk for coronary heart disease and between MTHFR polymorphism status and risk for venous t-hromboembolism.

rows.text: Neonatal/infantile: feeding difficulties, lethargy, apnoea, seizures, microcephaly, severe developmental delay; often fatal without early treatment [1,4].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Update and new concepts in vitamin-responsive disorders of folate transport and metabolism. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):665–70.
judged.reason: The abstract does not describe the neonatal/infantile clinical features or mortality of MTHFR deficiency.

judged.citation: Froese DS et al. Structural basis for the regulation of human 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase by phosphorylation and S-adenosylmethionine inhibition. Nat Commun. 2018;9(1):2261.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses crystal structure and allosteric regulation of MTHFR, not neonatal clinical features or outcomes of MTHFR deficiency.

rows.text: Adult-onset: peripheral neuropathy, dementia-like cognitive decline, psychosis, ectopia lentis (rare, usually a CBS finding) and arterial/venous thrombosis — MTHFR should be considered in any unexplained thrombotic event with hyperhomocysteinaemia and low methionine [2,9].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders cblC, cblD, cblE, cblF, cblG, cblJ and MTHFR deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: The abstract supports considering these disorders (and measuring homocysteine) in unexplained vascular thrombosis and neurological/visual presentations, but does not describe adult-onset neuropathy, dementia-like decline, psychosis, ectopia lentis, or low methionine.
judged.quote: We strongly recommend measuring plasma total homocysteine in any patient presenting with the combination of neurological and/or visual and/or haematological symptoms, subacute spinal cord degeneration, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or unexplained vascular thrombosis.

judged.citation: Engelbrecht V et al. MR and proton MR spectroscopy of the brain in hyperhomocysteinaemia caused by methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency. Am J Neuroradiol. 1997;18(3):536–9.
judged.reason: The abstract reports neuroimaging (atrophy, hypomyelination, NAA reduction) and betaine response in a girl with MTHFR deficiency and says nothing about adult-onset features, neuropathy, psychosis, ectopia lentis, thrombosis, or methionine levels.
judged.quote: MR imaging showed severe atrophy and large areas without myelination in the brain of a girl with methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency.

rows.text: High-dose BETAINE (100–150 mg/kg/day in children, maximum ~9 g/day; up to 20 g/day in adults) — provides an alternative methyl source via BHMT for homocysteine-to-methionine remethylation; the mainstay of therapy and can dramatically lower tHcy and raise methionine [10].

judged.citation: Strauss KA et al. Prevention of brain disease from severe 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2007;91(2):165–75.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses betaine therapy in severe MTHFR deficiency but reports a much higher dose (534±222 mg/kg/day, with the recommendation for a large early dose) and explicitly states betaine did not normalize plasma total homocysteine, contradicting both the stated 100–150 mg/kg/day dosing and the claim of dramatic tHcy lowering.
judged.quote: In all affected children, treatment with betaine (534+/-222 mg/kg/day) increased plasma S-adenosylmethionine, improved markers of tissue methyltransferase activity, and resulted in a threefold increase of calculated brain methionine uptake. Betaine therapy did not normalize plasma total homocysteine

rows.text: Avoid methotrexate and nitrous oxide — both inhibit remethylation further [1,11].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Update and new concepts in vitamin-responsive disorders of folate transport and metabolism. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):665–70.
judged.reason: The abstract says nothing about methotrexate or nitrous oxide exposure or contraindications in remethylation defects.

rows.text: Monitor plasma tHcy, methionine and psychometric development [1,10].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Update and new concepts in vitamin-responsive disorders of folate transport and metabolism. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):665–70.
judged.reason: No monitoring parameters such as plasma total homocysteine, methionine or psychometric follow-up are addressed.

judged.citation: Strauss KA et al. Prevention of brain disease from severe 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2007;91(2):165–75.
judged.reason: The abstract shows biochemical monitoring of plasma total homocysteine and amino acids (methionine) during betaine treatment, but says nothing about psychometric/developmental monitoring.
judged.quote: Plasma amino acid concentrations were used to estimate changes in cerebral methionine uptake resulting from betaine therapy.

rows.text: Treated from neonatal period with betaine: near-normal cognitive outcomes have been reported [1,10].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Update and new concepts in vitamin-responsive disorders of folate transport and metabolism. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):665–70.
judged.reason: The abstract offers no outcome or prognosis data for neonatally betaine-treated patients.

judged.citation: Strauss KA et al. Prevention of brain disease from severe 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2007;91(2):165–75.
judged.reason: The abstract reports a child diagnosed and started on betaine as a newborn who is healthy at age three, in contrast to the four older patients with irreversible brain damage.
judged.quote: The youngest child, diagnosed and started on betaine therapy as a newborn, is healthy at her present age of three years.

rows.text: The common c.677C>T/1298A>C polymorphisms are benign and should not be treated with high-dose folate unless tHcy is elevated [6,7].

judged.citation: Frosst P et al. A candidate genetic risk factor for vascular disease: a common mutation in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase. Nat Genet. 1995;10(1):111–3.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses the common c.677C>T polymorphism but offers no treatment guidance about high-dose folate and, rather than calling the variant benign, proposes it as a vascular disease risk factor.
judged.quote: This mutation in MTHFR may represent an important genetic risk factor in vascular disease.

judged.citation: Hickey SE et al. ACMG Practice Guideline: lack of evidence for MTHFR polymorphism testing. Genet Med. 2013;15(2):153–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that the polymorphisms lack demonstrated clinical significance (implying benign status and no need for testing), but says nothing about folate treatment or conditioning any therapy on elevated tHcy.
judged.quote: There is growing evidence that MTHFR polymorphism testing has minimal clinical utility and, therefore should not be ordered as a part of a routine evaluation for thrombophilia.

rows.text: Severe forms present with neonatal/infantile failure to thrive, neurological deterioration and megaloblastic anaemia; dramatic response to parenteral hydroxocobalamin is diagnostic and therapeutic [1,2].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders cblC, cblD, cblE, cblF, cblG, cblJ and MTHFR deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: The abstract supports prompt parenteral hydroxocobalamin as effective in any suspected remethylation disorder (which includes cblE/cblG) and notes neurological/haematological presentation, but does not specify neonatal failure to thrive or megaloblastic anaemia in these specific defects.
judged.quote: We strongly recommend to initiate treatment with parenteral hydroxocobalamin without delay in any suspected remethylation disorder; it significantly improves survival and incidence of severe complications.

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inborn errors of cobalamin absorption and metabolism. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2011;157C(1):33–44.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the haematologic (megaloblastic anaemia) and neurologic consequences of the remethylation block, but says nothing about neonatal failure to thrive or about parenteral hydroxocobalamin response being diagnostic/therapeutic.
judged.quote: Hyperhomocysteinemia along with hypomethioninemia can result in hematologic (megaloblastic anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) and neurologic (subacute combined degeneration of the cord, dementia, psychosis) defects.

rows.text: cblE (MTRR) and cblG (MTR) defects were delineated biochemically in the 1980s–1990s by somatic-cell complementation studies [3,4].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Functional methionine synthase deficiency (cblE and cblG): clinical and biochemical heterogeneity. Am J Med Genet. 1989;34(3):427–34.
judged.reason: This 1989 paper explicitly divides functional methionine synthase deficiency into cblE and cblG by complementation analysis with accompanying biochemical (fibroblast) studies, matching the claim's timeframe and method.
judged.quote: Patients are divided into two classes, cblE and cblG, on the basis of complementation analysis.

judged.citation: Rosenblatt DS et al. New disorder of vitamin B12 metabolism (cobalamin F) presenting as methylmalonic aciduria. Pediatrics. 1985;75(1):1–9.
judged.reason: The abstract describes a distinct complementation class (cblF) presenting with methylmalonic aciduria and a lysosomal cobalamin efflux defect, and never addresses the delineation of the cblE (MTRR) or cblG (MTR) defects or somatic-cell complementation analysis.
judged.quote: Despite excessive incorporation of [57Co]cyano-B12 by fibroblasts from the patient, free vitamin B12 was unable to efflux from lysosomes, and, therefore, synthesis of both adenosyl-B12 and methyl-B12 was impaired.

rows.text: Methylmalonic acid NORMAL (distinguishes from combined MMA+HCY disorders cblC/D/F/J and TCN2) [2,5].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inborn errors of cobalamin absorption and metabolism. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2011;157C(1):33–44.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly classifies cblE/cblG as isolated hyperhomocysteinemia (i.e., without methylmalonic acidemia) in contrast to the combined cblC/cblD/cblF disorders.
judged.quote: These can give rise to isolated methylmalonic acidemia (cblA, cblB, cblD variant 2), isolated hyperhomocysteinemia (cblD variant 1, cblE, cblG) or combined methylmalonic acidemia and hyperhomocysteinemia (cblC, classic cblD, cblF).

judged.citation: Watkins D et al. Novel inborn error of folate metabolism: identification by exome capture and sequencing of mutations in the CD320 gene. J Med Genet. 2011;48(9):590–2.
judged.reason: The abstract describes an MTHFD1-deficient proband with elevated methylmalonic acid and says nothing about methylmalonic acid being normal in cblE/cblG remethylation defects.
judged.quote: elevated blood levels of homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, and a selective decreased synthesis of methylcobalamin in cultured fibroblasts

rows.text: Somatic-cell complementation analysis on fibroblasts distinguishes cblE from cblG historically; modern practice uses molecular testing of MTR/MTRR [5].

judged.citation: Watkins D et al. Novel inborn error of folate metabolism: identification by exome capture and sequencing of mutations in the CD320 gene. J Med Genet. 2011;48(9):590–2.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns exome-based discovery of MTHFD1 mutations and does not discuss somatic-cell complementation analysis or molecular testing of MTR/MTRR to distinguish cblE from cblG.

rows.text: Both autosomal recessive. >30 variants per gene [6,7].

judged.citation: Leclerc D et al. Human methionine synthase: cDNA cloning and identification of mutations in patients of the cblG complementation group of folate/cobalamin disorders. Hum Mol Genet. 1996;5(12):1867–74.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that MTR mutations cause the inherited cblG disorder but reports only one missense mutation and a 3 bp deletion, so it does not carry the specific counts (">30 variants per gene") nor explicitly state autosomal recessive inheritance.
judged.quote: We have identified one missense mutation and a 3 bp deletion in patients of the cblG complementation group of inherited homocysteine/folate disorders by SSCP and sequence analysis

judged.citation: Leclerc D et al. Cloning and mapping of a cDNA for methionine synthase reductase, a flavoprotein defective in patients with homocystinuria. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 1998;95(6):3059–64.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms MTRR mutations in cblE patients (a 4-bp frameshift and a 3-bp deletion) but gives no support for the specific counts (>30 variants per gene) and does not state autosomal recessive inheritance.
judged.quote: The authenticity of the cDNA sequence was confirmed by identification of mutations in cblE patients, including a 4-bp frameshift in two affected siblings and a 3-bp deletion in a third patient.

rows.text: Neonatal/infantile (commonest severe form): feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, developmental delay, megaloblastic anaemia, hypotonia, progressive encephalopathy, sometimes seizures and stroke-like episodes [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Huemer M et al. Guidelines for diagnosis and management of the cobalamin-related remethylation disorders cblC, cblD, cblE, cblF, cblG, cblJ and MTHFR deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(1):21–48.
judged.reason: The abstract only gives broad symptom categories (neurological, visual, haematological) and does not enumerate feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, megaloblastic anaemia, hypotonia, seizures or stroke-like episodes as the commonest severe cblE/cblG presentation.
judged.quote: We strongly recommend measuring plasma total homocysteine in any patient presenting with the combination of neurological and/or visual and/or haematological symptoms, subacute spinal cord degeneration, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or unexplained vascular thrombosis.

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inborn errors of cobalamin absorption and metabolism. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2011;157C(1):33–44.
judged.reason: Megaloblastic anaemia and neurologic deterioration are supported, but feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures and stroke-like episodes in neonates are not mentioned.
judged.quote: Hyperhomocysteinemia along with hypomethioninemia can result in hematologic (megaloblastic anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) and neurologic (subacute combined degeneration of the cord, dementia, psychosis) defects.

judged.reason: The abstract confirms megaloblastic anaemia and developmental delay (plus nystagmus/mental retardation) in infancy, but does not mention feeding difficulties, failure to thrive, hypotonia, progressive encephalopathy, seizures or stroke-like episodes.
judged.quote: manifests with megaloblastic anaemia and developmental delay in early childhood

rows.text: Thrombotic events reported in late-onset cases [2,8].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inborn errors of cobalamin absorption and metabolism. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2011;157C(1):33–44.
judged.reason: The abstract enumerates the clinical consequences of hyperhomocysteinemia but does not mention thrombotic events or late-onset presentations.
judged.quote: Hyperhomocysteinemia along with hypomethioninemia can result in hematologic (megaloblastic anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) and neurologic (subacute combined degeneration of the cord, dementia, psychosis) defects.

rows.text: Parenteral HYDROXOCOBALAMIN is the cornerstone therapy (1 mg IM daily initially, then weekly maintenance — titrated to homocysteine and methionine) [2,9].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inborn errors of cobalamin absorption and metabolism. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2011;157C(1):33–44.

judged.citation: Carrillo-Carrasco N et al. Hydroxocobalamin dose escalation improves metabolic control in cblC. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(6):728–31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports intramuscular hydroxocobalamin as the main treatment titrated against homocysteine/methionine (in cblC), but explicitly states no formal dosing guidelines exist and argues for doses far above 1 mg, so the specific "1 mg IM daily then weekly maintenance" regimen is not carried.
judged.quote: Intramuscular (IM) hydroxocobalamin (OHCbl) is the main treatment for patients with cblC, but formal dosing guidelines do not exist.

rows.text: Avoid nitrous oxide — oxidises cobalamin cofactor and can precipitate acute deterioration [10].

judged.citation: Ilniczky S et al. MR imaging and clinical correlates in nitrous oxide induced subacute combined degeneration. Eur J Neurol. 2002;9(1):101–4.
judged.reason: The abstract documents nitrous oxide anaesthesia precipitating acute neurological deterioration (subacute combined degeneration) in the context of vitamin B12 deficiency, but it does not state the mechanism of cobalamin cofactor oxidation nor address cblE/cblG remethylation defects.
judged.quote: We report two cases of SCD induced by nitrous oxide (N2O) anaesthesia.

rows.text: Neonatal treatment significantly improves outcome [2,9].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inborn errors of cobalamin absorption and metabolism. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2011;157C(1):33–44.
judged.reason: No treatment or outcome data appear in the abstract.

judged.citation: Carrillo-Carrasco N et al. Hydroxocobalamin dose escalation improves metabolic control in cblC. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(6):728–31.
judged.reason: The abstract implies that prompt treatment of the acute neonatal presentation is life-saving, but it does not demonstrate that neonatal treatment significantly improves outcome and in fact notes long-term complications persist despite treatment.
judged.quote: This condition can be detected by expanded newborn screening and can have an acute neonatal presentation that is life-threatening if not suspected and promptly treated.

rows.text: Early-treated neonatal-onset cases: substantial neurological improvement achievable with lifelong cobalamin therapy, though residual developmental disability is common [2,9].

judged.citation: Watkins D, Rosenblatt DS. Inborn errors of cobalamin absorption and metabolism. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2011;157C(1):33–44.
judged.reason: The abstract does not discuss treatment response, developmental outcome or prognosis.

judged.citation: Carrillo-Carrasco N et al. Hydroxocobalamin dose escalation improves metabolic control in cblC. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2009;32(6):728–31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports clinical/biochemical improvement on cobalamin therapy alongside common residual developmental delay, but this is for cblC rather than cblE/cblG and it does not address neonatal-onset early-treated outcomes specifically.
judged.quote: It is well recognized that despite treatment, long-term complications such as developmental delay and progressive visual loss, may still develop.

rows.text: Most patients identified through NBS (high methionine) are clinically asymptomatic or very mildly affected — the condition is the commonest cause of isolated hypermethioninaemia and is usually benign [1,2].

judged.citation: Mudd SH et al. Isolated persistent hypermethioninemia. Am J Hum Genet. 1995;57(4):882–92.
judged.reason: The abstract reports a cohort of 30 biochemically ascertained isolated persistent hypermethioninaemia patients (presumed partial hepatic MAT deficiency) with no neurological abnormalities and near-universally normal development, supporting the benign/asymptomatic characterisation, though the phrase 'commonest cause' is not explicitly stated.
judged.quote: Patients ascertained on biochemical grounds had no neurological abnormalities, and 27/30 had IQs or Bayley development-index scores within normal limits or were judged to have normal mental development.

judged.citation: Chien YH et al. Spectrum of hypermethioninemia in neonatal screening. Early Hum Dev. 2005;81(6):529–33.
judged.reason: The abstract supports MAT deficiency being the commonest cause of isolated hypermethioninaemia detected by newborn screening, but it explicitly states the natural history is unresolved rather than asserting the condition is asymptomatic/benign.
judged.quote: Therefore methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency is the most prevalent cause of isolated hypermethioninemia in Taiwanese.

rows.text: MAT1A deficiency (OMIM #250850 recessive, #610550 dominant) was described by Gaull and Gahl in the 1970s–1980s [3].

judged.citation: Gaull GE et al. Hypermethioninemia associated with methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency: clinical, morphologic, and biochemical observations on four patients. J Pediatr. 1981;98(5):734–41.
judged.reason: The 1981 Gaull paper does describe hypermethioninemia with hepatic methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency, supporting Gaull's early description, but the abstract does not confirm the OMIM numbers, the dominant/recessive forms, Gahl's involvement, or a 1970s–1980s span.
judged.quote: Four patients with hypermethioninemia were ascertained in neonatal mass metabolic screening programs. ... Hepatic methionine adenosyltransferase activity was found to be low, ranging from 7.8 to 17.5% (mean 11.4%) of the normal adult control value.

rows.text: The dominant form with a single c.1132G>A (p.Arg264His) heterozygous variant causes mild isolated hypermethioninaemia and is particularly common [4,5].

judged.citation: Chadwick S et al. Thirteen patients with MAT1A mutations detected through newborn screening: 13 years' experience. JIMD Rep. 2014;14:71–6.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies R264H as the common autosomal dominant mutation in newborns with isolated persistent hypermethioninaemia without clinical consequence, matching the claim (nucleotide notation differs but designates the same variant).

judged.citation: Chamberlin ME et al. Demyelination of the brain is associated with methionine adenosyltransferase I/III deficiency. J Clin Invest. 1996;98(4):1021–7.
judged.reason: The abstract reports MATA1 mutations in eight hypermethioninaemic individuals but never mentions the c.1132G>A (p.Arg264His) variant, dominant heterozygous inheritance, or its frequency.
judged.quote: Mutations that abolish or reduce the MAT activity were detected in the MATA1 gene of all eight individuals.

rows.text: Urinary methionine transamination products (e.g. 2-oxo-4-methylthiobutyrate, 3-methylthiopropionate) may be elevated in severe cases — responsible for the 'boiled-cabbage' odour reported historically [6].

judged.citation: Chamberlin ME et al. Mutations in methionine adenosyltransferase I/III in hypermethioninaemia. Am J Hum Genet. 2000;66(2):347–55.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses MAT1A genotype–phenotype correlation and plasma methionine/homocysteine levels but says nothing about urinary methionine transamination products or a 'boiled-cabbage' odour, so the claim's topic is not engaged.
judged.quote: Methionine adenosyltransferase (MAT) I/III deficiency, caused by mutations in the MAT1A gene, is characterized by persistent hypermethioninemia without elevated homocysteine or tyrosine.

rows.text: Autosomal dominant (heterozygous c.1132G>A p.Arg264His — MILD hypermethioninaemia, clinically benign in most) [4,5].

judged.quote: Most individuals with isolated hypermethioninemia have been free of major clinical difficulties.

rows.text: Heterozygous dominant form (most patients): ASYMPTOMATIC, detected by NBS; normal growth and development — no treatment required [4,5].

judged.quote: Most individuals with isolated hypermethioninemia have been free of major clinical difficulties.

rows.text: Homozygous/compound heterozygous severe form: most are also clinically well but a subset shows neurological features — demyelination on MRI, developmental delay, dystonia — at very high methionine levels (>800 µmol/L) [7,8].

rows.text: Like upstream histidinaemia, the condition is rare and has generally been associated with a mild or absent clinical phenotype; a subset of published patients have had intellectual disability but causal attribution to UROC1 deficiency remains uncertain [1,2].

judged.citation: Espinós C et al. Mutations in the urocanase gene UROC1 are associated with urocanic aciduria. J Med Genet. 2009;46(6):407–11.

rows.text: Clinical phenotype: infantile failure to thrive, metabolic acidosis and 'swimming-pool' urinary odour during introduction of tyrosine-rich diets, resolving spontaneously by 1–2 years of age, with an excellent long-term prognosis [1,2].

judged.citation: Brownlee JM et al. Product analysis and inhibition studies of a causative Asn to Ser variant of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase suggest a simple route to the treatment of Hawkinsinuria. Biochemistry. 2010;49(33):7218–26.
judged.reason: The abstract supports infantile failure to thrive (slowed growth), metabolic acidosis, vomiting and diarrhoea, but says nothing about the 'swimming-pool' urinary odour, tyrosine-rich diet trigger, spontaneous resolution by 1–2 years, or excellent long-term prognosis (it instead calls the condition severe and proposes NTBC therapy).
judged.quote: The disease manifests as metabolic acidosis that significantly slows the growth rate and induces persistent diarrhea and vomiting.

rows.text: Hawkinsinuria (OMIM #140350) was first reported by Niederwieser et al. in 1977 in two related Australian families [3].

judged.citation: Niederwieser A et al. A new sulfur amino acid, named hawkinsin, identified in a baby with transient tyrosinemia and her mother. Clin Chim Acta. 1977;76(3):345–56.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms Niederwieser's 1977 first identification of hawkinsin in an affected child and her mother, but it describes only a single mother–child pair and never mentions two related Australian families.
judged.quote: An unknown compound present in the urine of a girl with prolonged transient tyrosinemia and her mother was isolated and identified as (2-L-cystein-S-yl-1,4-dihydroxycyclohex-5-en-1-yl)-acetic acid (IVa). The new amino acid was named hawkinsin (Haw)

rows.text: The condition is distinctive in being the only DOMINANT form of tyrosine metabolism disorder: affected individuals have a functional HPD enzyme on one allele and a gain-of-dysfunction variant (most commonly p.Ala33Thr) on the other that diverts 4-OH-phenylpyruvate into hawkinsin synthesis [4].

judged.citation: Tomoeda K et al. Mutations in the 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid dioxygenase gene are responsible for Tyrosinaemia type III and Hawkinsinuria. Mol Genet Metab. 2000;71(3):506–10.
judged.reason: The abstract supports autosomal dominant inheritance and the heterozygous p.Ala33Thr variant in HPD, but does not state that this is the only dominant tyrosine metabolism disorder nor describe a gain-of-dysfunction diverting 4-OH-phenylpyruvate into hawkinsin synthesis.
judged.quote: hawkinsinuria, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the excretion of 'hawkinsin,' may also be a result of HPD deficiency

rows.text: Characteristic urinary metabolites: HAWKINSIN (4-α-hydroxy-cyclohexyl-acetic acid) — a sulphur-containing cysteine conjugate — along with 4-hydroxycyclohexylacetate and elevated 4-hydroxyphenyl-lactate and 4-hydroxyphenyl-pyruvate [3,4].

judged.citation: Niederwieser A et al. A new sulfur amino acid, named hawkinsin, identified in a baby with transient tyrosinemia and her mother. Clin Chim Acta. 1977;76(3):345–56.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms hawkinsin as a urinary sulphur-containing cysteine conjugate in a setting of transient tyrosinaemia, but it does not mention 4-hydroxycyclohexylacetate or elevated 4-hydroxyphenyl-lactate and 4-hydroxyphenyl-pyruvate, and its structural name differs from the one given.
judged.quote: An unknown compound present in the urine of a girl with prolonged transient tyrosinemia and her mother was isolated and identified as (2-L-cystein-S-yl-1,4-dihydroxycyclohex-5-en-1-yl)-acetic acid (IVa). The new amino acid was named hawkinsin (Haw)

judged.citation: Tomoeda K et al. Mutations in the 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid dioxygenase gene are responsible for Tyrosinaemia type III and Hawkinsinuria. Mol Genet Metab. 2000;71(3):506–10.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms hawkinsin is a sulfur (cysteine-conjugated) amino acid excreted in urine, but gives a different chemical name and says nothing about 4-hydroxycyclohexylacetate or elevated 4-hydroxyphenyl-lactate/pyruvate.
judged.quote: Hawkinsin is a sulfur amino acid identified as (2-l-cystein-S-yl, 4-dihydroxycyclohex-5-en-1-yl)acetic acid.

rows.text: Ascorbate level may be low from the 'swimming-pool' odour's sulphur chemistry draining reduced glutathione/ascorbate [2].

judged.reason: The abstract engages the sulphur chemistry of hawkinsin formation (Michael addition of quinolacetic acid with cellular thiols) but never mentions ascorbate, ascorbate depletion, or the urinary odour compound.
judged.quote: Quinolacetic acid reacts readily by Michael addition with cellular thiols to form a two-electron oxidized form of hawkinsin.

rows.text: The canonical mutation is c.97G>A (p.Ala33Thr) — a missense change producing a structurally altered HPD that mis-channels its substrate [4,5].

judged.reason: The abstract reports the p.Ala33Thr missense mutation in hawkinsinuria patients and attributes disease to altered HPD structure/activity, though the nucleotide designation c.97G>A and 'mis-channelling' wording are not spelled out.

judged.reason: The abstract does state that hyperlysinemia is generally regarded as a benign metabolic variant, but its own cohort consisted of 8 patients with distinct neurological features, so it does not support that almost all reported individuals are asymptomatic.

rows.text: Plasma ammonia NORMAL (distinguishes from lysinuric protein intolerance, where lysine is LOW in plasma and urinary lysine is HIGH, with secondary hyperammonaemia) [1,2].

rows.text: Distinguishing context is essential: ELEVATED PIPECOLIC ACID is far more commonly a marker of PEROXISOMAL BIOGENESIS DISORDERS (Zellweger spectrum) or of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1, antiquitin deficiency) — isolated PIPOX deficiency is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion and has uncertain clinical significance [1,2].

judged.citation: Mihalik SJ et al. Peroxisomal L-pipecolic acid oxidation is deficient in liver from Zellweger syndrome patients. Pediatr Res. 1989;25(5):548–52.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that pipecolic acid accumulates in generalized peroxisomal (Zellweger spectrum) disorders due to deficient peroxisomal oxidation, but says nothing about pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy/ALDH7A1 or about isolated PIPOX deficiency being a diagnosis of exclusion with uncertain significance.
judged.quote: L-Pipecolic acid, a cyclic imino acid produced during the degradation of lysine, accumulates in body fluids of infants with the generalized peroxisomal disorders, including Zellweger syndrome, neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy, and infantile Refsum disease.

judged.citation: IJlst L et al. Molecular cloning and expression of human L-pipecolate oxidase. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 2000;270(3):1101–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that hyperpipecolic acidaemia has an unclear underlying mechanism (consistent with uncertain significance of isolated PIPOX deficiency), but it says nothing about Zellweger spectrum/peroxisomal biogenesis disorders or pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) being the more common causes of elevated pipecolic acid.
judged.quote: In literature, several patients have been described with hyperpipecolic acidaemia. The underlying mechanism responsible for the impaired degradation of pipecolate has remained unclear through the years.

rows.text: Whether a pure PIPOX defect alone causes clinical disease remains uncertain; most individuals identified biochemically have had coexisting pathology explaining the clinical picture, or have been asymptomatic [1,3].

judged.citation: Mihalik SJ et al. Peroxisomal L-pipecolic acid oxidation is deficient in liver from Zellweger syndrome patients. Pediatr Res. 1989;25(5):548–52.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns loss of pipecolic acid oxidation in Zellweger syndrome liver and does not address whether an isolated PIPOX defect causes clinical disease or the phenotypes of biochemically identified individuals.

judged.citation: Wanders RJA et al. Peroxisomal disorders: the single peroxisomal enzyme deficiencies. Biochim Biophys Acta. 2006;1763(12):1707–20.
judged.reason: The abstract is a general overview of single peroxisomal enzyme deficiencies and does not mention pipecolic acidemia, PIPOX, or the clinical significance/asymptomatic status of an isolated pipecolate oxidase defect.

rows.text: DISTINGUISHING CONTEXT is essential: (1) peroxisomal biogenesis disorders have elevated pipecolate PLUS elevated VLCFA, plasmalogen deficiency, bile-acid intermediates and phytanic acid — a combined biochemical signature distinguishing them from isolated PIPOX [4]; (2) ALDH7A1/antiquitin deficiency (pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy) causes elevated pipecolate PLUS elevated α-aminoadipic semialdehyde (α-AASA) and piperidine-6-carboxylate — a specific diagnostic biomarker [5,6].

judged.citation: Mills PB et al. Mutations in antiquitin in individuals with pyridoxine-dependent seizures. Nat Med. 2006;12(3):307–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that ALDH7A1/antiquitin deficiency causes accumulation of α-AASA and P6C as a diagnostic marker, but says nothing about accompanying elevated pipecolate (nor the peroxisomal biogenesis disorder signature).
judged.quote: these mutations abolish the activity of antiquitin as a delta1-piperideine-6-carboxylate (P6C)-alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde (alpha-AASA) dehydrogenase... Measurement of urinary alpha-AASA provides a simple way of confirming the diagnosis of PDS

judged.citation: Plecko B et al. Pipecolic acid as a diagnostic marker of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. Neuropediatrics. 2005;36(3):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms markedly elevated pipecolic acid in plasma and CSF of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy patients and its discriminatory value, but says nothing about α-aminoadipic semialdehyde, piperidine-6-carboxylate, ALDH7A1/antiquitin, or the peroxisomal biogenesis disorder signature (VLCFA, plasmalogens, phytanic acid).
judged.quote: Pipecolic acid in plasma was 4.3- to 15.3 fold elevated compared to the upper normal range before pyridoxine and remained in the mildly elevated range while on pyridoxine. Pipecolic acid was even more markedly elevated in CSF.

rows.text: Peroxisomal matrix enzyme; its mRNA/protein characterisation is well documented but pathogenic variants in humans have been few [7].

judged.citation: Dodt G et al. L-Pipecolic acid oxidase, a human enzyme essential for the degradation of L-pipecolic acid, is most similar to the monomeric sarcosine oxidases. Biol Chem. 2000;381(12):1341–8.
judged.reason: The abstract documents cloning of the cDNA, the encoded protein, its PTS1 signal and peroxisomal co-localization with catalase, supporting the mRNA/protein characterisation and peroxisomal matrix localization, but it says nothing about the number or scarcity of pathogenic human variants (nor the 17q11.2 locus/inheritance).
judged.quote: The complete cDNA, obtained by conventional library screening and 5' rapid amplification of cDNA ends, encompassed an open reading frame of 1170 bases, translating to a 390-residue protein. The translated protein terminated with the sequence AHL, a peroxisomal targeting signal 1. Indirect immunofluorescence studies showed that the protein product was expressed in human fibroblasts in a punctate pattern that co-localized with the peroxisomal enzyme catalase.

rows.text: Whenever elevated pipecolic acid is found, FIRST exclude: (a) Zellweger spectrum (VLCFA, plasmalogens); (b) ALDH7A1 deficiency (α-AASA / P6C); (c) secondary elevations from liver dysfunction or vitamin B6 insufficiency [1,5].

judged.citation: Mihalik SJ et al. Peroxisomal L-pipecolic acid oxidation is deficient in liver from Zellweger syndrome patients. Pediatr Res. 1989;25(5):548–52.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that Zellweger spectrum disorders cause high circulating pipecolic acid (supporting exclusion of Zellweger), but does not mention VLCFA/plasmalogen testing, ALDH7A1/α-AASA-P6C, or secondary elevations from liver dysfunction or B6 insufficiency.
judged.quote: Thus, the high circulating levels of L-pipecolic acid in Zellweger syndrome probably result from defective peroxisomal oxidation of L-pipecolic acid to AAA.

judged.citation: Mills PB et al. Mutations in antiquitin in individuals with pyridoxine-dependent seizures. Nat Med. 2006;12(3):307–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports item (b), that ALDH7A1 deficiency is identified by α-AASA/P6C, but does not address Zellweger spectrum testing or secondary pipecolate elevations from liver dysfunction or B6 insufficiency.
judged.quote: Measurement of urinary alpha-AASA provides a simple way of confirming the diagnosis of PDS and ALDH7A1 gene analysis provides a means for prenatal diagnosis.

rows.text: If elevated pipecolate turns out to represent antiquitin deficiency, PYRIDOXINE therapy (30 mg/kg/day initial, then maintenance) is life-changing — this is a key reason to carry out the differential diagnosis rigorously [5,6].

judged.citation: Mills PB et al. Mutations in antiquitin in individuals with pyridoxine-dependent seizures. Nat Med. 2006;12(3):307–9.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that antiquitin/ALDH7A1 deficiency underlies pyridoxine-dependent seizures (implying pyridoxine responsiveness) but gives no dosing regimen such as 30 mg/kg/day initial or maintenance therapy.
judged.quote: We show here that children with pyridoxine-dependent seizures (PDS) have mutations in the ALDH7A1 gene, which encodes antiquitin

judged.citation: Plecko B et al. Pipecolic acid as a diagnostic marker of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. Neuropediatrics. 2005;36(3):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that pyridoxine is the treatment for pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy and that withdrawal is dangerous, but gives no dosing (30 mg/kg/day initial, then maintenance) and does not name antiquitin deficiency.
judged.quote: It will in addition prevent patients with pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy from experiencing potentially dangerous pyridoxine-withdrawal, which until now has been necessary to prove the diagnosis.

rows.text: The much more important clinical lesson is not to miss the differential diagnoses — particularly ALDH7A1 deficiency — because they have major treatment implications [5,6].

judged.citation: Mills PB et al. Mutations in antiquitin in individuals with pyridoxine-dependent seizures. Nat Med. 2006;12(3):307–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the diagnosability of ALDH7A1 deficiency via a specific biomarker but does not itself discuss its treatment implications or the differential with isolated pipecolic acidemia.
judged.quote: Measurement of urinary alpha-AASA provides a simple way of confirming the diagnosis of PDS

judged.citation: Plecko B et al. Pipecolic acid as a diagnostic marker of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. Neuropediatrics. 2005;36(3):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract states that pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy remains underdiagnosed, that pipecolic acid measurement discriminates it from other causes of elevated pipecolate, and that recognising it has direct treatment/diagnostic consequences.
judged.quote: This clearly discriminates pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy from other possible defects with elevated pipecolic acid. Determination of pipecolic acid in plasma and/or CSF should be included in the diagnostic work-up of patients with therapy-resistant seizures.

rows.text: Separately, DHTKD1 variants have been implicated as a susceptibility factor for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2Q and for an adolescent-onset neurodegenerative phenotype in some kindreds — but these associations remain debated [1,2].
