rows.text: Deficiency produces systemic glutamine depletion with devastating neonatal encephalopathy: congenital malformations, severe seizures, multi-organ failure, and usually perinatal lethality — a unique reverse-image of all the standard urea-cycle disorders (where glutamine is HIGH because of ammonia trapping) [1,2].

judged.citation: Häberle J. Clinical and biochemical aspects of primary and secondary hyperammonaemic disorders. Arch Biochem Biophys. 2013;536(2):101–8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms glutamine synthetase is required alongside the urea cycle for ammonia removal, but it gives none of the claimed clinical content (congenital malformations, seizures, multi-organ failure, perinatal lethality) nor the contrast of high glutamine in urea-cycle disorders.
judged.quote: For removal of ammonia, mammals require the action of glutamine synthetase in addition to the urea cycle, in order to ensure lowering of plasma ammonia concentrations to the normal range.

judged.citation: Spodenkiewicz M et al. Minireview on glutamine synthetase deficiency, an ultra-rare inborn error of amino acid biosynthesis. Biology (Basel). 2016;5(4):40.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms neonatal-onset severe epileptic encephalopathy with low glutamine, chronic hyperammonaemia and incompatibility with normal life, but does not mention congenital malformations, multi-organ failure, perinatal lethality, or the contrast of high glutamine in urea-cycle disorders.
judged.quote: This disease was reported until now in only three unrelated patients, all of whom suffered from neonatal onset severe epileptic encephalopathy. The hallmark of GS deficiency in these patients was decreased levels of glutamine in body fluids, associated with chronic hyperammonemia.

rows.text: Glutamine synthetase deficiency (OMIM #610015) was first described by Häberle et al. in 2005 in two unrelated newborns with a devastating phenotype [3].

judged.citation: Häberle J et al. Congenital glutamine deficiency with glutamine synthetase mutations. N Engl J Med. 2005;353(18):1926–33.
judged.reason: The 2005 abstract reports two unrelated newborns with congenital glutamine synthetase deficiency and a fatal phenotype, matching the first-description claim.
judged.quote: We report on two unrelated newborns who had congenital human glutamine synthetase deficiency with severe brain malformations resulting in multiorgan failure and neonatal death.

rows.text: A heterozygous form causing an adult-onset mild phenotype has also been described recently [4].

judged.quote: Glutamine deficiency with hyperammonemia due to an inherited defect of glutamine synthetase (GS) was found in a 2 year old patient.

rows.text: Markedly LOW plasma, urinary and CSF glutamine (often <200 µmol/L in plasma vs normal 400–800) — THE DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARK, since every other inborn error of nitrogen metabolism features elevated or normal glutamine [1,3].

judged.citation: Häberle J. Clinical and biochemical aspects of primary and secondary hyperammonaemic disorders. Arch Biochem Biophys. 2013;536(2):101–8.
judged.reason: This structural review abstract discusses ammonia as a marker and promises an overview of conditions, but says nothing about plasma/CSF glutamine concentrations or diagnostic thresholds.
judged.quote: This paper will discuss the biochemical background of primary and secondary hyperammonemia and will give an overview of the various underlying conditions including a brief clinical outline and information on the genetic backgrounds.

judged.citation: Häberle J et al. Congenital glutamine deficiency with glutamine synthetase mutations. N Engl J Med. 2005;353(18):1926–33.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms glutamine is largely absent from serum, urine and CSF but gives no numeric threshold (<200 µmol/L vs normal 400–800) and does not state that all other nitrogen-metabolism errors have elevated or normal glutamine.
judged.quote: Glutamine was largely absent from their serum, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid.

rows.text: Other amino acids may also be low because glutamine is a major anabolic nitrogen donor [1,2].

judged.citation: Häberle J. Clinical and biochemical aspects of primary and secondary hyperammonaemic disorders. Arch Biochem Biophys. 2013;536(2):101–8.
judged.reason: The abstract does not address amino acid profiles or glutamine's role as an anabolic nitrogen donor.

judged.quote: two unrelated newborns who had congenital human glutamine synthetase deficiency with severe brain malformations resulting in multiorgan failure and neonatal death

rows.text: HSD17B10 deficiency (OMIM #300438; also known as 'MHBD deficiency') was originally described as an isolated organic aciduria but later recognised as a mitochondrial RNase P subunit defect — one of the first inborn errors to illustrate 'moonlighting' enzyme biology [3,4]. ~30 male patients reported with the classical phenotype; heterozygous females with milder variants more recently recognised.

judged.reason: The abstract supports the identification of a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase-family protein (HSD17B10) as a subunit of human mitochondrial RNase P — the 'moonlighting' basis — but says nothing about the organic aciduria phenotype, OMIM number, ~30 reported male patients, or heterozygous female carriers.
judged.quote: composed of a tRNA methyltransferase, a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase-family member, and a protein of hitherto unknown functional and evolutionary origin

judged.quote: 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase (MHBD) deficiency is a novel inborn error of isoleucine degradation.

rows.text: The biochemical pattern overlaps with β-ketothiolase (BKT/ACAT1) deficiency, but HSD17B10 patients ALSO have lactic acidosis and mitochondrial features (lactate elevated, respiratory chain defects on muscle biopsy) — this combined presentation should raise suspicion [1,5].

rows.text: Historical case reports linking GA-III to neurological symptoms almost certainly reflect ascertainment bias — patients were biochemically tested for other reasons [1,2,5].

judged.citation: Sherman EA et al. Genetic mapping of glutaric aciduria type 3 to chromosome 7 and identification of mutations in C7orf10. Am J Hum Genet. 2008;83(5):604–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that GA3 individuals detected by biochemical screening were healthy with no consistent phenotype, but says nothing about ascertainment bias in historical neurological case reports.
judged.quote: There was no consistent clinical phenotype associated with GA3.

judged.citation: La Serna-Infantes J et al. Novel contiguous gene deletion in Peruvian girl with trichothiodystrophy type 4 and glutaric aciduria type 3. Eur J Med Genet. 2018;61(7):388–92.
judged.reason: The abstract asserts GA3 has no distinctive phenotype (with the girl's neurological features attributable to the co-deleted MPLKIP/TTD4), but does not address ascertainment bias in historical case reports.
judged.quote: Glutaric aciduria type 3 is caused by a homozygous mutation in SUGCT gene with no distinctive phenotype.

rows.text: If urinary glutaric acid elevation is found, acylcarnitine profile (C5DC), 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, and GCDH molecular testing should be checked to exclude GA-I before concluding the diagnosis is GA-III [1,6].

judged.citation: Sherman EA et al. Genetic mapping of glutaric aciduria type 3 to chromosome 7 and identification of mutations in C7orf10. Am J Hum Genet. 2008;83(5):604–9.
judged.reason: The abstract shows GA3 was distinguished from GA1 by low 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and absence of the GCDH mutation, but it does not recommend acylcarnitine/C5DC testing as part of a diagnostic exclusion workflow.
judged.quote: None of these children had the GCDH c.1262C-->T mutation that causes GA1 among the Amish.

judged.citation: Kölker S et al. Guideline for the diagnosis and management of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type I). J Inherit Metab Dis. 2007;30(1):5–22.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that GA-I is diagnosed biochemically via 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and glutarylcarnitine (C5DC) by acylcarnitine tandem MS, but it does not mention GCDH molecular testing or the specific need to exclude GA-I before diagnosing GA-III.
judged.quote: Biochemically, the disease is characterized by accumulation of glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, glutaconic acid, and glutarylcarnitine, which can be detected by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of organic acids or tandem mass spectrometry of acylcarnitines.

rows.text: The clinical significance of the condition lies ONLY in avoiding misclassification as GA-I [1,2,5].

judged.citation: Sherman EA et al. Genetic mapping of glutaric aciduria type 3 to chromosome 7 and identification of mutations in C7orf10. Am J Hum Genet. 2008;83(5):604–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the absence of a clinical phenotype and relevance to GA1 understanding, but does not state normal life expectancy or that the sole significance is avoiding misclassification as GA-I.
judged.quote: There was no consistent clinical phenotype associated with GA3.

judged.citation: La Serna-Infantes J et al. Novel contiguous gene deletion in Peruvian girl with trichothiodystrophy type 4 and glutaric aciduria type 3. Eur J Med Genet. 2018;61(7):388–92.
judged.reason: Although the abstract touches on GA3's lack of a distinctive phenotype, it makes no statement about prognosis, life expectancy, or the risk of misclassification as GA-I.
judged.quote: Glutaric aciduria type 3 is caused by a homozygous mutation in SUGCT gene with no distinctive phenotype.

rows.text: Thiamine and ketogenic diet are key therapeutic options [1,2].

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: No treatment data are reported in this natural-history review, so thiamine and ketogenic diet cannot be assessed.

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: No treatment data are reported in this natural-history review, so thiamine and ketogenic diet cannot be assessed.

rows.text: DLD (E3) is shared with other 2-ketoacid dehydrogenases and produces a more complex multi-ketoacid phenotype [1,3].

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: The abstract includes E3 defects in the cohort but never states that E3/DLD is shared with other 2-ketoacid dehydrogenases or that it causes a multi-ketoacid phenotype, and in fact reports no clinical differentiation between biochemical etiologies.
judged.quote: Neither gender nor any clinical or neuroimaging feature differentiated the various biochemical etiologies of the disease.

judged.citation: Brown GK. Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 alpha deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1992;15(4):625–33.
judged.reason: The abstract is confined to PDH E1 alpha (PDHA1) deficiency and its X-linked features, saying nothing about DLD/E3 being shared with other 2-ketoacid dehydrogenases or a multi-ketoacid phenotype.

rows.text: Enzyme assay: PDC activity <40% of normal in cultured fibroblasts, lymphocytes or muscle [1,4].

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that residual PDC enzyme activity is measured and varies in PDC deficiency, but it does not state the <40%-of-normal diagnostic threshold or specify fibroblasts, lymphocytes or muscle as assay tissues.
judged.quote: Patients who died were younger, presented clinically earlier and had higher blood lactate levels and lower residual enzyme activities than subjects who were still alive at the time of reporting.

rows.text: PDHA1 notably shows an essentially equal frequency of clinically affected males and females — affected females tend to carry insertion/deletion variants while affected males more often carry missense variants; ~60% of affected males and ~85–95% of affected females have de novo variants [3,5].

judged.citation: Brown GK. Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 alpha deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1992;15(4):625–33.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that PDHA1 deficiency is X-linked with a high proportion of heterozygous females manifesting the condition, but gives none of the specific variant-type distribution or de novo percentages (~60%, ~85–95%).
judged.quote: PDH E1 alpha deficiency is an X-linked inborn error of metabolism in which a high proportion of heterozygous females manifest the condition.

rows.text: Structural brain malformations (agenesis of corpus callosum, simplified gyral pattern, subependymal cysts) characteristic and should raise suspicion [1,6].

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms frequent structural brain abnormalities including corpus callosum dysgenesis and ventriculomegaly, but does not mention simplified gyral pattern or subependymal cysts or tie these to the neonatal-onset form specifically.
judged.quote: Structural brain abnormalities frequently included ventriculomegaly, dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and neuroimaging findings typical of Leigh syndrome.

judged.citation: Marsac C et al. Defect in the lipoyl-bearing protein X subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in two patients with primary lactic acidosis. J Clin Invest. 1993;91(3):1040–7.
judged.reason: The abstract is a biochemical/immunoblot characterization of protein X deficiency and never addresses structural brain malformations such as corpus callosum agenesis, simplified gyral pattern or subependymal cysts; imaging discussed is only 31P NMR of muscle.
judged.quote: Spectra obtained with 31P nuclear magnetic resonance showed alterations compatible with those found in mitochondrial myopathies.

rows.text: Some adult males have isolated intermittent cerebellar ataxia; heterozygous females often mild [2,7].

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: Although the abstract addresses the clinical spectrum and gender, it reports no gender-related differences and never describes adult males with isolated intermittent cerebellar ataxia or mild heterozygous females.
judged.quote: Survival bore no relationship to the underlying biochemical or genetic abnormality or to gender.

judged.citation: Head RA et al. Clinical and genetic spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency: dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase (E2) deficiency. Ann Neurol. 2005;58(2):234–41.
judged.reason: The abstract engages the clinical spectrum of PDH deficiency and milder phenotypes but describes two children with autosomal recessive DLAT (E2) mutations presenting with episodic dystonia; it says nothing about adult males with isolated intermittent cerebellar ataxia or about mild manifestations in heterozygous females.
judged.quote: Both patients are less severely affected than typical patients with E1alpha mutations and both have survived well into childhood. Episodic dystonia was the major neurological manifestation, with other more common features of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, such as hypotonia and ataxia, being less prominent.

rows.text: KETOGENIC DIET (ratios 1:1 to 4:1 fat to carbohydrate/protein, targeting plasma β-hydroxybutyrate ~3.0–3.5 mEq/L) — the gold-standard therapy; bypasses the block by providing acetyl-CoA directly from β-hydroxybutyrate; ~50% of patients achieve seizure remission within the first year [8,9].

judged.citation: Wexler ID et al. Outcome of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency treated with ketogenic diets: studies in patients with identical mutations. Neurology. 1997;49(6):1655–61.
judged.reason: The abstract supports ketogenic diet (with carbohydrate restriction) as beneficial therapy in E1/PDC deficiency, but gives none of the specific quantitative details in the sentence — no fat:carbohydrate ratios, no plasma β-hydroxybutyrate target of ~3.0–3.5 mEq/L, and no ~50% seizure-remission rate within the first year (seizure outcomes are not mentioned at all).
judged.quote: Subjects who either had the diet initiated earlier in life or who were placed on greater carbohydrate restriction had increased longevity and improved mental development.

judged.citation: Sofou K et al. Ketogenic diet in pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: short- and long-term outcomes. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(2):237–45.
judged.reason: The abstract supports ketogenic diet as an effective, safe therapy and a target ketone level consistent with ~3.0–3.5 mmol/l (median 3.3), but it does not give the 1:1–4:1 diet ratios, the acetyl-CoA bypass mechanism, or the ~50% seizure-remission-within-one-year figure.
judged.quote: The median plasma concentration of ketone bodies (3-hydroxybutyric acid) was 3.3 mmol/l.

rows.text: THIAMINE 300–1000 mg/day (divided in three doses) — essential cofactor of E1; response is more likely in patients with missense variants, particularly exon 3 mutations; always trial [8].

judged.citation: Wexler ID et al. Outcome of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency treated with ketogenic diets: studies in patients with identical mutations. Neurology. 1997;49(6):1655–61.
judged.reason: The abstract mentions cofactor replacement only in passing as a treatment modality and gives no thiamine dose range, dosing schedule, or genotype-based (missense/exon 3) response prediction; its data concern ketogenic diet outcomes.
judged.quote: Treatment of E1 deficiency hs included cofactor replacement, activation of PDC with dichloroacetate, and ketogenic diets.

rows.text: Dichloroacetate (activates PDC by inhibiting PDH kinase, dosed per GSTZ1 haplotype) — trialled with biochemical and modest clinical response; peripheral neuropathy is a dose-limiting toxicity [10].

judged.citation: Stacpoole PW et al. Controlled clinical trial of dichloroacetate for congenital lactic acidosis in children. Pediatrics. 2006;117(5):1519–31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that DCA was trialled in congenital lactic acidosis including PDH deficiency with a biochemical (lactate) response, but it reports no clinical benefit rather than a modest clinical response, and it does not mention GSTZ1 haplotype-based dosing, PDH kinase inhibition, or peripheral neuropathy as a dose-limiting toxicity (it states DCA was well tolerated).
judged.quote: DCA significantly decreased the rise in blood lactate caused by carbohydrate feeding. ... However, it did not improve neurologic or other measures of clinical outcome.

rows.text: Later-onset phenotypes with partial enzyme activity: much more favourable, with some patients leading near-normal lives [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: Later presentation and greater residual activity are associated with survival, but the claim's assertion of near-normal lives is not in the abstract.
judged.quote: Patients who died were younger, presented clinically earlier and had higher blood lactate levels and lower residual enzyme activities than subjects who were still alive at the time of reporting.

judged.citation: Patel KP et al. The spectrum of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency: clinical, biochemical and genetic features in 371 patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;105(1):34–43.
judged.reason: Later presentation and greater residual activity are associated with survival, but the claim's assertion of near-normal lives is not in the abstract.
judged.quote: Patients who died were younger, presented clinically earlier and had higher blood lactate levels and lower residual enzyme activities than subjects who were still alive at the time of reporting.

judged.citation: Wexler ID et al. Outcome of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency treated with ketogenic diets: studies in patients with identical mutations. Neurology. 1997;49(6):1655–61.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses outcome as a function of ketogenic diet timing/intensity in seven boys with defined mutations, not the prognosis of later-onset phenotypes with partial residual enzyme activity.

rows.text: Lactate:pyruvate ratio is NORMAL (distinguishes from respiratory chain) and citrulline is frequently elevated (unique marker reflecting urea cycle involvement through aspartate depletion) [1,2].

judged.citation: Marin-Valencia I et al. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency: mechanisms, mimics and anaplerosis. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;101(1):9–17.
judged.reason: The abstract signals that the review emphasizes biochemical features distinguishing PC deficiency from other causes of lactic acidemia, but it does not state the normal lactate:pyruvate ratio or elevated citrulline/aspartate-depletion mechanism.
judged.quote: emphasizing features that distinguish PC deficiency from other causes of lactic acidemia

rows.text: PC deficiency (OMIM #266150) was first described by Hommes in 1968 [3].

judged.citation: Hommes FA et al. Two cases of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase deficiency. Acta Paediatr Scand. 1976;65(2):233–40.
judged.reason: This 1976 Hommes paper describes phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase deficiency, a different gluconeogenic enzyme defect, and does not report a 1968 first description of pyruvate carboxylase deficiency.
judged.quote: Assays of gluconeogenic enzymes in liver samples taken immediately after death demonstrated a deficiency of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, a key enzyme of gluconeogenesis.

rows.text: Three clinical subtypes (A, B, C) were delineated in the 1970s–1980s and remain the standard classification [2,4].

judged.citation: Marin-Valencia I et al. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency: mechanisms, mimics and anaplerosis. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;101(1):9–17.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the three-subtype (A, B, C) classification as standard but gives no indication that it was delineated in the 1970s–1980s.
judged.quote: Three clinical forms of PC deficiency have been identified: an infantile form (Type A), a severe neonatal form (Type B), and a benign form (Type C)

judged.citation: Robinson BH, Oei J, Saudubray JM et al. The French and North American phenotypes of pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, correlation with biotin containing protein by 3H-biotin incorporation, 35S-streptavidin labeling, and Northern blotting with a cloned cDNA probe. Am J Hum Genet. 1987;40(1):50–9.
judged.reason: The abstract documents distinct clinical phenotypes of PC deficiency (French vs North American, i.e., types B and A) with biochemical correlates, but never names three subtypes A/B/C nor establishes their delineation in the 1970s–1980s or their status as the standard classification.
judged.quote: Thus, whereas the North American presentation of PC deficiency is associated with the presence of a mature biotin containing protein of the correct molecular weight, the French presentation may, in some (but not in all) cases, have both absent PC protein and absent PC mRNA.

rows.text: ELEVATED CITRULLINE (a unique marker, typically 100–300 µmol/L) — reflects reduced aspartate available for argininosuccinate synthesis (aspartate depletion secondary to OAA/malate shortage) [1,5].

judged.citation: Garcia-Cazorla A et al. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency: metabolic characteristics and new neurological aspects. Ann Neurol. 2006;59(1):121–7.
judged.reason: The abstract supports hypercitrullinemia as a characteristic biochemical feature but does not provide the stated 100–300 µmol/L range or the argininosuccinate-synthesis mechanism.
judged.quote: Hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hypercitrullinemia were invariably found.

rows.text: Urine organic acids: elevated α-ketoglutarate and 3-hydroxybutyric acid [1,2].

judged.citation: Marin-Valencia I et al. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency: mechanisms, mimics and anaplerosis. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;101(1):9–17.
judged.reason: The abstract makes only a general reference to biochemical aspects and does not address urine organic acid findings such as α-ketoglutarate or 3-hydroxybutyric acid.
judged.quote: dissect the major clinical, biochemical, and genetic aspects of its dysfunction

rows.text: Type A (infantile, classic 'American' form): early-infancy onset with metabolic and lactic acidosis, delayed motor development, intellectual disability, seizures; most children die in infancy or early childhood, though survival to teenage years has been reported [1,2].

judged.citation: Marin-Valencia I et al. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency: mechanisms, mimics and anaplerosis. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;101(1):9–17.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the infantile Type A designation with early-age lactic acidemia/neurological dysfunction and death in early life, but does not mention motor delay, intellectual disability, seizures, or survival to teenage years.
judged.quote: an infantile form (Type A), a severe neonatal form (Type B), and a benign form (Type C), all of which exhibit clinical or biochemical correlates of impaired anaplerosis. There is no effective treatment for these patients and most, except those affected by the benign form, die in early life.

rows.text: Type B (severe neonatal, 'French' form): neonatal or infantile onset of hypothermia, respiratory distress, vomiting, severe lactic acidosis and hyperammonaemia; typically fatal by age 8 months [2].

judged.citation: Marin-Valencia I et al. Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency: mechanisms, mimics and anaplerosis. Mol Genet Metab. 2010;101(1):9–17.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies Type B as the severe neonatal form that typically dies in early life, but does not give the specific features (hypothermia, respiratory distress, vomiting, hyperammonaemia) or the 8-month survival figure.
judged.quote: a severe neonatal form (Type B)

rows.text: N-acetylcysteine + metronidazole (reduces gut H₂S production) is the rational and now evidence-based therapy [1,2].

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Loss of ETHE1, a mitochondrial dioxygenase, causes fatal sulphide toxicity in ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Nat Med. 2009;15(2):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the mechanistic rationale (ETHE1 loss causes toxic sulfide accumulation detoxified by a mitochondrial sulfur dioxygenase) but says nothing about N-acetylcysteine, metronidazole, gut H₂S production, or any evidence of therapeutic efficacy.
judged.quote: Therefore, ETHE1 is a mitochondrial sulfur dioxygenase involved in catabolism of sulfide that accumulates to toxic levels in ethylmalonic encephalopathy.

judged.citation: Viscomi C et al. Combined treatment with oral metronidazole and N-acetylcysteine is effective in ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Nat Med. 2010;16(8):869–71.
judged.reason: The abstract reports that metronidazole reduces sulfide-producing gut bacteria and NAC buffers sulfide, with the combination producing marked clinical improvement in affected children — i.e., the mechanistic rationale plus evidence.
judged.quote: Metronidazole, a bactericide, or N-acetylcysteine, a precursor of sulfide-buffering glutathione, substantially prolonged the lifespan of Ethe1-deficient mice, with the combined treatment being additive. The same dual treatment caused marked clinical improvement in five affected children, with hardly any adverse or side effects.

rows.text: Ethylmalonic encephalopathy (OMIM #602473) was first described by Burlina et al. in 1994 [3].

judged.citation: Burlina AB et al. A new syndrome with ethylmalonic aciduria and normal fatty acid oxidation in fibroblasts. J Pediatr. 1994;124(1):79–86.
judged.reason: The 1994 Burlina paper describes a novel clinical/biochemical phenotype with marked ethylmalonic aciduria and encephalopathy, i.e., the first description of ethylmalonic encephalopathy.
judged.quote: This unique clinical and biochemical phenotype identifies a new metabolic encephalopathy of yet undetermined cause.

rows.text: The causative gene ETHE1 was identified in 2004 [4].

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Ethylmalonic encephalopathy is caused by mutations in ETHE1, a gene encoding a mitochondrial matrix protein. Am J Hum Genet. 2004;74(2):239–52.
judged.reason: The 2004 paper reports identification of the gene responsible for ethylmalonic encephalopathy and its renaming to ETHE1, matching the claim's gene and year of publication.
judged.quote: we identified GenBank D83198 as the gene responsible for EE

rows.text: Elevated C4 (butyryl- + isobutyryl)-carnitine and C5 (2-methylbutyryl + isovaleryl)-carnitine on acylcarnitine profile (reflects secondary inhibition of short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases by H₂S) [1,5].

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Loss of ETHE1, a mitochondrial dioxygenase, causes fatal sulphide toxicity in ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Nat Med. 2009;15(2):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract reports high blood C4 and C5 acylcarnitines and states sulfide inhibits short-chain fatty acid oxidation, matching both the marker and the proposed mechanism.
judged.quote: high concentrations of C4 and C5 acylcarnitines in blood and high excretion of ethylmalonic acid in urine

judged.citation: Mineri R et al. Identification of new mutations in the ETHE1 gene in a cohort of 14 patients with ethylmalonic encephalopathy. J Med Genet. 2008;45(8):473–8.
judged.reason: The abstract reports ETHE1 mutation findings and general clinical features only, with no mention of acylcarnitine profiles, C4/C5 species, or H₂S-mediated inhibition of short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases.
judged.quote: 14 patients with EE were investigated for mutations in the ETHE1 gene. Of the 14 patients, 5 were found to carry novel mutations.

rows.text: Muscle biopsy: reduced cytochrome c oxidase activity with preserved SDH — a characteristic pattern [4].

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Ethylmalonic encephalopathy is caused by mutations in ETHE1, a gene encoding a mitochondrial matrix protein. Am J Hum Genet. 2004;74(2):239–52.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms decreased cytochrome c oxidase activity in skeletal muscle but says nothing about preserved SDH activity or the contrast constituting a characteristic pattern.
judged.quote: cytochrome c oxidase activity is decreased in skeletal muscle

rows.text: Founder alleles documented in Mediterranean and Arab populations [6].

judged.citation: Barth M et al. Multiple sources of metabolic disturbance in ETHE1-related ethylmalonic encephalopathy. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(Suppl 3):S443–53.
judged.reason: The abstract is a single-case metabolic loading study reporting a homozygous ETHE1 mutation and says nothing about founder alleles or population/ethnic distribution of variants.
judged.quote: We report on a 15-month-old male presenting with typical EE associated with a homozygous ETHE1 mutation.

rows.text: Brain MRI: bilateral symmetric T2 hyperintensity in putamen, caudate and cerebral + cerebellar cortex — Leigh-like pattern [1,7,8].

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Loss of ETHE1, a mitochondrial dioxygenase, causes fatal sulphide toxicity in ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Nat Med. 2009;15(2):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract describes clinical and biochemical features but never addresses brain MRI findings or a Leigh-like imaging pattern.

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Ethylmalonic encephalopathy is caused by mutations in ETHE1, a gene encoding a mitochondrial matrix protein. Am J Hum Genet. 2004;74(2):239–52.
judged.reason: The abstract is a gene-identification paper and does not address brain MRI findings or a Leigh-like radiological pattern.

judged.citation: Grosso S et al. Ethylmalonic encephalopathy: further clinical and neuroradiological characterization. J Neurol. 2002;249(10):1446–50.
judged.reason: The abstract documents T2 hyperintensity in the basal ganglia and cerebellar/cerebral atrophy in EE patients, but does not specify bilateral symmetric involvement of putamen and caudate plus cerebral and cerebellar cortex or describe a Leigh-like pattern.
judged.quote: Neuroradiological follow-up of patient 1 detected a diffuse hyperintensity on the T2 images at the basal ganglia which remained stable during a period of four years.

rows.text: Combination therapy with N-ACETYLCYSTEINE (thiol donor/H₂S scavenger, 100 mg/kg/day) + METRONIDAZOLE (reduces gut H₂S-producing flora, 20 mg/kg/day) — currently the only pharmacotherapy shown to slow disease progression [1,9].

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Loss of ETHE1, a mitochondrial dioxygenase, causes fatal sulphide toxicity in ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Nat Med. 2009;15(2):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract is a mechanistic study of sulfide toxicity and does not mention N-acetylcysteine, metronidazole, doses, or any pharmacotherapy outcome.

judged.citation: Olivieri G et al. Ethylmalonic encephalopathy and liver transplantation: long-term outcome of the first treated patient. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2021;16(1):229.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns liver transplantation outcome and never addresses N-acetylcysteine, metronidazole, their doses, or their effect on disease progression.
judged.quote: we successfully attempted liver transplantation in a 9-month-old EE girl

rows.text: Emerging: liver transplantation has been used in severe cases to supply hepatic ETHE1 activity (expressed in hepatocytes) — preliminary reports encouraging [10].

judged.citation: Dionisi-Vici C et al. Liver transplant in ethylmalonic encephalopathy: a new treatment for an otherwise fatal disease. Brain. 2016;139(Pt 4):1045–51.
judged.reason: The abstract reports living donor liver transplantation in an infant with ethylmalonic encephalopathy with striking neurological and biochemical improvement, supporting liver transplantation as an emerging encouraging option.
judged.quote: Unlike the invariably progressive deterioration of the disease, 8 months after liver transplantation, we observed striking neurological improvement with remarkable achievements in psychomotor development, along with dramatic reversion of biochemical abnormalities. These results clearly indicate that liver transplantation is a viable therapeutic option for ETHE1 disease.

rows.text: With NAC + metronidazole therapy begun early: clinical improvement and survival into the second decade reported, with stabilisation or slowed progression of the neurological phenotype [1,2,9].

judged.citation: Tiranti V et al. Loss of ETHE1, a mitochondrial dioxygenase, causes fatal sulphide toxicity in ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Nat Med. 2009;15(2):200–5.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses disease mechanism and states the disorder is invariably fatal, but does not report treated outcomes, survival into the second decade, or effects of NAC plus metronidazole.

judged.citation: Viscomi C et al. Combined treatment with oral metronidazole and N-acetylcysteine is effective in ethylmalonic encephalopathy. Nat Med. 2010;16(8):869–71.
judged.reason: The abstract documents clinical improvement on the dual treatment but gives no follow-up duration, no survival into the second decade, and no statement about stabilisation or slowed neurological progression.
judged.quote: The same dual treatment caused marked clinical improvement in five affected children, with hardly any adverse or side effects.

judged.citation: Olivieri G et al. Ethylmalonic encephalopathy and liver transplantation: long-term outcome of the first treated patient. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2021;16(1):229.
judged.reason: The abstract documents clinical/biochemical stabilisation and improvement after early intervention in EE, but the intervention is liver transplantation rather than NAC + metronidazole, and no survival into the second decade is reported (follow-up just over 6 years).
judged.quote: The long-term follow-up of the first EE transplanted patient demonstrates that liver transplantation stabilizes, or even improves, disease course

rows.text: Malonic aciduria (OMIM #248360) was first described by Brown et al. in 1984 [3].

judged.citation: Brown GK et al. Malonyl coenzyme A decarboxylase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1984;7(1):21–6.
judged.reason: The abstract reports the first recognized case of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency with malonic acid excretion, matching the 1984 Brown et al. first description.
judged.quote: A patient is described with a deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme, malonyl CoA decarboxylase - an inborn error of metabolism not recognized previously.

rows.text: The malonic:methylmalonic ratio is typically >1 (distinguishes from MMUT mutase deficiency, where ratio <1) [1,4].

judged.citation: FitzPatrick DR et al. The molecular basis of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency. Am J Hum Genet. 1999;65(2):318–26.
judged.reason: The abstract contains no biochemical/metabolite data on malonic or methylmalonic acid excretion and does not discuss differentiation from mutase deficiency.

judged.citation: Gao J et al. Cloning and mutational analysis of human malonyl-coenzyme A decarboxylase. J Lipid Res. 1999;40(1):178–82.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns cloning and mutation identification and mentions malonic aciduria only as a clinical feature; it never discusses methylmalonic acid levels or a malonic:methylmalonic ratio distinguishing MLYCD from mutase deficiency.
judged.quote: The genetic mutation underlying malonyl CoA decarboxylase deficiency was determined in a patient with clinical features of this defect, malonic aciduria, and markedly reduced malonyl CoA decarboxylase activity.

rows.text: Some founder variants identified [5,6].

judged.citation: Sacksteder KA et al. MCD encodes peroxisomal and cytoplasmic forms of malonyl-CoA decarboxylase and is mutated in malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency. J Biol Chem. 1999;274(35):24461–8.
judged.reason: The abstract describes a single severe mutation (c.947-948delTT) in one MCD-deficient patient but says nothing about founder variants or recurring population-specific alleles.
judged.quote: a malonyl-CoA decarboxylase-deficient patient has a severe mutation in the MCD gene (c.947-948delTT)

judged.reason: The abstract explicitly states autosomal recessive inheritance for all forms and names MOCS1, MOCS2 and GEPH as mutated loci.
judged.quote: All forms of molybdenum cofactor deficiency are inherited as autosomal recessive traits.

judged.citation: Reiss J et al. A mutation in the gene for the neurotransmitter receptor-clustering protein gephyrin causes a novel form of molybdenum cofactor deficiency. Am J Hum Genet. 2001;68(1):208–13.
judged.reason: The abstract identifies a GEPH deletion causing MoCo deficiency but never addresses the mode of inheritance, so the claim that all these gene defects are autosomal recessive cannot be evaluated from it.
judged.quote: The present report describes the identification of a gephyrin gene (GEPH) deletion in a patient with symptoms typical of MoCo deficiency.

rows.text: Usually fatal within weeks to months without cPMP therapy in type A [1,6,7].

judged.citation: Reiss J, Johnson JL. Mutations in the molybdenum cofactor biosynthetic genes MOCS1, MOCS2, and GEPH. Hum Mutat. 2003;21(6):569–76.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms a severe, usually fatal course but times death to "early childhood" rather than weeks to months, and says nothing about cPMP therapy or type A specifically.
judged.quote: The resultant severe phenotype, which includes progressive neurological damage leading in most cases to early childhood death, results primarily from the deficiency of sulfite oxidase.

judged.citation: Bayram E et al. Molybdenum cofactor deficiency: review of 12 cases. Eur J Paediatr Neurol. 2013;17(1):1–6.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the severe neonatal phenotype and lack of effective treatment in MoCD but gives no mortality timeline (weeks to months), no type A distinction, and does not address cPMP therapy.
judged.quote: The major clinical symptoms are intractable neonatal seizures, progressive encephalopathy, facial dysmorphic features and feeding difficulties. ... Although the therapeutic treatment strategies have not been improved, genetic analysis is essential to elucidate the disease.

judged.citation: Schwahn BC et al. Efficacy and safety of cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate substitution in severe molybdenum cofactor deficiency type A: a prospective cohort study. Lancet. 2015;386(10007):1955–63.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms rapidly progressive encephalopathy leading to severe disability and early death without effective prior treatment, but gives no specific 'weeks to months' survival interval.
judged.quote: Molybdenum cofactor deficiency (MoCD) is characterised by early, rapidly progressive postnatal encephalopathy and intractable seizures, leading to severe disability and early death.

rows.text: TYPE A (MOCS1): Daily IV FOSDENOPTERIN (synthetic cPMP) — FDA approved 2021 (Nulibry®) — replaces the missing biosynthetic intermediate and restores MoCo generation [3,8].

judged.citation: Schwahn BC et al. Efficacy and safety of cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate substitution in severe molybdenum cofactor deficiency type A: a prospective cohort study. Lancet. 2015;386(10007):1955–63.
judged.reason: The abstract supports intravenous cPMP substitution restoring molybdenum cofactor-dependent enzyme activities in type A, but does not mention the 2021 FDA approval or the Nulibry brand name (carried by the co-cited approval summary).
judged.quote: Intravenous cPMP (80-320 μg/kg per day) was started in neonates diagnosed with MoCD (type A and type B) following a standardised protocol.

rows.text: Genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis for future pregnancies [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Reiss J, Johnson JL. Mutations in the molybdenum cofactor biosynthetic genes MOCS1, MOCS2, and GEPH. Hum Mutat. 2003;21(6):569–76.
judged.reason: The abstract reports mutation identification in patients and relatives but does not discuss genetic counselling or prenatal diagnosis.

judged.citation: Veldman A et al. Successful treatment of molybdenum cofactor deficiency type A with cPMP. Pediatrics. 2010;125(5):e1249–54.
judged.reason: The abstract reports cPMP treatment and newborn-screening detection but says nothing about genetic counselling or prenatal diagnosis for future pregnancies.

rows.text: Type B/C: no disease-modifying therapy currently, prognosis remains poor [1,8].

judged.citation: Reiss J, Johnson JL. Mutations in the molybdenum cofactor biosynthetic genes MOCS1, MOCS2, and GEPH. Hum Mutat. 2003;21(6):569–76.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a generally poor prognosis in molybdenum cofactor deficiency but says nothing about therapy availability or a distinction between type A and types B/C.
judged.quote: progressive neurological damage leading in most cases to early childhood death

rows.text: Clinical phenotype: hypermethioninaemia + elevated SAH + myopathy + hepatopathy + developmental delay + coagulopathy + hypotonia — a combined muscle-liver-brain presentation distinctive from other hypermethioninaemia disorders (MAT1A, GNMT) which are typically much milder [1,2].

judged.citation: Barić I et al. S-Adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: a second patient, the first with homozygosity for a novel missense mutation. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2005;28(6):885–902.
judged.reason: The abstract documents hypermethioninaemia, markedly elevated AdoHcy, raised CK (myopathy), raised aminotransferases (hepatopathy), hypotonia and psychomotor delay, but does not mention coagulopathy or any comparison showing MAT1A/GNMT hypermethioninaemias are milder.
judged.quote: The laboratory abnormalities are markedly increased creatine kinase and elevated aminotransferases, as well as specific amino acid aberrations that pinpoint the aetiology. The latter include, most importantly, markedly elevated plasma AdoHcy.

judged.citation: Stender S et al. Adult-onset liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma in S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2015;116(4):269–74.
judged.reason: The abstract supports hypermethioninaemia with elevated SAH/SAM, myopathy (muscle weakness) and hepatopathy, but says nothing about developmental delay, coagulopathy or hypotonia, and makes no comparison with MAT1A or GNMT hypermethioninaemia disorders.
judged.quote: She developed muscle weakness in her mid-20s, and was diagnosed with hepatocellular carcinoma at age 29... markedly elevated serum levels of SAH, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), and methionine, which are hallmarks of SAH hydrolase deficiency.

rows.text: AHCY deficiency (OMIM #613752) was first described by Barić et al. in 2004 [3].

judged.citation: Barić I et al. S-Adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency in a human: a genetic disorder of methionine metabolism. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2004;101(12):4234–9.
judged.reason: The 2004 paper by Barić et al. reports the first proven human case of AdoHcy hydrolase deficiency, matching the claim of first description in 2004.
judged.quote: We report studies of a Croatian boy, a proven case of human S-adenosylhomocysteine (AdoHcy) hydrolase deficiency.

rows.text: Biochemistry requires specialist laboratories able to measure SAH [1,4].

judged.citation: Barić I et al. S-Adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: a second patient, the first with homozygosity for a novel missense mutation. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2005;28(6):885–902.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that plasma AdoHcy (SAH) measurement is the key diagnostic marker but says nothing about the need for specialist laboratories capable of assaying it.
judged.quote: The latter include, most importantly, markedly elevated plasma AdoHcy.

judged.citation: Buist NR et al. S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency in a 26-year-old man. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(4):538–45.
judged.reason: The abstract shows that diagnosis rested on specialised measurements of plasma AdoHcy/AdoMet plus erythrocyte enzyme activity and gene sequencing, and that it was only achieved at age 26 despite lifelong follow-up, but it never states that such SAH assays require specialist laboratories.
judged.quote: The diagnosis was based on markedly elevated plasma concentrations of both AdoHcy and S-adenosylmethionine, some 20% of the mean control activity of AdoHcy hydrolase activity in haemolysates of his red-blood cells, and two missense mutations in his gene encoding AdoHcy hydrolase.

rows.text: Heterogeneous variants including missense hypomorphs; heterozygotes asymptomatic [5,6].

judged.citation: Grubbs R et al. S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: two siblings with fetal hydrops and fatal outcomes. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(6):705–13.
judged.reason: The abstract documents compound heterozygosity for two novel missense variants, supporting variant heterogeneity, but says nothing about heterozygous carriers being asymptomatic or about hypomorphic residual activity.
judged.quote: deficient S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase (AHCY) activity due to compound heterozygosity for two novel mutations, c.145C>T; p.Arg49Cys and c.257A>G; p.Asp86Gly

judged.citation: Motzek A et al. Abnormal hypermethylation at imprinting control regions in a patient with S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency. JIMD Rep. 2016;29:21–8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms AHCY deficiency is autosomal recessive and caused by AHCY mutations (implying unaffected carriers), but says nothing about variant heterogeneity, missense hypomorphic alleles, or the clinical status of heterozygotes.
judged.quote: S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase (AHCY) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder in methionine metabolism caused by mutations in the AHCY gene.

rows.text: Phenotype generally more severe than MAT1A or GNMT — AHCY should be specifically considered in hypermethioninaemia + hepatopathy + myopathy [1,7].

judged.citation: Barić I et al. S-Adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: a second patient, the first with homozygosity for a novel missense mutation. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2005;28(6):885–902.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the combination of hypermethioninaemia with hepatopathy (elevated aminotransferases) and myopathy (markedly increased CK) as the recognisable picture, but makes no severity comparison with MAT1A or GNMT deficiency.
judged.quote: The laboratory abnormalities are markedly increased creatine kinase and elevated aminotransferases, as well as specific amino acid aberrations that pinpoint the aetiology.

judged.citation: Honzík T et al. Clinical picture of S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency resembles phosphomannomutase 2 deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2012;107(3):611–3.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses the clinical picture of SAHH deficiency but frames it as resembling PMM2-CDG, with no comparison of severity to MAT1A or GNMT deficiency and no mention of hepatopathy or myopathy as the diagnostic triad prompting consideration of AHCY.
judged.quote: Retrospective analysis of clinical features revealed striking similarities between SAHH deficiency and the PMM2-CDG Ia.

rows.text: METHIONINE-restricted diet (0.5–1 g/kg/day in infants) is the mainstay — reduces substrate flux through methionine adenosyltransferase and lowers SAH [1,5].

judged.citation: Barić I et al. S-Adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: a second patient, the first with homozygosity for a novel missense mutation. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2005;28(6):885–902.
judged.reason: Dietary methionine restriction as therapy is supported, but the specific infant dose of 0.5–1 g/kg/day and the stated mechanism of lowering SAH via reduced methionine adenosyltransferase flux are not given.
judged.quote: The disease seems to be at least to some extent treatable, as shown by improved myelination and psychomotor development during dietary methionine restriction and supplementation with creatine and phosphatidylcholine.

judged.citation: Grubbs R et al. S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: two siblings with fetal hydrops and fatal outcomes. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(6):705–13.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms dietary methionine restriction was used as treatment but gives no infant dose of 0.5–1 g/kg/day, no mechanistic statement about methionine adenosyltransferase flux, and no demonstrated lowering of SAH (the patient died despite treatment).
judged.quote: treatment by means of dietary methionine restriction and supplementation with phosphatidylcholine and creatine did not prevent her death at age 122 days

rows.text: Creatine and phosphatidylcholine supplementation (replace products of blocked methyltransferases) [4,5].

judged.citation: Buist NR et al. S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency in a 26-year-old man. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(4):538–45.
judged.reason: The abstract documents the biochemical rationale (low phosphatidylcholine/free choline and elevated guanidinoacetate from inhibited methyltransferases) but reports no creatine or phosphatidylcholine supplementation or its effect.
judged.quote: He had low values of erythrocyte phosphatidylcholine and plasma free choline and marginally elevated excretion of guanidinoacetate, suggesting that the elevated AdoHcy may have been inhibiting methylation of phosphatidylethanolamine and guanidinoacetate.

judged.citation: Grubbs R et al. S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: two siblings with fetal hydrops and fatal outcomes. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2010;33(6):705–13.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly reports creatine and phosphatidylcholine supplementation as part of the therapeutic regimen, though it does not spell out the product-replacement rationale.
judged.quote: supplementation with phosphatidylcholine and creatine

rows.text: Some patients respond well to early diagnosis and methionine restriction with stabilisation or modest improvement; late-diagnosed patients with established myopathy have less benefit [1,2].

judged.citation: Barić I et al. S-Adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: a second patient, the first with homozygosity for a novel missense mutation. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2005;28(6):885–902.
judged.reason: The abstract supports benefit in a patient monitored and treated from birth, but does not address reduced benefit in late-diagnosed patients with established myopathy.
judged.quote: This younger brother has the same two mutations in the gene encoding AdoHcy hydrolase, and has been monitored since birth.

judged.citation: Stender S et al. Adult-onset liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma in S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2015;116(4):269–74.
judged.reason: The abstract describes an undiagnosed adult case and an asymptomatic child but never addresses methionine restriction or any treatment response, early or late.

rows.text: Liver transplantation has been used in severe hepatopathy, and in one severe case corrected the SAH elevation that dietary therapy alone had failed to shift [8].

judged.citation: Strauss KA et al. Liver transplantation for treatment of severe S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2015;116(1–2):44–52.
judged.reason: The abstract describes a single severe AHCY case with hepatopathy in whom dietary therapy failed to normalize markers and liver transplantation reduced AdoHcy by 96%, matching the claim.
judged.quote: Dietary therapy failed to normalize biochemical markers or alter the AdoMet to AdoHcy molar concentration ratio. At 40 months of age, the proband received a liver segment from a healthy, unrelated living donor. Mean AdoHcy decreased 96%

rows.text: The rarity of the disorder limits outcome data [1,2].

judged.citation: Barić I et al. S-Adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency: a second patient, the first with homozygosity for a novel missense mutation. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2005;28(6):885–902.
judged.reason: The abstract states the condition had been proven in only one prior human, directly evidencing the extreme rarity that limits outcome data.
judged.quote: S-Adenosylhomocysteine (AdoHcy) hydrolase deficiency has been proven in a human only once, in a recently described Croatian boy.

judged.citation: Stender S et al. Adult-onset liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma in S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency. Mol Genet Metab. 2015;116(4):269–74.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the disorder is rare but does not state or discuss that this rarity limits outcome data.
judged.quote: inactivating mutations in this enzyme cause a rare autosomal recessive disorder, SAH hydrolase deficiency, that typically presents in infancy

rows.text: Multiple variants; some missense variants produce a pyridoxine-responsive biochemical phenotype [5].

judged.citation: Wang J et al. Mutations in the human gene encoding cystathionine γ-lyase cause cystathioninuria. Hum Mol Genet. 2003;12(4):451–7.
judged.reason: The abstract documents multiple CTH mutations including two missense variants, but says nothing about pyridoxine responsiveness of any variant.
judged.quote: We found two nonsense mutations, namely exon 8 c.940-941delCT and exon 11 c.1220delC, and two missense mutations, namely exon 2 c.356C>T (T67I) and exon 7 c.874C>G (Q240E).

rows.text: Also part of the Neu-Laxova severity continuum at the severe end [1,2].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Serine biosynthesis and transport defects. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;118(3):153–9.
judged.reason: The abstract states that defects of PGDH, PSAT or PSP share one phenotypic spectrum whose severe end is Neu-Laxova syndrome.
judged.quote: Serine biosynthesis defects present in a broad phenotypic spectrum that includes, at the severe end, Neu-Laxova syndrome, a lethal multiple congenital anomaly disease

judged.citation: de Koning TJ. Treatment with amino acids in serine deficiency disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(2–3):347–51.
judged.reason: The abstract recognises only PHGDH and PSPH deficiencies and never mentions PSAT1 deficiency or the Neu-Laxova spectrum.

rows.text: PSAT1 deficiency (OMIM #610992) was first described by Hart et al. in 2007 [3].

judged.citation: Hart CE et al. Phosphoserine aminotransferase deficiency: a novel disorder of the serine biosynthesis pathway. Am J Hum Genet. 2007;80(5):931–7.
judged.reason: The 2007 paper by Hart et al. explicitly reports the first identified cases of phosphoserine aminotransferase deficiency, matching the first-description claim (OMIM number aside).
judged.quote: We present the first two identified cases of phosphoserine aminotransferase deficiency.

rows.text: Biallelic loss-of-function variants typically cause the severe form; hypomorphic variants may produce later-onset milder disease [3,5].

judged.citation: Hart CE et al. Phosphoserine aminotransferase deficiency: a novel disorder of the serine biosynthesis pathway. Am J Hum Genet. 2007;80(5):931–7.
judged.reason: The abstract documents a severe neonatal phenotype with a frameshift plus a markedly hypofunctional missense variant (15% Vmax), supporting the loss-of-function/severe half, but says nothing about hypomorphic variants producing later-onset milder disease.
judged.quote: mutational analysis revealed compound heterozygosity for two mutations in the PSAT1 gene--one frameshift mutation (c.delG107) and one missense mutation (c.299A-->C [p.Asp100Ala])--in both siblings. Expression studies of the p.Asp100Ala mutant protein revealed a V(max) of only 15% of that of the wild-type protein.

judged.citation: Brassier A et al. Two new cases of serine deficiency disorders treated with l-serine. Eur J Paediatr Neurol. 2016;20(1):53–60.
judged.reason: The abstract reports clinical presentation and l-serine treatment response in two serine synthesis defect patients but never mentions specific variants, loss-of-function versus hypomorphic alleles, or genotype–phenotype correlation, so the claim's topic is not addressed.

rows.text: Neu-Laxova syndrome presentation in severe biallelic variants — with intrauterine growth restriction, ichthyosis, limb contractures, often perinatal lethality [6].

judged.citation: Acuna-Hidalgo R et al. Neu-Laxova syndrome is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder caused by defects in enzymes of the L-serine biosynthesis pathway. Am J Hum Genet. 2014;95(3):285–93.
judged.reason: The abstract reports three different missense and frameshift PSAT1 mutations segregating with Neu-Laxova syndrome, a disorder defined by severe malformations and prenatal/early postnatal lethality, matching the claim's core assertion (though the individual features such as ichthyosis and contractures are not itemized).
judged.quote: We identified six families with three different missense and frameshift PSAT1 mutations fully segregating with the disease.

rows.text: Milder later-onset variants with progressive polyneuropathy described [7].

judged.citation: Méneret A et al. A serine synthesis defect presenting with a Charcot-Marie-Tooth phenotype. Neurology. 2012;79(24):2302–4.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns a milder polyneuropathic presentation of PHGDH (3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase) deficiency and explicitly localises the mutations to the PGDH gene, providing no evidence for later-onset polyneuropathy in PSAT1 deficiency.
judged.quote: genetic analysis revealed 2 heterozygous mutations in the PGDH gene

rows.text: Neu-Laxova presentation: perinatal lethality regardless [1,2].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Serine biosynthesis and transport defects. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;118(3):153–9.
judged.reason: The abstract describes the Neu-Laxova end of the serine biosynthesis defect spectrum as lethal.
judged.quote: at the severe end, Neu-Laxova syndrome, a lethal multiple congenital anomaly disease

judged.citation: de Koning TJ. Treatment with amino acids in serine deficiency disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(2–3):347–51.
judged.reason: Neu-Laxova syndrome and perinatal lethality are not addressed anywhere in the abstract.

rows.text: Surprisingly, PSPH deficiency is reported to account for ~25% of all serine-biosynthesis-disorder cases — the second most common after PHGDH [1,2].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Serine biosynthesis and transport defects. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;118(3):153–9.
judged.reason: The abstract reviews all three serine biosynthesis defects but provides no relative frequency data, so neither the ~25% figure nor the ranking of PSPH as second most common after PHGDH appears.
judged.quote: Serine biosynthesis defects result from impairments of PGDH, PSAT, or PSP leading to systemic serine deficiency.

judged.citation: de Koning TJ. Treatment with amino acids in serine deficiency disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(2–3):347–51.
judged.reason: The abstract discusses serine biosynthesis defects including PSPH deficiency but gives no epidemiological or relative-frequency data, so the ~25% share and rank as second most common are absent.
judged.quote: At present two disorders have been reported: 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency and 3-phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency.

rows.text: PSPH deficiency (OMIM #614023) was first described by Jaeken et al. in 1997 in a child with a Williams-syndrome-like phenotype [3].

judged.citation: Jaeken J et al. 3-Phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency in a patient with a Williams-like syndrome. J Med Genet. 1997;34(7):594–6.
judged.reason: The 1997 abstract reports the first case of phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency in a boy with Williams syndrome features, matching the claim of first description.
judged.quote: This seems to be the first report of phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency.

rows.text: Identical biochemistry to PHGDH and PSAT1 deficiencies — differentiation requires molecular testing of all three genes [1,4].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Serine biosynthesis and transport defects. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;118(3):153–9.
judged.reason: The abstract groups PGDH, PSAT and PSP defects as causing the same systemic serine deficiency but does not state that biochemistry is identical or that molecular testing of all three genes is required.
judged.quote: Serine biosynthesis defects result from impairments of PGDH, PSAT, or PSP leading to systemic serine deficiency.

judged.citation: van der Crabben SN et al. An update on serine deficiency disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(4):613–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms identical biochemical hallmarks in all three disorders but does not address the need for molecular testing of all three genes to differentiate them.
judged.quote: The biochemical hallmarks of all three disorders are low concentrations of serine in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma.

rows.text: Hypomorphic missense variants reported in the index case [3,5].

judged.citation: Jaeken J et al. 3-Phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency in a patient with a Williams-like syndrome. J Med Genet. 1997;34(7):594–6.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the index case with residual (~25%) phosphoserine phosphatase activity, consistent with a hypomorphic defect, but reports no molecular/variant analysis and does not identify missense variants (which the co-cited mutation paper would carry).
judged.quote: Further investigation showed that the phosphoserine phosphatase (EC 3.1.3.3.) activity in lymphoblasts and fibroblasts amounted to about 25% of normal values.

judged.citation: Veiga-da-Cunha M et al. Mutations responsible for 3-phosphoserine phosphatase deficiency. Eur J Hum Genet. 2004;12(2):163–6.
judged.reason: The abstract reports two missense mutations in the only known case, with residual/partial enzyme activity consistent with hypomorphic effects.
judged.quote: The two mutations correspond to the replacement of the semiconserved Asp32 residue by an asparagine and of the extremely conserved Met52 by a threonine... Met52Thr almost abolished the enzymatic activity, whereas the Asp32Asn mutation caused a 50% decrease in Vmax.

rows.text: Congenital microcephaly, neonatal/infantile-onset intractable epilepsy, severe developmental delay — identical to the phenotype of other serine biosynthesis disorders [1,2].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Serine biosynthesis and transport defects. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;118(3):153–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a shared phenotypic spectrum across the three enzyme defects with severe neurological manifestations, but does not specify congenital microcephaly or neonatal/infantile intractable epilepsy.
judged.quote: intermediately, infantile serine biosynthesis defects with severe neurological manifestations and growth deficiency, and at the mild end, the childhood disease with intellectual disability

judged.citation: de Koning TJ. Treatment with amino acids in serine deficiency disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(2–3):347–51.
judged.reason: The abstract supports congenital microcephaly and severe psychomotor retardation for both serine biosynthesis defects, but attributes intractable seizures specifically to PHGDH deficiency rather than describing an identical phenotype.
judged.quote: These enzyme defects lead to severe neurological symptoms such as congenital microcephaly and severe psychomotor retardation and in addition in patients with 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase deficiency to intractable seizures.

rows.text: By analogy with PHGDH and PSAT1: strongly dependent on age at treatment initiation — early treatment can markedly improve long-term outcome [1,2].

judged.citation: El-Hattab AW. Serine biosynthesis and transport defects. Mol Genet Metab. 2016;118(3):153–9.
judged.reason: The abstract states benefit depends on starting L-serine before neurological damage occurs, i.e. outcome depends on timing of treatment initiation.
judged.quote: l-serine therapy may be beneficial in preventing or ameliorating symptoms in serine biosynthesis and transport defects, if started before neurological damage occurs

judged.citation: de Koning TJ. Treatment with amino acids in serine deficiency disorders. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(2–3):347–51.
judged.reason: The abstract notes only variable response to treatment and does not discuss age at treatment initiation or long-term outcome.

rows.text: Particularly frequent among Ashkenazi Jewish populations (carrier frequency ~1:40) [1,2].

judged.citation: Matalon R, Michals-Matalon K. Canavan disease. GeneReviews®. 1999 [updated 2021].
judged.reason: The abstract covers phenotype, diagnosis, management and autosomal recessive inheritance of Canavan disease but never addresses ethnic prevalence or carrier frequency, so the ~1:40 Ashkenazi figure cannot be evaluated.

judged.citation: Hoshino H, Kubota M. Canavan disease: clinical features and recent advances in research. Pediatr Int. 2014;56(4):477–83.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms higher prevalence among Ashkenazi Jewish people but gives no carrier frequency figure such as ~1:40.
judged.quote: The prevalence of CD is higher among Ashkenazi Jewish people

rows.text: Canavan disease (OMIM #271900) was first described by Canavan in 1931 [3]; the enzymatic and molecular defect was established by Matalon et al. in 1988 and 1993 [4,5].

judged.citation: Matalon R et al. Aspartoacylase deficiency and N-acetylaspartic aciduria in patients with Canavan disease. Am J Med Genet. 1988;29(2):463–71.
judged.reason: This 1988 Matalon paper establishes the enzymatic defect (aspartoacylase deficiency with N-acetylaspartic aciduria) in Canavan disease, the portion of the sentence attributed to it; the 1931 description and 1993 molecular defect are carried by the co-cited papers.
judged.quote: Aspartoacylase was assayed in cultured skin fibroblasts from one patient of each family and a profound deficiency of this enzyme was found.

judged.citation: Kaul R et al. Cloning of the human aspartoacylase cDNA and a common missense mutation in Canavan disease. Nat Genet. 1993;5(2):118–23.
judged.reason: This 1993 paper carries the molecular-defect portion of the sentence by reporting the cloning of the human aspartoacylase cDNA and a common missense mutation in Canavan disease, with the 1931 description and 1988 enzymatic work covered by the co-cited papers.
judged.quote: We have cloned the human aspartoacylase (ASP) cDNA spanning 1,435 basepairs, and show that the isolated cDNA expresses aspartoacylase activity in bacteria. Furthermore, an A to C base change, at nucleotide 854, has been found in 85% of the 34 Canavan alleles tested so far.

rows.text: Brain MR SPECTROSCOPY shows dramatically elevated NAA peak — often the first clue when leukodystrophy imaging is obtained [1,6].

judged.citation: Matalon R, Michals-Matalon K. Canavan disease. GeneReviews®. 1999 [updated 2021].
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly states that elevated NAA can be demonstrated in the brain by proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy as a diagnostic biochemical finding, though it does not comment on MRS being the first clue.
judged.quote: The biochemical diagnosis is established in an individual with suggestive clinical findings and elevated N-acetylaspartic acid (NAA) in urine (using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry) or in the brain by proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy.

judged.citation: Tavazzi B, Janson CG, Francis JS et al. Simultaneous high performance liquid chromatographic separation of purines, pyrimidines, N-acetylated amino acids, and dicarboxylic acids for the chemical diagnosis of inborn errors of metabolism. Clin Biochem. 2005;38(11):997–1008.
judged.reason: The abstract describes an HPLC method for NAA in plasma, urine and amniotic fluid and says nothing about MR spectroscopy or brain NAA peaks.

rows.text: MRI characteristic: diffuse bilateral SYMMETRICAL white-matter T2 hyperintensity with subcortical U-fibre involvement — a 'spongiform' leukodystrophy pattern — progressing to brain atrophy [1,6,9].

judged.citation: Matalon R, Michals-Matalon K. Canavan disease. GeneReviews®. 1999 [updated 2021].
judged.reason: The abstract identifies Canavan disease as a leukodystrophy but gives no MRI description of diffuse symmetrical T2 white-matter hyperintensity, subcortical U-fibre involvement, spongiform change, or progression to atrophy.
judged.quote: Canavan disease is a leukodystrophy characterized by neurodevelopmental delays, macrocephaly, and tone abnormalities.

judged.citation: Tavazzi B, Janson CG, Francis JS et al. Simultaneous high performance liquid chromatographic separation of purines, pyrimidines, N-acetylated amino acids, and dicarboxylic acids for the chemical diagnosis of inborn errors of metabolism. Clin Biochem. 2005;38(11):997–1008.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns a biochemical HPLC assay and does not address MRI findings or white-matter imaging patterns.

rows.text: Lithium, glyceryl triacetate (acetate supplementation) and ketogenic diet have been trialled in small series with no proven benefit [2,10].

judged.citation: Hoshino H, Kubota M. Canavan disease: clinical features and recent advances in research. Pediatr Int. 2014;56(4):477–83.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that no curative therapy exists and that dietary supplementation is only a candidate approach, but it does not name lithium, glyceryl triacetate or the ketogenic diet, nor report small trial series lacking proven benefit.
judged.quote: Although there is currently no curative therapy for CD, dietary supplements are candidates that may retard the progression of the symptoms associated with CD.

judged.citation: Baslow MH, Guilfoyle DN. Canavan disease, a rare early-onset human spongiform leukodystrophy. Mol Genet Metab. 2013;108(2):85–95.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms it discusses possible clinical interventions for Canavan disease (consistent with no established therapy), but it never names lithium, glyceryl triacetate or ketogenic diet, nor states that such trials showed no proven benefit.
judged.quote: In this article we also evaluate current hypotheses, and discuss possible clinical interventions that may be of value in treatment of CD.

rows.text: GENE THERAPY is actively in development — AAV9-ASPA trials have shown safety and some biochemical response in phase I/II studies; longer-term clinical outcome data awaited [11,12].

judged.citation: Leone P et al. Long-term follow-up after gene therapy for Canavan disease. Sci Transl Med. 2012;4(165):165ra163.
judged.reason: The abstract supports gene therapy safety and biochemical (NAA) response in a prospective clinical study, but the vector was AAV2-ASPA, not the AAV9-ASPA specified in the claim, and long-term follow-up data are in fact reported rather than awaited.
judged.quote: Safety data collected over a minimum 5-year follow-up period showed a lack of long-term adverse events related to the AAV2 vector.

judged.citation: Francis JS et al. Preclinical biodistribution, tropism, and efficacy of oligotropic AAV/Olig001 in a mouse model of congenital white matter disease. Mol Ther Methods Clin Dev. 2021;20:520–34.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that gene therapy for Canavan disease is actively in development but reports only preclinical mouse data with AAV/Olig001, not phase I/II AAV9-ASPA trial safety or biochemical response.
judged.quote: These results support the continued development of AAV/Olig001 for advancement to clinical application to white matter disease.

rows.text: Gene therapy offers the first disease-modifying prospect — outcomes of ongoing trials may shift the prognostic landscape [11,12].

judged.citation: Leone P et al. Long-term follow-up after gene therapy for Canavan disease. Sci Transl Med. 2012;4(165):165ra163.
judged.reason: The abstract reports disease-modifying effects of ASPA gene therapy—reduced brain NAA, slowed atrophy, and clinical stabilization—consistent with the claim that gene therapy offers a disease-modifying prospect that may alter prognosis.
judged.quote: AAV2-ASPA gene therapy resulted in a decrease in elevated NAA in the brain and slowed progression of brain atrophy, with some improvement in seizure frequency and with stabilization of overall clinical status.

judged.citation: Francis JS et al. Preclinical biodistribution, tropism, and efficacy of oligotropic AAV/Olig001 in a mouse model of congenital white matter disease. Mol Ther Methods Clin Dev. 2021;20:520–34.
judged.reason: The abstract demonstrates disease-modifying efficacy (rescue of ASPA activity, motor function, vacuolation) in a Canavan mouse model, but says nothing about outcomes of ongoing human trials shifting prognosis.
judged.quote: resulted in a dose-dependent rescue of ASPA activity, motor function, and a near-total reduction in vacuolation

rows.text: Clinical phenotype is highly variable — from completely asymptomatic through childhood speech delay and neurological symptoms to adult leukoencephalopathy — but outcome is generally better than the 'secondary' 3-methylglutaconic acidurias (types II–IX) which reflect mitochondrial dysfunction [1,2].

judged.citation: Wortmann SB et al. Inborn errors of metabolism with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria as discriminative feature: proper classification and nomenclature. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(6):923–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the primary (type I) versus secondary 3-MGA-uria distinction and that the secondary forms reflect mitochondrial/pathomechanistic defects, but says nothing about the variable clinical phenotype (asymptomatic to adult leukoencephalopathy) or the comparative outcome.
judged.quote: One should distinguish between "primary 3-methylglutaconic aciduria" formerly known as type I (3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase deficiency, AUH defect) due to defective leucine catabolism and the--currently known--three groups of "secondary 3-methylglutaconic aciduria"

judged.citation: IJlst L et al. 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria type I is caused by mutations in AUH. Am J Hum Genet. 2002;71(6):1463–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports clinical variability in type I but does not mention asymptomatic cases, adult leukoencephalopathy, or any comparison of outcome with the secondary 3-methylglutaconic acidurias.
judged.quote: 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria type I is an autosomal recessive disorder clinically characterized by various symptoms ranging from delayed speech development to severe neurological handicap.

rows.text: 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type I (OMIM #250950) was first described by Duran et al. in 1982 [3].

judged.citation: Duran M et al. Inherited 3-methylglutaconic aciduria in two brothers: another defect of leucine metabolism. J Pediatr. 1982;101(4):551–4.
judged.reason: This 1982 Duran report describes two brothers with inherited 3-methylglutaconic aciduria attributed to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase deficiency, i.e., the first description of what is now 3-MGA type I, matching the claimed author and year.
judged.quote: Two brothers, aged 7 and 5 years, who excreted large amounts of the leucine metabolites 3-methylglutaconic acid, 3-methylglutaric acid, and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid, are described. ... A (partial) deficiency of 3-methylglutaconyl coenzyme A hydratase is proposed to be the most likely underlying defect.

rows.text: Type I is the only PRIMARY form (direct enzyme defect); types II (TAZ / Barth syndrome), III (OPA3 / Costeff syndrome), IV (heterogeneous mitochondrial), V (DNAJC19), VI, VII (CLPB), VIII, IX (TMEM70) are SECONDARY forms caused by various mitochondrial disorders that share 3-methylglutaconic aciduria as a biochemical signature [2,4].

judged.citation: IJlst L et al. 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria type I is caused by mutations in AUH. Am J Hum Genet. 2002;71(6):1463–6.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes type I as a direct enzyme (AUH/3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase) defect, consistent with it being the primary form, but says nothing about types II–IX or their genes and mitochondrial basis.
judged.quote: This disorder is caused by a deficiency of 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase, one of the key enzymes of leucine degradation.

rows.text: In SECONDARY 3-MGA disorders the clinical context (cardiomyopathy for Barth, optic atrophy for Costeff, cataracts for DNAJC19, encephalopathy ± neutropenia for CLPB) and targeted gene panels distinguish from type I [2,5].

judged.citation: IJlst L et al. 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria type I is caused by mutations in AUH. Am J Hum Genet. 2002;71(6):1463–6.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns the molecular cause of type I and does not discuss the secondary 3-MGA disorders, their clinical features, or gene panel testing.

judged.citation: Engelke UF et al. NMR spectroscopic studies on the late-onset form of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type I. NMR Biomed. 2006;19(2):271–8.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns NMR discrimination of inborn errors of leucine metabolism in a late-onset 3-MGA type I patient and never addresses secondary 3-MGA disorders (Barth, Costeff, DNAJC19, CLPB), their clinical contexts, or gene panels.
judged.quote: Our data demonstrate that (1)H-NMR spectroscopy of urine can easily discriminate between the known inborn errors of leucine metabolism and provide the correct diagnosis.

rows.text: Heterogeneous variants; biallelic loss-of-function variants produce the adult leukoencephalopathy phenotype; hypomorphic variants often asymptomatic or mild [6,7].

judged.citation: Ly TB et al. Mutations in the AUH gene cause 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type I. Hum Mutat. 2003;21(4):401–7.
