judged.reason: The abstract supports variant heterogeneity in AUH and that some patients with complete loss of function are asymptomatic, but it does not support (and arguably contradicts) the specific genotype–phenotype mapping that biallelic loss-of-function causes the adult leukoencephalopathy phenotype while hypomorphic variants are mild.
judged.quote: Molecular analyses in five patients from four independent families revealed homozygosity or compound heterozygosity for mutations in the AUH gene; most mutations are predicted to completely abolish protein function. ... Complete absence of 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase/AUH appears to be compatible with normal development in some cases.

judged.citation: Wortmann SB et al. Inborn errors of metabolism with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria as discriminative feature: proper classification and nomenclature. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(6):923–8.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns nomenclature and classification and does not discuss AUH variant types or genotype–phenotype correlation.

rows.text: Clinical cases report speech delay, mild developmental difficulties, or rarely adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with cognitive decline, ataxia, dystonia — MRI showing bilateral symmetric deep white-matter signal change and basal ganglia involvement [1,8].

judged.citation: Wortmann SB et al. Inborn errors of metabolism with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria as discriminative feature: proper classification and nomenclature. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(6):923–8.
judged.reason: The abstract does not describe clinical features, speech delay, leukoencephalopathy or MRI findings in AUH deficiency.

rows.text: Supportive care for any neurological features [1,2].

judged.citation: Wortmann SB et al. Inborn errors of metabolism with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria as discriminative feature: proper classification and nomenclature. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(6):923–8.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses classification and diagnostic flow, not management or supportive care.

judged.citation: IJlst L et al. 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria type I is caused by mutations in AUH. Am J Hum Genet. 2002;71(6):1463–6.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses gene identification and mutation analysis, not management or supportive care.

rows.text: Adult leukoencephalopathy has slow progression but significant long-term morbidity in the minority of patients who develop it [1,8].

judged.citation: Wortmann SB et al. Inborn errors of metabolism with 3-methylglutaconic aciduria as discriminative feature: proper classification and nomenclature. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(6):923–8.
judged.reason: The abstract makes no statement about disease course, progression rate or long-term morbidity.

rows.text: Clinical spectrum: mild (isolated haemolytic anaemia) → moderate (+ 5-oxoprolinuria + metabolic acidosis) → severe (+ progressive neurological dysfunction) [1,2].

judged.citation: Ristoff E, Larsson A. Inborn errors in the metabolism of glutathione. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:16.
judged.reason: The abstract describes the severe-form features (haemolytic anaemia, acidosis, 5-oxoprolinuria, CNS damage) and implies a range of severity, but does not lay out the graded mild/moderate/severe three-tier spectrum as written.
judged.quote: Glutathione synthetase deficiency is the most frequently recognized disorder and, in its severe form, it is associated with hemolytic anemia, metabolic acidosis, 5-oxoprolinuria, central nervous system (CNS) damage and recurrent bacterial infections.

judged.citation: Njålsson R. Glutathione synthetase deficiency. Cell Mol Life Sci. 2005;62(17):1938–45.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly describes the three-tier clinical spectrum with haemolytic anaemia, added metabolic acidosis, and added neurological defects, plus 5-oxoprolinuria in all groups.
judged.quote: Mildly affected patients have mutations affecting the stability of the enzyme, causing a compensated haemolytic anaemia; moderately affected patients have, in addition, metabolic acidosis; and severely affected patients also develop neurological defects and show increased susceptibility to bacterial infections.

rows.text: Severity correlates with residual enzyme activity and produces a three-tier clinical classification [1,4].

judged.citation: Ristoff E, Larsson A. Inborn errors in the metabolism of glutathione. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:16.
judged.reason: It notes leaky mutations with residual enzyme activity and a 'severe form' with variable prognosis, but does not state that severity correlates with residual activity nor a three-tier classification.
judged.quote: Most of the mutations are leaky so that many patients have residual enzyme activity.

judged.citation: Njålsson R et al. Genotype, enzyme activity, glutathione level, and clinical phenotype in patients with glutathione synthetase deficiency. Hum Genet. 2005;116(5):384–9.
judged.reason: The abstract implies mild/moderate/severe tiers and genotype-based prediction, but it explicitly states enzyme activity did not distinguish moderate from severe phenotypes, so the claimed correlation of severity with residual enzyme activity is not carried.
judged.quote: The moderate and severe clinical phenotypes could not be distinguished based on enzyme activity, GSH or gamma-glutamylcysteine levels in cultured fibroblasts.

rows.text: Acquired 5-oxoprolinuria — from flucloxacillin, paracetamol overdose, or severe malnutrition — should be excluded in new adult presentations [5,6].

judged.citation: Fenves AZ et al. Increased anion gap metabolic acidosis as a result of 5-oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid): a role for acetaminophen. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2006;1(3):441–7.
judged.reason: The abstract documents acquired 5-oxoproline accumulation in adults linked to acetaminophen exposure and malnutrition, supporting the acquired causes and adult presentation; flucloxacillin is covered by the co-cited paper.
judged.quote: Twenty-one patients had major exposure to acetaminophen (one only acute exposure). Eighteen (82%) of the 22 patients were women. Most of the patients were malnourished as a result of multiple medical comorbidities

judged.citation: Liss DB et al. What is the clinical significance of 5-oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid) in high anion gap metabolic acidosis following paracetamol (acetaminophen) exposure? Clin Toxicol (Phila). 2013;51(9):817–27.
judged.reason: The abstract supports paracetamol- and flucloxacillin-associated acquired 5-oxoprolinuria/oxoprolinemia and the need to exclude other causes, but does not mention severe malnutrition as a cause.
judged.quote: Concomitant use of flucloxacillin, another medication associated with oxoprolinemia or oxoprolinuria, confounded several of the cases.

rows.text: RBC glutathione concentration MARKEDLY LOW — often <20% of normal [1,4].

judged.citation: Ristoff E, Larsson A. Inborn errors in the metabolism of glutathione. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:16.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes GSS as a defect of glutathione synthesis diagnosed by measuring gamma-glutamyl cycle metabolites and enzyme activity, which implies deficient glutathione, but it never states erythrocyte glutathione levels nor the quantitative "<20% of normal" threshold.
judged.quote: Diagnosis is made by measuring the concentration of different metabolites in the gamma-glutamyl cycle, enzyme activity and in glutathione synthetase and gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase deficiency, also by mutation analysis.

judged.citation: Njålsson R et al. Genotype, enzyme activity, glutathione level, and clinical phenotype in patients with glutathione synthetase deficiency. Hum Genet. 2005;116(5):384–9.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms low glutathione levels are assessed in GS deficiency and correlate with residual enzyme activity, but reports fibroblast (not RBC) GSH and gives no quantitative threshold such as <20% of normal.
judged.quote: From some of the patients, data on glutathione (GSH) levels and gamma-glutamylcysteine levels in cultured fibroblasts were also available.

rows.text: Severity tracks residual enzyme activity: hypomorphic missense variants → mild (haemolytic anaemia only); severe biallelic loss-of-function → severe (systemic) disease [4,7].

judged.citation: Njålsson R et al. Genotype, enzyme activity, glutathione level, and clinical phenotype in patients with glutathione synthetase deficiency. Hum Genet. 2005;116(5):384–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that truncating/splice (loss-of-function) mutations associate with moderate-to-severe disease and that mutation type partly predicts mild versus severe, but it contradicts severity tracking residual enzyme activity and does not state that hypomorphic missense variants give haemolytic anaemia only.
judged.quote: All mutations causing frameshifts, premature stop codons or aberrant splicing were associated with moderate or severe clinical phenotypes including haemolytic anaemia, 5-oxoprolinuria, and (in several forms) neurodevelopmental signs.

judged.citation: Shi ZZ et al. Mutations in the glutathione synthetase gene cause 5-oxoprolinuria. Nat Genet. 1996;14(3):361–5.
judged.reason: The abstract shows a homozygous missense variant causing a mild erythrocyte-restricted form with haemolytic anaemia only, versus splice-site/deletion/missense variants in severe systemic cases, but it does not establish the claim's mechanistic correlation with residual enzyme activity levels.
judged.quote: We also characterized a fifth case, an homozygous missense mutation in the gene in an individual affected by a milder-form of the GSS deficiency, which is apparently restricted to erythrocytes and only associated with haemolytic anaemia.

rows.text: Neonatal presentation can include profound metabolic acidosis requiring emergency treatment [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Ristoff E, Larsson A. Inborn errors in the metabolism of glutathione. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:16.
judged.reason: Metabolic acidosis is listed as a feature of the severe form, but the abstract does not specify neonatal onset or emergency treatment of profound acidosis.
judged.quote: in its severe form, it is associated with hemolytic anemia, metabolic acidosis, 5-oxoprolinuria

judged.citation: Njålsson R. Glutathione synthetase deficiency. Cell Mol Life Sci. 2005;62(17):1938–45.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms metabolic acidosis requiring bicarbonate correction but does not specify neonatal onset or emergency-level severity.
judged.quote: and bicarbonate to correct metabolic acidosis

judged.citation: Corrons JL et al. Hereditary non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia due to red blood cell glutathione synthetase deficiency in four unrelated patients from Spain: clinical and molecular studies. Br J Haematol. 2001;112(2):475–82.
judged.reason: The abstract does describe a neonatal presentation of GSH-S deficiency but reports only haemolytic anaemia with oxoprolinuria, with no mention of profound metabolic acidosis or emergency treatment.
judged.quote: One case exhibited a neonatal haemolytic anaemia associated with oxoprolinuria, but without neurological manifestations.

rows.text: Supportive care for any neurological phenotype [1,2,9].

judged.citation: Ristoff E, Larsson A. Inborn errors in the metabolism of glutathione. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:16.
judged.reason: The abstract states treatment aims for glutathione synthesis defects but confines them to avoiding haemolytic crises and boosting antioxidant defence, with no mention of supportive care for neurological phenotypes.
judged.quote: The aims of the treatment of glutathione synthesis defects are to avoid hemolytic crises and to increase the defense against reactive oxygen species.

judged.citation: Njålsson R. Glutathione synthetase deficiency. Cell Mol Life Sci. 2005;62(17):1938–45.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that only supportive/symptomatic management (antioxidants, bicarbonate) is available since no cure exists, but says nothing specifically about supportive care for the neurological phenotype.
judged.quote: Today, no cure can be offered these patients; they are given vitamins C and E to boost their antioxidant levels, and bicarbonate to correct metabolic acidosis.

judged.citation: Ristoff E et al. Long-term clinical outcome in patients with glutathione synthetase deficiency. J Pediatr. 2001;139(1):79–84.
judged.reason: The abstract documents treatment of patients with neurologic phenotypes (acidosis correction, vitamins C/E) but does not explicitly address generic supportive care for the neurological phenotype.
judged.quote: The treatment varied but usually included correction of acidosis and supplementation with vitamins C and/or E. Sixteen patients were severely affected with neurologic symptoms such as seizures and psychomotor retardation

rows.text: Severe form: significant disability and shortened life expectancy, though aggressive early treatment has led to improved outcomes in some cases [1,2,9].

judged.citation: Ristoff E, Larsson A. Inborn errors in the metabolism of glutathione. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2007;2:16.
judged.reason: The abstract notes CNS damage in the severe form and highly variable, unpredictable prognosis, but says nothing about shortened life expectancy or improved outcomes with aggressive early treatment.
judged.quote: The prognosis is difficult to predict, as few patients are known, but seems to vary significantly between different patients.

judged.citation: Njålsson R. Glutathione synthetase deficiency. Cell Mol Life Sci. 2005;62(17):1938–45.
judged.reason: The abstract documents severe disease features (neurological defects, infection susceptibility) implying significant disability, but gives no data on shortened life expectancy or improved outcomes with aggressive early treatment.
judged.quote: severely affected patients also develop neurological defects and show increased susceptibility to bacterial infections

judged.citation: Ristoff E et al. Long-term clinical outcome in patients with glutathione synthetase deficiency. J Pediatr. 2001;139(1):79–84.
judged.reason: The abstract reports severe neurologic involvement with deaths and states early vitamin C and E supplementation may improve long-term outcome, matching the claim.
judged.quote: Sixteen patients were severely affected with neurologic symptoms such as seizures and psychomotor retardation; 7 had died at the time of the study. None of the severely affected patients had been treated with both vitamins C and E from the neonatal period.

rows.text: D-2-HG and L-2-HG are BOTH neurotoxic oncometabolites but produce different clinical syndromes (D-2-HGA more systemic; L-2-HGA pure cerebellar/leukodystrophy) — stereospecific analysis is essential [1,2].

judged.citation: Struys EA. D-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria: unravelling the biochemical pathway and the genetic defect. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(1):21–9.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns only D-2-HGA biochemistry and genetics; it makes no mention of L-2-HG, the contrasting clinical syndromes, oncometabolite neurotoxicity, or the need for stereospecific analysis.
judged.quote: Much progress has been made in the last five years in various studies, revealing two human enzymes that play a role in the metabolism of D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG): hydroxyacid-oxoacid transhydrogenase (HOT) and D-2-HG dehydrogenase.

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. Progress in understanding 2-hydroxyglutaric acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):571–87.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that D-2-HG and L-2-HG accumulation defines distinct disorders requiring isomer distinction, but gives no phenotypic contrast (systemic vs cerebellar/leukodystrophy) or statement on stereospecific analysis methods.
judged.quote: Accumulation of D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG) and/or L-2-hydroxyglutarate (L-2-HG) in body fluids are the biochemical hallmarks of these disorders.

rows.text: D-2-HGA types I and II were delineated biochemically and genetically separately — D2HGDH in 2004 [3] and IDH2 in 2010 [4].

judged.citation: Struys EA et al. Mutations in the D-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase gene cause D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Am J Hum Genet. 2005;76(2):358–60.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes the genetic delineation of D-2-HGA (type I) by identifying disease-causing D2HGDH mutations, which is the part of the sentence this paper carries; the year 2004 corresponds to its e-publication (printed 2005) rather than anything stated in the abstract.
judged.quote: In the genes of two unrelated patients affected with d-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, we identified disease-causing mutations.

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. IDH2 mutations in patients with D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Science. 2010;330(6002):336.
judged.reason: This 2010 paper reports the germline IDH2 mutations defining D-2-HGA type II, carrying the IDH2/2010 half of the sentence (the 2004 D2HGDH half is cited to the other paper).
judged.quote: We have detected heterozygous germline mutations in IDH2 that alter enzyme residue Arg(140) in 15 unrelated patients with d-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (D-2-HGA), a rare neurometabolic disorder characterized by supraphysiological levels of D-2-HG.

rows.text: The IDH2 discovery was transformative because the same gain-of-function variants (at Arg140 and Arg172) are also acquired somatic drivers of 15–20% of AML and of IDH-mutant gliomas, linking an inborn error to oncogene biology and enabling IDH inhibitors (enasidenib, ivosidenib) as a treatment paradigm [4,5].

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. IDH2 mutations in patients with D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Science. 2010;330(6002):336.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the gain-of-function link between germline Arg140 IDH2 mutations and somatic IDH mutations in neoplasia, but gives no Arg172 residue, no 15–20% AML frequency, no gliomas, and no IDH inhibitors.
judged.quote: Heterozygous somatic mutations in the genes encoding isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 and -2 (IDH1 and IDH2) were recently discovered in human neoplastic disorders.

judged.citation: Stein EM et al. Enasidenib in mutant IDH2 relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia. Blood. 2017;130(6):722–31.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms somatic IDH2 mutations in AML and enasidenib as a mutant-IDH2 inhibitor therapy, but gives the AML frequency as ~12% rather than 15–20%, and does not mention Arg140/Arg172 residues, IDH-mutant gliomas, or ivosidenib.
judged.quote: Recurrent mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 ( IDH2 ) occur in ∼12% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

rows.text: STEREOSPECIFIC chiral chromatographic analysis is essential (reporting only 'total 2-hydroxyglutarate' misses the diagnosis and may cause confusion with L-2-HGA — a clinically and molecularly different disorder) [6,7].

judged.citation: Struys EA et al. Measurement of urinary D- and L-2-hydroxyglutarate enantiomers by stable-isotope-dilution LC-MS/MS. Clin Chem. 2004;50(8):1391–5.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly states that only enantiomer-specific measurement (achieved here via chiral derivatization and chromatographic separation) can differentiate D-2-HGA from L-2-HGA, which is the substance of the claim.
judged.quote: The use of DATAN as chiral derivatization reagent provided very well separated peaks of the formed diastereomers of D- and L-2-HG

judged.citation: Rzem R et al. L-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria, a defect of metabolite repair. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2007;30(5):681–9.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that L-2-HGA is a distinct disorder with its own molecular/enzymatic basis (FAD-linked L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency), supporting the contrast drawn, but it says nothing about the need for stereospecific chiral chromatography or the diagnostic pitfall of reporting only total 2-hydroxyglutarate.
judged.quote: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria is a metabolic disorder in which L-2-hydroxyglutarate accumulates as a result of a deficiency in FAD-linked L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme converting L-2-hydroxyglutarate to alpha-ketoglutarate.

rows.text: In somatic IDH-mutant tumours, 2-HG is also elevated in plasma and can be used as a treatment biomarker during IDH-inhibitor therapy [5].

judged.citation: Stein EM et al. Enasidenib in mutant IDH2 relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia. Blood. 2017;130(6):722–31.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms mutant IDH2 neomorphically produces 2-HG and that pharmacodynamic profiling was performed during enasidenib therapy, but it does not state that 2-HG is elevated in plasma or used as a treatment biomarker.
judged.quote: Mutated IDH2 proteins neomorphically synthesize 2-hydroxyglutarate resulting in DNA and histone hypermethylation, which leads to blocked cellular differentiation.

rows.text: TYPE II: IDH2 at 15q26.1 — heterozygous gain-of-function missense variants (most commonly p.Arg140Gln, p.Arg172Lys/Trp) producing a NEOMORPHIC enzyme that synthesises D-2-HG from 2-oxoglutarate [1,4].

judged.citation: Struys EA. D-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria: unravelling the biochemical pathway and the genetic defect. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(1):21–9.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses the genetic defect in D-2-HGA but identifies only D2HGD (type I) mutations, with no mention of IDH2, its locus, gain-of-function missense variants, or neomorphic D-2-HG synthesis.
judged.quote: We demonstrated pathogenic mutations in the D2HGD gene in patients with D-2-HGA, helping to unravel the primary defect causing D-2-HGA.

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. IDH2 mutations in patients with D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Science. 2010;330(6002):336.
judged.reason: The abstract supports heterozygous germline IDH2 Arg140 variants and the neomorphic conversion of 2-KG to D-2-HG, but does not give the 15q26.1 locus or the p.Arg172Lys/Trp variants.
judged.quote: confer on the enzymes a new function: the ability to convert 2-KG to d-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG). We have detected heterozygous germline mutations in IDH2 that alter enzyme residue Arg(140) in 15 unrelated patients

rows.text: Somatic IDH1/IDH2 variants at the same codons are oncogenic in AML and gliomas [5].

judged.citation: Stein EM et al. Enasidenib in mutant IDH2 relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia. Blood. 2017;130(6):722–31.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes recurrent somatic IDH2 mutations in AML but says nothing about IDH1, gliomas, or the specific codons shared with germline D-2-HGA type II.
judged.quote: Recurrent mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 ( IDH2 ) occur in ∼12% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

rows.text: Typical: infantile/childhood developmental delay, hypotonia, epilepsy, cardiomyopathy, cerebral atrophy on MRI [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Struys EA. D-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria: unravelling the biochemical pathway and the genetic defect. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(1):21–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports a broad phenotypic spectrum from severe neonatal to asymptomatic but lists none of the specific features claimed (developmental delay, hypotonia, epilepsy, cardiomyopathy, cerebral atrophy on MRI).
judged.quote: it became clear that the clinical phenotype of the disease varies widely from severe neonatal to asymptomatic

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. Progress in understanding 2-hydroxyglutaric acidurias. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(4):571–87.
judged.reason: The abstract announces clinical characterization of D-2-HGA types I and II but lists none of the claimed features (developmental delay, hypotonia, epilepsy, cardiomyopathy, cerebral atrophy).
judged.quote: whereas for D-2-HGA type I and type II novel clinical information is presented which was derived from questionnaires

judged.citation: van der Knaap MS et al. D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria: biochemical, clinical, magnetic resonance imaging and neuropathological findings. Ann Neurol. 1999;45(1):111–9.
judged.reason: The abstract supports infantile-onset developmental delay, hypotonia, epilepsy and cardiomyopathy, but the MRI findings reported are ventriculomegaly, enlarged subarachnoid spaces, subependymal cysts and delayed cerebral maturation rather than cerebral atrophy.
judged.quote: Ten of the patients had a severe early-infantile-onset encephalopathy characterized by epilepsy, hypotonia, cerebral visual failure, and little development. Five of these patients had a cardiomyopathy.

rows.text: TYPE II: more consistently severe — cardiomyopathy (often prominent), severe infantile epilepsy, developmental delay, dysmorphic features; mortality in infancy common [8,9].

judged.citation: van der Knaap MS et al. D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria: biochemical, clinical, magnetic resonance imaging and neuropathological findings. Ann Neurol. 1999;45(1):111–9.
judged.reason: The abstract documents a severe infantile phenotype with epilepsy, cardiomyopathy and minimal development consistent with the severe end of the spectrum, but it predates and does not use the type I/type II distinction and mentions neither dysmorphic features nor infantile mortality.
judged.quote: D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria is a distinct neurometabolic disorder with at least two phenotypes

judged.citation: Nota B et al. Deficiency in SLC25A1 causes a new syndrome with combined D-2- and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Am J Hum Genet. 2013;92(4):627–31.
judged.reason: The abstract reports gene discovery for combined D-2/L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria and gives no clinical phenotype data on D-2-HGA type II (cardiomyopathy, epilepsy, dysmorphism, infant mortality).

rows.text: IDH inhibitors (enasidenib for IDH2) have transformed treatment of IDH-mutant AML but have NOT been evaluated in germline D-2-HGA type II and use in that setting remains experimental [4,5,9].

judged.citation: Kranendijk M et al. IDH2 mutations in patients with D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Science. 2010;330(6002):336.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns mutation discovery and pathophysiology only and does not address IDH inhibitors, enasidenib, or any therapeutic evaluation.

judged.citation: Stein EM et al. Enasidenib in mutant IDH2 relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia. Blood. 2017;130(6):722–31.
judged.reason: The abstract supports enasidenib's clinical efficacy in mutant-IDH2 relapsed/refractory AML but does not address germline D-2-HGA type II, the part carried by the co-cited papers.
judged.quote: Among patients with relapsed or refractory AML, overall response rate was 40.3%, with a median response duration of 5.8 months.

judged.citation: Nota B et al. Deficiency in SLC25A1 causes a new syndrome with combined D-2- and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Am J Hum Genet. 2013;92(4):627–31.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses molecular etiology only and says nothing about IDH inhibitors, enasidenib, AML, or any therapy.

rows.text: TYPE II: significantly worse — cardiac and neurological morbidity drive mortality and long-term disability [1,8,9].

judged.citation: Struys EA. D-2-Hydroxyglutaric aciduria: unravelling the biochemical pathway and the genetic defect. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2006;29(1):21–9.
judged.reason: The abstract discusses D-2-HGA phenotype and genetics but never distinguishes a type II (IDH2) form nor comments on cardiac/neurological morbidity or mortality driving prognosis.
judged.quote: However, in approximately 50% of the patients with D-2-HGA examined, no pathogenic mutations have yet been found.

judged.citation: van der Knaap MS et al. D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria: biochemical, clinical, magnetic resonance imaging and neuropathological findings. Ann Neurol. 1999;45(1):111–9.
judged.reason: The abstract conveys severe neurological morbidity and cardiomyopathy in the severe phenotype but reports no mortality data and does not classify patients as type II or compare outcomes between types.
judged.quote: Ten of the patients had a severe early-infantile-onset encephalopathy characterized by epilepsy, hypotonia, cerebral visual failure, and little development. Five of these patients had a cardiomyopathy.

judged.citation: Nota B et al. Deficiency in SLC25A1 causes a new syndrome with combined D-2- and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. Am J Hum Genet. 2013;92(4):627–31.
judged.reason: No outcome, mortality, or disability data for D-2-HGA type II appear in this gene-discovery abstract.

rows.text: Bridge from 'organic aciduria' to 'autoinflammatory disease' — a unique position in metabolic medicine [1,2].

judged.citation: Haas D, Hoffmann GF. Mevalonate kinase deficiencies: from mevalonic aciduria to hyperimmunoglobulinaemia D syndrome. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2006;1:13.
judged.reason: The abstract frames MVA and HIDS as two ends of one clinical spectrum from a single enzyme deficiency, i.e. a continuum from organic aciduria to a periodic fever/autoinflammatory phenotype.
judged.quote: Mevalonic aciduria (MVA) and hyperimmunoglobulinemia D syndrome (HIDS) represent the two ends of a clinical spectrum of disease caused by deficiency of mevalonate kinase (MVK), the first committed enzyme of cholesterol biosynthesis.

judged.citation: van der Burgh R et al. Mevalonate kinase deficiency, a metabolic autoinflammatory disease. Clin Immunol. 2013;147(3):197–206.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly frames MVK deficiency as an inborn error of metabolism with an autoinflammatory phenotype, i.e. the bridge the sentence describes.
judged.quote: Mevalonate kinase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism with an autoinflammatory phenotype.

rows.text: Mevalonate kinase deficiency (OMIM #610377) was first described by Hoffmann et al. in 1986 [3].

judged.citation: Hoffmann G et al. Mevalonic aciduria — an inborn error of cholesterol and non-sterol isoprene biosynthesis. N Engl J Med. 1986;314(25):1610–4.
judged.reason: This 1986 NEJM paper is the original description of mevalonate kinase deficiency, reporting the first patient with massive mevalonic aciduria and severe mevalonate kinase deficiency.
judged.quote: These observations identify an inherited disorder of cholesterol and nonsterol isoprene biosynthesis in humans.

rows.text: HIDS (hyper-IgD with periodic fever syndrome) was described separately by van der Meer in 1984 [4] and only later recognised as partial MVK deficiency through work by Drenth et al. [5].

judged.citation: van der Meer JW et al. Hyperimmunoglobulinaemia D and periodic fever: a new syndrome. Lancet. 1984;1(8386):1087–90.
judged.reason: The abstract is van der Meer's 1984 report describing six patients with high serum IgD and recurrent fever as a new syndrome, which is the portion of the sentence attributed to this reference (the MVK link is carried by the co-cited Drenth paper).
judged.quote: Six patients of Dutch ancestry with a long history of recurrent attacks of fever of unknown cause were found to have a high serum IgD level and a large number of plasma cells with cytoplasmic IgD in the bone marrow.

judged.citation: Drenth JP et al. Mutations in the gene encoding mevalonate kinase cause hyper-IgD and periodic fever syndrome. Nat Genet. 1999;22(2):178–81.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes that Drenth et al. identified MVK mutations with diminished mevalonate kinase activity as the cause of HIDS, which is the portion of the sentence this paper carries (the 1984 van der Meer description is cited to the other paper).
judged.quote: Functional analysis demonstrated diminished MK activity in fibroblasts from HIDS patients. Our data establish MVK as the gene responsible for HIDS.

rows.text: Particularly common in Dutch and Northern European populations (founder variants) [2].

judged.citation: van der Burgh R et al. Mevalonate kinase deficiency, a metabolic autoinflammatory disease. Clin Immunol. 2013;147(3):197–206.
judged.reason: The abstract covers pathogenesis, phenotype, diagnosis and treatment but says nothing about population frequency, ethnic distribution or founder variants.

rows.text: Enzyme assay: MVK activity in cultured fibroblasts/leukocytes — <1% severe form, 1–10% HIDS [1,6].

judged.citation: Haas D, Hoffmann GF. Mevalonate kinase deficiencies: from mevalonic aciduria to hyperimmunoglobulinaemia D syndrome. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2006;1:13.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that reduced/low MVK enzyme activity underlies and confirms both disorders, but gives no residual-activity percentages (<1% vs 1–10%) or the assay tissue (fibroblasts/leukocytes).
judged.quote: A reduced activity of MVK and pathogenic mutations in the MVK gene have been demonstrated as the common genetic basis in both disorders.

judged.citation: Hoffmann GF et al. Clinical and biochemical phenotype in 11 patients with mevalonic aciduria. Pediatrics. 1993;91(5):915–21.
judged.reason: The abstract supports virtually absent enzyme activity in the severe mevalonic aciduria form but gives no residual-activity range for HIDS (1–10%) nor the specific tissue/percentage thresholds.
judged.quote: Varying degrees of severity of clinical illness were observed despite uniform, virtual absence of residual activity of the enzyme.

rows.text: Severe loss-of-function biallelic variants → classic mevalonic aciduria [2,7].

judged.citation: van der Burgh R et al. Mevalonate kinase deficiency, a metabolic autoinflammatory disease. Clin Immunol. 2013;147(3):197–206.
judged.reason: The abstract states biallelic MVK mutations block the pathway and that phenotype severity, including the severe multi-system presentation, tracks the severity of the enzyme defect.
judged.quote: Mutations in both copies of the MVK-gene lead to a block in the mevalonate pathway... The clinical phenotype ranges widely, depending on the severity of the enzyme defect. Severely affected patients have antenatal disease onset, dysmorphic features, growth retardation, cognitive impairment and progressive ataxia.

judged.citation: Houten SM et al. Mutations in MVK, encoding mevalonate kinase, cause hyperimmunoglobulinaemia D and periodic fever syndrome. Nat Genet. 1999;22(2):175–7.
judged.reason: The abstract engages MVK mutations and enzyme activity but describes the milder HIDS phenotype with partially reduced MK activity; it never addresses severe biallelic loss-of-function variants producing classic mevalonic aciduria.
judged.quote: Subsequent analysis of cells from four unrelated HIDS patients revealed reduced activities of mevalonate kinase (MK; encoded by the gene MVK), a key enzyme of isoprenoid biosynthesis.

rows.text: Usually with normal development and life span [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Haas D, Hoffmann GF. Mevalonate kinase deficiencies: from mevalonic aciduria to hyperimmunoglobulinaemia D syndrome. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2006;1:13.
judged.reason: The abstract indicates HIDS is limited to febrile attacks (with a neurologically affected subgroup), consistent with generally normal development, but says nothing about normal life span.
judged.quote: In HIDS, only febrile attacks are present, but a subgroup of patients may also develop neurological abnormalities of varying degree such as mental retardation, ataxia, ocular symptoms and epilepsy.

judged.citation: van der Burgh R et al. Mevalonate kinase deficiency, a metabolic autoinflammatory disease. Clin Immunol. 2013;147(3):197–206.
judged.reason: The abstract implies mild patients lack the severe features by restricting growth retardation and cognitive impairment to severely affected patients, but it never states that milder (HIDS) patients have normal development and normal life span.
judged.quote: Severely affected patients have antenatal disease onset, dysmorphic features, growth retardation, cognitive impairment and progressive ataxia.

judged.citation: van der Hilst JC et al. Long-term follow-up, clinical features, and quality of life in a series of 103 patients with hyperimmunoglobulinemia D syndrome. Medicine (Baltimore). 2008;87(6):301–10.
judged.reason: The abstract documents a large HIDS cohort with attacks persisting into adulthood and only rare amyloidosis, implying survival to adult life, but it never states that development or life span is normal and in fact reports lower autonomy and social development plus impaired quality of life.
judged.quote: The frequency of attacks decreased with the patient's increasing age, although 50% of patients over the age of 20 years still had 6 or more attacks per year.

rows.text: HIDS: IL-1 blockade (anakinra/canakinumab) is HIGHLY EFFECTIVE — standard of care since the mid-2000s for moderate-severe disease [9,10].

judged.citation: De Benedetti F et al. Canakinumab for the treatment of autoinflammatory recurrent fever syndromes. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(20):1908–19.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms canakinumab efficacy in controlling and preventing flares in mevalonate kinase deficiency (HIDS), but it does not support the 'standard of care since the mid-2000s' framing (this is a 2018 trial), says nothing about anakinra, and the reported MKD response rate (35% vs 6%; 57% with dose escalation) is more modest than 'highly effective'.
judged.quote: canakinumab was effective in controlling and preventing flares in patients with colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever, mevalonate kinase deficiency, and TRAPS

judged.citation: Bodar EJ et al. On-demand anakinra treatment is effective in mevalonate kinase deficiency. Ann Rheum Dis. 2011;70(12):2155–8.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that anakinra (IL-1 blockade) is effective in HIDS, but does not address canakinumab or establish IL-1 blockade as standard of care since the mid-2000s for moderate-severe disease.
judged.quote: On-demand treatment with anakinra in HIDS decreases the duration and severity of fever attacks.

rows.text: CLASSIC MEVALONIC ACIDURIA: supportive; anakinra may reduce fever frequency; haematopoietic stem cell transplant has been used in selected severe cases with some success [11].

judged.citation: Neven B et al. Allogeneic bone marrow transplantation in mevalonic aciduria. N Engl J Med. 2007;356(26):2700–3.
judged.reason: The abstract supports HSCT use in a severe mevalonic aciduria case with sustained remission, but says nothing about supportive care or anakinra reducing fever frequency (and notes only anti-inflammatory treatment failure).
judged.quote: A 3-year-old boy with mevalonic aciduria whose condition had failed to improve with antiinflammatory treatment underwent allogeneic bone marrow transplantation from an HLA-identical sister who was a heterozygous carrier of the mutant gene. We observed sustained remission of febrile attacks and inflammation during a 15-month follow-up period.

rows.text: Classic mevalonic aciduria: poor — many die in infancy/early childhood, though a subset reach adolescence or adulthood with significant disability [1,2,11].

judged.citation: Haas D, Hoffmann GF. Mevalonate kinase deficiencies: from mevalonic aciduria to hyperimmunoglobulinaemia D syndrome. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2006;1:13.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms compromised life expectancy and no established treatment in MVA but gives no timing of death in infancy/early childhood nor a subset surviving to adolescence/adulthood.
judged.quote: Life expectancy is often compromised.

judged.citation: van der Burgh R et al. Mevalonate kinase deficiency, a metabolic autoinflammatory disease. Clin Immunol. 2013;147(3):197–206.
judged.reason: The abstract documents severe multi-system disability and the need for stem cell transplantation in severe cases, but gives no mortality data or statement that many die in infancy/early childhood or that a subset survives to adolescence/adulthood.
judged.quote: Severely affected patients have antenatal disease onset, dysmorphic features, growth retardation, cognitive impairment and progressive ataxia... Severe cases require allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

judged.citation: Neven B et al. Allogeneic bone marrow transplantation in mevalonic aciduria. N Engl J Med. 2007;356(26):2700–3.
judged.reason: The abstract describes disease features and a single transplant case but does not address mortality in infancy/early childhood or survival into adolescence/adulthood.

rows.text: Most reported patients have had mitochondrial-like phenotypes with lactic acidosis [1].

judged.citation: Marcadier JL et al. Mutations in ALDH6A1 encoding methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase are associated with dysmyelination and transient methylmalonic aciduria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:98.
judged.reason: The abstract describes a single case with transient/variable lactate elevation and stresses an extremely variable phenotype, but makes no claim that most reported patients have mitochondrial-like phenotypes with lactic acidosis.
judged.quote: Existing reports describe a highly variable clinical and biochemical phenotype, which can make diagnosis a challenge.

rows.text: 3-Hydroxyisobutyric aciduria (OMIM #614105) was first described in 1991 [2].

judged.citation: Ko FJ et al. 3-Hydroxyisobutyric aciduria: an inborn error of valine metabolism. Pediatr Res. 1991;30(4):322–6.
judged.reason: The 1991 paper presents 3-hydroxyisobutyric aciduria as a newly identified disorder of valine metabolism in a patient, matching the claimed date and identity of the first description (OMIM number itself is administrative and not expected in the abstract).
judged.quote: 3-Hydroxyisobutyric aciduria, a disorder of valine metabolism, has been found in a boy in whom the clinical picture was that of a typical organic acidemia

rows.text: ALDH6A1 mutations were identified in 2000 [3].

judged.citation: Chambliss KL et al. Molecular characterization of methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2000;23(5):497–504.
judged.reason: This 2000 paper reports the first molecular characterization of MMSDH (ALDH6A1) deficiency, identifying a homozygous coding mutation.
judged.quote: Only the first patient had alterations in the MMSDH coding region, revealing homozygosity for a 1336G > A transversion, which leads to substitution of arginine for highly conserved glycine at amino acid 446. ... These data provide the first molecular characterization of an inborn error of metabolism specific to the L-valine catabolic pathway.

rows.text: Acylcarnitines: some patients have mildly elevated C4-OH (3-hydroxybutyrylcarnitine) [4].

judged.citation: Gray RG et al. Methylmalonic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency: demonstration of defective valine and beta-alanine metabolism and reduced malonic semialdehyde dehydrogenase activity in cultured fibroblasts. Biochem Med Metab Biol. 1987;38(1):121–4.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns fibroblast valine/beta-alanine oxidation and enzyme activity, and says nothing about acylcarnitine profiles or C4-OH elevation.

rows.text: Genotype-phenotype correlation is incomplete; several biallelic patients have been essentially asymptomatic while others with similar residual activity have had severe disease — suggesting additional modifier loci [3,5].

judged.citation: Chambliss KL et al. Molecular characterization of methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2000;23(5):497–504.
judged.reason: The abstract documents strikingly divergent biochemical phenotypes among putative MMSDH-deficient patients and shows that only one had coding-region variants, which speaks to incomplete genotype-phenotype correlation, but it does not report asymptomatic biallelic patients versus severe disease at similar residual activity, nor propose modifier loci.
judged.quote: The urine metabolic pattern was strikingly different in all... Only the first patient had alterations in the MMSDH coding region... No abnormalities of the MMSDH cDNA were detected in the other patients.

judged.citation: Pollitt RJ et al. 3-Hydroxyisobutyric aciduria: heterogeneity within a common biochemical phenotype. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1985;8(Suppl 2):75–6.
judged.reason: The abstract documents a biochemically affected patient who developed normally, supporting the existence of essentially asymptomatic cases, but provides no genotype, residual enzyme activity comparison, or evidence bearing on modifier loci.
judged.quote: The patient is now aged 4 years and has developed normally.

rows.text: Severe infantile form: psychomotor delay, hypotonia, lactic acidosis, seizures, dysmorphic features, cerebral atrophy on MRI — mitochondrial-like phenotype with organic aciduria overlay [1,6].

judged.citation: Marcadier JL et al. Mutations in ALDH6A1 encoding methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase are associated with dysmyelination and transient methylmalonic aciduria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:98.
judged.reason: The abstract supports severe developmental delay, lactate elevation and abnormal brain MRI, but reports dysmyelination rather than cerebral atrophy and does not mention hypotonia, seizures or dysmorphic features.
judged.quote: We report a child with severe developmental delays, abnormal myelination on brain MRI, and transient/variable elevations in lactate, methylmalonic acid, 3-hydroxyisobutyric and 3-aminoisobutyric acids.

judged.citation: Sass JO et al. 3-Hydroxyisobutyrate aciduria and mutations in the ALDH6A1 gene coding for methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(3):437–42.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms a severe infantile presentation with developmental delay and death from hepatoencephalopathy at age 2, but does not mention hypotonia, lactic acidosis, seizures, dysmorphic features or cerebral atrophy on MRI.
judged.quote: We present two unrelated patients who presented with developmental delay and increased urinary concentrations of 3-hydroxyisobutyric acid... One patient developed a febrile illness and subsequently died from a hepatoencephalopathy at 2 years of age.

rows.text: Developmental support [1].

judged.citation: Marcadier JL et al. Mutations in ALDH6A1 encoding methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase are associated with dysmyelination and transient methylmalonic aciduria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:98.
judged.reason: The abstract addresses diagnosis, genetics and enzyme assay only, with no mention of management or developmental support.

rows.text: Small patient numbers limit prognostic confidence [1,6].

judged.citation: Marcadier JL et al. Mutations in ALDH6A1 encoding methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase are associated with dysmyelination and transient methylmalonic aciduria. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2013;8:98.
judged.reason: The abstract documents that only three molecularly confirmed cases existed before this fourth one and emphasises extreme phenotypic variability, directly supporting that patient numbers are too small for prognostic confidence.
judged.quote: To date, only three reported cases have been confirmed at the molecular level, through identification of homozygous mutations in ALDH6A1, the gene encoding MMSDH.

judged.citation: Sass JO et al. 3-Hydroxyisobutyrate aciduria and mutations in the ALDH6A1 gene coding for methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2012;35(3):437–42.
judged.reason: The abstract documents that only a single genetically confirmed case existed previously and adds just two more patients, directly establishing the very small patient numbers underlying the claim.
judged.quote: However, to date methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency has only been demonstrated at the gene level for a single individual.

rows.text: DLD deficiency has a distinctive multi-2-ketoacid dehydrogenase phenotype because DLD is shared with PDH and BCKDH [1,2].

judged.citation: Koike K, Urata Y, Goto S. Cloning and nucleotide sequence of the cDNA encoding human 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (lipoamide). Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1992;89(5):1963–7.
judged.reason: The abstract reports only the cloning and sequence of the human OGDH (E1) cDNA and says nothing about DLD, its sharing with PDH/BCKDH, or any clinical phenotype.
judged.quote: We have cloned a human cDNA encoding OGDH from a fetal liver cDNA library by plaque hybridization with a mixture of oligonucleotide probes designed from the amino acid sequences of porcine OGDH.

judged.citation: Bonnefont JP et al. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency presenting as congenital lactic acidosis. J Pediatr. 1992;121(2):255–8.
judged.reason: The abstract reports alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency clinically and never addresses DLD/E3 deficiency or its shared role with PDH and BCKDH.
judged.quote: We report an inborn error of the tricarboxylic acid cycle, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency, in three siblings with hypotonia, metabolic acidosis, and hyperlactatemia immediately after birth.

rows.text: OGDH deficiency was described in the 1980s–1990s [3].

judged.citation: Guffon N et al. 2-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency, a rare cause of primary hyperlactataemia: report of a new case. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1993;16(5):821–30.
judged.reason: This 1993 report of new cases of 2-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency, including enzymatic demonstration of the defect, is consistent with the disorder being described in the 1980s–1990s.
judged.quote: Two new familial cases of 2-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (2-KGD) deficiency are reported

rows.text: DLST (E2) variants have been associated with susceptibility to paraganglioma in adults as well as metabolic phenotypes in children [4].

judged.citation: Remacha L et al. Recurrent germline DLST mutations in individuals with multiple pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas. Am J Hum Genet. 2019;104(4):651–64.
judged.reason: The abstract establishes DLST as a PPGL-susceptibility gene in affected individuals but says nothing about metabolic phenotypes in children.
judged.quote: we found positive DLST immunostaining exclusively in tumors carrying TCA-cycle or EPAS1 mutations. In summary, this study reveals DLST as a PPGL-susceptibility gene

rows.text: DLD deficiency adds: elevated branched-chain amino acids (partial MSUD-like picture), elevated alpha-keto acids, elevated plasma pyruvate, elevated urinary lactate/2-hydroxybutyrate, and elevated glycine (reflecting the glycine cleavage system which also uses DLD as its L-protein subunit). 2-Hydroxyglutarate may be secondarily elevated [1,5,6].

judged.citation: Koike K, Urata Y, Goto S. Cloning and nucleotide sequence of the cDNA encoding human 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (lipoamide). Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1992;89(5):1963–7.
judged.reason: The abstract is a molecular cloning report with no biochemical or metabolite data on patients (branched-chain amino acids, pyruvate, glycine, 2-hydroxyglutarate) and no mention of DLD deficiency.
judged.quote: This cDNA spans 4156 bases and contains an open reading frame of 3009 nucleotides encoding a presequence of 40 amino acid residues and a mature protein of 963 amino acid residues (Mr = 108,642).

judged.citation: Shany E et al. Lipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency due to a novel mutation in the interface domain. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 1999;262(1):163–6.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms lactic acidemia and impaired branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase activity (mechanistic basis for a MSUD-like picture), but reports no metabolite data on BCAAs, glycine, pyruvate, 2-hydroxybutyrate or 2-hydroxyglutarate.
judged.quote: An infant with a neurodegenerative disorder accompanied by lactic acidemia is described.

rows.text: All autosomal recessive [4,5,7].

judged.citation: Remacha L et al. Recurrent germline DLST mutations in individuals with multiple pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas. Am J Hum Genet. 2019;104(4):651–64.
judged.reason: The abstract describes germline DLST variants acting as dominant tumour-susceptibility alleles with somatic loss of heterozygosity, not autosomal recessive inheritance, and says nothing supporting recessive transmission.
judged.quote: We identified five germline variants affecting DLST in eight unrelated individuals (∼7%); all except one were diagnosed with multiple PPGLs.

judged.citation: Shany E et al. Lipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency due to a novel mutation in the interface domain. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 1999;262(1):163–6.
judged.reason: The abstract reports a specific DLD coding change but never addresses the mode of inheritance for OGDH, DLST or DLD.

rows.text: Heterozygous DLST variants have been associated with hereditary paraganglioma [4].

judged.citation: Remacha L et al. Recurrent germline DLST mutations in individuals with multiple pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas. Am J Hum Genet. 2019;104(4):651–64.
judged.reason: The abstract reports recurrent germline (heterozygous, with tumour LOH) DLST variants in individuals with pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas, identifying DLST as a susceptibility gene.
judged.quote: p.Gly374Glu-DLST tumors exhibited loss of heterozygosity ... this study reveals DLST as a PPGL-susceptibility gene

rows.text: MRI: Leigh-like pattern with basal ganglia T2 hyperintensity [2,6].

judged.citation: Bonnefont JP et al. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency presenting as congenital lactic acidosis. J Pediatr. 1992;121(2):255–8.
judged.reason: The abstract describes neonatal lactic acidosis, hypotonia and neurologic deterioration but reports no neuroimaging or Leigh-like basal ganglia findings.
judged.quote: Neurologic deterioration resulted in death at about 30 months of age.

rows.text: DLD: variable — classical neonatal 'multi-oxoacid dehydrogenase' phenotype with severe lactic acidosis + BCAA elevation + encephalopathy; or Ashkenazi-founder late-onset form with episodic liver failure and Reye-like episodes, recurrent encephalopathy, sometimes adult presentation [5,8].

judged.citation: Shany E et al. Lipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency due to a novel mutation in the interface domain. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 1999;262(1):163–6.
judged.reason: The abstract supports phenotypic variability in DLD deficiency and an infantile neurodegenerative presentation with lactic acidemia, but does not describe the Ashkenazi-founder late-onset form with episodic liver failure or Reye-like episodes.
judged.quote: The phenotypic heterogeneity in LAD deficiency is not directly correlated with the residual LAD activity but rather with its impact on the multienzymatic complex activity.

judged.citation: Hong YS et al. Identification of the E3 subunit gene (DLD) mutation in a Korean patient with dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency. J Korean Med Sci. 2003;18(3):428–30.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms an Ashkenazi-founder DLD/E3 genotype (Gly194Cys) with a distinct clinical phenotype, but gives none of the claimed phenotypic specifics (late onset, episodic liver failure, Reye-like episodes, adult presentation) nor the neonatal multi-oxoacid dehydrogenase picture with BCAA elevation.
judged.quote: Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3) deficiency with a clinical phenotype and genotype (Gly194Cys homozygous) previously identified only in Ashkenazi Jewish patients, was diagnosed in two Palestinian Arab siblings and two unrelated Ashkenazi Jewish patients.

rows.text: DLD Ashkenazi-founder form: episodic decompensations can be fatal but between episodes function may be preserved [1,2,5,8].

judged.citation: Koike K, Urata Y, Goto S. Cloning and nucleotide sequence of the cDNA encoding human 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (lipoamide). Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1992;89(5):1963–7.
judged.reason: The abstract contains no clinical, outcome, or population-founder information relevant to an Ashkenazi DLD form or episodic decompensations.

judged.citation: Bonnefont JP et al. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency presenting as congenital lactic acidosis. J Pediatr. 1992;121(2):255–8.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency with progressive fatal course and says nothing about the DLD Ashkenazi-founder form or episodic decompensations with preserved interval function.

judged.citation: Shany E et al. Lipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency due to a novel mutation in the interface domain. Biochem Biophys Res Commun. 1999;262(1):163–6.
judged.reason: The abstract describes a single infant's enzymology and a novel interface-domain mutation and provides no information on episodic decompensations, mortality, or interepisode function in the Ashkenazi-founder form.

judged.citation: Hong YS et al. Identification of the E3 subunit gene (DLD) mutation in a Korean patient with dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency. J Korean Med Sci. 2003;18(3):428–30.
judged.reason: The abstract documents fatal outcomes in childhood and one patient surviving to age 18 in the Ashkenazi-founder (Gly194Cys) form, but does not describe episodic decompensations or preserved function between episodes.
judged.quote: While three of the four patients died in childhood without specific treatment, the surviving patient at age 18 years may have benefited from long-term daily supplementation with a cocktail of riboflavin, biotin, coenzyme Q and carnitine.

rows.text: Immediate lactose/galactose elimination is life-saving, but despite early treatment, long-term complications (ovarian failure in females, speech and cognitive deficits, tremor) persist — making GALT one of the most paradigmatic 'treated but still affected' inborn errors [1,2].

judged.citation: Welling L et al. International clinical guideline for the management of classical galactosemia: diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(2):171–6.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms dietary treatment and follow-up of clinical complications are core to CG management, but it never states that galactose elimination is life-saving nor names the persisting complications (ovarian failure, speech/cognitive deficits, tremor).
judged.quote: Recommendations addressing diagnosis, dietary treatment, biochemical monitoring, and follow-up of clinical complications were formulated.

rows.text: The 'Duarte variant' (N314D in compound heterozygosity with a classical allele) reduces GALT activity to ~25% and is generally benign — no treatment required [5].

judged.citation: Elsas LJ, Lai K et al. Functional analysis of the human galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase promoter in Duarte and LA variant galactosemia. Mol Genet Metab. 2001;72(4):297–305.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms N314D defines the Duarte allele and that it reduces GALT activity (via reduced transcription), but it gives ~50% activity in the homozygous state rather than the claimed ~25% in compound heterozygosity with a classical allele, and says nothing about the variant being benign or requiring no treatment.
judged.quote: One missense mutation, an aspartate to asparagine substitution at amino acid 314 (N314D), impairs 50% activity in the homozygous state in some patients but gives near normal activity in others. The former condition is called Duarte (D)

rows.text: FSH elevated later in affected females (ovarian failure) [1,6].

judged.citation: Schweitzer S et al. Long-term outcome in 134 patients with galactosaemia. Eur J Pediatr. 1993;152(1):36–43.
judged.reason: The abstract documents gonadal dysfunction in affected females (delayed puberty in 6 of 11) but never reports FSH levels or biochemical evidence of ovarian failure.
judged.quote: Physical findings revealed that puberty was delayed in 1 out of 18 males and 6 out of 11 females.

rows.text: Molecular genotyping informs prognosis: Q188R homozygotes have poorer long-term outcomes than some other genotypes [7,8].

judged.citation: Lin HC, Reichardt JK. Linkage disequilibrium between a SacI restriction fragment length polymorphism and two galactosemia mutations. Hum Genet. 1995;95(3):353–5.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns a SacI RFLP and its linkage disequilibrium with Q188R and N314D haplotypes, and says nothing about clinical outcomes or genotype-based prognosis.
judged.quote: The polymorphic allele is found on about 11% of normal chromosomes and is in linkage disequilibrium with the two most common mutations identified in GALT thus far: Q188R and N314D.

judged.citation: Elsas LJ, Lai K. The molecular biology of galactosaemia. Genet Med. 1998;1(1):40–8.
judged.reason: The abstract explicitly links genotype to clinical outcome, associating Q188R with classic galactosemia and impaired GALT function while S135L is associated with good outcomes, which carries the claim that genotyping informs prognosis and that Q188R fares worse than some other genotypes.
judged.quote: Two common mutations, Q188R and K285N, account for more than 70% of G alleles in the white population and are associated with classic galactosemia and impaired GALT function. In the black population, S135L accounts for 62% of the alleles causing galactosemia and is associated with good outcomes.

rows.text: Untreated: fatal within weeks [1,2,6].

judged.citation: Welling L et al. International clinical guideline for the management of classical galactosemia: diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(2):171–6.
judged.reason: The abstract describes guideline methodology and consensus, and says nothing about the untreated natural history or neonatal mortality of classical galactosemia.

judged.citation: Schweitzer S et al. Long-term outcome in 134 patients with galactosaemia. Eur J Pediatr. 1993;152(1):36–43.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms galactosaemia can be lethal (20 patients died of disease sequelae) but gives no information on the untreated course or a fatal outcome within weeks.
judged.quote: the remaining 20 patients had died due to sequelae of the underlying disease

rows.text: A notable exception: African-American patients homozygous for p.Ser135Leu, when adequately treated, do NOT develop POI [9,10].

judged.citation: Waggoner DD et al. Long-term prognosis in galactosaemia: results of a survey of 350 cases. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1990;13(6):802–18.
judged.reason: The brief abstract reports only that long-term outcomes are poor and unrelated to studied variables; it says nothing about genotype (p.Ser135Leu), ethnicity, or ovarian function, so the exception cannot be judged from it.

judged.citation: Gubbels CS et al. Primary ovarian insufficiency in classic galactosaemia: role of FSH dysfunction and timing. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(1):29–34.
judged.reason: The abstract studies mechanism and timing of POI in classic galactosemia but never addresses genotype (p.Ser135Leu) or ethnicity-specific exceptions, so it cannot speak to this claim.

rows.text: NO established treatment prevents the long-term complications despite best-practice dietary management — a major area of ongoing research (substrate reduction, gene therapy, aldose reductase inhibition) [1,2,9].

judged.citation: Welling L et al. International clinical guideline for the management of classical galactosemia: diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2017;40(2):171–6.
judged.reason: The abstract's statement that knowledge gaps exist foremost in treatment and follow-up is consistent with unresolved long-term outcomes, but it does not state that no treatment prevents long-term complications nor mention substrate reduction, gene therapy, or aldose reductase inhibition.
judged.quote: During the development of this guideline, gaps of knowledge were identified in most fields of interest, foremost in the fields of treatment and follow-up.

judged.citation: Waggoner DD et al. Long-term prognosis in galactosaemia: results of a survey of 350 cases. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1990;13(6):802–18.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that long-term outcomes remain poor and are not explained by dietary compliance (i.e. diet does not prevent complications), but it says nothing about the named research directions (substrate reduction, gene therapy, aldose reductase inhibition).
judged.quote: An international survey of the long term results of treating galactosaemia has shown poor results. These do not seem to be related to any of the relevant variables studied, for example delayed diagnosis or poor dietary compliance.

rows.text: Long-term: the 'cognitive burden' and premature ovarian insufficiency of classical galactosaemia persist despite optimal dietary management — an unresolved clinical challenge [9,10].

judged.citation: Waggoner DD et al. Long-term prognosis in galactosaemia: results of a survey of 350 cases. J Inherit Metab Dis. 1990;13(6):802–18.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that poor long-term outcomes persist independent of dietary compliance, but does not specify cognitive burden or premature ovarian insufficiency as the persisting complications.
judged.quote: These do not seem to be related to any of the relevant variables studied, for example delayed diagnosis or poor dietary compliance.

judged.citation: Gubbels CS et al. Primary ovarian insufficiency in classic galactosaemia: role of FSH dysfunction and timing. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2013;36(1):29–34.
judged.reason: The abstract supports that primary ovarian insufficiency is present and of early onset in classic galactosemia patients, but says nothing about cognitive burden and does not explicitly address persistence despite optimal dietary management.
judged.quote: Fifteen patients with primary ovarian insufficiency underwent ovarian stimulation with gonadotropins... ovarian imaging results point to an early onset of ovarian failure in this disease.

rows.text: Duarte variant: benign with no treatment required [5].

judged.citation: Elsas LJ, Lai K et al. Functional analysis of the human galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase promoter in Duarte and LA variant galactosemia. Mol Genet Metab. 2001;72(4):297–305.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns the molecular/promoter basis of reduced GALT expression in the Duarte allele and makes no statement about the Duarte variant being clinically benign or not requiring treatment.
judged.quote: The -119 to -116delGTCA reduces hGALT transcription resulting in reduced GALT activity in the Duarte allele.

rows.text: Distinct from the clinically more benign hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI, aldolase B deficiency) [1,2].

judged.citation: Pagliara AS et al. Fructose-1,6-diphosphatase deficiency: a cause of lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia in infancy. J Clin Invest. 1972;51(8):2115–23.
judged.reason: The abstract biochemically distinguishes this disorder from HFI by showing normal fructose-1-phosphate aldolase activity alongside absent FDPase, but says nothing about HFI being clinically more benign.
judged.quote: Hepatic phosphorylase, glucose-6-phosphatase, amylo-1,6-glucosidase, phosphofructokinase, fructose-1-phosphate aldolase, and fructose-1,6-diphosphate aldolase levels were normal, but no fructose-1,6-diphosphatase (FDPase) activity was detected.

judged.citation: Gorce M et al. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency causes fatty liver disease and requires long-term hepatic follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(2):215–22.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns hepatic manifestations of FBP1 deficiency and never mentions hereditary fructose intolerance or aldolase B deficiency, so the contrast in severity cannot be assessed.

rows.text: Plasma glucose typically 1–2 mmol/L during crisis; lactate often 10–20 mmol/L; ketones elevated [1,4].

judged.citation: Pagliara AS et al. Fructose-1,6-diphosphatase deficiency: a cause of lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia in infancy. J Clin Invest. 1972;51(8):2115–23.
judged.reason: The case documents hypoglycaemia (40 mg/100 ml ≈ 2.2 mmol/L) and lactate up to 20 mM, but the abstract does not report elevated ketones.
judged.quote: admitted with severe lactic acidosis (20 mM) and hypoglycemia

judged.citation: Moey LH et al. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency as a cause of recurrent hypoglycemia and metabolic acidosis: clinical and molecular findings in Malaysian patients. Pediatr Neonatol. 2018;59(4):397–403.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis and hyperlactacidemia during crises but gives no numeric values for glucose (1–2 mmol/L) or lactate (10–20 mmol/L) and does not mention ketosis.
judged.quote: All the patients presented with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperlactacidemia and hepatomegaly.

rows.text: Enzyme assay on liver tissue (ideally) or cultured fibroblasts confirms diagnosis; peripheral leukocytes may show reduced activity [1,5].

judged.citation: Pagliara AS et al. Fructose-1,6-diphosphatase deficiency: a cause of lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia in infancy. J Clin Invest. 1972;51(8):2115–23.
judged.reason: Diagnosis by hepatic enzyme assay showing absent FDPase activity is supported, but the abstract does not address cultured fibroblasts or peripheral leukocytes.
judged.quote: no fructose-1,6-diphosphatase (FDPase) activity was detected

rows.text: Missense, splice and large deletions all described [6,7].

judged.citation: el-Maghrabi MR et al. Human fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase gene (FBP1): exon-intron organisation, localisation to chromosome 9q22.2-q22.3. Genomics. 1995;27(3):520–5.
judged.reason: The abstract screens FBP1 in two deficient patients but explicitly reports only non-pathogenic substitutions and no identified missense, splice, or large deletion mutations causing disease.
judged.quote: These nucleotide substitutions were also found in normal unaffected subjects and thus are not the cause of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency in the two subjects studied.

judged.citation: Kikawa Y et al. Identification of genetic mutations in Japanese patients with fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency. Am J Hum Genet. 1997;61(4):852–61.
judged.reason: The abstract documents missense variants (G164S, A177D) plus a nonsense and a frameshift insertion in FBP1, but describes no splice-site variants and no large deletions, so those elements of the claim are not carried here.
judged.quote: three novel mutations--a G-->A transition at base 490 in exon 4 (G164S) (3 alleles [14%]), a C-->A transversion at base 530 in exon 4 (A177D) (1 allele [4%]), and a G-->T transversion at base 88 in exon 1 (E30X) (2 alleles [9%])

rows.text: Fructose-containing foods can precipitate episodes (as in HFI) but less reliably [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Pagliara AS et al. Fructose-1,6-diphosphatase deficiency: a cause of lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia in infancy. J Clin Invest. 1972;51(8):2115–23.
judged.reason: The abstract shows symptoms began on weaning to baby food and that fructose administration lowered glucose and raised lactate, with fructose/sucrose exclusion needed for control.
judged.quote: experienced numerous attacks of hyperventilation when weaned to baby food ... intravenous fructose, glycerol, and alanine caused a 40-50% fall in plasma glucose and a significant rise in lactate

judged.citation: Gorce M et al. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency causes fatty liver disease and requires long-term hepatic follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(2):215–22.
judged.reason: The abstract describes liver abnormalities during follow-up and acute crises but says nothing about fructose ingestion as a trigger of episodes.

judged.citation: Pinto A et al. International practices in the dietary management of fructose 1-6 biphosphatase deficiency. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2018;13(1):21.
judged.reason: The abstract engages fructose/sucrose as a dietary issue in FBPase deficiency and notes uncertainty about restriction, but it does not state that fructose-containing foods can precipitate episodes (or that they do so less reliably than in HFI).
judged.quote: Although the need for an emergency regimen to avoid metabolic decompensation is well established at times of illness, there is uncertainty about the need for other dietary management strategies such as sucrose or fructose restriction.

rows.text: Practice varies widely and is not guideline-backed: in an international survey of 36 centres treating 126 patients, three-quarters restricted sucrose or fructose to some degree while a quarter imposed no restriction when the patient was well [8].

judged.citation: Pinto A et al. International practices in the dietary management of fructose 1-6 biphosphatase deficiency. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2018;13(1):21.
judged.reason: The abstract reports exactly the survey scope (36 centres, 126 patients) and the 75%/25% split in dietary restriction practice, plus the call for guidelines.
judged.quote: Thirty-six centres reported the dietary prescriptions of 126 patients with FBPase deficiency. ... Seventy-five per cent of centres advocated dietary restrictions. ... Twenty-five per cent of centres (n = 9), advised no dietary restrictions when patients were well.

rows.text: Monitoring: blood glucose, lactate, urinary ketones during illness [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Pagliara AS et al. Fructose-1,6-diphosphatase deficiency: a cause of lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia in infancy. J Clin Invest. 1972;51(8):2115–23.
judged.reason: Plasma glucose and lactate are used to follow the patient's dietary response, but the abstract does not address urinary ketone monitoring or monitoring during intercurrent illness.
judged.quote: Normal plasma glucose and lactate levels were maintained on an 800 cal diet of 66% carbohydrate (sucrose and fructose excluded).

judged.citation: Gorce M et al. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency causes fatty liver disease and requires long-term hepatic follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(2):215–22.
judged.reason: The abstract recommends only a hepatic monitoring protocol and does not address monitoring of blood glucose, lactate or urinary ketones during intercurrent illness.

judged.citation: Pinto A et al. International practices in the dietary management of fructose 1-6 biphosphatase deficiency. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2018;13(1):21.
judged.reason: The abstract covers illness/emergency management in FBPase deficiency but says nothing about monitoring blood glucose, lactate or urinary ketones during illness.
judged.quote: All centres advocated an emergency regimen mainly based on glucose polymer for illness management.

rows.text: The episodic nature means lifelong vigilance is required especially during illness [1,2,8].

judged.citation: Pagliara AS et al. Fructose-1,6-diphosphatase deficiency: a cause of lactic acidosis and hypoglycaemia in infancy. J Clin Invest. 1972;51(8):2115–23.
judged.reason: The abstract shows crises recur when dietary management lapses, implying ongoing vigilance, but says nothing about lifelong follow-up or risk specifically during intercurrent illness.
judged.quote: When carbohydrate was reduced to 35% and protein or fat increased to 23 and 53% respectively, lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia recurred.

judged.citation: Gorce M et al. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency causes fatty liver disease and requires long-term hepatic follow-up. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2022;45(2):215–22.
judged.reason: The abstract supports the need for lifelong follow-up and notes that symptoms cluster around acute crises, but the specific framing of vigilance during intercurrent illness (rather than hepatic surveillance) is not stated.
judged.quote: a liver monitoring protocol should be set up for these patients, during lifelong follow-up

judged.citation: Pinto A et al. International practices in the dietary management of fructose 1-6 biphosphatase deficiency. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2018;13(1):21.
judged.reason: The abstract states management aims to prevent decompensation particularly during febrile illness, that all patients were prescribed an emergency regimen, and that restrictions did not relax with age, consistent with lifelong illness-focused vigilance.
judged.quote: management aims to prevent hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis by avoiding prolonged fasting, particularly during febrile illness

rows.text: Uncooked cornstarch dietary therapy (from the 1980s) transformed outcomes [1,2].

judged.citation: Kishnani PS et al. Diagnosis and management of glycogen storage disease type I: a practice guideline of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics. Genet Med. 2014;16(11):e1.
judged.reason: The guideline abstract confirms that nutritional management is central to GSD I care but never mentions uncooked cornstarch specifically, its introduction in the 1980s, or the resulting transformation in outcomes.
judged.quote: Aspects of diagnostic evaluation and nutritional and medical management, including care coordination, genetic counseling, hepatic and renal transplantation, and prenatal diagnosis, are also addressed.

rows.text: Fasting HYPOGLYCAEMIA (often within 2–4 h) + LACTIC ACIDOSIS (lactate paradoxically rises rather than falls with fasting — because accumulating G6P feeds glycolysis rather than being hydrolysed) + HYPERURICAEMIA (G6P → ribose-5-P → purine production) + HYPERTRIGLYCERIDAEMIA + HYPERCHOLESTEROLAEMIA (G6P → acetyl-CoA → de novo lipogenesis during fasting) [1,5].

judged.citation: Kishnani PS et al. Diagnosis and management of glycogen storage disease type I: a practice guideline of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics. Genet Med. 2014;16(11):e1.
judged.reason: The abstract lists the same biochemical constellation (hypoglycaemia, lactic acidaemia, hyperlipidaemia, hyperuricaemia) and gives a 3–4 hour fasting interval consistent with the claimed 2–4 h window, though the mechanistic explanations are not spelled out.
judged.quote: Patients with GSD I have a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations, including hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, lactic acidemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and growth retardation. Individuals with GSD type Ia typically have symptoms related to hypoglycemia in infancy when the interval between feedings is extended to 3–4 hours.

judged.citation: Greene HL et al. Continuous nocturnal intragastric feeding for management of type I glycogen-storage disease. N Engl J Med. 1976;294(8):423–5.
judged.reason: The abstract implies the biochemical abnormalities of hypoglycaemia, elevated lactate, uric acid and triglycerides (all fell with treatment) but does not mention hypercholesterolaemia, the 2–4 h fasting interval, or the G6P-based mechanisms.
judged.quote: This regimen stabilized blood glucose levels above 70 mg per deciliter and decreased serum uric acid, triglyceride, lactate and serum oxalacetic transaminase levels, as well as hepatic size, in all patients.

rows.text: Genotype–phenotype correlation is partial [6,7].

judged.citation: Lei KJ et al. Genetic basis of glycogen storage disease type 1a: prevalent mutations at the glucose-6-phosphatase locus. Am J Hum Genet. 1995;57(4):766–71.
judged.reason: The abstract reports mutation spectrum and ethnic prevalence of G6PC variants but never examines clinical phenotype or its relationship to genotype, so it cannot speak to whether genotype–phenotype correlation is partial.
judged.quote: Sixteen mutations were uncovered that were shown by expression to abolish or greatly reduce G6Pase activity and that therefore are responsible for the GSD type 1a disorder.

judged.citation: Veiga-da-Cunha M et al. The putative glucose 6-phosphate translocase gene is mutated in essentially all cases of glycogen storage disease type I non-a. Eur J Hum Genet. 1999;7(6):717–23.
judged.reason: The abstract notes that patients with differing mutations and prior subtype labels (Ib/Ic/Id) had indistinguishable clinical phenotypes, which bears indirectly on limited genotype–phenotype correlation, but it never assesses genotype–phenotype correlation in G6PC1/GSD Ia, the disorder of the claim.
judged.quote: the clinical phenotype of the four new patients who had been diagnosed as GSD Ic and the one diagnosed as GSD Id was no different from the GSD Ib patients
