rows.text: Adult complications: HEPATIC ADENOMAS (40–70% of patients by young adulthood; 10% risk of malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis / proteinuria / chronic kidney disease, osteoporosis, gout, PCOS in females [1,2,8,9].

judged.citation: Kishnani PS et al. Diagnosis and management of glycogen storage disease type I: a practice guideline of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics. Genet Med. 2014;16(11):e1.
judged.reason: The guideline abstract confirms GSD I involves multi-organ evaluation including hepatic, kidney and reproductive systems (and hepatic/renal transplantation), but none of the specific adult complications named in the claim—hepatic adenomas at 40–70%, 10% malignant transformation to HCC, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, osteoporosis, gout, or PCOS—appear in the abstract.
judged.quote: This management guideline specifically addresses evaluation and diagnosis across multiple organ systems (hepatic, kidney, gastrointestinal/nutrition, hematologic, cardiovascular, reproductive) involved in GSD I.

judged.citation: Chou JY et al. Type I glycogen storage diseases: disorders of the glucose-6-phosphatase complex. Curr Mol Med. 2002;2(2):121–43.
judged.reason: The abstract reviews the molecular basis and general childhood phenotype of GSD-I but does not address adult/long-term complications such as hepatic adenomas, HCC risk, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, osteoporosis, gout, or PCOS, nor any of the cited percentages.
judged.quote: Both GSD-Ia and GSD-Ib patients manifest phenotypic G6Pase deficiency, characterized by growth retardation, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, nephromegaly, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, and lactic academia and the current treatment is a dietary therapy.

judged.citation: Rake JP et al. Glycogen storage disease type I: diagnosis, management, clinical course and outcome. Results of the European Study on Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (ESGSD I). Eur J Pediatr. 2002;161(Suppl 1):S20–34.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the spectrum of adult complications (liver adenomas and carcinomas, progressive renal disease, osteopenia, hyperuricaemia) as major causes of morbidity/mortality, but gives no prevalence figures for adenomas (40–70%) or the 10% malignant transformation risk, and does not mention PCOS.
judged.quote: Data on dietary treatment, pharmacological treatment, and outcome including mental development, hyperlipidaemia and its complications, hyperuricaemia and its complications, bleeding tendency, anaemia, osteopenia, hepatomegaly, liver adenomas and carcinomas, progressive renal disease

rows.text: GSD Ib: G-CSF for neutropenia, empaglifozin (newer use — inhibits 1,5-anhydroglucitol-6-P accumulation and improves neutrophil function) [10].

judged.citation: Wortmann SB et al. Treating neutropenia and neutrophil dysfunction in glycogen storage disease type Ib with an SGLT2 inhibitor. Blood. 2020;136(9):1033–43.
judged.reason: The abstract reports off-label empagliflozin (an SGLT2 inhibitor) in GSD-Ib patients lowering 1,5AG6P and improving neutrophil function, with G-CSF as the background/prior therapy for neutropenia.
judged.quote: the glucose-lowering SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin, used for type 2 diabetes, was successfully repurposed for treating neutropenia and neutrophil dysfunction in the rare inherited metabolic disorder GSD-Ib without causing symptomatic hypoglycemia. We ascribe this to an improvement in neutrophil function resulting from the reduction of the intracellular concentration of 1,5AG6P.

rows.text: GENE THERAPY (AAV8-G6PC1) in phase II/III trials 2022+ with promising early results [11].

judged.citation: Weinstein DA et al. Safety and efficacy of DTX401, an AAV8-mediated liver-directed gene therapy, in adults with glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSDIa). J Inherit Metab Dis. 2025;48(2):e70014.
judged.reason: The abstract supports AAV8-mediated G6PC1 gene therapy (DTX401) with promising early results (favorable safety, 68% cornstarch reduction), but it reports a phase 1/2 dose-escalation trial rather than phase II/III trials, and gives no 2022+ trial timing.
judged.quote: This open-label, phase 1/2, dose-escalation, 52-week gene therapy trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of a single DTX401 infusion in 12 adults with GSDIa

rows.text: GSD Ib has additional morbidity from immune dysfunction but empaglifozin has recently revolutionised that aspect of care [2,10,11].

judged.citation: Wortmann SB et al. Treating neutropenia and neutrophil dysfunction in glycogen storage disease type Ib with an SGLT2 inhibitor. Blood. 2020;136(9):1033–43.
judged.reason: The abstract documents the immune-related morbidity of GSD-Ib (serious infections, IBD, neutrophil dysfunction) and its resolution with empagliflozin, allowing GCSF discontinuation or tapering, consistent with the claim of transformed care.
judged.quote: Clinically, symptoms of frequent infections, mucosal lesions, and inflammatory bowel disease resolved, and no symptomatic hypoglycemia was observed. GCSF could be discontinued in 2 patients and tapered by 57% and 81%, respectively, in the other 2.

judged.citation: Weinstein DA et al. Safety and efficacy of DTX401, an AAV8-mediated liver-directed gene therapy, in adults with glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSDIa). J Inherit Metab Dis. 2025;48(2):e70014.
judged.reason: The abstract concerns DTX401 gene therapy in GSD Ia and says nothing about GSD Ib immune dysfunction or empagliflozin.

rows.text: Tissue-specific expression explains the IIIa/IIIb distinction [6].

judged.citation: Bao Y et al. Human glycogen debrancher enzyme gene (AGL): complete structural organisation and characterisation of the 5' flanking region. Genomics. 1996;38(2):155–65.
judged.reason: The abstract documents tissue-specific AGL isoforms and promoters in liver versus muscle, but never mentions the GSD-IIIa/IIIb subtype distinction or that tissue-specific expression accounts for it.
judged.quote: These results suggest that the human AGL gene contains at least 2 promoter regions that confer differential expression of isoform mRNAs in a tissue-specific manner.

rows.text: Founder variants: c.4456delT in North African Jewish and Inuit populations; additional founder alleles in Faroese and other populations. >100 pathogenic variants total [7].

judged.citation: Shen J et al. Mutations in exon 3 of the glycogen debranching enzyme gene are associated with GSD IIIa that is differentially expressed in liver and muscle. J Clin Invest. 1996;98(2):352–7.
judged.reason: The abstract reports AGL mutation spectrum (exon 3 17delAG and Q6X in GSD-IIIb, plus R864X/R1228X frequencies in Caucasian patients) but says nothing about the c.4456delT founder variant in North African Jewish or Inuit populations, Faroese founder alleles, or a total of >100 pathogenic variants.
judged.quote: The R864X and R1228X were not unique for GSD-IIIb as they were also found in GSD-IIIa patients (frequency of 10.3% and 5.2% in Caucasian patients, respectively).

rows.text: Physical therapy for progressive myopathy [1,2,9].

judged.citation: Kishnani PS et al. Glycogen storage disease type III diagnosis and management guidelines. Genet Med. 2010;12(7):446–63.
judged.reason: The abstract notes that neuromuscular and musculoskeletal evaluation and management are addressed but says nothing about physical therapy for myopathy.
judged.quote: This management guideline specifically addresses evaluation and diagnosis across multiple organ systems (cardiovascular, gastrointestinal/nutrition, hepatic, musculoskeletal, and neuromuscular) involved in glycogen storage disease type III.

judged.citation: Sentner CP et al. Glycogen storage disease type III: diagnosis, genotype, management, clinical course and outcome. J Inherit Metab Dis. 2016;39(5):697–704.
judged.reason: The abstract reports muscle pain prevalence but does not address physical therapy or any non-dietary intervention for myopathy.

judged.citation: Schreuder AB, Rossi A, Grunert SC, Derks TGJ. Glycogen storage disease type III. GeneReviews®. 2010 [updated 2022].
judged.reason: The abstract describes slowly progressive skeletal myopathy in GSD III and explicitly lists physical therapy/musculoskeletal assessment as part of management and surveillance.

rows.text: The HPRT1 disorder spectrum has three clinically recognised phenotypes, stratified by residual enzyme activity: Lesch-Nyhan disease (LND) at the severe end (<2% activity; motor dysfunction, cognitive impairment, and compulsive SELF-INJURIOUS BEHAVIOUR — lip and finger biting, head banging — distinctive and disturbing for families); HPRT1-related neurologic dysfunction (HND) at the intermediate range (2–8% activity; motor and cognitive findings similar to but milder than LND, without self-injury); and HPRT1-related hyperuricaemia (HRH) at the mild end (>10% activity; hyperuricaemic gout without overt neurologic deficits — historically called 'Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome') [1,2].

judged.citation: Jinnah HA et al. Delineation of the motor disorder of Lesch-Nyhan disease. Brain. 2006;129(Pt 5):1201–17.

judged.quote: Affected individuals exhibit over-production of uric acid, along with a characteristic neurobehavioural syndrome that includes mental retardation, recurrent self-injurious behaviour and motor disability.

judged.reason: The abstract confirms loss/impairment of UMP synthase enzymatic activity in mutant constructs expressed in E. coli and Sf21 cells, but gives no quantitative residual activity threshold (<5% of normal) and does not report assays in erythrocytes or patient cultured cells.
judged.quote: Expression of human UMP synthase cDNAs containing these mutations in pyrimidine auxotrophic Escherichia coli and in recombinant baculovirus-infected Sf21 cells demonstrates impaired activity

rows.text: The enzyme has dual activities from a single polypeptide — both are typically reduced in patients but residual OMP decarboxylase activity can be higher than orotate phosphoribosyltransferase, producing varying profiles. <20 pathogenic variants reported [3,4].

judged.citation: Suchi M et al. Molecular cloning of the human UMP synthase gene and characterisation of point mutations in two hereditary orotic aciduria families. Am J Hum Genet. 1997;60(3):525–39.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms UMP synthase is a bifunctional single-gene enzyme carrying both OPRT and ODC activities with impaired activity in patients, but it does not state that residual ODC activity exceeds OPRT activity nor that fewer than 20 pathogenic variants have been reported (it describes mutations in only two families).
judged.quote: Uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase is a bifunctional enzyme catalyzing the last two steps of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (OPRT) and orotidine-5'-monophosphate decarboxylase (ODC).

judged.citation: Yablonski MJ et al. Intrinsic activity and stability of bifunctional human UMP synthase and its two separate catalytic domains, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and orotidine-5'-phosphate decarboxylase. J Biol Chem. 1996;271(18):10704–8.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms the enzyme is a bifunctional protein with two catalytic domains (OPRT and ODCase) in a single polypeptide, but says nothing about patient residual activity profiles or the number of reported pathogenic variants.
judged.quote: Human UMP synthase is a bifunctional protein containing two separate catalytic domains, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (EC 2.4.2.10) and orotidine-5'-phosphate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.23).

judged.quote: Thus, a deficiency of DPD appears to be an important pharmacogenetic syndrome.

rows.text: The pharmacogenomic significance of DPYD heterozygosity became clear in the 1990s after recognition of severe 5-FU toxicity in carriers of the c.1905+1G>A splice variant [4].

judged.reason: The 1988 abstract establishes DPD deficiency as the biochemical basis of severe 5-FU toxicity and identifies partial (heterozygous) enzyme deficiency in relatives, but it does not mention the c.1905+1G>A splice variant, any genotype, or the 1990s recognition of risk in carriers.
judged.quote: we demonstrated complete deficiency of enzyme activity in the patient and partial deficiency of enzyme activity in her father and children consistent with an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. rows.text: Both 'inborn error' and 'pharmacogenomic' frames are now well established; modern guidelines (e.g. CPIC 2018 [5]) recommend DPYD testing before 5-FU therapy.

rows.text: Molecular testing of DPYD (especially the four CPIC-recommended variants: c.1905+1G>A *2A, c.1679T>G *13, c.2846A>T, and HapB3) has largely replaced enzymology for both diagnostic and pharmacogenomic indications [5,6].

rows.text: ADSL deficiency (OMIM #103050) was first described by Jaeken and van den Berghe in 1984 [3]. ~100 patients reported worldwide.

judged.citation: Jaeken J, Van den Berghe G. An infantile autistic syndrome characterised by the presence of succinylpurines in body fluids. Lancet. 1984;2(8411):1058–61.
judged.reason: The abstract is the 1984 first description of adenylosuccinase deficiency by these authors, supporting the first-description claim, but it reports only 3 children and says nothing about ~100 patients reported worldwide.
judged.quote: Their presence indicates a deficiency of this enzyme, which is involved in both de novo synthesis of purines and the formation of adenosine monophosphate from inosine monophosphate.

rows.text: The characteristic urinary purines (SAdo, SAICA riboside) are not detected on routine organic-acid screens and require specific HPLC or LC-MS/MS analysis [4,5].

judged.citation: Edery P, Marie S et al. Intrafamilial variability in the phenotypic expression of adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency: a report on three patients. Am J Med Genet A. 2003;120A(2):185–90.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that diagnosis requires a dedicated urinary screen for succinylpurines, but it does not state that these purines escape routine organic-acid screening nor specify HPLC or LC-MS/MS methodology.
judged.quote: this diagnosis should be considered and assessed using a simple urinary screening method for the presence of succinylpurines in any patient with mental retardation of unexplained origin

judged.citation: Jaeken J, Wadman SK, Duran M, van Sprang FJ, Beemer FA, Holl RA, Theunissen PM, de Cock P, van den Bergh F, Vincent MF, et al. Adenylosuccinase deficiency: an inborn error of purine nucleotide synthesis. Eur J Pediatr. 1988;148(2):126–31.
judged.reason: The abstract confirms that SAdo and SAICA riboside accumulate in urine and other body fluids of ADSL-deficient patients, but says nothing about their non-detection on routine organic-acid screens or the need for specific HPLC/LC-MS/MS analysis.
judged.quote: This newly discovered inborn error of purine metabolism is characterized by an accumulation in body fluids of succinyladenosine (S-Ado) and succinylaminoimidazole carboxamide riboside (SAICA riboside), the dephosphorylated derivatives of the two substrates of adenylosuccinase.

rows.text: The S-Ado:SAICA-riboside ratio correlates with phenotype, and the direction is the opposite of what is often assumed — a LOW ratio marks severe disease: in Jaeken's original eight-patient series the ratio was between 1 and 2 in CSF, plasma and urine in the seven severely retarded patients, and around 5 in the one markedly milder patient, whose fibroblast enzyme activity was also the lowest (6% of normal) [5].

judged.citation: Jaeken J, Wadman SK, Duran M, van Sprang FJ, Beemer FA, Holl RA, Theunissen PM, de Cock P, van den Bergh F, Vincent MF, et al. Adenylosuccinase deficiency: an inborn error of purine nucleotide synthesis. Eur J Pediatr. 1988;148(2):126–31.
judged.reason: The abstract reports exactly the ratio values, the number of severely retarded patients, the milder patient's ~5 ratio, and her 6% fibroblast enzyme activity.
judged.quote: In the cerebrospinal fluid, plasma and urine of these patients, the S-Ado/SAICA riboside ratio was between 1 and 2. In striking contrast, the eighth patient (a girl) was markedly less mentally retarded. Most noteworthy, the S-Ado/SAICA riboside ratio in her body fluids was around 5

rows.text: Note that bacterial deribosylation of both biomarkers in urine has caused false-negative screening, so a normal urine purine screen does not exclude the diagnosis [10].

judged.quote: Screening methods for the diagnosis of dADSL may be falsely negative due to bacteria-mediated deribosylation of SAICA-riboside and SAdo.

rows.text: Type I (classic infantile, commonest): psychomotor delay from infancy, microcephaly, severe to profound intellectual disability, seizures (myoclonic, tonic-clonic), autism-like behaviours, self-mutilation in some, feeding difficulties, failure to thrive [1,2,8].

rows.text: Riboflavin transporter deficiency (OMIM #211530 / #211500) was recognised as a disease entity in the 1890s (Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere) and 1930s (Fazio-Londe) but its molecular basis (RFVT variants) was identified only in 2010–2011 [3,4].

judged.quote: We identified a candidate gene, C20orf54, by studying a consanguineous family with multiple affected individuals and subsequently demonstrated that mutations in this gene were the cause of disease in other, unrelated families.

judged.quote: Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome was first described in 1894 as a rare neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive sensorineural deafness in combination with childhood amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Mutations in the gene, SLC52A3 (formerly C20orf54), one of three known riboflavin transporter genes, have recently been shown to underlie a number of severe cases of Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome

rows.text: The small number of reported milder cases suggests limited phenotypic variation, though later-onset forms may have somewhat longer survival with lifelong severe disability [1,2,3].

judged.reason: The abstract does not discuss phenotypic variability, milder later-onset forms, or survival in combined D,L-2-HGA.
